# THE ANCIENT

Published in 1696 in Franeker, it remains a foundational text in the study of ecclesiastical history and Jewish-Christian relations.</summary>

# DEDICATION.

...[we may have] a more solid and more extensive [foundation]. On the contrary, indeed, ***our salvation is from the Jews.*** <note>original: "salus nostra est ex Judæis"; a quotation from the Gospel of John 4:22</note> Regarding everything we believe in our Religion, we are not ashamed to depend upon the authority of Moses and the Prophets, whom the Jewish People revere as the principal Ministers of their own Religion. We profess that the Holy Divinity whom we worship (for we worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit) is commended to us by the Writings of Moses and the Prophets as the Unique, True, and Supreme God, the Creator and Governor of this Universe. We do not blush to profess that the very Author of our restored Salvation, Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, was born a man among men and a Jew among Jews; he was most clearly designated and depicted by the oracles and ceremonies of that very Jewish Nation. Furthermore, whatever excellence there is in Divine Worship as celebrated by Christians, and whatever it possesses of splendor and decorum—although among us Religion is truly practiced more with piety than with magnificence <note>Vitringa refers here to the "Plain Style" of Reformed/Protestant worship versus the elaborate rituals of other traditions</note>—they acknowledge they received from the Jews. This was the only nation that was in the light for many centuries, while all other men, as many as this world contains, were deserted and destitute of God and wandered in thick darkness. Therefore, we read in the books of Moses how Jacob, seeking the prophetic prayers of his Father Isaac, by the clever advice of his Mother, [clothed] himself in the most precious garments of his Brother Esau...

<summary>In this dedication, Vitringa argues that Christianity is deeply rooted in Jewish tradition, asserting that Christian concepts of God, the authority of the prophets, and even the person of Jesus himself are inseparable from their Jewish origins.</summary>
<keywords>salvation, Jews, Moses, Prophets, Trinity, Jesus Christ, divine worship, Jacob and Esau, religious history</keywords>

...[garments] had put on, and those prosperous things which seemed destined for his brother through the blessing of the Parent—deceived by this artifice—he derived for himself; this we not undeservedly relate to the Christians from among the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" refers to non-Jewish people who converted to Christianity</note>. For they truly transferred into their own sacred rites whatever was beautiful and praiseworthy in Religion as it was practiced by the Jews; the Oracles of the Prophets <note>original: "Oracula Vatum"</note>, which promised the prerogatives of exceptional benefits to the Jews, they interpreted as being about themselves and applied to themselves. That unfeigned and sincere faith, with which the Patriarchs received the promises of such great blessings made to them by God with a simple mind—setting aside the merits of their own virtues—they themselves have, as it were, put on. And in this particular garment, which the Esau-ites <note>A term used by the author to compare the Jewish people to Esau, who sold his birthright</note> (I mean, the carnal Jews) long ago set aside, they commend themselves to God. They have pursued Divine Grace through a kind of trick and cunning, beyond and contrary to God’s plan as it appeared externally, and they have, as it were, snatched away the benefits that seemed destined for the Jews and claimed them for themselves. Indeed, Christians themselves—as many of them as are truly what they ought to be—are to be counted among the Jews according to the Doctrine of the Apostle Paul, and are to be called and held as Jews. On the contrary, the Jews who are still called by this name today, just as they long ago departed from the faith and true Religion of their Fathers, are thus entirely unworthy of this title— <note>catchword: titu- (referring to "titul-o" or title)</note>

...owe an account to no one except God; otherwise, it will undoubtedly seem different to others who are familiar with the norms and laws of our **Academic Life**. For the occupations and duties by which we are distracted for the benefit of the **Studious Youth** <note>original: "Studiosæ Juventutis"; referring to the university students the author teaches</note> so greatly restrict and cut short our time that we can hardly apply any efforts to our scholarly labors except "stolen" hours <note>original: "furtivas"; hours snatched away from his official responsibilities</note>. Therefore, if these works are less polished and refined, they deserve some measure of pardon. 

I might fear with greater justification, however, that someone might charge these efforts of mine with **Ambition**. They might say that I am not content with teaching **Theology** and interpreting the **Divine Word** <term>Verbum Divinum: The Holy Scriptures or the Gospel</term>—a province in which I certainly have plenty to do if I have any talent at all—and that I have "put my sickle into another man’s harvest" <note>A proverbial expression (original: "falcem meam in alienam messem mittam") meaning to meddle in a field of study belonging to someone else</note> and excessively sought the praise of expertise in **Hebrew Matters and Antiquities**.

...[pre]sumption regarding my own resources and abilities, which I know and feel to be very small. Instead, it was a certain destiny of Divine Providence—whose laws I have obeyed almost against my will and not without a certain resistance and hesitation—that brought this offspring <note>original: "hunc foetum"; a common metaphor for a newborn book or intellectual work</note> into the light. Since my younger years (I mention a fact not unknown to you), I was affected by a no small desire for making progress in **Hebrew Literature** <term>Literis Hebræis: The study of the Hebrew language, its grammar, and the vast body of Jewish scholarly writing</term>, the profession of which I was meant to adorn. With no less pleasure than effort, I turned over the works that the leading men in this science—drawing from the rites and ceremonies of the Hebrew nation—had produced with great diligence to illuminate the sacred practices of Christians. At last, my gaze remained fixed on the SYNAGOGUE, specifically its **Form of Government** and **Administration of Sacred Rites**, as it has been described elsewhere—though with many an error—by **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English clergyman and scholar who was a pioneer in using Rabbinic literature to provide context for the New Testament</note>.

I then began to compare these descriptions with what I encountered on the same subject in the works of **Grotius**, **Selden**, **Petit**, **Cappell**, and **Burman** <note>A list of the greatest legal and theological minds of the 17th century, including Hugo Grotius and John Selden, who applied "oriental" or Hebrew scholarship to European law and theology</note>. The latter, Frans Burman, was a most learned man who deserved highly of the Church and followed in their footsteps; at that time, his **Nine Disputations on Synagogues** existed, which were later published among his own **Academic Exercises**. To these, I added the few things I had gathered myself to illustrate that same material from the **Codex Sopherim** <term>Massekhet Soferim: A minor tractate of the Talmud detailing the rules for scribes and the public reading of the Torah</term>, the **Kol Bo** <term>An anonymous 13th-century Hebrew legal compendium</term>, and the definitions of **Rabbi Jacob ben Asher**, as they were arranged by **Rabbi Karo** <note>Referring to the *Shulchan Aruch*, the most authoritative code of Jewish law, compiled by Joseph Karo based on the earlier work of Jacob ben Asher</note>...

-># DEDICATION.<-

...[demon]strating <note>original: "strandam"; the completion of "illustrandam"</note> what I had collected, I conceived so much confidence from it that I dared to send a book into the public under the title *The Ruler of the Synagogue* <note>original: "Archisynagogi"</note>. It was intended to describe the *Form of Government and Administration of Sacred Rites*, as they existed in the *Ancient Synagogue*, insofar as the *Church Government and Form of Public Worship* among *Christians* were ordered and established according to that model. 

For the Illustrious Buxtorfs, Father and Son <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Elder (1564–1629) and his son (1599–1664) were the preeminent Christian Hebraists of their era</note>, had already written learnedly and skillfully about the public and private rites and ceremonies of the Jews in their **THE JEWISH SYNAGOGUE** <note>original: "S Y N A G O G A J U D A I C A"</note>, following the example of *Leon of Modena* <note>A prominent Venetian Rabbi (1571–1648) who wrote an influential guide to Jewish life for Christian readers</note>. While I left most of their work in its rightful place and respected its value, it was of little use for my specific purpose. 

Indeed, although that book of mine was received by many with more affection than it deserved, it was by no means polished with such care, or furnished and adorned with such an abundance of material, that I did not realize—should God grant me a longer life and preserve my mental strength—that it would eventually need to be revised and given a "new dress" <note>original: "novâ veſte donandum"; a scholarly metaphor for a revised and expanded edition</note>. 

However, because of the duties of my Theological Professorship, I was becoming more and more separated from **Rabbinic Literature** <term>Literis Rabbinicis: The vast body of post-biblical Jewish scholarly writing, including the Talmud and medieval commentaries</term>, which requires a person’s almost total and constant devotion. I would undoubtedly have procrastinated and put this work off from day to day, had I not pledged my word to the reader in that very book to compare—when the opportunity arose—the *Sacred Rites and Ministries of the Synagogue* with the *Sacred*...

These qualities I know, first of all, to be very modest and small in myself; furthermore, time did not permit [more], nor, even if it had permitted it most greatly, [would I have obtained] from my mind...

For I know well that I am here *dealing with a work*, as they say, *full of dangerous hazard* <note>original: "periculosae... plenum opus aleae"; a famous quote from the Roman poet Horace (*Odes* 2.1.6) regarding the risks of writing about sensitive historical or political topics</note>; and in weaving this work together, I had more reason to object to myself than Jerome had when about to write the Epitaph for Nepotianus: *Small talents cannot sustain great subjects* <note>original: "Grandes materias ingenia parva non sustinent"; Saint Jerome (Hieronymus) was a 4th-century Bible translator and scholar; Nepotianus was his friend and a young clergyman to whom Jerome was very attached</note>. There are many things here that are doubtful and obscure, for which a great expertise in facts, a perspicacity of judgment, and the tools of a vast and solid erudition are required to successfully unearth them from Antiquity and harmonize them. These qualities, I know first of all, are very modest and meager in my case; furthermore, time did not permit, nor, even if it had permitted in the greatest degree, [could I obtain] from my mind...

To take care for myself...

You wish to be praised by your son-in-law <term>Son-in-law: original "Gener." In the 17th-century academic world, familial ties often doubled as professional networks.</term>; yet you have no need to be praised, seeing as there has always been such high regard for your Learning, Prudence, and Eloquence, that the most flourishing Churches of Holland <note>The "flourishing Churches" refers to the Dutch Reformed Church during its Golden Age of scholarship and influence.</note> have never possessed you without the envy of others—even those of Amsterdam and Leiden <note>original: "Amstelædamensis & Lugdunensis." Furthermore, you have bestowed upon me so many and such great benefits for your sake and mine, that I would be the most ungrateful of mortals if I did not acknowledge myself most strictly bound to you in all duties of reverence, love, and gratitude which can be expected from a son-in-law toward a father-in-law, or a son toward a father.

## INTRODUCTORY PREFACES.

<margin>Page 1.</margin>
**CHAPTER I.**
*The usefulness, and indeed the necessity, of this treatise is commended, in which the origin of the Sacred Rites of the Early Christian Church is traced from elsewhere (whether from the Temple or from the Synagogue).*

<margin>6.</margin>
**CHAPTER II.**
*The opinion of certain most learned men of both this and ancient times is reported, who attempt to trace the Form of Government and the Rituals of the Christian Church back to the <term>JEWISH TEMPLE</term> <note>original: "TEMPLO JUDAICO." Referring to the centralized worship in Jerusalem.</note>; and the reasons that gave rise to this opinion are investigated.*

<margin>15.</margin>
**CHAPTER III.**
*The view of many other learned and famous men is set forth, who maintain that the Government of the Christian Church was formed according to the model of the <term>JEWISH SYNAGOGUES</term> <note>original: "SYNAGOGARUM JUDAICARUM." Referring to local community gathering places for prayer and study.</note>. The reasons by which they were persuaded of this opinion, or by which they could be persuaded, are added.*

<margin>27.</margin>
**CHAPTER IV.**
*A way is prepared for discerning which of the aforementioned opinions regarding the Origin of Church Rites—whether they are to be sought from the <term>TEMPLE</term> or the <term>SYNAGOGUE</term>—is more true. To this end, it is first established: 1. That within the Temple, whether in ordinary or extraordinary cases, those ceremonies were also occasionally observed which were customary in the Synagogues. 2. That the Jewish authors themselves often compare the Ministry of the Synagogues in various parts with the Worship of the Temple. In passing, it is examined where the King’s station or Chair was located in the Temple, and also whether there was any Synagogue located within the Temple.*

<column-break/>

<margin>44.</margin>
**CHAPTER V.**
*Notwithstanding those points granted in the preceding Chapter, it is proven by evident arguments that the Exercise of Religion in the Christian Church approaches much nearer to the Form of Divine Worship as it was celebrated in the Synagogues, than to the <term>divine service</term> <note>original Greek: "λατρείαν" (latreian). Refers specifically to the ritual service or worship of the Temple.</note> of the Temple; because in those parts where the Worship of the Synagogue differs from the Ceremonies of the Temple—such as in the distinction of Places, Persons, Clothing, Age, Degrees of Holiness, etc.—the Church aligns with the Synagogue, not with the Temple; and furthermore because the Doctors of the Hebrews themselves distinguish the Worship of the Synagogue, insofar as it agrees with the Church's worship, from the Religion of the Temple.*

<margin>53.</margin>
**CHAPTER VI.**
*The arguments of James Ussher of Armagh <note>original: "Usserii Armachani." James Ussher (1581–1656) was the Archbishop of Armagh and a famous scholar of biblical chronology.</note> and other most learned men, reviewed in Chapter II, are discussed at length; by these arguments they intend to prove that the external Government of the Church and the mode of Divine Worship under the Gospel Economy was formed by the Apostles according to the type of the Temple Religion and its Administration. At the same time, the importance of this question is indicated, and the testimonies produced from Holy Scripture to establish this opinion are explained.*

->SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.<-

# BOOK ONE.
## PART I.

### CHAPTER I.

Following the preliminary outline of this book's structure, we investigate the original meaning of the word **Synagogue** <note>original: "ΣΥΝΑΓΩΓΗ"</note>, drawing from the lexicographer *Hesychius*, the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, and the specific usage of the Hebrew word **Edah** <note>original: "עדה"; usually referring to a formal assembly or congregation</note>; which has much in common with the Greek *Synagogue*. At the same time, we ask: what is the true meaning of the concept **Qahal** <note>original: "קהל"; an assembly or convocation</note>? How is it used in the Septuagint? How is it distinguished from **Edah**? And how does it align with the Greek word **Ecclesia** <note>original: "ἐκκλησία"; the word used for 'Church'</note>, and the Latin terms **People** <note>original: "Populus"</note>, **City-State** <note>original: "Civitas"</note>, **Assembly** <note>original: "Concio"</note>, and **Summoned Comitia** <note>original: "Comitia Calata"; referring to ancient Roman religious assemblies called by a priest</note>? We also explore whether the Greek word *kaleo* <note>original: "καλέω"; to call</note> and the ancient Latin *calo* <note>to call or summon</note> might be derived from the Hebrew. Finally, after resolving certain objections, we offer observations on the phrases **Holy Community** <note>original: "קהילא קדישא" (Qehila Qadisha)</note> and **Holy Church** <note>original: "ἁγία ἐκκλησία"</note>, which were used frequently by the Apostles. 77.

### CHAPTER II.

After examining the well-known opinions of *Jerome* and *Augustine* <note>two influential early Church Fathers</note> regarding the difference in meaning between the words **Synagogue** and **Church**, the notes of the illustrious scholar *Grotius* on these same words are presented and debated. We also include an exposition of the word **Ecclesia** as found in the *Suda* <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>. Furthermore, we investigate in what sense the concept of **Church** should be understood in that debated saying of Christ, "**Tell it to the Church**" <note>original: "Dic Ecclesiæ"; from Matthew 18:17</note>, examining the arguments of *Cameron* and *Cappellus* in favor of the accepted explanation. We also note a very singular use of the phrase **Holy Community** <note>original: "קהילא קדישא"</note> in the **Talmud**, which might seem to contradict our opinion. Finally, we discuss the original meaning of the words **Knesset** <note>original: "כנסת"; gathering</note> and **Tzibur** <note>original: "צבור"; the public or congregation</note>, which are likewise usually translated as **Synagogue**. 89.

### CHAPTER III.

We move to a closer consideration of the word **Synagogue**, establishing with solid arguments its dual meaning: it is used in the writings of the New Testament to mean either a **Place of Meeting** or the **Assembly** itself. 

<column-break/>

Next, we investigate why this word came to be used for the **Place** and the **building of the assembly**, since by its origin it signifies the **Gathering** itself. To make this easier to understand, we explain that it is quite common for words that originally mean a "Gathering" to be transferred over time to designate the places where that gathering meets. We provide examples such as the words **Sanhedrin** <note>original: "סנהדרין" or "συνέδριον"; meaning a sitting-together or council</note>, **Curia** <note>the origin of which is sought from the Greek "kyria," meaning authority</note>, **Assembly** <note>original: "Concio"</note>, and **Comitium** <note>the Roman place of assembly</note>. Additionally, we note that the word **Ecclesia** underwent this same shift in meaning among both Sacred and Secular authors. On this occasion, the opinion of *Fuller* regarding the true meaning of **Ecclesia** in 1 Corinthians 11:18, 22 is weighed, alongside *Spanheim’s* arguments against it. Finally, we inquire into the validity of what *Elias Levita* <note>a famous 15th-16th century Hebrew grammarian</note> wrote concerning the word **Qehila** <note>original: "קהילה"; congregation</note>. 102.

### CHAPTER IV.

It is observed that the word **Synagogue**, when used for a **place of sacred assembly**, shifts toward the meaning of the word **Knishta** <note>original: "כנישתא / כנישה"</note>, which is commonly used by Hebrew writers for the **House of Assembly** <note>original: "בית כנישתא" or "בית הכנסת" (Beit HaKnesset)</note> through a shortening of the phrase common to Sacred Authors. Then we proceed to the explanation of other names by which **Synagogues** are usually designated by various writers. Among these, we first examine the term **Proseucha** <note>original: "PROSEUCHA"; a place of prayer</note>, as used by *Juvenal*, *Philo*, and *Josephus*. We investigate whether it carries the same meaning in two passages of the New Testament: Luke 6:12 and Acts 16:13. To understand these, the commentaries of *Schindler*, *Drusius*, *Heinsius*, and others are brought forward and examined. Afterward, other names for Synagogues are touched upon, such as **sacred places** <note>original: "ἱερὰ"</note>, **Sabbath-houses** <note>original: "σαββατεῖα"</note>, **men's halls** <note>original: "ἀνδρῶνες"</note>, **houses of prayer** <note>original: "προσευκτήρια"</note>, and **places of study** <note>original: "φροντιστήρια"</note>, all of which can be found in the works of *Philo* and *Josephus*. Finally, an observation is added regarding the expression **Beit HaKnesset** <note>original: "בית הכנסת"; House of Assembly</note>. 115.

<summary>This page contains the table of contents for the first part of Book One, detailing a linguistic and historical investigation into the terms "Synagogue" and "Ecclesia." It explores how the names for religious assemblies transitioned from describing the people to describing the physical buildings.</summary>

->SUMMARIES OF THE CHAPTERS.<-

## CHAPTER V.
Synagogues, strictly so-called, which are named **Houses of Assembly** <note>original: "בתי כנסיות" (Battei Kenesiyot)</note>, are more significantly distinguished from **Houses of Study** <note>original: "בתי מדרשות" (Battei Midrashot)</note>, whether Academies or Public Schools. These are sometimes included under the broader meaning of the word **Synagogue** <note>original: "Συναγωγὴ"</note> in the writings of the New Testament, a point agreed upon by the scholar *Lightfoot*. Then, the following names are explained as far as is necessary: **House of Study** <note>original: "בי מדרש" (Bei Midrash)</note>, and several others; **House of the Rabbis** <note>original: "בי רבנן" (Bei Rabbanan)</note>, **Academy** <note>original: "ישיבה" (Yeshiva)</note>, **Lecture Hall** <note>original: "תרביצא" (Tarbitza)</note>, **House of Instruction** <note>original: "בי אולפנא" (Bei Ulpana)</note>, **House of Meeting** <note>original: "בי וועד" (Bei Va'ad)</note>, **House of the Master** <note>original: "בי רב / בי רבן" (Bei Rav / Bei Rabban)</note>, **House of the Student** <note>original: "בי תלמיד" (Bei Talmid)</note>, **The Vineyard** <note>original: "כרם" (Kerem); a metaphor for an academy</note>, and **The Row** <note>original: "סדרא" (Sidra)</note>. These are the terms by which Gymnasia <note>places of intellectual training</note> are designated in the writings of the Talmudists. A distinction is added between Private and Public Schools. — 133.

## CHAPTER VI.
This chapter discusses **Schools** and Private **Prayer Rooms** <note>original: "Oratoriis Domesticis"</note> and their use among the teachers of the Jewish nation. The true meaning of the terms **Upper Room** <note>original: "עלית" (Aliyah)</note>, **upper chamber** <note>original: "ὑπερῷον" (hyperōon)</note>, **upstairs room** <note>original: "ἀνάγαιον" (anagaion)</note>, **Dining Room** <note>original: "Cœnaculum"</note>, and **Hall** <note>original: "Chalcidium"</note>, which pertain to this subject, is investigated. The use of such consecrated upper rooms is demonstrated from the writings of the Old and New Testaments, with mention of the opinion of the distinguished *de Dieu* regarding the Upper Room where the Apostles gathered on the Feast of Pentecost. The windows of these rooms and their use are also discussed. Finally, *private gymnasia*, which belong to many individuals, are described. — 145.

## CHAPTER VII.
The form and method of Public Education observed in public lecture halls or schools is explained. A doubt is discussed beforehand: whether the Sanhedrins <note>the high Jewish courts</note>, both Great and Small, had their own lecture halls distinct from the courtrooms or judgment chambers. Then, the method of teaching used in the schools is debated, and the question is answered: did students traditionally stand before the death of Prince *Gamaliel*? This is addressed by citing examples from the history of the New Testament and examining the arguments of *Petit* against *Scaliger* on the opposing side. Afterward

<column-break/>

the nature and method of Interpretation are discussed. The author defends against *Rabbi Abraham Ben David* the view that an interpreter was not allowed to deviate from the opinions of the preaching teachers. These points are confirmed by the famous history of the disagreement that once arose between *Gamaliel* and *Joshua*. — 156.

## CHAPTER VIII.
The main structural parts of the Synagogue building are listed, specifically two: the **Library Chest** <note>the Ark where scrolls are kept</note> and the **Platform** <note>the raised stage for the speaker</note>. # CHAPTER SUMMARIES.
## BOOK ONE.
### PART I.

### CHAPTER I.
Following the general outline of this book’s contents, we investigate the true meaning of the word **Synagogue** <note>original: ΣΥΝΑΓΩΓΗ</note>, based on the works of **Hesychius** <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian</note>, the **Septuagint** <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, and the specific meaning of the Hebrew word **Assembly** <note>original: עדה ('edah)</note>, which has much in common with the Greek word for Synagogue. Simultaneously, we ask: what is the true meaning of the concept **Congregation** <note>original: קהל (qahal)</note>? How is it used in the Septuagint? How does it differ from the word for "Assembly"? We also explore its similarities with the Greek word **Church** <note>original: ἐκκλησία (ekklesia)</note> and the Latin terms for **The People, The State, Public Assembly,** and **Summoned Assembly** <note>original: Populus, Civitas, Concio, Comitia Calata</note>. We even attempt to see if the Greek verb "to call" <note>original: καλέω (kaleo)</note> and the ancient Latin verb **to summon** <note>original: *calo*</note> can be derived from it. Finally, after resolving certain objections, we offer observations on the phrase **Holy Community** <note>original: קהילא קדישא (Kehilla Kadisha)</note> or **Holy Church** <note>original: ἁγία ἐκκλησία (hagia ekklesia)</note>, which the Apostles used frequently. 77.

### CHAPTER II.
After examining the famous opinions of **Jerome** and **Augustine** regarding the difference in meaning between the words *Synagogue* and *Church*, we present and debate the notes of the illustrious **Hugo Grotius** on these same terms. We also include an exposition of the word "Church" found in the **Suda** <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>. Furthermore, we investigate how the concept of "Church" should be understood in the controversial saying of Christ: **Tell it to the Church** <note>original: *Dic Ecclesiae*</note>, examining the arguments of **John Cameron** and **Louis Cappellus** <note>prominent 17th-century Protestant theologians</note> for the accepted explanation. We also note a very singular use of the phrase **Holy Community** <note>original: קהילא קדישא</note> in the Talmud, which might seem to contradict our opinion. Finally, we discuss the true meaning of the words **Assembly** <note>original: כנסת (Keneset)</note> and **Public Body** <note>original: צבור (Tsibbur)</note>, which are likewise commonly translated as *Synagogue*. 89.

### CHAPTER III.
We move to a closer consideration of the word **Synagogue** <note>original: συναγωγή</note> and establish with solid arguments its dual meaning in the New Testament, where it is understood as either the **Place of Meeting** or the **Gathering** itself.

<column-break/>

Then, we investigate why this word is used for a place and a building when its original meaning refers to the gathering of people. For a easier understanding, we explain that it is quite common for words that strictly signify a group of people to be transferred over time to designate the places where that group meets. We provide examples such as the words **Sanhedrin** <note>original: סנהדרין / συνέδριον</note>, **Council Chamber** <note>original: *Curia*, derived from the Greek word for authority, κυρία</note>, **Assembly**, and **Meeting-place**. Additionally, we show that the word **Church** <note>original: ἐκκλησία</note> underwent this same change in meaning among both sacred and secular authors. On this occasion, we weigh the opinion of **Thomas Fuller** regarding the true meaning of "Church" in 1 Corinthians 11:18, 22, while also considering the arguments of **Friedrich Spanheim** against it. Finally, we inquire into the validity of what **Elias Levita** <note>a famous 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note> wrote concerning the word **Congregation** <note>original: קהילה (Kehillah)</note>. 102.

### CHAPTER IV.
We observe that the word **Synagogue**, when used for a place of sacred meeting, shifts toward the meaning of the word **Assembly** or **Gatherings** <note>original: כניסת / כנסיות (Keneset / Kenesiyot)</note>, which is familiarly used by Hebrew writers for the **House of Assembly** <note>original: בית הכנסת (Beit ha-Knesset)</note>, often using a shorthand common among sacred authors. Then we proceed to explain other names by which the *Synagogue* is usually designated by various writers. Among these, we first examine the word **Prayer-house** <note>original: PROSEUCHA</note> as it is used by the Roman poet **Juvenal** and the historians **Philo** and **Josephus**. We investigate whether it has the same meaning in two New Testament passages, Luke 6:12 and Acts 16:13, bringing in and examining the commentaries of scholars like **Schindler, Drusius,** and **Heinsius**. Afterward, we touch upon other names for Synagogues, such as **Sacred places, Sabbath-houses, Men's halls, Prayer-houses,** and **Study-centers** <note>original: ἱερά, σαββατεῖα, ἀνδρῶνες, προσεuktήρια, φροντιστήρια</note>, which can be found in Philo and Josephus. Finally, we add an observation regarding the phrase **House of Assembly**. 115.

## BOOK ONE.

### PART I.

#### CHAPTER I.

**F**ollowing the introduction to the sequence of topics in this Book, an investigation is made into the true meaning of the word **Synagogue** <note>original: ΣΥΝΑΓΩΓΗ</note>, drawing from Hesychius, the translators of the Septuagint, and the specific nuances of the Hebrew word **Assembly** <note>original: עדה (Edah)</note>, which shares much in common with the Greek *Synagoge*. At the same time, the true significance of the concept of **Congregation** <note>original: קהל (Qahal)</note> is sought: how it was used by the Septuagint translators, how it differs from the word *Edah*, and its relationship to the Greek **Church** <note>original: εκκλησία (Ekklesia)</note> and the Latin terms **The People**, **The City-State**, **The Gathering**, and the **Summoned Assembly** <note>original: Populus, Civitas, Concio, Comitia Calata</note>. It is also considered whether the Greek verb **to call** <note>original: καλεῖν (kalein)</note> and the ancient Latin **to summon** <note>original: calo</note> might be derived from these sources. Finally, after resolving certain objections, observations are made regarding the phrases **Holy Community** <note>original: קהילא קדישא (Qehila Qadisha)</note> and **Holy Church** <note>original: ἁγία ἐκκλησία</note>, which were used frequently by the Apostles. 77.

#### CHAPTER II.

After examining the well-known opinions of Jerome and Augustine regarding the difference in meaning between the words *Synagogue* and *Church*, the annotations of the illustrious scholar Grotius on these same terms are presented and debated. This includes an exposition of the word **Church** <note>original: ἐκκλησία</note> as found in the lexicon of Suidas. Furthermore, the text investigates the sense in which the concept of the "Church" should be understood in the controversial saying of Christ: "Tell it to the Church" <note>Matthew 18:17</note>; here, the arguments of Cameron and Cappel in favor of the accepted explanation are examined. Also noted is a singular use of the phrase **Holy Community** <note>original: קהילא קדישא</note> in the Talmud, which might seem contrary to our opinion. Finally, the genuine meaning of the words **Assembly** <note>original: כנסת (Knesset)</note> and **Public Body** <note>original: צבור (Tsibur)</note>, which are likewise commonly translated as *Synagogue*, is discussed. 89.

#### CHAPTER III.

The text moves to a closer consideration of the word **Synagogue** <note>original: συναγωγή</note>, establishing through solid arguments its double meaning: it is used in the writings of the New Testament to mean either the **Place of Meeting** or the **Assembly itself**.

<column-break/>

Next, the reason is sought as to why this word is used for the Place and the building of the meeting, when by its very origin it denotes the Assembly of people. For a easier understanding, it is explained that it is quite common for words which properly signify a "gathering of people" to be transferred over time to designate the "places" in which that gathering is collected. Examples are provided, such as the words: **Sanhedrin** <note>original: סנהדרין / συνέδριον; the high council</note>, **Senate** <note>original: Curia; whose origin is traced to the Greek word for "lordly," *kyria*</note>, **Assembly** <note>original: Concio</note>, and **Meeting Place** <note>original: Comitium</note>. Furthermore, it is added that the word **Church** <note>original: ἐκκλησία</note> underwent the same change in meaning among both Sacred and Secular authors. On this occasion, the opinion of Fuller is weighed regarding the genuine meaning of "Church" in 1 Corinthians 11:18, 22, while also considering Spanheim’s arguments against it. Finally, the text inquires into the validity of what Elias Levita wrote concerning the word **Congregation** <note>original: קהילה (Qehila)</note>. 102.

#### CHAPTER IV.

It is observed that the word **Synagogue** <note>original: ΣΥΝΑΓΩΓΗ</note>, when used for the place of a sacred meeting, takes on the meaning of the word **Assembly-house** <note>original: כנישתא / כנישה (Kenishta/Kenisha)</note>, which is commonly used by Hebrew writers for **House of Assembly** <note>original: בית כנישתא / בית הכנסת (Beit Kenishta or Beit ha-Knesset)</note>; this is often shortened in a way familiar to the Sacred Authors. Then, the text proceeds to explain other names by which Synagogues are typically distinguished by various writers. Among these, it first examines the term **Place of Prayer** <note>original: PROSEUCHA</note>, as used by Juvenal, Philo, and Josephus, and inquires whether it has the same meaning in two passages of the New Testament: Luke 6:12 and Acts 16:13. To understand these, the commentaries of Schindler, Drusius, Heinsius, and others are brought forward and examined. Afterward, other names for Synagogues are touched upon: **Sacred places**, **Sabbath-houses**, **Men's halls**, **Prayer-houses**, and **Study-houses** <note>original: ἱερά, σαββατεῖα, ἀνδρῶνες, προσευκτήρια, φροντιστήρια</note>, which can be found in Philo and Josephus. Finally, an observation is added regarding the expression **House of Assembly** <note>original: בית הכנסת (Beit ha-Knesset)</note>.

### CHAPTER V.

**Synagogues**, strictly so-called, which are termed **Houses of Assembly** <note>original: בתי כנסיות (Batei Knesiyot)</note>, are more significantly distinguished from **Houses of Study** <note>original: בתי מדרשות (Batei Midrashot)</note>, meaning the Academies or Public Schools. ### CHAPTER II.

The opinions of *Josephus*, *Philo*, and even the *later Masters* are examined, who trace the origin of the explanation of the Divine Law—frequented on Sabbath days—back to the times and precepts of Moses. Testimonies from the *Law of Moses* regarding the "Holy Convocation" <note>Hebrew: מקרא קדש (*mikra kodesh*)</note>, which they translate as a sacred assembly (Lev. 23:3), and the *sanctification of the seventh day* (Exod. 20:8) are unfolded. *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a major Dutch legal scholar and theologian</note> is believed to have looked to these same passages without disagreement. It is proven, however, that the origin of the Synagogues is not to be sought in either of those, once the expression "Holy Convocation" has been explained and the precept concerning the *sanctification of the Sabbath* has been declared. 282.

### CHAPTER III.

It is taken into consideration whether *that Tent* which *Moses* is read to have fixed outside the camp—to be approached by the repentant Israelites—should be thought to have been similar to the *Synagogues*, or the *Theological Auditoriums* <note>lecture halls for religious study</note> which were in use among the Jews of later times. Likewise, the reason is brought forth as to why *that Tabernacle* was called the TENT OF MEETING. Afterward, it is explored whether, in the famous promise found in Exodus 24, the *Structure* of Synagogues was tacitly either commanded or permitted, once the genuine meaning of that passage has been produced and confirmed. 297.

### CHAPTER IV.

The opinion of the illustrious man, *Hugo Grotius*, concerning the *first origin of Synagogues* is examined; it is built upon the precept found in *Moses* regarding the *reading of the Law*, which was to be repeated every seven years during the *Festival of Tabernacles*. Likewise, the view of *Cornelius Bertram* <note>A 16th-century Hebraist known for his work on the Republic of the Hebrews</note> on the same argument is explored, and it is argued against him that Synagogues do not owe their origin to the dispersion of the Levites throughout the region of the land of Canaan, which was ordained by a singular decree of God. 308.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER V.

It is disputed whether the *Chaldean Interpreter* <note>The Aramaic Targumist</note> at Judges 5:9 mentions *Synagogues* appropriately enough in his *Paraphrase*; and it is asked at the same time what should be understood in 그 text by the "Legislators of Israel" <note>Hebrew: חוקקי ישראל (*chokeke Yisrael*)</note>, after the opinions of Jewish Interpreters have been explored. Further, it is asked whether *Mizpah*, which was once a famous meeting place for the Hebrew people, existed as a Synagogue in the time of the Judges; the Dutch Interpreters <note>referring to the Statenvertaling or related commentators</note> seem to lean toward this opinion along with *Kimchi* and *Abarbanel* <note>Medieval Jewish commentators David Kimchi and Isaac Abarbanel</note>. To this question, it is answered in the negative for various reasons that are brought forward. It is also taught that this *Mizpah* was different from the "land of Mizpah" in Joshua 11:3, near which Joshua defeated the Kings of Northern Canaan; and finally, the genuine meaning of the phrase "before the Lord" <note>Hebrew: לפני יהוה (*lifne Adonai*)</note> in Judges 20:1 is explained. 315.

### CHAPTER VI.

The transition is made to *another interval of time in the Jewish Commonwealth*, as it was governed by *Kings* up until the *Babylonian captivity*; it is asked whether that era gave rise to the *Synagogues*? To this question it is answered that *Synagogues*, strictly speaking, do not seem to have arisen during all that time, but that the Jewish people did not, for that reason, lack all *public instruction*. Before that prior proposition (denying Synagogues to this interval of time) is proven, the *nature and manner of Public Instruction* is discussed in advance; particularly, the *public Schools of the Prophets* are described, in which they were accustomed to preach before the common people, illustrated by various texts of Holy Scripture. It is then proven that such institutions were not entirely lacking even under the *Judges*, although at that point in time they were very rare. On this occasion, the meaning of a praiseworthy and obscure passage, 2 Chronicles 15:3–5, is tracked down, after the commentaries of the Hebrew Interpreters have been thoroughly examined. 329.

# CHAPTER HEADINGS.

## C H A P T E R VII.
The dissertation on the *public Schools of the Prophets* is continued, particularly concerning the *established Listeners of the Prophets*, who are usually called *Prophets* and *Sons of the Prophets* <note>original: "Prophetæ & Prophetarum Filii" — a biblical term for disciples of a prophet</note> in Sacred History. Their entire way of life is described with the help of Hebrew Commentators, showing how they lived, ate, and devoted themselves to study together and yet *separately*, under the leadership of one or more famous Teachers; in a manner not much different from the <term>Cenobites</term> <note>original: "Cœnobitæ" — members of a monastic community</note> of subsequent centuries. The restoration of these types of Prophetic institutions is traced back to the times of *Samuel*, and the parts of his history relating to this are illustrated, while certain interpretations by *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century Jewish statesman and philosopher</note> are rejected. Finally, a comparison is established between the *Schools of the Prophets* among the Hebrews and the *Schools of Philosophers* among the Greeks. 349.

## C H A P T E R VIII.
The nature of the duty imposed upon the *Levites* for *teaching* the Jewish people is investigated through various testimonies of Holy Scripture. It is proven that they, more than other Israelites from the common people, were obligated to learn the Law and to draw out its genuine meaning. This *knowledge* served a practical use: they could answer those asking about the meaning of the Law, determine doubtful cases, and frequently preside over the judgments of the people. It is also suggested by conjecture that the poorer among them were often received into the families of Israelites to preside over their domestic sacred rites and to take charge of instructing the household. Appended to this dissertation is an exposition of *three* highly noteworthy passages of Holy Scripture pertaining to this subject. 362.

## C H A P T E R IX.
Various arguments are produced, illustrated, and emphasized, drawn from the Holy Scriptures, to prove that *Synagogues* (as they are specifically named) were not at all known

<column-break/>

or accepted under the *Jewish Kings* up until the *Babylonian Captivity*. In particular, the notable history of the *Book of the Law*—found in the Temple by *Hilkiah*, the presiding High Priest, and delivered to King *Josiah*—is narrated and explained. 380.

## C H A P T E R X.
An objection raised by very learned men based on Psalm 74:8 <note>In many translations, this verse mentions "meeting places" or "synagogues of God," which some use to argue for their pre-exilic existence</note> against the opinion confirmed in the previous dissertation is resolved. This is done by indicating the scope and argument of this entire Psalm (in the determination of which even experienced interpreters of Scripture disagree), and especially by explaining the *words* containing the difficulty that opposes our view. 396.

## C H A P T E R XI.
Certain other doubts are resolved which are, or could be, raised by Jewish or Christian Doctors against the opinion proven above, based on interpretations of certain passages of Holy Scripture. Regarding the *Fast* that was proclaimed by *Jezebel* and observed in *Samaria*, a brief discussion is provided toward the end. 405.

## C H A P T E R XII.
It is posited, alongside other learned men, that *Synagogues* and their principal ceremonies *were born* in Canaan after the return of the Jews from the Babylonian Captivity, and this is confirmed by the words of *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>. Following this, it is argued that the precise moment in time to which the origin of Synagogues should be assigned is uncertain, as there is no memory of them even in the history of the Maccabees. It is noted, however, that their principal ceremonies are to be traced back to that solemn public reading of the Divine Law, with the blessings joined to it, which is described in the Book of *Nehemiah*. After illustrating that text, other causes that promoted the origin of Synagogues are also reviewed. Finally, this dissertation concludes with certain passages added from *Philo* and *Josephus* concerning the progress of this first institution of Synagogues. 413.

# CHAPTER HEADINGS.
## PART III.
### CHAPTER I.
The meeting places of the early Church are investigated; these are divided into *Private and Public*, and the former are further divided into *fixed and discretionary*. It is established from the *Acts of the Apostles* that *Private* locations were used for a time and were *discretionary*, following a discussion of the explanations by the famous scholars *de Dieu* <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch orientalist</note> and *Cloppenburg* regarding the phrase *from house to house* <note>original: "κατ' οἶκον"</note>. Then, *Public* places are discussed, and it is argued that *Public Oratories* <note>prayer houses</note> of this kind should not be entirely denied to Christians of the first centuries, even if they were rare. Reasons are also presented as to why Christians of the earliest times both needed and chose to remain hidden in the exercise of their religion. Finally, some observations are made regarding the famous testimonies of the Gentiles <note>non-Christians, specifically Romans and Greeks</note> concerning Christians, claiming that Christians have no Temples or Altars. 429.
### CHAPTER II.
Certain reasons are brought forward to prove,

<column-break/>

that the sacred buildings of the early Christians were formed after the model of the Jewish Synagogues; this is further emphasized by a brief comparison between the *Names, Parts, and Accidental features* of Synagogues and *Christian Oratories*. 444.
### CHAPTER III.
It is shown that the custom of praying *toward the East* <note>original: "versus Orientem"</note>, and of directing the *rear part* of their Oratories toward it—which was observed by Christians of old—is not as contrary to the customs of the Jews as is commonly thought. Meanwhile, other reasons that they offered for this custom are reviewed. Finally, it is noted that the *Christian Oratories* grew so much in size and splendor under the rule of Christian Princes that they seemed more similar to *Temples*—whether Jewish or Gentile—than to Synagogues; indeed, they were frequently compared to the *Temple of Jerusalem* by authors of those times. 456.

## BOOK SECOND.
### CHAPTER I.
After a preface concerning the difficulty of the following treatise, various passages are selected from the *Commentaries of Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist and theologian</note> on the New Testament, in which he discusses the *Form of Government* of both the *Synagogue* and the *Church*, and the agreement between the two, from which the entire opinion of *Grotius* on this matter can be drawn. 467.
### CHAPTER II.
It is proven that the Apostolic churches were everywhere ruled by a College of <term>Presbyters</term> <note>original: "Presbyterorum" — elders or priests</note> of the same kind and order, certainly with some President, but one distinguished from the other Presbyters by no certain mark or prerogative of his presidency; indeed, the right of teaching is claimed for all the others just as much as for the *President*, both from the Holy Scriptures and from the monuments of Ecclesiastical History. Furthermore, a greater force of reasoning is applied to subvert the distinction of *Presbyters* into *Teaching and Ruling*—or *Lay* elders, as they are specifically called: 

<column-break/>

on which occasion the office of the *Presbyters of the Early Christian Church* is explained from the *History of the Ancient Church*, to make it clear that they had almost nothing in common with our *common Presbyters* <note>referring to lay elders in the author's contemporary church</note> except for the name. 474.
### CHAPTER III.
Three passages—1 Timothy 5:17, Romans 12:8, and 1 Corinthians 12:28—which are usually brought forward from the Epistles of Paul in favor of *Ruling Elders from the Common People*, are explained at length, their genuine sense having been investigated, produced, and confirmed. Regarding the first passage, taken from the *First Epistle to Timothy*, it is necessary to ask what kind of *Teaching Presbyters* those are who are mentioned by *Cyprian* <note>a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note>, after weighing the opinion of the most learned *Dodwell* <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an Anglo-Irish scholar</note> regarding them. Finally, the *Seniors of the people* <note>original: "Seniores plebis"</note> are called to the scene, whose memory exists in the writings of the Ancients; it is proven that they betray the cause of *Ruling Elders* more than they help it. 490.

### CHAPTER IV.
**Grotius's Hypothesis** regarding the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church is examined against the truths already proven, and it is defined to what extent it should be accepted or rejected. 512. <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist and theologian who argued for strong parallels between Jewish and Christian administrative structures.</note>

### CHAPTER V.
**The Structure of the Synagogue**, which the most learned **Petit** <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar of ancient law</note> reconstructed from the Body of Civil Law, is surveyed: in which case it is debated how the various titles of dignity—such as **Patriarchs**, **Primates**, **Majors**, **Nobles**, **Rulers of the Synagogue**, **Fathers of the Synagogues**, **High Priests**, **Priests**, **Presbyters**, and **Elders**—should be understood in the Roman Laws that deal with the Jews. 516. <note>original Latin terms: "Patriarcharum, Primatum, Majorum, Procerum, Archisynagogorum, Patrum Synagogarum, Archiereorum, Hiereorum, Presbyterorum, Seniorum"</note>

### CHAPTER VI.
**The Form of the Ancient Synagogue**, as the famous **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English Hebraist</note> conceived it in his mind, is set before the eyes: in which, since it is supposed that the Sacred duties of the Synagogue were distributed among the **Ten Men** who are called <term>The Idle Men</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Batlanim*. These were men of leisure who were paid or volunteered to be constantly available for communal service and prayer</note>, first the primary passages found in the Code of Jewish Law concerning the **Ten Idle Men** are brought forward; then the double interpretation of this title—one by **Lightfoot** and **Cappellus**, the other by **Buxtorf**, which is accepted among the interpreters of the Talmudic Code—is presented. 530.

### CHAPTER VII.
Those things are brought forward which are suitable for illustrating and probably establishing the opinion of **Lightfoot** and **Cappellus** regarding the **Ten Idle Men**; namely: 1. That **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler</note> interpreted the "Ten Idle Men" as *Ten learned Men*, free for instruction and legal judgments. 2. That not only in the Hebrew language but also in others, it is common for studious and learned men to be called "Idle" <note>meaning "at leisure" for study</note>. 3. The <term>Meticulousness</term> <note>original Greek: "Περίεργον" (Periergon)</note> of these Idle Men; <term>being occupied with public needs</term> <note>original Hebrew: "עוסקים בצרכי צבור" (oskim be-tzorkhei tzibur)</note>; fits Lightfoot's exposition well. 534.

### CHAPTER VIII.
**The Offices of the Synagogue**, as they

<column-break/>

were distributed among the **Ten Idle Men** by **Lightfoot**, are each reviewed, and it is debated whether they suit the Ancient Synagogue. Among other things, it is proved by solid arguments that the *Collectors of Alms* should not properly be reckoned among the official officers of the Synagogue. 542.

### CHAPTER IX.
It is assumed that **Ancient Synagogues** were not ruled in only one way; and first it is proved that the more famous synagogues of the larger cities were governed by a Senate of Learned Men. 549.

### CHAPTER X.
It is proved that **Other Synagogues**—either because they were less famous and subordinate to larger ones, or because they lacked a wealth of Learned Men—were ruled by a certain **MASTER OF SACRED RITES**, called a <term>Rabbi</term> <note>original Hebrew: "רב" (Rav)</note>; his status and office are described at some length; to which is added a description of the <term>Pastors</term> <note>original Hebrew: "פרנסים" (Parnasim)</note> of the **modern Synagogue**. Many other things are interspersed regarding titles of masterly honor: <term>Wise Man</term> <note>Hebrew: "חכם" (Chakham) / Greek: "σοφὸς" (Sophos)</note>, <term>Master</term> <note>Hebrew: "רב" (Rav)</note>, <term>Associate</term> <note>Hebrew: "חבר" (Chaver)</note>, <term>Sophist</term> <note>Greek: "σοφιστής"</note>, <term>Notable</term> <note>Greek: "γνώσιμος"</note>, etc. 565.

### CHAPTER XI.
Those things which occur in the history of the New Testament, the statutes of Roman Law, in the works of **Epiphanius**, and elsewhere concerning the **Governance of Synagogues** are brought forward to illustrate the preceding hypotheses and are reconciled with them. Especially discussed is the genuine meaning of the terms <term>Head of the Assembly</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ראש הכנסת" (Rosh HaKnesset)</note> among the Hebrews, and **RULER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>original: "ARCHISYNAGOGI"</note> among the Greeks and Latins. 580.

### CHAPTER XII.
The **Various types of Synagogue Governance** proposed above are compared with the **Form of Governance of the early Christian Church**, and it is proved by solid arguments that none of them can be applied to the **Form of Governance of the Apostolic Church** except that first one, by which the more famous synagogues are supposed to be ruled by a Senate of several Learned Men, who constituted a certain sacred **Consistory** or **Presbytery**. 592.

# BOOK THREE.

## PART I.

### CHAPTER I.
After outlining the **schema** <note>original Greek: "σχῆμα," meaning the structure or outline</note> of the following treatise, a more specialized discussion begins regarding the **NAMES OF THE LEADERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE**, which occur in the New Testament Scriptures; these are conveniently compared with the names or titles of the Leaders of the Early Christian Church. Among these, the first place is given to the title of **ELDERS** <note>original Hebrew: "זקנים" (Zekenim)</note>, a title common to the leaders of both the Synagogue and the Church, which is explained and illustrated from suitable authors according to our purpose. 609.

### CHAPTER II.
After explaining the title of Elders, the distinguished title of **PASTORS** <note>original Greek: "Ποιμένων" (Poimenon), meaning shepherds</note> is taken up, by which the Leaders of the Christian Church are noted by Paul. This is traced back to the term **PASTORS** <note>original Hebrew: "פרנסים" (Parnasim), literally "providers" or "sustainers"</note>, very well known in the modern, but especially in the Ancient Synagogue; its origin and genuine meaning are unearthed and further illuminated and confirmed. Specifically, after examining the opinion of **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist</note>, who attributed this title to the collectors of alms, it is proven by many arguments that in common ancient usage it was ascribed to those Rectors of the Synagogue who were also Teachers, excelling in learning and piety. 621.

### CHAPTER III.
The power of the word **OVERSEER** <note>original Greek: "ΕΠΙΣΚΟΠΟΣ" (Episkopos), from which the word "Bishop" is derived</note>, by which the Leaders of the Church are likewise designated in the New Testament writings, is first extracted from the Greek language, then illustrated from the Hebrew, by comparing it with the name **OFFICER** <note>original Hebrew: "ממונה" (Memunneh), an appointed official or overseer</note>, a term familiarly used for the Leaders of the Synagogue. To this same category are reduced the Greek term **Leader** <note>original: "προεστὼς" (Proestos)</note> and the Latin term **Provost** <note>original: "Præpositus"</note>, which are titles also granted to the Elders of the Church. Finally, the name **LEADER** <note>original Greek: "Ἡγούμενος" (Hegoumenos)</note> is treated, applied to those same Rectors of the early Church in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which is compared with the Hebrew title of the same force and usage, **GUIDE** <note>original Hebrew: "מנהיג" (Manhig)</note>, known in the Synagogue. 640.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER IV.
The **QUALITIES** or conditions which Paul requires for the choosing of Bishops in the First Epistle to Timothy are recounted and distinguished into certain classes. Then, two of these are selected to be explained more broadly: the first, that a Bishop must be **apt to teach** <note>original Greek: "διδακτικὸν" (didaktikon)</note>, which it is proven should be translated as "fit for teaching"; the second, that a Bishop must be the **husband of one wife** <note>original Greek: "μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα" (mias gynaikos andra)</note>. It is demonstrated through many points that this phrasing excludes not only "successive" polygamy (remarriage after death/divorce), as some say, but also "simultaneous" polygamy. Both of these conditions, as they were observed among the ancient Elders of the Jewish assemblies, are investigated from Hebrew writings. 649.

### CHAPTER V.
A treatise begins regarding the **DUTIES** of the Elders of the Ancient Synagogue and the Church, which are reduced to two types: **Teaching** and **Governing**. It is thus proven by clear testimonies that sermons were once held in the Synagogues; the nature of these is then diligently investigated, explaining (as much as is sufficient) the meaning of the three principal terms by which Synagogal sermons are designated: **Haggadah** <note>original Hebrew: "אגדה," homiletic or narrative teaching</note>, **Words of Admonition** <note>original Hebrew: "דברי כיבושין" (Divrei Kivushin), speeches intended to humble or rebuke the heart</note>, and **Derashah** <note>original Hebrew: "דרשה," a formal sermon or exposition</note>. In the exposition of the first term, it is shown that the method of teaching through **allegories and parables** <note>original Greek: "ἀλληγορίας & παραβολὰς"</note> formerly flourished in the Synagogues. 667.

### CHAPTER VI.
The specific circumstances of holding sermons among the Jews are discussed; namely, the **Place, Time, and Occasions** on which this act was celebrated in the Synagogue. In particular, a double kind of Synagogal sermon is observed: one which was mixed with the Divine reading of the Law, and another which followed it. 685.

### CHAPTER VII.
The authority to preach in the Synagogues is vindicated first of all for the <term>Archisynagogis</term> <note>Rulers of the Synagogue; the presiding officers who managed the services and communal affairs</note>; and on that occasion, the origin and genuine meaning of the term are disputed...

# CHAPTER HEADINGS.

...the meaning of the term **laying on of hands** <note>original Greek: "χειροθεσία" (cheirothesia)</note> in **Roman Law**. However, two **qualifications** of this opinion are primarily set forth regarding the **Rulers of the Synagogue** <note>original Latin: "Archisynagogos"</note>. 1. That they did not *ordinarily* perform this act, but only in certain established and rarer cases, although customs here easily varied. 2. That they alone did not perform this act of preaching in the Synagogues, but granted it with great freedom to any **Teachers** <note>original Latin: "Doctoribus"</note>; from which the reason is sought why **Christ** and the **Apostles** preached so familiarly in the Synagogues. 696.

->CHAPTER VIII.<-

The **Sermons of the Teachers** of the Christian Church are compared with those of the **Synagogue**—from which they derive their origin—in terms of their **Name**, **Method**, and various **Circumstances**; certain phrases of Holy Scripture pertaining to this are explained. 712.

->CHAPTER IX.<-

The **Governance of the Prefects of the Synagogue** is discussed, which is organized into three acts: the **Guidance of Synagogue Acts**, the **Coercion of the Disobedient**, and the **Care of Alms**. After explaining the first part, the text moves to an exposition of **Synagogue Coercions**, which are divided into two types: **Excommunication** and **Flogging**. Furthermore, **Jewish Excommunication** and the **Rebuking** that precedes it are discussed, as well as the **Origin of Excommunication** and the **Persons** in whom the power of **Excommunicating** resided, as far as it relates to this subject. In particular, these two points are examined more specifically: 1. Whether Christ's words in Matthew chapter XVIII. 15, 16, 17 are to be referred to the Synagogue customs of that time? 2. Whether those who were **Excommunicated** among the Jews were also excluded from the Synagogue building itself? 727.

->CHAPTER X.<-

It is disputed more precisely and at greater length against **Erastus** <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss theologian who argued that the power of excommunication should lie with the state rather than the church</note> and others, that **Excommunication** in the Apostolic Christian Church was received following the example of the **Synagogue**. It is taught what that **Excommunication** of ancient times primarily consisted of, after resolving exceptions or

<column-break/>

objections to the opposing view. It is also proven that **private Excommunication** was in use among Christians just as it was among Jews; and it is finally added that this power was exercised in the Church by **Bishops** and **Presbyters**. 752.

->CHAPTER XI.<-

A discussion is held regarding **Flogging** in the Synagogues, which the Sacred Writers mention in more than one place. The opinions of **Theodore Beza** <note>A French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note> and **Hugo Grotius** <note>A Dutch jurist and theologian who wrote extensively on law and scripture</note> are examined; against their views, it is demonstrated that this type of punishment was instituted and practiced in the Synagogues in place of **Excommunication**, and is attributed to the **Elders of the Synagogue**. It is also inquired whether any similar kind of coercion took place in Christian Assemblies. Finally, the reason is given why Christ is never read to have been Excommunicated in the Gospel Histories. 768.

->CHAPTER XII.<-

The dissertation on the **Duties of the Rulers of the Synagogue** moves to their **third act** of Governance: namely, the **Care of Alms**. Before reaching that point, however, two very noble questions are discussed and settled: why **Alms** among the Jews is called **Justice** <note>original Hebrew: "צדקה" (Tzedakah)</note>; and how much difference there is between this same **Justice** and another duty of piety and charity, which among them is designated by the name **Liberal Beneficence** <note>original Hebrew: "גמילות חסדים" (Gemilut Hasadim), often translated as "Acts of Loving-kindness"</note>. Both questions are treated in such a way that many notable sayings of Holy Scripture are shed in a new light. Indeed, it is proven that almost every work of Christ was, and the work of Christians ought to be, **Liberal Beneficence**. 782.

->CHAPTER XIII.<-

The **Care for the Poor** maintained by God in organizing the state of the Jewish Republic is briefly indicated; the **Alms** of that nation are distinguished into **obligatory** and **liberal** or **voluntary**. It is conjectured that those of the latter type only began to be solemnly collected after the end of the Babylonian Captivity and distributed to the poor by **Collectors** <note>original Hebrew: "גבאים" (Gabbaim)</note> appointed for that purpose; the **Alms** are again distinguished into those given to the **Poor of the land of Canaan**, and those...

->### CHAPTER HEADINGS.<-

...distributed to the poor of each place. Finally, it is proved that the right of distributing these alms rested with both the **Presidents of the Synagogues** and the **Bishops of the Christian Churches**. 806.

### CAP. XIV.
We move to the **incidental features** of Jewish and Christian **Presbyters** <note>leaders or elders</note> to be compared with one another, first dealing with the **Ordination** of both—that is, both their **ELECTION** and their **CONFIRMATION**. In this dissertation, the method of electing and confirming the leaders of the **Early Church** is presented and explained from the undisputed monuments of antiquity, especially from **Cyprian** <note>St. Cyprian, a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note>. The act of election is defended as belonging to the **People**, rather than the ordaining Bishops, contrary to the views of the famous **Beveridge** <note>William Beveridge, a 17th-century Anglican bishop and scholar</note>. 818.

### CAP. XV.
How the **Presidents of the Jewish Presbyteries** were elected and confirmed in their office is explained from Hebrew authors. It is shown that the customs used by Christians in this matter were derived from the **Synagogue** into the **Church**. In particular, various doubts are cleared up regarding the **laying on of hands** <note>original Hebrew: "סמיכה" (Semikhah)</note> or the **Doctoral laying on of hands** <note>original Greek: "χειροθεσία" (cheirothesia)</note> of the Jews, and its significance. 828.

### CAP. XVI.
It is proved once again that **Bishops** and **Presbyters** constituted the same council and were of the same **Order**, not only in the Apostolic age but also in those following. This section refutes the recent objections of **Henry Dodwell** <note>a prominent 17th-century scholar and theologian</note>, a most learned man, regarding the argument produced by **Blondel** <note>David Blondel, a French Protestant who argued for the original equality of bishops and presbyters</note> from the **laying on of hands** <note>original Greek: "χειροθεσία" (cheirothesia)</note> of the Clergy among the ancients. It is then proved that the **Heads of the Academies** <note>original Hebrew: "ראשי ישיבות" (Roshei Yeshivot)</note> of the Jewish Presbyteries were considered to be of the same Order and council as the **Assessor Presbyters** <note>assistant elders</note>. 844.

### CAP. XVII.
It is considered whether individual churches or their **Rectors** <note>leaders</note> had any **relationship** <note>original Greek: "σχέσιν" (schesin)</note> among themselves, such that the Council of Elders of one church depended on the Council or Councils of other churches as being superior in authority. It is proved that after the removal of the **Sanhedrin in Jerusalem**, which was fortified by Apostolic authority, all churches and the

<column-break/>

**Presbyteries** of the early churches became **independent**, while still maintaining the necessary acts of communion. Small Christian societies are obliged by the **Law of Christ** to cultivate this communion. It is then shown what those acts of communion are, as well as how and when **Metropolitans** <note>bishops with authority over a province</note> arose. A clear conformity in this part is also shown between the **Synagogue** and the **Church**. 857.

### CAP. XVIII.
It is established that the **number of Presbyters** in both Jewish and Christian councils varied according to the reason of the places and circumstances. Next, the **honorariums** or **stipends** of the Presbyters of both the Church and the Synagogue are discussed, showing again the agreement of customs between the two in this regard. Afterwards, some points are added concerning the **hereditary transfer** of the presiding office from father to son, again comparing the customs of the Synagogue and the Ancient Church. 874.

## PART II.

### CAP. I.
After a preliminary outline of the following treatise, the **MINISTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUES** of modern times, known by the titles **Envoy**, **Minister**, and **Treasurer** <note>original Hebrew: "שליח" (Shaliach), "חזן" (Chazzan), and "גבאי" (Gabbai)</note>, are described. However, a proven distinction is noted between these titles and the persons so named in the **Ancient Synagogue**. In the ancient setting, the **ENVOYS OF THE CHURCH** <note>original Hebrew/Latin: "שליחי צבור" (Shaliach Tzibbur) / "LEGATI ECCLESIÆ"</note> were specifically those appointed—either ordinarily or extraordinarily—to pour out prayers on behalf of the assembly; the **MINISTERS** <note>original Hebrew: "חזנים" (Chazzanim)</note> were those who performed the lowlier services of the Synagogue. 889.

### CAP. II.
The genuine meaning of the names **Envoy**, **Minister**, and **Treasurer** <note>original Hebrew: "שליח" (Shaliach), "חזן" (Chazzan), and "גבאי" (Gabbai)</note> is revealed and illustrated from many testimonies. The somewhat obscure origin of the word **Minister** <note>original Hebrew: "חזן" (Chazzan)</note> is likewise investigated. In particular, it is proved that the term **Chazzan** is usually used by Hebrew authors for an **attendant** <note>original Greek: "ὑπηρέτῃ" (hyperete)</note> or **MINISTER OF AN INFERIOR ORDER**, and that **Shaliach Tzibbur** should be translated not as **MESSENGER**, but as **ENVOY OF THE CHURCH**. 895.

## CHAPTER III.

The opinion of **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English scholar of Hebrew and rabbinic literature</note> is refuted, who attempted to compare the name and office of the **Messenger of the Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *shaliach tzibbur*, the individual who leads the congregation in prayer</note> with the name and office of the **Bishop** <note>original Greek: *episkopou* (overseer)</note> in the Christian Church. However, the same learned man is praised for comparing the title **Messenger of the Assembly** with the designation **Angel of the Church** <note>original Greek: *angelou ekklesias*</note> found in the Book of Revelation. It is proved that the **Presidents of the Elders** in the Christian Church performed the same work as the **Messengers of the Church** in the Synagogue. A final word is added regarding Paul’s paraphrase: **Apostle of the church** <note>original Greek: *apostolos ekklesias*</note>. 908.

## CHAPTER IV.

The opinion of certain learned men is praised, who began to compare the **Deacons** of the Church described by Paul in the Epistle to Timothy with the **Chazzanim** <note>original: *Chazzanitis*; the *Chazzan* was a synagogue official or attendant</note> of the Synagogue; this view is supported by the similarity of both their **Names** and **Offices**. In particular, the genuine meaning of the terms **Servant** <note>original Greek: *hyperetes*</note> and **Deacon of the Church** <note>original Greek: *diakonos tes ekklesias*</note> is discussed in comparison with the Hebrew terms **Synagogue Attendant** <note>original Hebrew: *chazzan keneset*</note> and **Attendant** <note>original Hebrew: *chazzan*</note>. 914.

## CHAPTER V.

It is established by various arguments that the seven **Stewards** <note>original Greek: *oeconomos*</note> of the Jerusalem Church, who were ordained by the Apostles for the **Service of Tables** <note>original Greek: *eis diakonian trapezon*</note>, were very different from the **Deacons** of whom Paul speaks in his Epistles to Timothy and the Philippians, and from those known by that name throughout the early Christian churches. This was observed long ago by **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note> and the **Quinisext Council** <note>also known as the Council in Trullo (692 AD), which dealt with church discipline</note>. It is proved that these were extraordinary ministers, noting the opinion that compares them with the **Collectors of Alms** <note>original Hebrew: *gabbaim*</note> among the Hebrews. 920.

## CHAPTER VI.

The qualities or **Virtues** that the Hebrews require in their **Messengers of the Assembly** are recounted and compared with the **Virtues** that Paul requires in **Bishops**, who performed the duties of the Messengers of the Church in the Christian community. Likewise, the requirements that the Jews look for in their **Chazzanim** <note>attendants</note>, or Deacons of the Synagogue properly so called, are briefly com-

<column-break/>

pared with the conditions required by Paul in the **Deacons of the Christian Church**. 934.

## CHAPTER VII.

A transition to the **Rituals of the Jewish Religion**, the performance of which was granted to any literate men in the ancient Synagogue by the **Rulers of the Synagogue**. In later times, however, these tasks were entrusted to the **Synagogue Ministers**, who also began to be called **Messengers of the Church**. Among these rituals, we begin with the sacred rite of the **Reading of the Mosaic Law**. This chapter deals with the underlying subject of that rite, discussing notable doubts: whether the entire Law of Moses was read in the synagogues; whether it was read according to the **Keri** <note>the traditional way the word is spoken/read</note> or the **Ketiv** <note>the way the word is written in the text</note>; and whether it was permitted to read the Holy Scripture in **Greek**. The views of **Scaliger**, **Walton**, and **Simon** <note>prominent 16th and 17th-century biblical scholars and philologists</note> are noted, along with other requirements the Jews had for the **Scroll of the Law** from which the reading was to be performed. 946.

## CHAPTER VIII.

This chapter deals distinctly with the **Prerequisites**, as they are called—the preliminary steps of the sacred rite of **Reading the Mosaic Law** as celebrated in the synagogues—as well as its methods, accompanying rituals, and following actions. The statutes of the **Masters** <note>the Rabbis</note> on this subject are presented. Among other relevant matters, the formula of the most holy prayer, the **Kaddish**, is presented from the works of **Maimonides** <note>a preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>, and the **Major and Minor divisions** of the Mosaic Law are discussed in passing. 961.

## CHAPTER IX.

The **Circumstances** of this sacred exercise are discussed regarding both **Time** and **Place**. A passage from **Tertullian** <note>a 2nd-century Christian author from Carthage</note> is explained, in which he calls the public reading of the Law, as it was performed by the Jews in his age, a **Taxable Liberty** <note>original Latin: *vectigalem libertatem*; referring to the tax Jews paid to Rome for the right to practice their religion</note>. The **Qualities and Requirements** of the readers are given, as well as the rules for their **Order and Number**. Finally, the duties of **Reverence** required from the synagogue congregation during this act are described from the **Hebrew Canons**. 977.
