-># CHAPTER HEADINGS.<-

### CHAPTER X.

This chapter treats the **Reading of the Prophets**, as is customary in the synagogue, including its *subject matter*, methods, and circumstances, while describing the rules of the Masters <note>The "Masters" refers to the Rabbis of the Talmudic period who established these laws (Halakha).</note> regarding this ritual. In passing, an inquiry is made into the reason why the **Writings** <note>original Hebrew: כתובים (*Ketuvim*); the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible, including Psalms, Proverbs, and Job.</note>, or the third part of the Biblical Codex, are generally not read in the synagogue (with the exception of the five Minor Scrolls <note>The *Megillot*: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther.</note>). Finally, some observations are added regarding the genuine meaning of the word **Haftarah** <note>original Hebrew: הפטרה; meaning "conclusion" or "dismissal," it refers to the selection from the Prophets read after the Torah portion.</note>, which is the term used to designate the Prophetic reading. 984.

### CHAPTER XI.

The passages concerning the reading of the Law and the Prophets found in the writings of the New Testament are identified, not omitting the example of Christ as the **Reader of the Prophet Isaiah** in the synagogue of Nazareth. The origin of the **reading of the Law**, and especially of the **Prophets**, is then discussed, and the opinion of **Elias Levita** <note>Elia Levita (1469–1549) was a famous Hebrew grammarian and scholar whose theories on the history of the biblical text were highly influential.</note> is examined. Finally, it is proven that the ritual of **reading both the Gospels and the Prophets**, divided into certain **sections** <note>original Greek: περικοπὰς (*perikopas*)</note> or **readings** <note>original Greek: ἀναγνώσματα (*anagnosmata*)</note>, was transferred from the Synagogue into the Church, with examples provided of the similarities between the two. 998.

### CHAPTER XII.

This chapter deals with the public **Interpretation** of the Law and the Prophets, as was the custom in the synagogues, and its methods are explained according to the statutes of the Hebrews. It is then asked whether Paul, in the fourteenth chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, was looking back to the customs of the synagogues when prescribing laws to the Corinthians regarding the interpretation of the Divine Word. 1015.

### CHAPTER XIII.

Here begins the treatise on the solemn **PRAYERS** and **BLESSINGS** of the Synagogue, the recitation of which is known among the Jews as the **Descending** or **Appearing** before the Ark <note>original Hebrew: ירידה לפני התיבה (*Yeridah lifnei ha-Teivah*); the "Ark" refers to the chest containing the Torah scrolls.</note>. To understand this ritual, the general parts of a man's prayer to God—**Blessing** <note>original Hebrew: ברכה (*Berachah*)</note> and **Prayer** <note>original Hebrew: תפלה (*Tefillah*)</note>—and the specific parts—**Thanksgiving and the Deprecation of Divine Perfections** <note>original Hebrew: שבח (*Shevach*, meaning "praise" or "extolling").</note>

<column-break/>

**Praise** <note>original Hebrew: שבah (*Shevach*)</note>; and **Thanksgiving** <note>original Hebrew: ותהודיה (*v'Tehodiyah*)</note>; **Supplication and Petition** <note>original Hebrew: תחנה ; ובקשה (*Tachanah v'Bakashah*)</note>; are noted according to **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note>, and are applied to illustrate certain passages from the Apostle Paul. Prayers are then distinguished into **Private and Public**; and both types are categorized into **Morning, Afternoon, and Evening** prayers. Finally, the meaning of the phrase **DESCENDING BEFORE THE ARK** is declared. 1022.

### CHAPTER XIV.

The prayer formula **Eighteen Benedictions** <note>original Hebrew: שמנה עשרה (*Shemoneh Esreh*); also known as the *Amidah*, the central prayer of Jewish liturgy.</note>, consisting of eighteen blessings, which is held most sacred by the Jews and to which nearly all other prayers are usually referred, is presented in its entirety according to **Maimonides**, compared with various **Liturgies**. Many observations are made regarding it, especially the **various ways** it is to be recited in different cases; and regarding the author and the time of the added **Nineteenth** prayer, which is called the **Blessing of the Heretics** <note>original Hebrew: ברכת המינים (*Birkat ha-Minim*); a prayer historically directed against sectarians or those who deviated from communal norms.</note> and is directed against heretics. 1031.

### CHAPTER XV.

The ritual of the **READING OF THE SHEMA** <note>original Hebrew: קריאת שמע (*Kriat Shema*); the recitation of the core confession of faith: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."</note>, which every free adult male Israelite is bound to perform twice daily, is described. The **Seven** blessings are presented, with **three** to be recited with the Morning Shema and **four** with the Evening Shema, along with certain observations on this ritual. 1052.

### CHAPTER XVI.

The entire **Jewish Liturgy**—that is, the prayers and blessings in the order they are recited in the synagogues at the Morning, Afternoon, and Evening hours—is described according to Maimonides, with his text on this subject cited and illustrated. Those matters which were not clearly taught by the famous **Buxtorf** <note>Likely Johannes Buxtorf the Younger (1599–1664), a leading Christian Hebraist.</note> on this subject (such as what he wrote regarding the **Hundred Blessings**) are elucidated. 1062.

# INTRODUCTION, ETC. CHAPTER I.
<sig>A</sig>

Those are to be judged to have looked out best for the common good who apply themselves to acquiring a true and solid understanding of these matters, and who also, by their own diligence in this kind of study, lead the way for others—even in the smallest details. For in Religion, nothing should be considered so small that it is not truly great and significant when compared to any other things or rituals of a different kind.

<margin>Persius, Satire II</margin> Indeed, I admit that the Christian Religion is practiced with a simple rite and without the pomp of many ceremonies. That arrogance which Pagan Superstition brought into the Worship of the Gods, and that splendor with which the Jewish Sacred Rites once shone (having been instituted by God himself for the benefit of the Church in its infancy), is largely neglected and rejected by Christianity, in its pure and uncorrupted state. It does not require *a bright and white garment so much as a pure heart, and*, to speak with the poet Persius:
->*A soul where duty and right are blended, and the sacred recesses*<-
->*of the mind,*<-
<note>original Latin: "Compositum jus fasque animi, sanctosque recessus mentis," a quote from Persius (34–62 AD) emphasizing that God values internal virtue over external sacrifice.</note>

<margin>Romans 12:1</margin> And even those very Ceremonies by which the Christian Religion is fulfilled are so simple, chaste, and pure, that not only is there nothing in them that offends Reason, but on the contrary, untainted Reason approves the Worship and Veneration of the Divine as it is practiced among Christians as "rational" <note>original Greek: $\lambda o \gamma \iota \kappa \eta \nu$ (*logikēn*), referring to the "reasonable service" mentioned by St. Paul in Romans 12:1.</note>, and supports it with its own strength and light. For Christians hold assemblies, and in them they celebrate Divine Virtues and blessings through Hymns composed by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit; they pour out Prayers and Thanksgivings to God, the author of all good; they read, interpret, and comment upon the Divine Word to encourage Virtue; they seal their Communion, which they have through one faith with the same Lord, with certain sacred symbols; they do this in *pure places*, without pomp, with *certain Elders presiding* (to borrow a phrase from Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was an early Christian author from Carthage who wrote extensively about church structure.</note>), *to whom the exercise of spiritual judgment has been entrusted by the Gathering of the Christian People*. Since these things constitute almost the whole of the Christian Religion, what is in them that could not withstand the most rigid scrutiny? Indeed, what is there that the fair and upright judgment of any man would not approve and praise?

Therefore, it might seem a *useless and least necessary* task to seek the origin of the Rites of the Christian Religion from any other principle than—

# CHAPTER I. ON THE OLD SYNAGOGUE.

...is spent on illustrating things from the light of Reason, or even from the Prerogatives of the New Covenant <note>original Latin: "Novi Fœderis," referring to the Christian era and the New Testament.</note>, to which the Sacred Rites and Government of the Christian Church had to be adapted. But if anyone weighs this matter more carefully and reflects upon it, they must either be of a stubborn mind, or they will change their opinion. For certainly, even if it is very true that the Christian Religion does not clash with Reason, if it can nevertheless be shown that Christ and the Apostles—the authors of the Doctrines and Rituals of our Religion—modeled it after another pattern which they had before their eyes, and from which they drew their ways of speaking about religious matters, it cannot be denied that the Rituals of our religion and the way the Christian Church is managed must first be explained by this Principle, and can only be solidly understood through it. Indeed, there are many things most worthy of attention which lead us to presume, quite reasonably, that Christ and the Apostles were focused on *Jewish Sacred Rites*—and especially the *Synagogal* ones, as will be discussed later—when they were establishing the Sacred Rites of the Church of the New Covenant.

1. In the Worship of the Temple and the *Synagogues*, certain Rites and ceremonies occur that are similar in every way to those observed in our own Sacred Rites. For if we turn our attention to the *Reading of the Law*, *Psalmody* <note>The singing or chanting of Psalms.</note>, *Sermons*, *Prayers*, *Blessings*, and other Sacred Acts and Rites of that kind, it is well established that they were no less in use among the Ancient Jews than they are now among Christians. For anyone who considers this with an attentive mind, what is more natural than to think about the common *Origin* of these Sacred Rites?

2. In the *Temple* and the *Synagogues* there were *Overseers* and *Ministers* <term>Præfecti & Ministri</term> of sacred things, who, in terms of their *Offices* (and even their *Names*, which we will discuss shortly), are comparable to those who *preside* over our Churches and perform *ministries* for them. Therefore, it is rightly asked: what is the reason for this similarity, or what could it be?

3. A point deserving special notice here is that not only do the *Officials* and *Customs* of the *Christian and Jewish* sacred assemblies agree with each other in many parts, but the Sacred Writers themselves repeatedly refer to the *Christian Church*, and its *Overseers*, *Ministers*, and *Customs* by the same names,

-># PROLEGOMENA, etc. Chapter I.<-

...they express in words and phrases which the Jews were accustomed to use to designate their own Sacred Persons and Ceremonies, either long ago, or even still today.

<margin>Acts 20:28; Ephesians 4:11; 1 Corinthians 6:5; 1 Timothy 5:17; 1 Timothy 3:8; Titus 1:5; Revelation 2:1; Hebrews 13:17; 2 Corinthians 9:12; Philippians 2:17; 1 Timothy 3:1; 1 Timothy 2:1; 1 Timothy 4:13; Acts 20:28; 1 Corinthians 14:15, 16, 26, 28.</margin>
1. Anyone who reads the Scripture of the New Testament carefully, I believe, will notice that names such as *Synagogue*, *Pastors*, *Teachers*, *Wise Men*, *Overseers*, *Leaders*, *Presbyters* <note>original: "Presbyterorum," refers to the elders or leaders of the early church community.</note>, *Angel of the Church*, and *Deacons* occur frequently within it. So too do the words and phrases by which their functions are expressed, such as *ministries* <note>original Greek: λειτουργίας (leitourgias)</note>, *worship* <note>original Greek: λατρείας (latreias)</note>, the *work* <note>original Greek: ἔργου (ergou)</note>, *To Bless*, *To Pray*, *To Sing*, *To lift up pure hands in every place*, *To Feed* <note>or "To Shepherd"</note>, *To Read*, *To Teach*, *To Interpret*, and *To answer Amen*. Indeed, there are many others besides these. Yet, in truth, these names, words, and expressions are the very same ones that are commonly used in the Ancient and Modern Synagogue. In the Synagogue, you find the words and names for the *Assembly* <note>original Hebrew: כנסת (Knesset)</note> and the *House of Assembly* <note>original Hebrew: בית הכנסת (Beit ha-Knesset)</note>, the *Congregation* <note>original Hebrew: צבור (Tsibbur), which corresponds to the Greek phrase meaning "the multitude of those who believed"</note>, the *Holy Congregation* <note>original Hebrew: קהילה קדושה (Kehilla Kedosha)</note>, the *Teachers* <note>original Hebrew: רבנים (Rabbanim)</note>, the *Wise Men* <note>original Hebrew: חכמים (Chachamim)</note>, the *Pastors* <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים (Parnassim), often referring to those who provided for the community's needs</note>, the *Presbyters* <note>original Hebrew: זקנים (Zekenim) or "Elders"</note>, the *Overseers* <note>original Hebrew: ממונים (Memunim)</note>, the *Leaders* <note>original Hebrew: מנהיגים (Manhigim)</note>, the *Angels of the Church* <note>original Hebrew: שליח צבור (Sheliach Tsibbur), literally the "Messenger of the Congregation" who led prayers</note>, and the *Deacons* <note>original Hebrew: חזנים (Chazzanim), the attendants or cantors of the synagogue</note>. Likewise, the actions of praying, reading, interpreting, shepherding, teaching, and excommunicating (though one must speak of this last one with discernment) are practiced there, as will become clear later, God willing.

<margin>1 Timothy 3:1, 2, etc.</margin>
2. But what seems even more wonderful is that the precepts which the Jewish Masters prescribe regarding the virtues and requirements of the Officials and Ministers of the Synagogue differ hardly at all from those which the Apostle *Paul* handed down in an entirely similar case.

3. Furthermore, the actions the Synagogue has, such as *Expounding upon the Shema* <note>The "Shema" is the central prayer of Judaism, beginning "Hear, O Israel."</note>, *Waving the napkin* <note>A ritual signal used in large ancient synagogues to indicate when the congregation should respond.</note>, and *Blessing*, bring much light either to certain famous sayings and deeds of Christ and the Apostles, or even to certain customs of the Early Church.

4. Indeed, regarding the very free Rites which the ancient Church observed in the admission of any of its members (who possessed the proper age and dignity) to perform sacred duties; the customs it held in sitting and teaching; and even other celebrated circumstances noted in sacred worship—there is scarcely one of these that does not receive light from the Ancient Synagogue. Since I shall provide the clearest arguments for all of these things in the following pages, I believe I shall have no reader of such poor and ignoble judgment who would not see the justice in this...

**W**e have noted that the most distinguished men, who *trace the Form of Governance and Ceremonies of the Christian Church from the Jewish Sacred Rites*, are divided, or can be divided, into two camps. There are those who *refer the Offices and Rites of the Christian Church to the Worship of the Jewish Temple*; there are others, on the other hand, who *attempt to derive the sacred practices of the Christians from the Synagogue*. The former view was held by a man of venerable name and the highest erudition, **James Ussher of Armagh** <note>original: "Usserius Armachanus," referring to the famous 17th-century Irish Archbishop and scholar known for his biblical chronology.</note>, whose words I shall transcribe from a *Treatise* <margin>In the little work, *On the Origin of Bishops and Metropolitans*, pages 1, 2.</margin> published in Latin not long ago, because they contain arguments for this opinion that are by no means to be disregarded: *The origin of the Episcopate is founded partly on the pattern prescribed by God in the Old Testament, and partly on the imitation of the same introduced by the Apostles and confirmed by Christ himself in the New Covenant. Governance in the Church under the Old Testament was entrusted to the Priests and Levites; in whose place the Ministers in the Church under the New [Testament] have succeeded, no differently than the Lord’s Day succeeded the place of the Sabbath. So that what was said by the Prophet regarding the calling of the Nations might be fulfilled:* <margin>Isaiah 66:21.</margin> *And I will take from them for Priests and for Levites, says the Lord. ### INTRODUCTION &c. CHAPTER 2.

<margin>Ziegler, chapter 2, page 16.</margin>
...New Testament; as observed by the most learned men. 3. Those things which pertained to the *customs* or *ways* <note>original Greek: τὰ ἤθη (ta ēthē) or τοὺς τρόπους (tous tropous)</note>—the behaviors and habits of the Priests—are subsequently applied to the *Overseers and Ministers of the Christian Church*.

And these are indeed the primary points that support this comparison; but besides these: 4. I believe that the rite or custom of the *offering of gifts*, introduced soon after the Church’s earliest infancy, contributed much toward illustrating and strengthening this comparison between Priests and Bishops, or between the form of Temple worship and that of the Church. I will explain the matter in a few words. <margin>See Tertullian, Apology, chapter 39.</margin> When the <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>The Eucharist or Communion.</note> was formerly to be celebrated, each person offered at the sacred table whatever they had ready—bread, wine, oil, incense, money, and other various gifts—which were received and arranged by the Deacons. For since there were no fixed revenues for the Church, it was necessary that offerings be made by the faithful themselves, both for what they were to consume at the Supper and for what served to sustain the *Bishops, Presbyters, Deacons, and the poor*, as well as for the necessary care of the meeting place and its rituals. <margin>Ecclesiastical Observations, chapter 5, concerning the Offerings of the Ancients.</margin> The faithful, says *Gabriel Albaspinæus* <note>Gabriel de L’Aubespine (1579–1630) was a French Bishop and scholar of early Church history.</note>, *in those early times on Sundays and feast days, rarely approached the altar without gifts and presents, provided their means were not so meager that they could not do so without hardship. These gifts were called offerings, which the Priest, having received from the hands of the faithful, would offer to God upon the altar and bless with specific prayers.* <margin>See Hildebrand, On Offerings for the Deceased, chapter 4, § 9.</margin> Who does not see in this act of the *offering of gifts*, so widely accepted in the early Church, something similar to the offerings that were frequently made at the altar in the Temple? For the priests of the Temple were sustained by those very gifts which were offered to God through them and in them, which the Apostle calls *living from the sanctuary*, or <margin>1 Corinthians 9:13</margin> *to share with the altar* <note>original Greek: συμμερίζεσθαι τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ (symmerizesthai tō thysiastēriō)</note>. Since this similarity of offering would strike anyone's eye, who wonders that the other Rites and Offices of the Church were designated by such names that corresponded to the ways of speaking used in the Temple? Added to this is the fact that a specific reasoning was offered as to why the gifts of *bread and wine*, offered on the sacred table, should be called sacrifices by a far greater right than any others. For since the body and blood of Christ the Lord, hanging from the cross, is considered in the Sacred Scriptures as a *sacrifice*, which [leads] toward the expiation— <note>The text ends mid-sentence here; the catchword "nem" on the following page completes the word "expiationem" or "expiation."</note>

<summary>This page argues that the early Christian practice of bringing physical offerings (bread, wine, and money) to the altar was a direct parallel to Jewish Temple sacrifices. This financial and ritual similarity helped justify using Old Testament titles like "Priest" for Christian ministers.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 2. Concerning the ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.</header>

...the sacrifice for the remission of our sins was offered to His Father; and since the *bread and wine in the Holy Supper represent the body and blood of Christ*, it seemed to the early Church that these sacred symbols of bread and wine in the Supper could, with the greatest right, be called a *sacrifice*. From this, it eventually came about that the *sacred table* was called an *altar*; the *Bishops* and *Presbyters* who blessed and distributed the gifts were called *Priests*; and the *Deacons* serving the Bishops were called *Levites*. Thus, the entire arrangement <note>original Greek: θέσις (thesis)</note> of the Jewish Temple was eventually introduced into the simple assemblies of the Christians. Just as we have already shown the antiquity of these ways of speaking from *Ignatius*, most learned men have likewise observed the same in the writings of *Justin*, *Irenaeus*, *Tertullian*, and *Cyprian*, the Fathers of the first centuries.

<margin>

</margin>
In *Eusebius* and other authors of Ecclesiastical History, and in the Canons of the Councils, these phrases occur with such frequency that it is abundantly clear that this comparison had taken deep root in the minds of people at that time.

5. Perhaps we will not be far from the truth if we add this cause among others: why the first Christians compared their rites and customs more with those of the *Temple* than with the *Synagogues*. It was because they were more ignorant of the Jewish language and ceremonies due to the extreme division of sentiments and recent wounds <note>The "recent wounds" likely refers to the social and religious conflicts following the destruction of the Temple and the separation of the early Church from Judaism.</note>; as is evident everywhere from many examples. ...they often wished to have nothing in common (which is evident again from the example of *Jerome* himself, who writes that he had a man named *Barrabanus* as a *nighttime* teacher <note>Jerome, a famous Bible translator, studied Hebrew in secret with this teacher to avoid public scandal or Jewish disapproval.</note> at a great price because of his fear of the Jews). 6. Although Christians cherished Jews with such charity as is proper, it cannot be denied that the first Christians made the greatest effort to ensure their religion was held as most distinct from that of the Jews. Consequently, they carefully avoided the names of the *Old Synagogue* and its rituals. It happens conveniently that I can confirm this with the words of *Casaubon* <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar and philologist.</note>, who discusses the genuine nature of the words <term>synaxis <note>original: σύναξις; meaning a gathering or assembly, especially for the Eucharist.</note></term> and <term>synagoga <note>original: συναγωγή; the Greek word for synagogue, meaning a "bringing together."</note></term>. <margin>Exercise XVI against the Annals of Baronius, Article XLII, page 474.</margin> "Properly," he says, "*synaxis* is exactly the same as *synagoga*, for both *synaxis* and *synagoga* are derived from the same verb <note>both come from the Greek verb 'synagein', meaning to bring together.</note>. *But it seems the first Christians deliberately used a new word formation to put a distinction between Christian 'synaxes' and Jewish 'synagogues.' Whereas among all the ancient Greeks, the name 'synagoga' is very commonly used.*" Further on: <margin>page 475.</margin> "*Otherwise, what we were saying before is most true; the first Christians used the name 'synaxis'*" SO THAT THEY MIGHT DISTINGUISH THEIR MEETINGS BY THE VERY NAME FROM JEWISH SYNAGOGUES, or those of heretics. <header>CHAPTER 2. On the OLD SYNAGOGUE.</header>

...if anyone during their festivals lights lamps, let him be excommunicated. <note>original Greek: ἐν ταῖς ἑορταῖς αὐτῶν, ἢ λύχνους ἅπτοι, ἀφοριζέσθω.</note> If any Christian brings oil to the sacrifices of the Pagans or to the Synagogue of the Jews on their feast days, or lights their lamps, let him be expelled from the community. <note>original Latin: Si quis Christianus oleum tulerit ad sacra Gentilium, vel Synagogam Iudaorum, festis ipsorum diebus, aut accenderit lampades, pellatur ex societate.</note> The Council of Constantinople, which sat in the Trullo <note>The Quinisext Council (692 AD), named after the domed hall (Trullus) where it met, which established many disciplinary canons for the Eastern Church.</note>, likewise took precautions in the same way. <margin>Canon 11.</margin> No one ranked among the clergy, nor any layman, should eat the unleavened bread of the Jews, or enter into familiarity with them, or call upon them in times of sickness, or receive medicines from them, or bathe with them in the public baths. If anyone attempts to do this, if he is a clergyman, let him be deposed; if a layman, let him be excommunicated. <note>original Greek: Μηδεὶς τῶν ἐν ἱερατικῷ...; original Latin: Nemo eorum, qui in sacro ordine censentur...</note> Many similar things could be added to these. Indeed, I ask you to read the *Orations of Chrysostom against the Jews* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an influential Archbishop of Constantinople; his "Adversus Judaeos" sermons were a series of harsh polemics designed to stop Christians from participating in Jewish festivals.</note>, and you will see with what seriousness and with what force of intellect and learning he exhorted and implored the Christians of his time not to admire or visit the Jewish Rites and Synagogues; and conversely, how vehemently he spoke against those who were delighted by the ceremonies of the Jewish Synagogues. Since, therefore, it was in the interest of the early Church to separate itself as far as possible from the Jewish Synagogue and from the heretics—of whom the Synagogue had been a fertile mother since the very times of the Apostles—it is easy to understand why the early Church diligently and solicitously avoided the names of the *Synagogue* and the offices and rituals held within it.

7. I do not know if I may add to what has been said that for the Pagans, who were converted from Heathenism to Christianity, the designations sought from the "Temple" were far more familiar and pleasing than those from the "Synagogue." For since the Pagans were accustomed in their own sacred rites to speak of Temples, Altars, Priests, and Sacrifices, it undoubtedly happened that it was most agreeable to them—or, to use softer words, they were inclined by a long custom of such names—to retain these words rather than exchange them for others altogether unknown and recent, provided they could find even the slightest use and <term>analogy <note>original: ἀναλογίαν; a correspondence or proportion between two things.</note></term> for them in their new sacred rites. Moreover, it is well known that many other terms besides these were transferred from Pagan superstition into the Christian Religion.

### PROLEGOMENA, etc. CHAPTER 3.

...indeed have led them away from the ceremonial worship of the Temple, what do you think they would have done in the sacred rites of the Synagogue—those simple and harmless rites which *no reason commanded to be changed?* But this point, which contains a new reasoning, must be pressed more closely in a few words.

<margin>On Matthew 4:23.</margin>
3. The most learned *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was a prominent English scholar of Hebrew and the Bible who sought to explain the New Testament through the lens of Jewish tradition.</note>, in the words cited above from him, very correctly observed that the entire worship of the synagogue was moral. It must be believed that he intended to say this very thing: that the worship of the synagogues was <term>logical</term> <note>original Greek: λογικὸς</note> or rational—that is, that nothing occurred in the worship of the synagogues which could not be perfectly reconciled with sound reason, or rather, be derived from it. Since indeed that which they call *moral* lasts for all time, he very rightly concluded that the Apostles did nothing strange in making the form of divine worship under the <term>Gospel Economy</term> <note>A theological term referring to the system or administration of God's dealings with humanity under the New Testament.</note> conform to it.

<margin>Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II.</margin>
Certainly, as soon as *reason* perceives that *God exists*, it simultaneously understands that *He is to be worshiped publicly with a pure, whole, and incorrupt mind and voice.* For the public worship of the <term>Deity</term> <note>original Latin: Numinis</note> requires both that we venerate and celebrate God with our prayers and praises, and that we instruct and admonish one another regarding that mutual duty toward God and our neighbor. In order for this to be done decently, there is a need for a *place* destined for these sacred rites, and for *overseers and ministers* of the assembly, to whose care those matters may be safely entrusted. In this way, God was celebrated in the synagogues by the Jewish people, with only a very few rites added on, without which almost all religion tends to become cheapened among the common people. But whatever pertained to the *ceremonial* or <term>typical</term> <note>original Greek: τυπικὸν; referring to rituals that "typify" or foreshadow future spiritual truths, as opposed to moral or rational duties.</note> part of the religion of the Jewish people was entirely confined to the inner sanctuaries of the Temple—which will be discussed a little more broadly hereafter. The words of *Ambrose* <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), an influential Bishop of Milan.</note>, praised elsewhere by the most eminent *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a famed English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>, agree strongly with our statements.

<margin>*On the Law of Nature and Nations*, Book I, Chapter 10.</margin>
*Natural law has three parts, of which the first is this: that once the Creator is acknowledged, He should be honored, and His brightness and majesty should not be attributed to any creature. The second part is moral—that is, that one should live well, governed by modesty. The third part is teachable, so that the knowledge of God the Creator may be handed down to others as an example of conduct.* Indeed, worship of this kind, which is entirely consistent with natural reason, was performed in the Synagogue. ## CHAPTER IV.

*The way is prepared to discern which of the aforementioned opinions regarding the Origin of Church Rites—whether derived **FROM THE TEMPLE** or **THE SYNAGOGUE**—is more true. Therefore, it is established in advance: 1. That in the Temple, in both ordinary and extraordinary cases, those ceremonies were also observed which were customary in the Synagogues. 2. That Jewish Authors themselves often compare the Ministry of the Synagogues in various parts with the worship of the Temple. In passing, it is investigated where the King’s station or Chair was in the Temple; and also whether there was any Synagogue within the Temple.*

Thus has been reported the double opinion—though they seem opposed to one another—concerning the Origin of the Rites and Offices of the Christian Church. One side brings them from the Temple, the other from the Synagogue. Therefore, before we advance our step much further, it is fitting that we state which of these pleases us most and—what is the heart of the matter here—seems to approach closest to the truth. To accomplish this properly, it will be useful to proceed with slow and safe steps.

First, therefore, I will establish that all the sacred Rites of the synagogue were also performed in the Temple; a point which I nevertheless wish you would interpret skillfully <note>The author is cautioning the reader to understand that while the "style" of worship was shared, the Temple still maintained its unique sacrificial functions.</note>. Therefore, consider with me: 1. That the Temple was the fixed and ordinary place for praying to God, praising Him, and giving Him thanks, and for blessing the people—acts which surely fulfill the greatest part of Synagogue Religion. That this is so is abundantly clear from the prayer of Solomon, by which the Temple was first dedicated. And you shall hear him speak thus: <margin>2 Chronicles 6:21, 22, 23, 24, 25, etc.</margin> *...to the supplications of your servant and of your people Israel, which they shall pray toward this place.* <note>original Hebrew: אל תחנוני עבדך ועמך ישראל אשר יתפללו אל המקום הזה</note> Thus it continues throughout his whole prayer. Hence it is that the Temple itself is called in Isaiah a **House of Prayer** <note>original Hebrew: בית תפלה (*Beit Tefillah*)</note>, or what is the same thing, <margin>chapter 56:7; Matthew 21:13</margin> a **house of prayer**. <note>original Greek: οἶκος προσευχῆς (*oikos proseuchēs*)</note>

*The way is prepared to discern which of the aforementioned opinions regarding the origin of the rites of the Church—whether they should be sought from the **Temple** or the **Synagogue**—is more true. Therefore, we first establish: 1. That in the Temple, whether in ordinary or extraordinary cases, those ceremonies which were customary in Synagogues were also observed. 2. That Jewish authors themselves often compare the ministry of the Synagogues in various parts to the worship of the Temple. In passing, it is discussed where the King’s station or Chair was in the Temple; and also whether there was any Synagogue in the Temple.*

Thus have been reported two opinions, which seem opposed to each other, regarding the origin of the rites and offices of the Christian Church. One side brings them from the Temple, the other from the Synagogue. Therefore, before we move much further, it is appropriate to state which of these most appeals to us and—the heart of the matter here—which seems to come closest to the truth. To accomplish this properly, it will be useful to proceed with slow and safe steps.

<margin>
2 Chronicles 6:21, 22, 23, 24, 25, etc.
Chapter 56:7.
Matthew 21:13.
</margin>
First, therefore, I will establish that all the sacred **rites** performed in the synagogue were also **carried out in the Temple**; though I would wish you to interpret this carefully. Consider with me: 1. That the Temple was the established and ordinary place for praying to God, praising Him, and giving Him thanks, and for blessing the people—acts which indeed constitute the greatest part of the **Synagogue's order of worship** <note>The author uses 'Religion of the Synagogue' to mean its liturgical structure and daily ritual life.</note>. That this is so is abundantly clear from the prayer of **Solomon**, by which the Temple was first dedicated. *And you shall hear*, he says, <note>original Hebrew: אל תחנוני עבדך ועמך ישראל אשר יתפללו אל המקום הזה — *el tachanunei avdecha v'amcha Yisrael asher yitpalelu el hamakom hazeh*</note> *the supplications of your servant and of your people Israel, which they shall pray toward this place.* Thus he continues throughout his entire prayer. This is why the Temple itself is called in **Isaiah** a "house of prayer" <note>original Hebrew: בית תפלה — *Beit Tefillah*</note> / or what is the same thing, a "house of prayer" <note>original Greek: οἶκος προσευχῆς — *oikos proseuchēs*</note>.

Indeed, I would also not deny that certain Synagogues in Jerusalem served the common needs of the Jerusalem Church itself, as the daily duties of Religion were observed far more *conveniently* in them than in the Temple. Let this much be certain for now: the *Temple* just as much as the *Synagogues* was dedicated to prayer, and any Israelite could fulfill the duty of praying just as well in the *Temple* as in the *Synagogues*. This is clearly seen from the example of *Peter and John* <note>The author refers to the passage where the Apostles go to the Temple at the hour of prayer, suggesting the Temple remained a primary place for communal prayer even after the establishment of the early Church.</note>.

In addition to the fact that the *Temple* was *ordinarily* intended for the same spiritual exercises as the *Synagogues*, in extraordinary or rare cases, the exact same acts and the same ceremonies were observed in the *Temple* as in the *Synagogues*. To me, an extraordinary case is when the *Kings* ordered *bronze* or *wooden* <term>platforms</term> <note>original: "suggesta," referring to a raised pulpit or rostrum for public speaking.</note> to be built in the Temple courtyard, and from them spoke words both to *God* and to the *people*. The first author of this custom was indeed *Solomon*, about whom the sacred Historian writes in these express words: *For Solomon had made for himself a bronze basin* <note>original Hebrew: כִּיּוֹר נְחֹשֶׁת (*kiyyor nechoshet*). From this pulpit *Solomon* prayed to God and spoke to the people. His example was followed by Kings *Jehoshaphat*, *Hezekiah*, and *Josiah*, who likewise either poured out prayers to God or even read the *law* to the people; although certainly in these later passages there is no explicit mention of a <term>bema</term> <note>original Greek: βήματος (*bēmatos*), a raised step or rostrum used by orators and later in churches and synagogues.</note> in which they stood when they devoted themselves to these sacred exercises. *Jacob Judah Leon* <note>Jacob Judah Leon (1602–1675), a Jewish scholar and architect famous for creating a celebrated model of Solomon's Temple.</note> conjectures that a throne was established in the *Temple courtyard*, which he describes with magnificent words—if only they were true and worthy of trust—and that these Kings were positioned upon it. That the King did [not] sit, but stood, and indeed by the column (for thus the word *amud* <gloss>Hebrew: עמוד</gloss> is conveniently explained), as the custom required. But which *column*? It is possible that by it was designated the post of the Eastern gate of the *inner court*, where the Royal station was located. However, it must not be concealed that the Ancient Hebrew scholars, regarding what is asserted here about the post or column, explained it as a *Seat* or *throne*. The *Chaldee Paraphrast* <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> translates it thus: *And the King stood upon the dais.* <note>original: והא מלכא קאם על אסטונא</note>

<margin>On this passage]</margin> This, according to *Kimchi* <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a celebrated medieval rabbi and grammarian</note>, ought to be explained as: *The King stood by the Chair*. For he says: <gloss>The meaning is "near the column"; and likewise the word "upon" is taken as "near" in other places, such as when it says "and the tribe of Manasseh was upon him," meaning near him. In his opinion, the "column" would be an honorable place within that portico for the King to stand, and therefore it is called a column. Similarly, in the Book of Chronicles, it speaks of "standing in his place" [on the column], meaning the place appropriate for him to stand.</gloss> His words mean to say: *By the column*; *for the little word* <term>al <gloss>Hebrew: על, usually meaning "upon"</gloss></term> *is also understood this way in other places,*

<margin>Numbers 2:20</margin> *“And* <gloss>al / upon</gloss> *him the tribe of Manasseh,” that is, by or next to him. Jonathan, however, interprets it: "And he stood upon the* <term>astavana <gloss>Aramaic: אסטוונא, a platform or raised seat</gloss></term>,” *a chair or seat; which is explained by* <term>stio <gloss>ספסל, a bench or footstool</gloss></term>, *in which the Princes and Great Men are accustomed to sit. This is how it can be understood in*

<margin>2 Chronicles 23:13. Schindler <note>Valentin Schindler (died 1604), author of a famous polyglot dictionary</note> does so in the same way; *A Chair*, in which the Princes sat. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> has "upon the pillar" <gloss>Greek: ἐπὶ τοῦ στύλου / epi tou stylou</gloss>, which does not bring much light to this matter. 

If anyone truly wishes, along with the illustrious Coccejus, to understand by the word "column" <gloss>Hebrew: עמוד / amud</gloss> *some higher platform* in which the King was accustomed to stand in the Temple *so that he might stand out above the people*, I certainly will not argue spiritedly with him. For I confess that "column" can be understood as a *raised place for standing*; nor does it shrink from reason that the King stood in some higher and more prominent place in the Temple. What I am primarily disputing now is whether a throne was placed for the *King* in the Temple in which he might sit, and whether such a *throne* is designated by the word "column." Neither seems to me to agree with the truth. For in the Temple it was not the custom to sit, but to stand, which is the posture of those praying and serving. The Kings also, in the noted texts, are said *to have stood*, not *to have sat*; except that 
<margin>2 Chronicles 6:13</margin> Solomon was also *on his knees* <note>Referring to Solomon kneeling during the dedication of the Temple</note>. 

And the word "column" <gloss>Hebrew: עמוד / amud</gloss> is by no means translated as *throne or bench*. And with these points my argument could rest and be concluded. Nevertheless, let me add to this that there is no great reason urging us why we should not simply take the word "column" here to mean a *pillar*, by which the King, whenever he was present for the Temple's sacred rites, was accustomed to stand, consistent with what is said of the *Prince* in Ezekiel. For when I properly weigh those things brought forward by the Interpreters in favor of that accepted opinion, I do not feel myself carried toward this side by strong arguments. 
<margin>2 Chronicles 6:13</margin> They advise that by the "column" of *Joash* <note>The child-king Joash, whose coronation by a pillar is recorded in 2 Kings 11</note> one must understand the *bronze platform* <gloss>Hebrew: כִּיוֹר נְחֹשֶׁת / kiyor nechoshet</gloss> upon which King Solomon preached to the people and prayed to God. But on what foundation? 

For it is permitted to deny this with the same freedom with which others affirm it. On the contrary, what is declared concerning this very King Joash in the *Books of Chronicles* 
<margin>2 Chronicles 23:13</margin> seems to contradict the opinion that by "column" one should understand the Bronze Chair which Solomon prepared. For thus it is read there: 
<gloss>Hebrew: והנה המלך עומד על עמודו במבוא</gloss> 
*And behold, the King was standing in his station* (we translate: *by his column*)

...by Jehoiada it was publicly *read aloud*, so much so that no reason can be sought from this as to why *Joash* <note>original: "Joaz," the boy-king of Judah who was hidden in the Temple and later restored to the throne</note> would have been stationed upon any public platform. ### CHAPTER 4. CONCERNING THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

...parent, he ascended into the Temple and sat on the throne. I hesitate, however, whether it can be concluded from these words that he **sat on the throne** within any specific court of the Temple. For the account of *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian</note> is satisfied if we conceive that he **sat upon the throne** after he had departed from the Temple. But I also would plainly not want to have overlooked this: that the bronze shell-shaped platform, built by Solomon, was placed <gloss>original Hebrew: בתוך העזרה / betokh ha-azarah</gloss> *in the midst of the Court*. From this it also seems to be evident in a way that the position <gloss>original Hebrew: על העמוד / al ha-ammud</gloss> *by the column* <note>referring to the royal station mentioned in 2 Kings 23:3</note> was not the same as Solomon’s position on the **bronze platform**. I hold this reasoning because, by that *court* in which Solomon’s **rostrum** <term>suggestum: a raised platform or dais used by orators</term> was established, the **Court of the Priests** seems entirely meant, and not the **outer court**, or the **greater court**, as the Dutch and other interpreters maintain in all the notes they have given regarding the evidence observed previously. For the platform was set in the **middle of the Court**, before the altar, so that Solomon, standing upon it, would have had the faces of the Israelites turned toward him while he was preaching, as they stood in the **Porticoes of that Inner Court**. You might easily gather these points from the noted text, which I would be unable to explain if the platform itself had been placed in the **outer court** or the **Porticoes of the Inner Court**. But if Solomon's **rostrum** were truly located near the altar in the Court of the Priests, then I will easily prove that it is very different from the seat or station of the later Kings. For who will say that their station was in the **Court of the Priests**? Certainly, what Solomon did was altogether extraordinary, and his **platform** and its location seem to have been adapted only for that specific occasion. In any case, it has been observed by the most learned **Diodati** <note>Giovanni Diodati (1576–1649), a Protestant theologian famous for his Bible translations</note> that this **bronze rostrum** of Solomon was afterward consecrated for the Levites, who were appointed to praise God, even if other interpreters often seem to go in entirely different directions. Furthermore, in the fact that Solomon, having built the **platform** or **rostrum** in the Court of the Priests, **prayed** for the people and addressed them, one must recognize without doubt a prelude to the **worship of the Synagogues**. This worship, as is well known, consists chiefly in this: that prayers are poured out from a public place and addresses for instruction are delivered by a public person. That this was indeed done solemnly in this case has already been noted.

In the second place, it should now be noted that the Jewish Doctors themselves recognize such a great agreement and conformity between the **Synagogue** and the **Temple**, and the rites of both, that they not only compare the **worship of the Synagogues** with the <term>liturgy; liturgy (λειτουργίᾳ)</term> of the Temple, but they also commanded that various precepts belonging to the Temple be observed likewise in the **Synagogues**. "What is the worship of the heart? This is prayer." <note>Original Hebrew: עבודה שבלב זו תפלה. ## CHAPTER V.

*Notwithstanding those things which were granted in the preceding chapter, it is proven by clear arguments that the practice of the religion of the Christian Church approaches much more closely the form of divine worship as it was celebrated in the Synagogues, than to the service of the Temple; because in those aspects where the worship of the Synagogue differs from the ceremonies of the Temple—such as in the distinction of places, persons, garments, age, degrees of holiness, etc.—the Church aligns with the Synagogue, not with the Temple; and furthermore, because the Hebrew Doctors themselves distinguish the worship of the Synagogue, insofar as it agrees with the worship of the Church, from the religion of the Temple.*

Even though these two points we have already addressed do not seem at all obscure, it remains certain that the *sacred worship of the Temple*, appropriately so-called <note>Original Greek: φερωνύμως (*pheronymōs*), meaning "rightly named" or "bearing the name in a literal sense."</note>, retained many things unique to itself, none of which were transferred at all to the *Synagogues*. The *Synagogues*, in turn, had their own form and their own customs, which one would find with difficulty in the *sacred liturgy* <note>Original Greek: ἐν τῇ λειτουργίᾳ τῇ ἱερᾷ (*en tē leitourgia tē hiera*). While we use "liturgy" today for church services, in this context it refers specifically to the formal, ritualistic duties of the Temple priests.</note>. The principal portion of the ceremonial *Law*, which was observed for the most part in the Temple and could not be observed elsewhere, was excluded from the *Synagogues*. The Temple had its own Priests, its own Levites—men belonging to a specific family and tribe; the Temple had its own altars for various uses; it had its own sacrifices of diverse kinds; it also had its own instruments and most splendid apparatus; it had its own degrees of holiness; likewise its own secret *mysteries* <note>Original Greek: μυστήρια (*mystēria*). In the ancient world, this referred to sacred rites or truths revealed only to the initiated.</note> of religion, none of which were to be seen in the Synagogues. In the Synagogue, on the other hand, one notices a simplicity of sacred rites (and only those which are entirely necessary), and a freedom to exercise that <term>Rational Worship</term> <note>Latin: *Rationalis Cultus*. This refers to worship involving the mind and spirit—such as prayer and teaching—rather than physical animal sacrifices.</note> which appears nowhere in the religion of the Temple. *Prayers* also, and the *reading* and *interpretation of the Law*...

### CHAPTER 5. ON THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

...they are more strictly bound to Synagogues than to the Temple; so much so that a manifest divorce <note>Here meaning a "separation" or "distinction"</note> remains between the Temple and the Synagogues. Therefore, through those positions we have already established, the investigation has not yet been sufficiently satisfied as to whether the model of the Christian Church fits the Temple or the *Synagogue* better. Let us say more freely then, notwithstanding those reasons of suitability which can be noted between the customs of the Christian Church and the ceremonies of the Ancient Temple, that it seems most certain to us that the *Worship* of the New Testament Church draws its origin from the *Synagogue*, not from the *Temple*. Let us see the reasons that can confirm this hypothesis of ours.

1. It has already been observed in the preceding sections that the *Agreement* which exists between the *Synagogues* and the *Church* is so exact that not only the name of the *Synagogue*, but the names of *Pastors*, *Presbyters* <term>Elders</term>, the *Angel of the Church* <note>A title used in the Book of Revelation, often linked by scholars to the "Sheliach Tzibbur" or messenger of the congregation in the Synagogue</note>, *Deacons*, etc., were transferred without any change to the *Christian Church*; whereas, on the contrary, the name of the *Temple* never was. The names of *Priests* and *sacrifices* were never applied directly and properly, but always metaphorically <note>Original Greek: μεταφορικῶς (*metaphorikōs*)</note>, to the Place, the *Ministers of the Sacraments*, and the *Worship* of the Church of the New Covenant. From this, it is safe to gather that the form of the Christian Church agrees more with the *Synagogue* than with the *Temple*.

2. A very clear reason is sought from the fact that in those parts where the *Synagogue* differs from the Temple, the Christian Church sides entirely with the *Synagogue*, not with the *Temple*. Let this be for us a certain and undoubted criterion <note>Original Greek: κριτήריון (*kritērion*)</note> of the truth of our opinion. What we have said must be illustrated through examples.

### CHAPTER 5. OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

...his hands for blessing. There was a specific reason why a *minor* was not admitted to these later acts, which we should not overlook in the following sections. It must not be hidden that the Jewish Doctors desired experience, strengthened by a proper age, in those who were to be elected to the established duties of the Leader of the Synagogue or the Minister of the Synagogue; however, it remains certain that the Synagogue fixed no laws regarding *age*. Indeed, the Christian Church here again agrees so handsomely with the Synagogue that it could not do so more. For in the truly Apostolic Canons, no more was provided by law regarding a certain *age* than regarding *Persons*. <margin>1 Timothy 4:12</margin> *Timothy* was appointed as a minister of the Church by Paul while still a young man. I am not unaware that the Church of subsequent times again pre-defined a certain time for the *Priesthood*, and indeed that very same time which was thought to have been assigned to the ancient Priests; a fact which also did not escape the most perceptive <margin>On the Succession of the Pontiffs, book 2, chapter 4</margin> *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note>; but, as is again the mark of difference here, that entire determination depends equally on the very free opinion and consent of the Churches. For otherwise it is well known that every prerogative of age has been abolished under the New Covenant.

5. Beyond those things which have now been observed by us, many others can be brought forward in which one may note a similar difference between the ceremonies of the Temple and the Synagogue. It was required of the Priests that they be free from *vices and blemishes of the body*; <margin>Vessels of the Sanctuary, chapter 3, section 1</margin> (although the Levites were not rejected because of bodily blemishes, as *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a famous medieval Jewish scholar who codified Jewish law</note> expressly states); born of legitimate marriages; free from ceremonial impurity; set apart from mourning over a relative, and many more things that could be added from *Maimonides’* books, which are titled *Vessels of the Sanctuary* and *Entrance into the Sanctuary*. Yet none of these things at all were required of the person who performed the Sacred rites in the Synagogue. Not only the *lame*, but even the *blind*—notable physical defects—are called to celebrate certain public religious acts within it. Thus holds the Mishna, a part of which we described before. <margin>Megillah, chapter 4, section 6</margin> *A blind person recites the Shema and translates* <note>original: "סומא פורש את שמע ומתרגם" — The Shema is a central Jewish prayer. To "translate" refers to the ancient practice of providing an Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) for the congregation</note>. Regarding other matters, there is no need to give warning. Indeed, who is unaware that the Christian Church neglects these same laws regarding its own ministers, provided they are sufficiently trained for public edification?

After it has been proven by solid reasons and examples that the *Christian Church Ceremonies* agree much more with the *Sacred Rites of the Synagogue* than with the *Temple Worship*, we must now proceed to respond to the arguments of the opposing view, which we reviewed in our previous discourse. Among those, that which *first occurs to us* is that there is indeed a great agreement between *Priests* and *Levites*, and *Bishops*, or *Presbyters* and *Deacons*. But it must be observed that this *characteristic* alone is not sufficient to ground a comparison between the *Temple* and the *Church* on that basis, because there is almost no sacred or civil *College* or *Sanhedrin* <note>A governing assembly or council</note> flourishing among men in which similar ranks of *Presidents* and *Ministers* are not observed. That the Sanhedrins of the Hebrews had their own *ministers* <note>original Hebrew: שליחי (Shelichai), meaning messengers or agents</note> is too well known to need mention. In the sacred rites of the Gentiles <note>The non-Jewish, pagan world</note>, the exact same logic of distinction and order was maintained. There were *Priests* there: *the Greatest, the Greater, and the Lesser*, just as among the Hebrews, and at the same time *servants and attendants of the Priests*...

However, the entire system was regarded as *ceremonial*, because the *moral* Religion of the Temple served the *ceremonial* aspects. But that which was *moral* in the ceremonies of the Temple—such as, for example, *praying to God*, *celebrating Him with song*, *blessing the people in His name*, *etc.*—was transferred to the Synagogues, and from the Synagogues to the Oratories of the Christians. It is better, therefore, to say that the Church received these ceremonies from the *Synagogue* rather than from the *Temple*, because it accepted many other rites from the *Synagogue* while entirely neglecting those ceremonies and that apparatus which were unique to the Temple. These things, which we now assume, will be brought to light by the comparison itself, which is to be established hereafter.

It will perhaps be more to the point to address what is brought forward in the third place against our opinion from *Holy Scripture*; namely, that the Scripture: α. sometimes expresses the *Worship of the New Testament Church* in phrases taken from the *Worship of the Temple*. β. Namely, in that age when Israel was subject to the elements of the world <note>original: *elementis mundi* — a biblical phrase referring to the elementary religious stages or ritual laws of the Old Testament</note>, that manner of worshiping God, which consisted in the offering of *sacrifices*, was primarily known and accepted. ...distinguished by [times], and yet to be observed by all nations by some necessity as a criterion <note>original Greek: κριτήριον (*kritērion*)</note> of true religion—who would indicate this in the current state of time? For I do not think there would be anyone so foolish as to think that this phrase refers to the festivals of the *Appearance of Christ* <note>original Greek: ἐπιφανείας τοῦ Χριστοῦ (*epiphaneias tou Christou*); likely referring to Epiphany or Christ's manifestation</note>, *Passover*, and *Pentecost*, which are observed by Christians according to an ancient institution of the Church.

What, then, was finally signified by such expressions concerning the *Sabbath*, the *New Moon*, and *Feast days*? This, if I am not mistaken, means only that the Church of the New Covenant would celebrate God with that kind (though not that *form*) of worship which was once visible in the *Sabbaths*, *New Moons*, and the *Feast days* of *Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles*. The Sabbath was destined for *rest*; the New Moons and Festivals were consecrated to *joy and gladness*. The former [the Sabbath] indeed was for acknowledging and proclaiming God, the true Author of Light—whom the nations were ignorant of, yet sought to worship on those same days with certain ceremonies—while the latter [Festivals] were in memory of benefits granted to the Jewish people in various instances. Therefore, when the Church lives through such times, in which it constantly practices rest from sin and *evil* works; in which it proclaims and praises God as the Author of *Light and Redemption and all spiritual benefits*, with joy, a perfected conscience, and the fullest liberty in a crowded assembly of people,

# CHAPTER 6. CONCERNING THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

...acting <note>original: *agentibus*; completing the sentence from the previous page</note> and Levites, we will soon be forced to speak; therefore, let our discourse proceed now only on those things which pertain to the *Worship and ministry* themselves. That consisted, as is well known, of sacrifices and their offerings. Sacrifices were of various types and modes. Some were entirely consumed on the altar, except for the hide; of others, a part was consumed by the altar and a part by the Priests. Of others, a part was consumed by the altar and a part was burned outside the altar. Of others, a part went to the altar, a part to the Priests, and a part to those offering. Others again were given as a gift to the Priests alone. The purposes for whose sake these offerings were performed were likewise various. For either those who offered wished to give testimony of their reverence toward God, or they satisfied a required duty, or they sought to obtain pardon for sins committed through imprudence or ignorance, or to pray against an imminent evil, or to hasten an expected good, or to give thanks for a benefit received. Furthermore, certain times and a certain number were prescribed for the offerings, which varied on Sabbaths, New Moons, and Feast days from the ordinary offerings. These things had to be related by me, so that I might place the truth I intend to demonstrate in a clear light.

Consider therefore in your mind what you mean or understand when you say the *Old Temple Economy* <note>The word "Economy" here refers to the systematic organization and administration of the Temple’s laws and rituals.</note> is a type <note>A "type" is a theological term for a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of the *New*? Do you mean that in our Churches not only the thing itself, but even the same form of ministry, ought to be preserved which was observed in the Old Temple? This is what the Roman Catholics <note>original: *Pontificii*</note> want, and those who act with them—against whom we dispute in these pages—who build the entire form of their Church and opinions of great weight upon this hypothesis. Or do you truly mean only this: that there was nothing in the Temple Ministry that was symbolic <note>original Greek: τυπικὸν (*typikon*)</note> which is not truly found "according to the truth" <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἀλήθειαν (*kat’ alētheian*)</note> in the worship of the Church?

Certainly, if you choose the former, you will involve yourself in difficulties not easily overcome. Let us try with a few examples. *Sacrifices* in the worship of the Church ought to signify *prayers*. For regarding the fact that they foreshadowed the *sacrifice of Christ*, I will say nothing now, because in every prayer and thanksgiving of a Christian person, an offering of Christ's sacrifice is made. But there are various kinds of prayers, and various modes and ends. For they are instituted either for praising God, or for praying against evils, or for obtaining good things, or for giving thanks—

### PROLEGOMENA &c. CHAPTER 6,

...giving thanks for benefits received, either for exercising our communion with God, or for obtaining pardon for crimes committed. You might say, then, that these types of prayers were designated by the various types of sacrifices we have reviewed. Now, proceed. Burnt offerings <note>original: *holocausta*</note> were offered every day at fixed morning and evening hours. On Sabbaths, New Moons, and Feasts, other sacrifices were added to those fixed ones. On the Day of Atonement, a sacrifice for the sins of all *Israel* was consecrated with fasting through a unique ritual. In the Feast of Tabernacles, a completely mystical pattern of sacrifices was observed, with the number decreasing each day. If you wished to see a "type" <note>In this context, a "type" is a prophetic symbol or a physical foreshadowing of a spiritual reality.</note> of these things formed in the Christian Church, you would have to establish it in this way, and you could not do otherwise. It would be necessary first to establish *fixed* times, which were once observed among the *Jews*. It would be necessary at those *fixed* times to prescribe a certain *number* of prayers of a *certain kind* at *certain* hours. 

But that is truly <term>absurd</term> <note>original Greek: *atopon*, meaning out of place or improper</note>, and if anything else, it is entirely contrary to the liberty which Christ acquired for us with His own blood. For we are not bound by any precept to pray *more* on *this day* than another; to recite *this kind* of prayer rather than another; or to devote ourselves more to prayer at *this hour* than at another. From this we conclude that just because ceremonial worship was *typical* <note>meaning it served as a symbolic forerunner</note>, it by no means follows that the *entire* form of this worship should be expressed in the Church of the New Testament. Rather, it means only that the New Testament possesses the *truth of those things* which the *Old* once held in shadow. 

In what way, truly? Under the Old Testament, *burnt offerings* were offered; under the New, there are those who present themselves entirely to God as a sacrifice of <term>sweet fragrance</term> <note>original Greek: *euōdias*</note>. Under the Old, a *sacrifice for sin* took place; under the New, Christ presented Himself <term>for sin</term> <note>original Greek: *peri hamartias*</note>, through which we may approach God and obtain pardon for sins. Under the Old, there were *sacrifices* intended for warding off evils, asking for good things, and giving thanks for benefits received; under the New, because of the sacrifice of Christ, it is permitted to both ask for necessities and pray against misfortunes, and to celebrate God with praises and thanksgivings. Where this is present, we say that in the Church of the New Covenant there exists <term>the truth</term> <note>original Greek: *tēn alētheian*</note> of those things which prevailed under the Old Economy <note>The "Old Economy" refers to the legal and religious administration of the Mosaic Law.</note>. We do not believe the form must be sought in the entire complexity of the ministry; nor would it be easily found, if it were sought.

# CHAPTER 6. ON THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE. 69

But as time passed, it happened that those very sacred symbols—which were called **gifts** and **oblations** because they were presented to God by the faithful for the use of the Church—came to be regarded as ***sacrificies***, which were offered to God by the Pastors (the ***Bishops*** and ***Elders***) for the forgiveness of sins. Thus at last the mystery of the **Pontifical Mass** <note>original Latin: *Missæ Pontificiæ*; refers to the Roman Catholic Mass</note> was completed. Its foundation is the idea that under the New Testament there are ***Priests in the proper sense***, distinct from the common people in the same respect as the Aaronic Priests were once distinct from them—those who have the power to perform a sacrifice to God on behalf of others. This power is claimed as their own by law and right, such that the Christian people are no more to be admitted to performing this sacrifice now than the Israelites were once admitted to the altar of the Temple. What an error! What great evil has come from this error! We, therefore, deny that the Jewish Priests, as they were occupied in the ordinary ministry of the Temple, primarily prefigured the ***Leaders of the Church*** in their being distinct **from the people** <note>original Greek: *ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ* (apo tou laou)</note>. The most evident reason, which suffers no contradiction, is this: because Christ, through his death, has equally obtained for all the faithful the right and power to approach the Father toward himself and through himself (as through a Priest). This is taught through the whole Scripture of the **New Covenant** <note>original Latin: *Novi Fœderis*; the New Testament</note>.
<margin>Ephesians 2:18, 3:12.</margin>
This is the prerogative; this is that immense benefit of the faithful of the New Testament.
<margin>John 14:6.</margin>
The **Minister of the Church**, who pours out prayers in public, is not the one (except in the thinnest sense) through whom the faithful approach God. He enjoys no greater right of addressing God than any other member of the true Church. All, as priests, approach the Father together through Christ...

The Apostles and Ministers of the New Testament are not called **Priests** in the cited testimonies from the prophecies of **Isaiah** and the **Epistle to the Romans** in the sense that the **Papists** <note>original Latin: *Pontificii*; those supporting the authority of the Pope and the Catholic hierarchical system</note> and other most learned authors intend—as if they stood in relation to the **common people** <note>original Latin: *plebem*</note> just as the Israelite **people** once stood in relation to the Priests. When in the cited places the **Ministers** of the Gospel are compared with **Priests**, those **Priests** are considered in contrast to the **people** only in respect to the sacrifices, not in respect to the Israelite people as a social class. This is clear from those very passages, even at first glance. **The Priests and Levites brought an offering to the Lord in clean vessels**: in the same way, the Ministers of the New Testament bring the **Gentiles** <note>Non-Jewish nations</note> to God through the preaching of the Gospel, and present them to God as **sacrifices** to be devoted to Divine honor. The **people** here, therefore, are not considered as the <term>antitype <note>The reality or fulfillment that matches a symbolic 'type' or pattern from the Old Testament</note></term> of the Israelite people, but as the <term>antitype</term> of the **sacrifices**. This observation alone breaks the entire strength of that opposing argument. For in this sense, certainly not only is every Servant of the New Covenant—appointed to preach the Gospel and by this means lead people to the communion of God and Christ—a **Priest**, but even any faithful person from the lowest rank of the people is a Priest, if they lead any other person to Christ and the communion of His Kingdom, whether through teaching or the example of **their life**. 

Lest you think that this comparison implies even the slightest superiority of the **Ministers** of the Gospel over the **people**, please turn your mind to what Paul says in the **Epistle to the Philippians**, 
<margin>Chapter 2:17.</margin> 
where he compares the faithful themselves to **Priests** offering themselves to God through a **continual** profession of true faith; while he compares **his own blood** (to be poured out at some point to confirm the doctrine of the Gospel) with the **wine** that was once poured out over the **daily sacrifice**. "But," he says, "even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and share my joy with you all" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ', εἰ καὶ σπένδομαι ἐπὶ τῇ θυσίᾳ καὶ λειτουργίᾳ τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν, χαίρω καὶ συγχαίρω πᾶσιν ὑμῖν</note>. ### CONCERNING
# THE OLD SYNAGOGUE
## BOOK ONE.

### CONCERNING
## The Names and Structure of Synagogues.
### CHAPTER 1.

*Following the previously established order of this Book's treatment, the genuine meaning of the word SYNAGOGUE <note>original Greek: ΣΥΝΑΓΩΓΗ (Synagoge)</note> is investigated, drawing from Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note>, the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, and the specific notation of the Hebrew word for "assembly" <note>original Hebrew: עֵדָה ('edah)</note>, which has much in common with the Greek "Synagogue." At the same time, we ask: what is the true meaning of the concept of "congregation" <note>original Hebrew: קָהָל (qahal)</note>? What is its usage in the Septuagint? How is it distinguished from the word for "assembly" <note>Hebrew: 'edah</note>? What is its correspondence with the Greek "church" <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (ekklesia), meaning a called-out assembly</note>, and the Latin terms for People, City-State, Assembly, and the "Called Assembly" <note>original Latin: Populus, Civitas, Concio, Comitia Calata</note>? It is also explored whether the Greek "to call" <note>original: καλέω (kaleo)</note> and the ancient Latin "to call" <note>original: calo</note> can be derived from it. Finally, after certain objections are resolved, some observations are made regarding the phrase "the holy congregation" or "the holy church" <note>original: קְהִילָא קַדִישָׁא (Kehila Kadisha) and ἡ ἁγία ἐκκλησία (he hagia ekklesia)</note>, a phrase frequently used by the Apostles.*

# CONCERNING NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.

...to the "assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven" <note>original Greek: πρωτοτόκων ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἀπογεγραμμένων (prototokon en ouranois apogegrammenon); a reference to Hebrews 12:23</note>, the *universal gathering* and the **ASSEMBLY** (**The Church**), *of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven*. Who that is wise in the Hebrew language, reading these words, would not think that the Apostle, through the two words "festal gathering" <note>original Greek: πανήγυρις (panegyris)</note> and "church" <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (ekklesia)</note>, intended to express the force of the Hebrew word *Qahal* <note>original Hebrew: קהל (qahal), meaning a congregation or assembly</note>?

<margin>See Castellus in his Lexicon under this entry.</margin>
Indeed, it seems probable to me that the Greek word "to call" <note>original: καλέω (kaleo)</note> and the ancient Latin word "to call" <note>original: calo</note> derive their origin from this very Hebrew word *Qahal*. That the term *calare* among the Romans signified the same thing—and indeed even more—as the Greek *kalein*, is a fact too well known to need further mention.

<margin>Book 5, page 49.</margin>
Consult *Varro on the Latin Language* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE) was an ancient Roman scholar and writer</note>, where he explains the word "Calends" <note>original Latin: Calenda; the first day of the Roman month, traditionally when the priests called out the dates of festivals.</note>.

<margin>The Merchant, Act 5, Scene 2, line 11.</margin>
Evidence of this usage also exists in the works of the playwright *Plautus*. In the etymology itself, there is nothing difficult, because in the ancient pronunciation of the Hebrew language, the letter *He* [ ה ] in the word *Qahal* [ קהל ] was entirely absorbed. What we now read as *Kahal*, the ancient Hebrews read as *Kaal*, or *Kel*. This, with the addition of a verbal ending, was easily formed into *kaleo* among the Greeks and *calo* among the Latins. However, if anyone would rather derive the Greek *kaleo* from the Hebrew word for "to call" <note>original: קרא (qara)</note>—by changing the letter *R* [ ר ] into *L* [ l ], which we have demonstrated elsewhere happens very frequently—let him enjoy his own opinion.

<margin>Sacred Observations, book 1, chapter 8, page 101.</margin>
Moreover, the ancient Hebrews used the word *Qahal* not only as a noun but also as a verb. *Qahal* signifies *to come together*, and its causative form *Hiqhil* means *to gather a multitude to celebrate an assembly* <note>original Latin: comitia, referring to a formal Roman political gathering</note>. The Greek translators <note>The Septuagint authors</note>, besides other terms such as "to gather," "to bring together," and "to assemble," exceptionally well applied the words "to hold an assembly" <note>original: ἐκκλησιάζω (ekklesiazo)</note> and "to call out an assembly" <note>original: ἐξεκκλησιάζω (exekklesiazo)</note> when they wished to represent the force of these notions.

<margin>Antiquities, book 3, chapter 4.</margin>
The historian *Josephus* spoke very pointedly of "summoning the multitude into an assembly" <note>original Greek: συγκαλεῖν τὸ πλῆθος εἰς ἐκκλησίαν (synkalein to plethos eis ekklesian)</note>, or *calling together the crowd into a Church*, when he described that same gathering of the people for an assembly at Mount Sinai, which I mentioned just now. Furthermore, in an entirely similar case, he uses the word "to call an assembly" <note>original: ἐξεκκλησιάζειν (exekklesiazein)</note>.

<margin>Antiquities, book 4, chapter 8.</margin>
These are his own words concerning Moses, describing how he conducted himself near the final end of his life: "On the following days, for he continuously held assemblies, he gave them blessings and curses upon those who would not live according to the laws but would instead transgress what was determined in them" <note>original Greek: Ταῖς δ’ ἑξῆς ἡμέραις... (Tais d' hexes hemerais...)</note>. Gelenius <note>Sigismund Gelenius (1497–1554), a scholar known for his Latin translations of Greek classics.</note> translated this as: "On the following days in succession, for he was constantly calling convocations, he commended them to God with favorable prayers, just as he conversely devoted those to dire imprecations who, neglecting the laws, acted against their prescription." I am not sure, however, whether the word *exekklesiazein* in this context is not more correctly translated as "to address the assembly" or "to hold a speech to the people," rather than "to call an assembly together."
