# CHAPTER I. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

...so that the words, "he continuously held assemblies," <note>original Greek: συνεχῶς ἐξεκκλησίασε (synechos exekklesiase)</note> signify that Moses, near the end of his life, frequently preached to the people. But these two ideas go hand in hand, and both are hidden within the meaning of this word. It is certainly clear from the evidence already produced that the nuance <note>original Greek: ἔμφασις (emphasis); referring to the underlying weight or specific implication of a word</note> of the meaning of the term <term>Qahal</term> <note>Hebrew: קהל; generally meaning a summoned assembly or convocation</note> and its distinction from <term>Edah</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה; generally meaning a congregation or appointed meeting</note> is not obscure.

<margin>See Suidas under the word ἐκκλησιάζω <note>Suidas, or the Suda, is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world; the Greek word refers to holding a public assembly.</note>.</margin>

Yet we have not overcome every difficulty. For it is to be observed—as we touched upon before—that sometimes the entire gathering of the Jewish people is also called an <term>Edah</term>; further, that the translators of the Septuagint <note>The influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made in the 3rd century BCE</note> sometimes translate the term <term>Qahal</term> as "synagogue" <note>original Greek: συναγωγὴ (synagoge)</note>, a name they usually use to render the word <term>Edah</term>; and finally, that this very notion of <term>Qahal</term> sometimes seems to be applied to specific gatherings, not of the whole Republic, but perhaps of a single city or province. We must respond to each of these points briefly.

Regarding the *first* point, I would not deny that the entire multitude of the Jewish people can be called, and sometimes is called, an <term>Edah</term> or "assembly," because every society and gathering of men—whether large or small in number, whether universal or particular (as they say)—can be and is an <term>Edah</term>, a "gathering and coming together." Therefore, there is no *meeting* <note>original Latin: concio; a gathering called to hear a speech or sermon</note> and no *formal assembly* <note>original Latin: comitium; a legal or political gathering for voting or decision-making</note> that is not truly an <term>Edah</term> or "assembly." 

But one must pay attention to this: 1. By the word <term>Edah</term> considered in itself, without any context from the text, the universal multitude of a people is never indicated. When it is said in the text that this or that must be done <term>in the assembly of Israel</term> <note>original Hebrew: בעדת ישראל (be-edat Yisrael)</note>, or *by the assembly of Israel*, that phrase—considered in its genuine and proper meaning—never designates that it must be performed by the *entire* Jewish people, unless the circumstances of the text (from which alone a judgment on the more general meaning of this word can be formed) prove it. But the term <term>Qahal</term>, always and everywhere if I am not mistaken, designates the universal community of the people. What was done in the formal assemblies of the people can be said to have been done in an *assembly*, yet it does not rightly follow from this that the words *assembly* and *formal assembly* do not differ in meaning. 2. When the Sacred Writers strive to indicate the whole assembly of the people through the word <term>Edah</term>, they frequently do not express it simply by "Position," <note>original Greek: Θέσιν (thesin); here referring to a simple categorical statement</note> as in <term>Assembly of Israel</term>...

However, because it seemed otherwise to those Septuagint translators, one should not think that the words "The Whole Assembly" <note>Hebrew: Kol Edah</note> and <term>Qahal</term> differ in no way in their meaningful power. It often happens that translators either do not grasp the genuine meaning of words, or they translate words of varying meanings with the same Greek terms, provided there is some overlap in their definitions. Therefore, we need not labor any further on resolving this objection.

When **Jehoshaphat** is said to have stood in the "assembly of Judah," the term **assembly** must certainly be understood as the entire Jewish people, summoned by him to Jerusalem for a sacred gathering during a most difficult time for the Republic. The reason that the "assembly of Judah" does not there denote the people of Israel as well—who constituted a different Republic—is because the Ten Tribes, having separated from the tribe of Judah, were then considered an entirely different people, distinct from the assembly or people of Judah. # ON NAMES etc. Book I. Part I.

...corresponds to the Greek word **Synagogue** <note>original Greek: συναγωγή</note>, and the Hebrew word **Congregation** <note>original Hebrew: קהל (Qahal)</note> to the word **Assembly** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (Ecclesia)</note>.

Indeed, from this difference in the meanings of these two Greek words, *Synagogue* and *Assembly*, I believe it is clear enough why Christ and the Apostles chose to describe the multitude of Christians by the name **Assembly** <note>Ecclesia</note> rather than **Synagogue**. This choice should not be attributed primarily to a desire to distinguish the Christian Church from the Jewish one by using different names—as many faithful in later ages have assumed—for the Jews themselves were accustomed to calling their own gatherings "Assemblies," as has already been noted. Rather, it was because the term **Assembly** <note>Ecclesia</note> was much more suitable for designating the concept they intended to represent. A **Synagogue** <note>συναγωγή</note>, like the Hebrew term **Gathering** <note>original Hebrew: עדה (Edah)</note>, always signifies a *group joined and gathered together in person*, even if they are perhaps bound by no other link. But an **Assembly** <note>Ecclesia</note> designates a *certain multitude that constitutes a People, joined together by laws and bonds*, even if it often happens that they are not currently gathered or even able to be gathered.

<margin>
From the *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, page 261.
</margin>
This is very much how *Justin Martyr* <note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher and apologist</note> expresses the matter: *For both the People and the Assembly, though consisting of many men in number, are called and addressed by a single name, just as if they were one single thing.* For example, when the faithful are scattered throughout various regions of a land so that they are denied the ability to meet together, they then cease to be a **Gathering** <note>original Hebrew: עדה (Edah)</note> in the sense of a physical meeting, but they do not cease to be an **Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: קהל (Qahal)</note> or Church. That is, they do not cease to constitute one body, which is knit together by the closest bonds through the Spirit and faith. From this, I believe it is easy to see that the word *Ecclesia* was used much more appropriately than *Synagogue* to designate the multitude of believers. Indeed, you may easily gather that the writers of the New Testament did not seek out or affect anything particularly special in the word *Ecclesia* over *Synagogue* from the fact that they occasionally use this word *Ecclesia* to designate a **multitude of Pagans and secular people**.

<margin>
Acts of the Apostles, chapter 19:32.
</margin>
So it is in the Acts of the Apostles regarding the crowd of Ephesians: *For the Assembly* <note>Ecclesia</note> *was in confusion.*

<margin>
Annotation on this passage.
</margin>
However, it was excellently observed by *Beza* <note>Theodore Beza, a 16th-century Reformation scholar and translator</note> that the word *Ecclesia* does not lose its standard definition here. He says: *Assembly [Ecclesia]; That is (as they rightly explain...*

*After examining the famous opinions of Jerome and Augustine regarding the difference in meaning between the words Synagogue and Assembly <note>Ecclesia</note>, the notes of the illustrious Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius, a prominent 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian</note> on these same words are presented and examined; not neglecting the definition of the word **Assembly** <note>Ecclesia</note> found in Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedic lexicon</note>. **A**lthough we might seem to have discussed the genuine meaning of the terms **Congregation** <note>original Hebrew: עדה (Edah)</note> / **Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: קהל (Qahal)</note> / **Assembly** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (Ecclesia)</note>, and **Synagogue** <note>original Greek: συναγωγή</note> with no small diligence, we have not yet finished all that must be said about them, or at least what we proposed to say. For once we have recognized what is true and certain in this matter, it will be useful to understand what others have decided regarding these words, so that hereafter the path for us in treating other related matters may be smoother.

His <note>Referring to St. Augustine, the 4th-century theologian</note> words are these: *Although **SYNAGOGUE** is properly said of the Jews, but **CHURCH** <note>original Latin: ECCLESIA</note> of the Christians, because a "congregation" [congregatio] refers more to cattle, whereas a "convocation" [convocatio] refers more to men; nevertheless, we have found that [the Jewish assembly] was also called a Church, and perhaps it is more fitting for us to say: Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the Nations.*

It was indeed very well observed by Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon, a renowned 16th-century classical scholar</note> that the occasion for this clever wordplay was provided by the Latin word *congregate* [congrego] which is derived from *flock* [grex]. However, this distinction is absent in the Greek word **Synagogue** [συναγωγή], as well as in the Hebrew names for a Synagogue. Nor is it entirely true, as Casaubon adds, that the "Church" [Ecclesia] was named from a verb that belongs uniquely to rational beings. For the word *to call* [καλεῖν]—from which *Assembly* [ἐκκλησία] is derived—and *to recall* [ἀνακαλεῖσθαι] are used in reference to the calling and recalling of dogs in Xenophon’s *On Hunting* <note>An ancient Greek treatise on the sport of hunting</note>:

<margin>Chapter 10, section 3.</margin>
*indeed even in John: The Shepherd of the sheep calls [καλεῖ] the sheep.* <note>John 10:3</note> However much weight this example from Casaubon carries is for each reader to judge; yet the foundation of his criticism itself is sound.

<margin>In the preceding chapter, near the end.</margin>
For the reason, as I have already anticipated, why Christ and the Apostles called the gathering of believers an **Assembly** [Ecclesia] rather than a **Synagogue** is not to be sought in the idea that they detested the word "Synagogue" more than the other out of some hatred for the Jewish nation, but because the term *Assembly* [Ecclesia] is much more fitting and meaningful in this case. As for what Casaubon adds—that the word "to call" is used even for beasts, in order to prove that the word *Assembly* is not distinguished from the word *Synagogue* in this regard—I cannot help but illustrate this from *Aristophanes* <note>The most famous comic playwright of ancient Athens</note>, who elegantly represents a gathering of beasts with the same Greek words that he usually uses to describe the *public assemblies of the Athenians*.

<margin>In the Comedy titled "The Wasps," lines 31-32.</margin>
The words are:
> Sosias: "It seemed to me, during my first sleep, that in the Pnyx <note>The official meeting place of the Athenian democratic assembly</note>
> a group of sheep were sitting together in assembly [ἐκκλησιάζειν],
> holding staffs and wearing cloaks.
> And then it seemed to me that a Whale-monster, acting like a common innkeeper,

# CHAPTER 2. ON SYNAGOGUES.

Cattle hold assemblies. The Sea-Monster (*θηρίον θαλάττιον* [thērion thalattion] <note>original Greek: a sea beast</note>, a sea monster according to the Scholiast) holds a speech. By the "sea monster," *Aristophanes* <note>The Greek playwright; the author is referencing a scene from his comedy "The Wasps"</note> understands *Cleon* in this dream, and by the "cattle" he understands the *Athenians*. But though *Augustine* may have erred out of ignorance of the Hebrew language, what moved *Jerome*—who excelled in the knowledge of that language—to approve of this distinction between *Synagogue* and *Church* not just once but often? I will provide one passage from his own Commentaries on the words of *Proverbs*: *I was almost in all evil in the midst of the Church and the Synagogue.* <margin>Jerome's Commentary on Proverbs, chapter 5, verse 14. Also on chapter 1, verse 8.</margin> Thus says *Jerome*:

> Church and Synagogue are Greek names, and in Latin they signify one and the same thing: that is, a gathering of many people together. However, if they are more subtly distinguished, **CHURCH** <note>original Latin: ECCLESIA</note> is interpreted as a "calling together" [convocatio] and **SYNAGOGUE** as a "gathering" [congregatio]. And indeed, the ancient people of God were called by both names. But now, for the sake of distinction, that one is called the Synagogue, and ours the Church; this is earned by the merit of faith and greater knowledge, because even an irrational creature can be "gathered" [congregari].

<margin>Dialogue between an Orthodox and a Luciferian. Epistles, volume 11, folio 49, column 2; folio 50, column 4; folio 53, column 3.</margin>
Elsewhere, however, *Jerome* more clearly uses the word *Synagogue* in a derogatory sense. Attend to these words: *Your Church* (he introduces a *Luciferian* <note>A follower of Lucifer of Cagliari, a 4th-century bishop known for his strict stance against Arian heretics</note> speaking) *which receives bishops from the Arians, should be called the **SYNAGOGUE** of the Antichrist rather than the **CHURCH** of Christ.* Again: *But you, when among the Arians, do not say "Church," but "Synagogue."* And again: *Know that it is not the **CHURCH** of Christ, but the **SYNAGOGUE** of the Antichrist.* Yet, it has already been observed by learned men that the Greeks more than once used the term *συναγωγή* [synagōgē] in a positive sense. Let us take one example from the Epistles of *Ignatius*: *Without the Presbyters there is no chosen Church, no gathering of saints, no assembly of the holy ones* <note>original Greek: χωρίς πρεσβυτέρων ἐκκλησία ἐκλεκτή οὐκ ἔστιν, ου συνάθροισμα ἁγίων, ου συναγωγή ὁσίων</note>. <margin>See Suicer on the word συναγωγή. Epistle to the Trallians, p. 5. Ecclesiastical History, Book VII, chapter XI.</margin> *Suicer* <note>Johann Caspar Suicer, a 17th-century scholar of ecclesiastical Greek</note> reads "of the saints" [*ἁγίων*]. I also noted in *Eusebius*, in a letter from *Dionysius*, Bishop of Alexandria, to a certain *Germanus*, that the word *to gather* [*συνάγειν*] is used more than once in the same sense as *to assemble as a church* [*ἐκκλησιάζειν*]; likewise, the word *synagogue* [*συναγωγή*] is used for *the church* [*τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ*], a gathering of Christians.

<margin>Annotations on the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 16, verse 18.</margin>

# CONCERNING NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.

...occurs in this place, which the Syriac <note>The author refers to the Peshitta, the standard Syriac translation of the Bible.</note> most excellently translates as **עדה** (*Edah*): which signifies, as the Hebrew masters teach us, a chance assembly <note>original Greek: τὸν τυχόντα [ton tychonta]</note>, but one that consists of a certain kind of people; whereas **קהל** (*Qahal*) denotes an assembly of any sort. However, these words are usually used interchangeably in common practice, nor did the translators of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> distinguish between them. In the fifth chapter of Proverbs, where the Hebrew has **בתוך קהל ועדה** (*in the midst of the assembly and the congregation*), the Septuagint has: *in the midst of the assembly [ecclesia] and the congregation [synagoge]*. But in Psalm 26:5, they translated **קהל מרעים** (*the assembly of evildoers*) as *the assembly [ecclesia] of the wicked*. Similarly, in 1 Chronicles 13:2, they interpret **לכל קהל ישראל** (*to all the assembly of Israel*) as *to the whole assembly [ecclesia] of Israel*. Again, in Leviticus 4:13–14, where the Hebrew first uses **עדה** (*Edah*) and then **קהל** (*Qahal*), the Septuagint used *synagogue* in both places. And the writer of the book called Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach, a book of the Biblical Apocrypha.</note> calls a promiscuous collection of a crowd an *assembly [ecclesia] of the masses*. But for the most part, *ecclesia* is nothing other than the people of Israel, in the way that *Edah* is used in the cited passage of Leviticus. Stephen uses the word *ecclesia* in this way in Acts 7:38. Caleb is said to have received his inheritance "in the assembly" [*in the ecclesia*] in 1 Maccabees 2:56. And in the writer of Ecclesiasticus, "people" [*laos*] and "assembly" [*ecclesia*] are used for the same thing in chapters 24:1 and 44:15. Likewise, the author of the history of the Maccabees in 1 Maccabees 4:59 and 3:13 spoke of "the whole assembly [*ecclesia*] of Israel," and the tablets of the covenant are said to have been read "before the assembly [*ecclesia*]" in 14:19, where shortly after "assembly" is explained by the word for "the people" [*demou*] in 21:5. Nor should it be doubted that this meaning fits this passage perfectly. For that Israelite people, living in one region, bore the image of the Christian multitude dispersed throughout the whole world: therefore the Christian multitude is everywhere called by the name "people" [*laos*], as can be seen in Acts 15:14, Romans 9:21, and Titus 2:14. Moreover, as we have said, "people" [*laos*] and "church" [*ecclesia*] are the same. Thus far Grotius; regarding whose digression we observe these things:

<margin>Matthew 16:18.</margin>
1. We do not think Grotius was correct in stating that the Syriac did well to translate the word *ecclesia* in Matthew as **עדה** (*Edah*). The Septuagint never renders the word *Edah* as *ecclesia*, even if it is true that they occasionally translate the word *Qahal* as *synagogue*. 2. <margin>In the Lexicon under the word עדה (*Edah*)</margin> It should not be said so simply and without restriction that the word *Edah* does not signify a chance assembly <note>original Greek: τὸν τυχόντα [ton tychonta]</note>, but one consisting of a certain kind of men. For although *Edah*, by reason of its origin and use, sometimes denotes a specific determined assembly, it very frequently at other times signifies any chance assembly. Let the celebrated Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius, a 17th-century Dutch theologian and expert in Hebrew.</note> settle the dispute: "Every assembly of those meeting and coming toward one another (that is, any chance gathering) is an **עדה** (*Edah*). But an assembly of the people, a great consenting assembly distinct from others—especially one of citizens of a single Republic, State, or Kingdom—is properly called a **קהל** (*Qahal*)."

# CHAPTER 2. OF SYNAGOGUES.

The fact that the Masters <note>The "Masters" refers to the Rabbinical scholars of later Jewish history.</note> of later times often interpreted and used the word **Edah** <note>Hebrew: עדה [edah], usually translated as "congregation."</note> for a gathering of *judges*, or a fixed *meeting* of any group of men, does not hinder our opinion at all. Let it suffice that we maintain that the use of this concept is general and varied in the *Sacred Scriptures*. 3. It is not at all certain that the *words* **Edah** and **Qahal** <note>Hebrew: קהל [qahal], usually translated as "assembly" or "convocation."</note>—as well as *synagoge* and *ecclesia*—are usually interchanged by the *translators of the Septuagint* <note>The Septuagint, or LXX, is the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> themselves. We admit that the word **Qahal**, which properly denotes an *ecclesia* [assembly], is sometimes rendered by them as *synagoge*; however, it does not follow from this that the concepts of **Edah** and **Qahal** do not differ in meaning. This is because it happens a thousand times that Hebrew words with very different meanings (if you look at their *origin and more common use*) are nevertheless translated into the same *Greek* or *Latin* terms in certain cases and circumstances. An open-minded translator might convert the Hebrew words **Mikdash**, **Hechal**, and **Beyt YHWH** <note>Original Hebrew: מקדש / היכל / בית י׳—referring to the Sanctuary, the Temple Palace, and the House of the Lord.</note> each into the word *Temple* in their respective places, and not wrongly; yet who would conclude from this that these words do not differ in the power of their meaning? The Septuagint, however, does not mix these words up, as we have already reminded the reader once or twice. I confess that they translate the name **Qahal** as both *ecclesia* and *synagoge*, because certainly every *Church* [ecclesia] can be called a *Synagogue* in a healthy sense; but **Edah**, which they usually render as *synagoge*, they do not translate as *ecclesia*, because not every **Edah** [congregation] is an *ecclesia* [a formal assembly]. Of the passages brought forward by *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch jurist and theologian who wrote extensively on biblical interpretation.</note>, there is not one that proves what needed to be proven: that **Edah** signifies an *ecclesia*. Rather, they prove that the term *ecclesia* is uniquely to be referred to **Qahal**. 4. However, we concede without difficulty that it is possible for the Greek word *ecclesia* to be taken more loosely at times for any *crowd* or multitude of people; but such misuses <note>The author uses the term "catachresis," a technical term for using a word in an unconventional or strained way.</note> also occur with other words that often have very steady and indubitable meanings. The interpretation of *Hesychius* <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note> seems to belong here: *Ecclesia: A meeting, a synagogue, a public festival*;

</margin>

### CHAPTER 2. OF SYNAGOGUES.
M 3

The fact that the Masters <note>The author refers to Jewish scholars or Rabbis of later periods.</note> of later times have often interpreted and used the word **עדה** <note>original Hebrew: *Edah*, often translated as congregation.</note> for a *council of Judges*, or the *status of any assembly of men*, does not contradict our opinion. Let it suffice that we maintain that the use of this concept in the Holy Scriptures is promiscuous and general. 

3. As for the claim that the words **קהל** <note>original Hebrew: *Qahal*, often translated as assembly.</note> and **עדה** (*Edah*), as well as **συναγωγή** <note>original Greek: *synagoge*</note> and **ἐκκλησία** <note>original Greek: *ecclesia*</note>, are usually mixed in usage—even by the translators of the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX.</note>—this is not so certain. We admit that the word **קהל** (*Qahal*), which properly denotes an *ecclesia* <note>In its original Greek sense, a "called-out" assembly.</note>, is sometimes rendered by them as *synagogue*; but it does not follow from this that the notions of *Edah* and *Qahal* do not differ in meaning. It happens six hundred times <note>A Latin idiom meaning "countless times."</note> in usage that Hebrew words of very different meanings—if you look at their origin and more common use—are nevertheless translated by the same Greek or Latin words in certain cases and circumstances. A more liberal translator might convert the Hebrew terms **מקדש** (*Miqdash*), **היכל** (*Heichal*), and **בית יי** (*Beit YHWH*) <note>These terms signify "Sanctuary," "Palace or Temple," and "House of the LORD" respectively.</note> into *Temple* each in its place, and not incorrectly; yet who would conclude from this that these words do not differ in the power of their meaning? 

Indeed, the Septuagint does not mix these words, as we have already warned once or twice. I confess they translate the name **קהל** (*Qahal*) as both *ecclesia* and *synagogue*, because certainly every Church <note>original: *Ecclesia*</note> can be called a *Synagogue* in a sound sense; but **עדה** (*Edah*), which they usually translate as *synagogue*, they do not translate as *ecclesia*, because every *Edah* is not an *ecclesia*. Among the passages cited by Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian whose work "Annotationes in Novum Testamentum" is likely being referenced.</note>, there is none by which it is proved (as should have been proved) that *Edah* signifies *ecclesia*. Rather, they prove that *ecclesia* is to be referred uniquely to *Qahal*. 

4. However, we grant him without difficulty that it is possible for the Greek word *ecclesia* to sometimes be taken more loosely for any *crowd* or multitude of people; but such misuses <term>catachreses|the use of a word in a way that departs from its strict etymological meaning</term> also occur with other words that often have a very constant and indubitable meaning. The interpretation of **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note> seems to belong here: *Ecclesia: A meeting, a synagogue, a public festival*; although it is certain that Hesychius did not have other terms at hand by which he might designate the emphasis of the word *ecclesia*.

## CHAPTER 2. ON SYNAGOGUES.

I would by no means admit the principle, as it stands, that the Old Testament used a broader meaning [for "assembly"] than the **Church** <note>original Greek: *ekklesia*</note> in the New Testament writings—simply because the former designates any multitude whatsoever without any **relation** <note>original Greek: *schesis*</note> to religion, while the latter signifies a **gathering** with a **relation** to religion. It is certainly true that **Church** in the New Testament primarily denotes the **multitude of the people of God**, the **community** of believers. But that meaning was adopted for this word from its more frequent use in the New Testament writings because the Sacred Writers more often apply it to **religious gatherings**. Otherwise, by its very nature, *ekklesia* no more signifies a **sacred gathering** than the Hebrew word **Assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *Qahal* (קהל)</note>. Indeed, when **Assembly** <note>*Qahal*</note> is applied to the **gathering and assemblies of Israel** in the Old Testament writings, as happens very often, does it not then designate a **sacred multitude** just as much as **Church** <note>*ekklesia*</note> does in the writings of the Apostles? Therefore, this reasoning by **Cameron** <note>John Cameron (1579–1625) was a Scottish theologian who argued that the "Church" in Matthew 18:17 referred to a specific judicial body rather than the whole congregation.</note> carries no weight, at least it seems to me. For this reason, I judge it much better that the word **Church** <note>*ekklesia*</note> be taken here with the same meaning that we said the word **Assembly** <note>*Qahal*</note> was consistently understood previously.

Let **Church** <note>*ekklesia*</note> signify here, I say, the **entire multitude of believers**; what is absurd in that? Cameron claims the form of Church government would then be turned into a **democracy**, or even a **mob rule** <note>original Greek: *demokratian* or *ochlokratian*</note>. I deny that this follows. For the meaning of Christ is clear: he who has sinned and has been rebuked in vain **by two or three** must be reported to all the members of the **Church**, so that everyone (certainly not the elders of the Church alone) may, according to their ability, instruct, warn, and bring him back to the right path. For this duty is commanded to all the faithful: to have care for those who wander. Furthermore, it was accepted around the time of Christ in the Synagogues that those who stubbornly refused to perform the duties of charity and **fellowship** to others were reported to the **Church** assembled in the Synagogues. This will become clear from what must subsequently be said regarding **Excommunication**, when the true sense of this passage will be discussed more copiously.

On the other hand, *Tsibbur* has this advantage over *Edah*: it denotes a **solemn assembly of the whole people**, or at least the largest part of them, for **sacred rites**. *Edah* signifies more a **scheduled gathering of specific men**, whether they be many or few in number. ### CHAPTER 2. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<sig>N 3</sig>

It <note>The author is referring to the term *Knesset*, mentioned on the previous page.</note> denotes exactly the same thing as the Greek *synagogē* <note>original: "συναγωγὴ", meaning a gathering or assembly.</note>, the frequent use of which should primarily be derived from this source. However, <term>Knesset</term> <note>Hebrew: כנסת, from a root meaning "to gather" or "to collect."</note> does not by itself designate any entire *community* or *City* of people, but rather any sort of *Assembly* and *association*, or *gathering* of people—whether large or small, of good men or bad—depending on the circumstances of the text in which its use occurs. 

Because, however, the word <term>Edah</term> <note>Hebrew: עדה</note>—by the power of its origin from the root <term>Ad</term> <note>Hebrew: עד, implying a fixed time or place.</note>—means to appoint or proclaim, it often signifies a fixed, ordained, and composed gathering, such as a body of *Judges*, *Teachers*, and others. 

<margin>
Psalm 82:1.
</margin>

For this reason, <term>Knesset</term> usually takes that same meaning upon itself as well, even if its *origin* does not necessarily require such a specialized meaning. Thus, the "Assembly of God" <note>Hebrew: *Edat El* (עדת אל); see Psalm 82:1: "God stands in the congregation of the mighty."</note> or *Gathering of God*, in which *God himself is said to have stood*, and which referred to the *Great Council of the Jews*, is translated by the Paraphrast <note>Likely the Aramaic Targum, a translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible.</note> using the word <term>Knishta</term> <note>Aramaic: כנישתא, the equivalent of Knesset.</note>. 

<margin>
Regarding the <term>Knesset HaGedolah</term> <note>Hebrew: "The Great Synagogue."</note>
</margin>

Nothing is more well-known than that Hebrew writers speak of the <term>Knesset HaGedolah</term> or the *Great Synagogue*, by which they understand those one hundred and twenty Theologians and Prophets who, after the Babylonian Captivity, were the authors of the sacred *judgment* <note>original: "κρίσεως" (kriseōs)</note>—that is, the bringing of the Divine Law into a settled order. 

<margin>
Buxtorf, *Masoretic Commentary*, Ch. 10. 
Morin, *Exercises*, Book 2, Ch. 11, § 7. 
Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, Book 2, Ch. 26, § 7. 
Spencer, *On the Laws of Moses*, Book 3, Diss. 6.1, Ch. 10, § 5.
</margin>

These figures have been discussed at great length by most learned men. In this usage of the word, it is clear that <term>Knesset</term> signifies a *Sanhedrin* <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews.</note> and an *Assembly* called together for the sake of the religious community. 

But elsewhere, as is well known, it is accepted indiscriminately for any *Assembly*, whether sacred or profane. From this source, however, as I have already mentioned, the word **SYNAGOGUE** is properly to be derived. Yet we neither wish to nor can we deny that the word *ecclesia* <note>Greek: ἐκκλησία, usually translated as "Church" but literally meaning a "called-out assembly."</note> itself has been used in a few places by Sacred Writers with respect to this very word <term>Knesset</term>. Wherefore, it was recently said, and not entirely without merit, by a most learned man, that the word *ecclesia* should be traced back to <term>Knesset</term>. However, this holds true in only a few instances, as we shall argue in the following chapter; it is not generally true. 

Regarding the word <term>Atzeret</term> <note>Hebrew: עצרת, often referring to a solemn assembly or the "closing" day of a festival.</note>, which the Greek translators likewise tend to explain as a *gathering* or *assembly*—and certainly not absurdly in many places—I say nothing, because it has no use in this treatise.

But what, pray, is the reason that the word **synagoge**, which properly denotes an *assembly*, changes its meaning so much that it simultaneously denotes the **Place** itself in which that assembly gathers? It is our duty now to point this out. So that this may be done in some order, let us observe: 1. It happens not rarely that names which signify a *crowd, meeting*, or *congregation* pass over into the meaning of the **Place** in which such *colleges* of men are gathered. The reason for this does not seem to be obscure: since specific **Places** are usually assigned to fixed **meetings**, and since these places could hardly receive a name from anywhere else to distinguish them from other similar **Places**, it happens that the names of such **assemblies** often pass into the names of the **Places** assigned to those assemblies.

...sounds like something else: "to come together in the church" <note>original: *συνέρχεσθαι ἐν τῆ ἐκκλησίᾳ* (synerchesthai en tē ekklēsia)</note>—to convene in the Church—
<margin>1 Corinthians 14:23</margin>
if I am not entirely mistaken. What then? Will "Church" in these words denote only a place? I would not want that either. I think it more convenient that a double meaning be blended into one here, so that we may translate "to come together in the church" as: to convene in that place where the Church is gathered. I think that is what Paul intended to say. "Church" <note>original: *Ἐκκλησία* (Ekklēsia)</note> denotes the multitude of the faithful. But "to come together in the church" is to convene in that place where the multitude of the faithful is. Certainly **Theophylactus** <note>An 11th-century Archbishop of Bulgaria and influential Bible commentator</note>, in his comments on this later passage of Paul—in which, however, I do not find the same difficulty, 
<margin>In this place.</margin>
as I said—wants exactly the same thing. However, this passage is read differently in other Codices <note>ancient manuscript volumes</note>, in which case it contains nothing relevant to our matter. I would also not wish to overlook that the most learned men **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note> and **Selden** <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English polymath and legal scholar</note>, to whose judgment much weight must be given, were also entirely of the opinion that "church" here ought to be interpreted as a place. **Grotius** remarks (on the words: *Do you despise the Church of God?*):

Regarding Paul and Barnabas, Luke speaks thus in the Acts of the Apostles:
<margin>Chapter 11:26</margin>
"It happened that for a whole year they were gathered together in the church" <note>original Greek: *Ἐγένετο δὲ αὐτοὺς ἐνιαυτὸν ὅλον συναχθῆναι ἐν τῆ ἐκκλησίᾳ*</note>. What is "to be gathered together in the church" here other than to be gathered in that place where the Church is? Therefore, "Church" here does not denote the people alone, because a people is not without a place; nor does it denote the place alone, since a place cannot be called a "church" without the people; rather, it means the people gathered in a certain place. ...where it is gathered. Nor do I doubt that these very testimonies, and if there be any others like them, gave occasion to that very frequent use of the word *Ecclesia* <note>original: *ἐκκλησία* (ekklēsia) - meaning assembly or church</note> for the place of assembly among the writers of later times. But so that what we have said may become even clearer to the perception, let us compare with these testimonies of **Paul** a certain saying of **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria</note>, in which there is a similar use of the word *Ecclesia*. <margin>Book III, p. 187.</margin> *But both man and woman ought to be led to the church, modestly dressed, with an unaffected gait;* <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ δὲ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ἀκτέον τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ ἄνδρα, ἐστολισμένους κοסμίως, ἀπλάστῳ βαδίσματι</note> — <margin>p. 188.</margin> *For such they ought to appear and be fashioned throughout their whole life, those who are initiated into Christ, as they compose themselves with gravity and honesty in the churches.* <note>original Greek: Τοιούτους γ’ ἐχרῆν παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίון φαίνεσθαι καὶ διαπλάττεσθαι τοὺς χριστῷ τελουμένους, οἵους σφᾶס ἐν ἐκκλησίαις ἐπὶ τὸ σεμνότερον σχηματίזουσιν</note> One may certainly understand by *the church* in these words the People of the faithful, just as in the testimonies of **Paul**. Yet who doubts that **Clement** intended to indicate something more here by *church*? But what is that? He understood the multitude of the faithful, gathered in a certain place where they were accustomed to gather. What further advances our consideration is that **Elias Levita** <note>A famous 16th-century Jewish scholar and lexicographer</note> teaches that the Hebrew concept <term>קהלה</term> <note>Kehillah - meaning congregation or community</note> *Ecclesia* does not only denote the assembly of the People, but also the Place in which they dwell. I will add his entire commentary:
<margin>In *Tishbi* at this word.</margin>
> <term>קהל</term> <note>Kahal</note>. A large gathering. It is called a *Kahal* just like a *tzibur* <note>a public congregation</note>; another form is <term>קהלה</term> <note>Kehillah</note>. They are accustomed to distinguish between them thus: that they call a congregation of Jews living in one city a *Kahal*, but the city itself in which that congregation is located they call a *Kehillah*, such as the Church of Padua or the Church of Venice. In the plural, however, it has *Kehillot*. But *Kahal* is not used in the plural as *Kehalim*. Even the place in which the dwellings of the living are—that is, the burial grounds of the dead—is accustomed to be called *Kehillah* [Church], even if it is a village and there is no great crowd of Jews there. <gloss>A large congregation of people is called Kahal / Another form is called Kehillah. They are accustomed to distinguish those two in this way: that they call the congregation of Jews, dwelling in one place, Kahal; but the city itself, in which that congregation is, they call Kehillah, such as the Paduan Church, the Venetian Church. In the plural, however, it has Kehillot. "The Kahal" however is not used in the plural "Kehalim." Also the place in which there are dwellings of the living, that is, the burial grounds of the dead, is accustomed to be called Kehillah [Church]; even if it is a village, and there is no great gathering of Jews there.</gloss>

### OF NAMES etc. BOOK I. PART I. ###

...as the lexicographers hold. **Schindler** <note>Valentin Schindler (d. 1604), a Lutheran philologist and author of a famous five-language dictionary</note> states: *Kehillah* <note>original Hebrew: קהלה</note> is a "city or place" where the **Church** dwells. Likewise, it is where the bodies of the deceased rest. **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Hebraist</note> defines *Kehilla* <note>original Aramaic: קהלא</note> as a "Congregation, an assembly of men, especially gathered for sacred rites, a Church, a Synagogue, a place," and "the people gathered in a place." He adds: *Thus, when they describe the place in which someone lives, they name not the city but the assembly;* **In the Holy Congregation of Venice, etc.** <note>original Hebrew: בקהלת קדושה</note> **Castell** <note>Edmund Castell (1606–1686), author of the Lexicon Heptaglotton</note> holds these same views. 

But we believe the words of **Elias** <note>Elias Levita (1469–1549), a famous Jewish grammarian and teacher of Christian humanists</note> must be accepted with a healthy dose of caution. For what does he say? He claims that *Kahal* <note>original Hebrew: קהל</note> and *Kehillah* differ in that *Kahal* denotes the assembly, while *Kehillah* denotes the **place**. How can this be true, since beyond all controversy *Kehillah* is often used for the assembly itself? Furthermore, who could be persuaded to believe that the Jews, by the term **Holy Congregation** <note>original Hebrew: קהלה קדושה (Kehillah Kedoshah)</note>, always designate a **place** or a **city**? 

I also doubt very much whether by this phrasing—*The Holy Congregation of Prague, of Venice, of Altona*—the cities themselves are designated. For by what right would they call the city itself **Holy**, unless it were Jerusalem or the cities of Canaan? (For concerning Jerusalem, it is found on shekels, whether genuine or counterfeit: **Holy Jerusalem** <note>original Hebrew: ירושלים קדושה</note>). Therefore, I do not think what **Elias** teaches is so simply true. 

Yet I would not dare to say he writes something entirely false. For I saw in the *Preface of the Jewish Calendar*, published by **Rabbi Uri**, that the **city** of Jerusalem is called absolutely **K.K.** <note>An abbreviation for Kahal Kadosh (Holy Congregation)</note>, with only this familiar epithet: <margin>Hottinger presents this at the end of his Booklet on Monuments.</margin> **May it be built and established speedily in our days.** <note>original Hebrew: תבנה ותכונן במהרה בימינו — a traditional Jewish prayer for the restoration of Jerusalem</note> 

Let us say, then—until this is more clearly understood by us—that the term *Kehillah* signifies the multitude of believers, of whatever sect, who dwell in this or that fixed place. Thus, **The Holy Congregation of Prague** denotes the *Church of Prague*; or, if you prefer, the city of Prague insofar as it contains the **Church of the Jews**. Indeed, the fact that a **burial ground** where many dead are laid is designated by the same name follows the same reasoning. 

We conclude that the Greek word *ekklēsia* <note>original: ἐκκλησία</note> and the Hebrew *kehillah* in certain places signify something more than a mere multitude; that is, a multitude in relation to a **place**, or a **place** with respect to a certain multitude gathered within it. However, when the **Apostle Paul** uses the word *ekklēsia* in the phrase mentioned before—*you come together in the church*—I do not think he intended his mind toward the Hebrew word *kahal* or *kehillah*. Nor is there found, as far as I know, among the Hebrews any...

...some phrase <note>original Greek: φράσις (phrasis)</note> similar to this Greek one, in which the use of the word **Qoheleth** <note>original Hebrew: קהלת; referring to the "Preacher" or "Assembler"</note> is the same as the use of the word **Ecclesia** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία (assembly/church)</note> here. <margin>Deuteronomy 23:2</margin>

The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this as: *to enter into the assembly of the Lord* <note>original Greek: εἰσέρχεσθαι εἰς ἐκκλησίαν Κυρίου (eiserchesthai eis ekklêsian Kyriou)</note>. At first glance, this seems similar to our phrasing, but when well-considered and examined, it differs not a little. *First*, it is an entirely different thing to **enter into the assembly** <note>original Latin: ingredi in Ecclesiam</note> than it is to **meet in the assembly** <note>original Latin: convenire in Ecclesia</note>. This is because the latter phrase, as has already been proven, necessarily includes the meaning of a *place*, which can be entirely ignored in the *former* phrase. Furthermore, "to enter into the assembly" in that context does not mean to **enter into a multitude** gathered in a specific spot, but rather to become a part and member of the people of God. No more words are needed to dismiss this comparison.

Having established in the previous chapter that the word can refer to both a group of people and a physical location, the author now argues that the word "Synagogue" is often used as a shorthand (ellipsis) for "House of the Synagogue," much like Hebrew and classical languages omit the word "house" in common idioms.</meta>

<header>CONCERNING NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.</header>

...of the synagogue <note>original Greek: συναγωγῆς (synagoges)</note>, the house or Temple of the congregation. There are various reasons that suggest this. 1. Because "House of the Assembly" <note>original Hebrew: בי' הכנסת (Beit HaKnesset)</note> is much more frequently used by Hebrew writers than simply "Assembly" <note>original Hebrew: כנסת (Knesset)</note> or "Entry" <note>original Hebrew: כניסה (Kenisah)</note>: from which it is certainly clear that "House of Assembly" is the full term and "Assembly" is an abbreviation. 2. Because the logic behind the words "Assembly" <note>original Hebrew: כנסת (Knesset)</note> and "Inquiry" <note>original Hebrew: מדרש (Midrash)</note> in these cases seems to be exactly the same. For observe now, that *Midrash*—which signifies discussion and more subtle inquiry—is taken equally for the building and the School in which such inquiries are held, as it is for the inquiry itself. Thus, you find very frequently in the *Hebrew Grave-markers* <note>original Latin: Cippis Hebraicis; a 17th-century work on Jewish monuments and inscriptions</note>: *The second vault is called the School <note>Midrash</note> of Solomon the King*.

<margin>
p. 20.
p. 32.
p. 52.
</margin>
Again: *The place is very venerable, and there is a place of inquiry* <note>original Greek: τόπος ζητήσεως (topos zeteseos)</note>. In another place: *There is the Academy of Rabbi Simeon son of Yochai*. It is added: *There he himself was buried in his own School <note>Midrash</note> with his son Rabbi Elazar*. We see, certainly, in these and many other places that the word *Midrash* is taken to mean "School." Since, however, *Midrash* literally signifies "Inquiry," there is no doubt that the word *Beth* <note>original Hebrew: בית; meaning "House"</note> is missing, which is usually added to the expression to complete it. Therefore, we believe that "Assembly" <note>Knesset</note> is said instead of "House of Assembly" <note>Beth HaKnesset</note>, just as *Midrash* is said for *Beth Midrash* <note>House of Inquiry</note>.

<margin>
Sacred Grammar <note>Grammatica Sacra</note> concerning Names, book III. Treatise 1. Canon XXXIX. Chapter III. 1. Chapter IV. 2. Appendix III. 7. Isaiah XXII. 22. Acts II. 27. 31.
</margin>
3. Furthermore, the ellipsis <note>the grammatical omission of a word</note> of the little word "House" <note>original Hebrew: בית (Beth)</note> is very frequent in similar modes of speaking. Examples have long ago been noted by Glassius <note>Salomon Glassius, 1593–1656, a prominent Lutheran biblical scholar</note>; even if he overlooked our "synagogue." Thus in Micah: *Chiefs of Jacob* for *Chiefs of the house of Jacob*. Likewise: *mountain of the Lord* for *mountain of the house of the Lord*. So also *the key of David* <note>original Greek: κλεῖς τοῦ Δαβὶδ (kleis tou Dabid)</note> for *the key of the house of David*. Glassius adds: *To this, some refer the phrase "to Hades" <note>original Greek: εἰς ᾅδου (eis hadou)</note>, namely the "house" of Hades. Just as the Greeks say "to the teacher’s" <note>original Greek: εἰς διδασκάλου (eis didaskalou)</note>, meaning the teacher’s house. Euripides writes: "Brought up in a most pious man's," meaning in his house <note>original Latin: aedibus</note>. And among the Latins: "At Opis’s," "at Pollux’s," namely, their temples.* Thus far he speaks.

<margin>
Preparation for the Gospel <note>Praeparatio Evangelica; a work by the historian Eusebius</note> book VIII.
</margin>
Let us say, therefore, in a similar way of speaking and writing, that "Synagogue" <note>original Greek: συναγωγή</note> is said for "House of the Synagogue" <note>original Greek: οἴκῳ τῆς συναγωγῆς</note>, and "Assembly" <note>Knesset</note> for "House of Assembly" <note>Beth HaKnesset</note>. It is well known that this same word "Synagogue" was accepted by Philo and Josephus <note>Jewish writers of the 1st century AD</note> in the same sense as it is in the Gospels, and it will become clear from the testimonies to be cited in their proper place. ## CHAPTER 4. OF SYNAGOGUES. 119

<margin>
Chapter 11. 
Fuller, *Miscellanies*, Book 1, Chapter 11. 
*Every Good Man is Free*, page 679.

The things noted long ago by Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian</note> and others are manifest concerning the *Essenes* <note>A Jewish sect known for asceticism and communal living</note>: "Betaking themselves to sacred places, which are called synagogues, the younger men are accustomed to sit in order according to age under the elders." <note>original Greek: εἰς ἱερὰς ἀφικνούμενοι τόπες, οἳ καλένται συναγωγαὶ, καθ᾽ ἡλικίας ἐν τάξεσιν ὑπὸ πρεσβυτέροις νέοι καθίζοντες; original Latin: Ad LOCA SACRA se conferentes, qua SYNAGOGÆ dicuntur, secundum ætatem ordine sub senioribus juniores considere solent.</note>

Among the other names by which *Synagogues* are distinguished among foreign authors—and it is doubtful if even among the sacred writers—none is more familiar than the **PRAYER-HOUSE** <note>original Greek: προσευχή (proseucha)</note>. This is read in the works of *Juvenal* <note>A Roman satirist known for his critiques of Roman society</note>:

<margin>
Satire III, 
verse 215.
</margin>
> "Tell me where you stay; in what **PRAYER-HOUSE** should I look for you?" <note>original Latin: Ede, ubi consistas, in quâ te quæro PROSEUCHA.</note>

*Prayer-house* here, as the most learned men now generally agree, is a Jewish *oratory* <note>a place designated for prayer</note>; regarding this meaning, the most literate authors of old were once hesitant. They preferred it to be understood as a "hovel" for beggars, in which those seeking alms were accustomed to hide away. For it is well known that the word *Proseucha* is formed from the Greek "to pray" or "to make vows" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ προσεύχεσθαι (apo tou proseuchesthai)</note>. However, that usage of the word "prayer-house" did not seem to fit poorly with the aim and circumstances of *Juvenal's* text. But the most learned *Turnebus* <note>Adrianus Turnebus, a 16th-century French classical scholar</note> taught that both meanings of the word "prayer-house" are elegantly 

<margin>
*Adversaria*, Book 1, Chapter XIX.
</margin>
joined in this passage: "The *Prayer-houses*," he says, "were the temples of the Jews, as in Alexandria and Rome and other cities, having acquired this name because they were certain oracles, or as Christians say, oratories. ... Since, however, the Jews were most inclined toward giving alms, a gathering of beggars would assemble there. But both the Jews and the beggars themselves were hated by everyone, and because the beggars had no homes, they sometimes occupied these places as lodgers and slept in them; and thus the name of the prayer-house fell into contempt." Cleomedes <note>A Stoic philosopher</note>, mocking the absurdities of Epicurus in his *Philosophy*, says: "the talk from the middle of the prayer-house and of those praying in it, are some Jewish and debased things." <note>original Greek: τὰ δὲ ἀπὸ μέσης προσευχῆς καὶ τῶν ἐπ' αὐτῆς προσευχόντων, ἰουδαικά τινα καὶ παρακεχαραγμένα</note>. This latter way of reconciling the terms pleases me most, because Jews are elsewhere described by *Juvenal* as beggars.

Satire III, verse 14.
</margin>

### OF NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I. 120

Poor and begging Jews, who indeed had no furniture except for a **basket and hay** <note>original Latin: *cophinus & fœnum*. Roman writers often mocked Jews for carrying these items, likely to keep food kosher or for bedding</note>, were once accustomed to linger in the grove formerly sacred to the Muses <note>the Camenae, Roman fountain nymphs</note>, where there were also **Shrines**, and there they would sell to any passerby the knowledge of their own fate in exchange for a small coin. He speaks in the same way elsewhere:

<margin>Satire 6, verse 541.</margin>
> *Leaving behind the basket and the hay,*
> *The trembling Jewish woman begs into a secret ear,*
> *An interpreter of the laws of Jerusalem, a high Priestess*
> *Of the tree, and a faithful messenger from the highest heaven.*
<note>original Latin: *Cophino fœnoque relicto, Arcanam JUDÆA tremens mendicat in aurem, Interpres Legum Solymarum & magna Sacerdos Arboris ac ſummi fida internuntia cœli.*</note>

The Jews had no furniture other than a **basket and hay**; leaving these behind in their usual places, they go into the city to beg. **Martial** <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams</note> writes in the same vein:

<margin>Book 12, Epigram 57.</margin>
> *The Jew, taught by his mother, does not cease to beg.*
<note>original Latin: *A matre doctus nec (ceſſat) rogare Judæus.*</note>

Therefore, because Jewish beggars were frequently present at them, **PRAYER-HOUSES** <term>Proseucha: from the Greek word for prayer</term> are rightly noted as places where the poor were to be sought. Furthermore, **Turnebus** <note>Adrien Turnèbe, a 16th-century French classical scholar</note>, in addition to what we have already presented, observed a twofold testimony from **Philo Judaeus** <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria</note> in which "prayer-house" is taken to mean **Synagogue**. Both are sought from Philo's own book describing the *Embassy to Gaius* <note>An account of a Jewish delegation to the Roman Emperor Caligula</note>, one of which was also not overlooked by **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius, a famous Dutch jurist and theologian</note>. But indeed, Philo in that book repeats this word with this same meaning not twice or thrice, but many times. Let us note some of the texts.

<margin>Commentary on Matthew 4:23.</margin>
"Of the **prayer-houses**, there are many in each section of the city. Some they have stripped of trees..." <margin>page 782.</margin> <note>original Greek: Τῶν προσευχῶν, πολλαὶ δέ εἰσι καθ' ἕκαστον τμῆμα τῆς πόλεως. τὰς μὲν ἐδενδροτόμησαν;</note> Again: "The **prayer-houses**, as many as they were not able to destroy by fires and demolitions, they defiled in another way to overturn the laws and customs." <margin>page 783.</margin> <note>original Greek: Προσευχαὶ, ὅσας μὴ ἐδυνήθησαν ἐμπερήσεσι καὶ κατασκαφαῖς ἀφανίσαι, ἕτερον τρόπον ἐλυμήναντο κατὰ τῆς τῶν νόμων καὶ ἐθῶν ἀνατροφῆς.</note> Again, speaking of **Augustus** <note>The first Roman Emperor</note>: "They neglected the honors of this such and so great benefactor during the forty-three years he held Egypt, placing no statue, or image, or painting in his honor in the **PRAYER-HOUSES**." <margin>page 784.</margin> <note>original Greek: τοῦτον τὸν εὐεργέτην... παρεκαλύψαντο οὐδὲν ἐν προσευχαῖς ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ μὴ ἄγαλμα, μὴ ξόανον, μὴ γραφὴν ἱδρυσάμενοι;</note> *For this such and so great a benefactor, through the forty-three years in which he held Egypt, they neglected the honors, placing no statue or likeness of him in the PRAYER-HOUSES.* And so it is found here and there throughout the whole book, in many other places.

And not only Philo uses this term, but also **Josephus** <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>. These words, most worthy of note, are read in his writings: "On the following day, therefore, everyone gathered at the **prayer-house**, a very large building, capable of receiving a great crowd." <margin>In his *Life*, page 1020.</margin> <note>original Greek: Κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἐπιοῦσαν οὖν ἡμέραν συνάγονται πάντες εἰς τὴν προσευχὴν, μέγιστον οἴκημα, πολὺν ὄχλον ἐπιδέξασθαι δυνάμενον;</note> *Therefore, on the following day the people convened in the PRAYER-HOUSE, a very large building, capable of a very frequent multitude.* And then: "And when the beginning of the following day had dawned, coming there from Taricheae, I found the multitude already gathering in the **prayer-house**..."

# CHAPTER 4. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>
*Omissions*, Book 1, on Matthew 21:13.
</margin>
...the multitude already gathered in the **Prayer-house** <note>original: *Proseucha*</note>. Later again; He himself also dressed in a breastplate, and as secretly as possible girded with a sword **came into the prayer-house** <note>original Greek: *ἦλθεν εἰς τὴν προσευχὴν*</note>. From these examples, in my judgment, it is clear that the word **PRAYER-HOUSE** <note>Proseucha</note> was at that time most commonly used to mean a **Synagogue**. For this reason, I do not quite understand what I read in the works of **Drusius** <note>Joannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar of Hebrew and the Bible</note> concerning these houses; "Prayer-houses," he says, "belonged properly to the Jews, and in them they sold fruit; hence the nickname **Fruiterer** <note>original: *Pomarius*</note>. An old inscription reads: *TO P. CORFIDIUS SIGNINUS, FRUITERER, FROM THE PRAYER-HOUSE.*" We know that learned men feel that Synagogues were not held as sacred then as they are now, and it is possible that this is true. However, I do not accept it as proven by Drusius that the Jews were accustomed to sell apples in their Prayer-houses; though I am aware that these houses were commonly planted with trees, among which there might have been fruit-bearing ones. Perhaps a "Fruiterer from the Prayer-house" simply denotes a **Fruiterer of the Jewish Nation and Religion**. Yet, I would not dare to speak too confidently in a matter that is not entirely clear.

<margin>
Matthew 22:10.
Luke 21:4.
Hebrews 12:1.
*Sacred Rhetoric*, Treatise 1, ch. 4, § 3.
Isaiah 56:7.
Matthew 21:13.
In the lexicon at the word כנס (*kenes*)
</margin>
In the use of this word, the same shorthand <note>original: *ellipsis*</note> must be observed which we noted before in the word **synagogue** <note>original: *συναγωγή*</note>. For "prayer" <note>original: *προσευχὴ*</note> is said instead of "house" or "place of prayer." Thus, in Matthew 22, **the wedding** <note>original: *γάμοι*</note> refers to the place where the wedding is celebrated; **the gifts of God** in Luke 21:4 refers to the **treasury** <note>original: *δωροφυλάקιον*</note> itself, into which those gifts were usually sent; and **the contest** <note>original: *Ἀγών*</note> refers to the place where the contest is held. You will find more examples in the works of **Glassius** <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), a Lutheran theologian and biblical critic</note>, who did not neglect our term "prayer-house" among them. Indeed, a **House of Prayer** <note>original: *Οἶκος προσευχῆς*</note> is the same as what the Hebrews call a **House of Prayer** <note>original Hebrew: *בית תפלה* / *Beth Tephillah*</note>, or an **Oratory** <note>original Greek: *προσευκτήριον*</note>. This phrase is found in **Isaiah** regarding the Temple—which is similar to Synagogues in this regard—and it was repeated by Christ; "It is written," He said, "**my house shall be called a HOUSE OF PRAYER.**" <note>original: *ὁ οἶκός μου οἶκος προσευχῆς κληθήσεται*</note> This name applies to Synagogues with the greatest justice, because Synagogues were consecrated primarily for the pouring out of prayers. **Philippus Aquinas** <note>A 17th-century scholar and convert from Judaism who taught Hebrew in Paris</note> says aptly regarding our subject: **The fixed place dedicated to prayer is called the House of Assembly, because the congregation gathers there to pray.** <note>original Hebrew: *המקום הקבוע להתפלל נקרא בית הכנסת יען שמאספים שם הקהל להתפלל* / *Beth Ha-Keneset*</note> To this we may also refer the fact that the Synagogue, in the opinion of some, is called in the **Books of the Maccabees** a **place of prayer** <note>original: *τόπος τῆς προσευχῆς*</note>, as noted by the most excellent Glassius...

### ON NAMES, etc. BOOK I. PART I.

<margin>

I have found this noted by **Glassius** <note>Salomon Glassius (1593–1656), a German biblical critic</note> and, before him, by **Schindler** <note>Valentin Schindler (d. 1604), a Lutheran philologist and Hebraist</note>. The words go as follows: *And they gathered together and came to Maspha* (in the writings of the Old Testament מצפה / which, as it is now pointed with vowels, is read as *Mispa*) <note>original Greek: ὅτι τόπος προσευχῆς εἰς Μασσηφὰ τὸ πρότερον τῷ Ἰσραὴλ</note> *because there was a place of prayer in Mizpah formerly for Israel*. They understand the author's meaning to be that *Mizpah*, where the Tribes of Israel were accustomed to hold their assemblies, was a fixed place designated for prayers. However, it seems the words can be explained more simply: that in ancient times, the Israelites were accustomed to convene at *Mizpah* to pray.

It remains now for us to inquire whether this observation has any use in the exposition of Holy Scripture. Indeed, it has seemed so to very learned men, who have brought forward two passages from the books of the New Testament (for a long time I thought only one fell into this category) in which they thought the word **prayer-house** <note>original Greek: προσευχή / proseuchē</note> could be understood as a **Synagogue**. Both are found in *Luke*; one in the *Gospel*, the other in the *Acts of the Apostles*. The first goes like this:

<margin>
Gospel of Luke, chapter 6:12.
</margin>
*Now it came to pass in those days, that he went out to the mountain* <note>original Greek: προσεύξασθαι</note> *to pray, and he was spending the night in the prayer-house of God* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἦν διανυκτερεύων ἐν τῇ προσευχῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>. Thus **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a French Protestant theologian</note> translates it. The **Vulgate** <note>The 4th-century Latin Bible translation</note> and **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous Dutch humanist</note> translate it word-for-word: *And he was spending the night in the prayer of God*.

<margin>
In the place cited.
</margin>
The **Belgian Translators** <note>The Dutch Statenvertaling version</note>: **And he remained through the night in prayer to God.** <note>original Dutch: Ende hy bleef den nacht over in't gebedt tot Godt.</note> From *Glassius*, however, who noted only this one passage, I understood that the most learned *Schindler* takes "the prayer of God" here to mean a Synagogue or *Proseucha* [prayer-house], as it is called by secular authors. **Drusius** <note>Joannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish scholar</note> was of the same mind.

<margin>
In the Lexicon under the word תפלה [Tefillah / Prayer].

*What if*, he says, *he spent the night in the Prayer-house of God? so that the name of God is added for emphasis, or to distinguish the True God from other Prayer-houses in which false gods were worshiped*. A *Proseucha* [prayer-house] is elsewhere called a house of prayer and was located outside the city.

<margin>

</margin>
However, this conjecture does not find favor with me. For what is this: *in the Prayer-house of GOD*? Why not simply: *in the Prayer-house*?

<margin>

*Schindler* compared a certain passage from the Gospel of Matthew, in which "the Temple of God" seems to use a similar redundancy: *And Jesus entered into the Temple of God* <note>original Greek: καὶ εἰσῆλθεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>. Yet I do not admit this comparison. For the phrase "Temple of God" is directed entirely toward those most common Hebrew phrases, *The Palace of the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: היכל יהוה / Heikhal Yahweh</note> or *The House of the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: בית יהוה / Beit Yahweh</note>; therefore, I do not recognize a redundancy in it. Furthermore, the context, when properly weighed, refutes this explanation.

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the term "Proseucha" (prayer-house), specifically examining whether the "mountain" where Christ prayed in Luke 6:12 contained a physical building or was simply a place of solitary prayer. The author argues against the idea that a formal synagogue structure existed on the mountain.</meta>

### CHAPTER 4. ON SYNAGOGUES.

This opinion is deceptive. It is held in that passage that *Christ*, having departed from his disciples, went alone onto the mountain, into a place separated from the frequent commerce of men, destined not for public but for private and solitary exercises of piety. For if that had been a public oratory <note>A place designated for prayer, from the Latin "oratorium"</note>, Christ certainly would not have selected it for performing his private prayers. Let us hear *Matthew* in another place: <margin>Chapter 14:23.</margin> *And after he had sent the crowds away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀπολύσας τοὺς ὄχλους ἀνέβη εἰς τὸ ὄρος κατ᾽ ἰδίαν προσεύξασθαι; original Latin: Et postquam dimisisset turbas, ascendit in montem seorsum ad orandum.</note> While this is a different instance, the circumstance is the same. Furthermore, it should be observed that when it is written in the words of *Luke*, "he went out into the mountain to pray," and shortly thereafter follows, "and he was spending the night in prayer" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἦν διανυκτερεύων ἐν τῇ προσευχῇ</note>; it seems altogether that the word "prayer" <note>term: προσευχὴ (proseuchē) / A Greek word that can mean either the act of praying or a physical building used for prayer</note> must be understood in exactly the same way as the act of praying. Indeed, these phrases correspond to each other more naturally: "He went out to pray, and persisted through the whole night in prayer," than these: "He went out to pray and persisted in a Prayer-house or in a Synagogue." For it does not suit the intention of *Luke* that Christ spent a sleepless night in a Synagogue (for to what purpose would this pertain?), but rather that he spent the whole night in praying. And certainly, since this mountain was very close to Capernaum, in which there was a *Synagogue*, who would believe that a *Proseucha* <note>A prayer-building</note> was also on this mountain? Certainly in *Matthew*, <margin>Chapter 5:1.</margin> where he speaks of this same mountain, it is simply said that Christ ascended the *mountain*, and *sat* upon it to teach the people, with no mention made of a *Synagogue*. Let us add that it is not the custom among the Jews to sleep, or rather to "spend the night" <note>original Greek: διανυκτερεύειν / dianuktereuein</note> in Synagogues without a compelling necessity. Thus one may read in their modern constitutions: <margin>Orach Chaiim, Laws of the Synagogue. Title 151. § 3. § 4.</margin> **It is not permitted to sleep in the Synagogue, even a chance nap; however, in the House of Study it is permitted.** <note>original Hebrew: אין ישנין בבית הכנסת אפי׳ שינת עראי אבל בבית המדרש מותר</note> It is added: **For the needs of the Synagogue, it is permitted to eat and sleep within it; and for this reason, it is permitted to sleep in the Synagogue on the night of the Day of Atonement.** <note>original Hebrew: לצורך בית הכנסת מותר לאכול וליישן בתוכו ומטעם זה ישנים בליל יה׳ בבית הכנסת</note> We know, of course, that "to sleep" is one thing, and "to spend the night" is another; yet he who enters a Synagogue during the night must necessarily fall under the suspicion that he will not abstain from sleep within it. To us, therefore, it seems simpler, as we have already said,

...to translate "prayer of God" <note>original Greek: προσευχὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ; original Latin: orationem Dei</note> as *prayer to God* <note>original Latin: in Deum</note>. This phrase is indeed a little unusual, but we are not without examples by which it may be illustrated. Thus, the "high praises of God" <note>original Hebrew: רוממות אל (romemot El)</note> are songs by which God is exalted. "The fear of the Lord" <note>original Hebrew: יראת יהוה (yirat Yehovah)</note> is that fear which has God as its object. In the Psalms it is written: "Prayer to the God of my life" <note>original Hebrew: תפלה לאל חיי (tephillah l'El chayyay)</note>. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> renders this: "Prayer to the God of my life" <note>original Greek: Προσευχὴ τῷ Θεῷ τῆς ζωῆς μου</note>. We conclude, therefore, that nothing prevents "prayer of God" in this place from signifying prayers *poured out to God*.

<header>CHAPTER 4. ON SYNAGOGUES.</header>

...was accustomed to be. For who does not speak in this way? Saint Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father</note> says: "For it was not only where the synagogue was, but they also prayed outside, as if setting apart a certain place" <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἔνθα ἦν ἡ συναγωγὴ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔξω ηὔχοντο ὥσπερ τόπον τινὰ ἀφορίζοντες</note>. For the Synagogue was not only there, but they also prayed outside it, in a place defined for that purpose, as it were. Furthermore, just as the Praetors—whom we shall discuss—and the *Duumviri* <note>a municipal magistrate in Roman colonies</note> differed, so too did the Synagogue differ from the *Proseucha* <note>an informal place of prayer, often located outdoors or near water</note>. This is just as today: where Jews are more numerous, there are only "legitimate" Synagogues, properly so called. And thus, in the following chapter, a Synagogue is said to have been in Thessalonica, whereas in smaller places there were only *Proseuchae*. Hence, the Syriac translator himself calls the *Proseucha* here <margin>Verse 13</margin> a "House of Prayer" <note>original Syriac: בֵּית צְלוֹתָא (Beit Tzlota)</note>; while in the following chapter, the Synagogue is called an "Assembly" <note>original Syriac: כְּנוּשְׁתָּא (Kenushta)</note>. What of the fact that women were not admitted to the conversation of men in the Synagogues, being separated by lattices? Yet here it says: "we spoke to the women who had come together" <note>original Greek: ἐλαλοῦμεν ταῖς συνελθούσαις γυναιξί</note>. Thus far Heinsius <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a leading Dutch scholar of the Renaissance</note>. Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a Protestant reformer and biblical translator</note>, however, translates it: *where prayer was accustomed to be.* In Dutch: **Where prayer was wont to happen.** <note>original Dutch: Daer het gebedt plagh te geschieden</note>

I wish indeed that I did not hesitate more now in reconsidering this passage than I once did, when I quite freely <margin>In *The Archisynagogue*, chapter 12, pages 250, 257.</margin> defended the common translation approved by Beza and the Dutch. I wrote something like this: I find no fault in this latter version, because the true and most consistent meaning of the words *proseuchē* <note>prayer/prayer-house</note> and *nomizesthai* <note>to be customary or supposed</note> is retained. Unless perhaps someone wishes the word *proseuchē* to be taken in a broader sense, because here it signifies all the sacred worship performed in synagogues, the greatest part of which was *proseuchē*, or Prayer. In Dutch, we might not inelegantly translate this place: **Where people were accustomed to practice divine service.** <note>original Dutch: Daer men gewoon was Godts-dienst te oeffenen</note> And certainly, even now I am not fully satisfied with the explanation of the phrase: *where prayer was supposed to be* <note>original Greek: Οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι</note>, which Heinsius interprets as: *where, according to received custom, there was*, or *used to be, a Synagogue*. For what was this *custom* <note>original Greek: νόμισμα (nomisma)</note>, what was this received habit, by which a certain Synagogue was located outside the city of Philippi by the river? Why does Luke not say: "where there was a synagogue of the Jews"? Why does he say *it was thought to be* <note>original Greek: ἐνομίζετο εἶναι</note> or *was accustomed to be*? Or was it perhaps not there at that time? It certainly was; for Paul went there. It is possible that the Old Latin Translator sensed this difficulty, and therefore translated *it was thought to be* as *it seemed to be*; for the word *nomizomai* is sometimes understood in another sense. The meaning would then be: *As if Paul had guessed that there was some Oratory or Synagogue there, in which people of the Jewish nation were accustomed to meet.* It is doubtful, however, whether that Old Translator did not read *it seemed* <note>original Greek: ἐδόκει (edokei)</note> instead of *it was thought* <note>original Greek: ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto)</note>, as...

*Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and biblical scholar</note> reports that in a certain very ancient Manuscript of his, it was written:* More so since it is also consistent with that version of the Syriac Interpreter’s paraphrase: <note>original Syriac: ונפקן ביומא דשבתא לבר מן תרעא דמדינתא על יד נהרא מטל דתמן מתחזיא הוא בית צלותא — "And we went out on the Sabbath day outside the city gate by the river because a house of prayer was seen there."</note> The Latin translation of the Trostian Edition <note>The Syriac New Testament edited by Martin Trost in 1621</note> is expressed in this manner: *And we went out on the Sabbath day outside the city gate near the riverbank, where A HOUSE OF PRAYER WAS VISIBLE.* But it does not seem that the Syriac Interpreter intended to say that a certain Synagogue was visible outside the city. Not because that sense is more intricate than others, but because the Syriac Interpreter would then deviate greatly from all other Interpreters and Readings, with which he can easily be reconciled. The source of the error, it seems to me, lies in the Latin translation, not in the Syriac Interpreter. Clearly, the word חזא / חזי <note>haza/hazi</note>—*he saw, he looked at, he contemplated*—in the *Ethpehal* form <term>Ethpehal<note>The passive or reflexive verb conjugation in Syriac and Aramaic</note></term>, אתחזי <note>eth-hazi</note> (which occurs in this text), is indeed frequently taken to mean *to be looked at* or *to be seen*, but it also signifies *to be thought* or *to be considered*, corresponding to the Greek <note>original Greek: δοκεῖν (dokein)</note>; with that same variety of meaning that appears in the Latin word *videri* <note>meaning both "to be seen" and "to seem"</note>. Take some examples from our Syriac Interpreter himself.

<margin>Chapter xvii. 25.</margin> Thus we read in *Matthew*: *And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying:* "What do you think, <note>original Greek: Τί σοι δοκεῖ (Ti soi dokei)</note> Simon?" The Syriac: <note>original Syriac: מנא מתחזיא לך שמעון (Mana meth-hazya lak Shemon) — "How does it appear to you, Simon?"</note> Likewise in the following Chapter: "What do you <margin>Chapter xviii. 12.</margin> think <note>original Greek: Τί ὑμῖν δοκεῖ (Ti hymin dokei)</note>; if a man has a hundred sheep." The Syriac: <note>original Syriac: מנא מתחזיא לכון (Mana meth-hazya lekon)</note>. Likewise in <margin>Chapter xiv. 64.</margin> *Mark*: "how does it appear to you?" <note>original Greek: τί ὑμῖν φαίνεται (ti hymin phainetai)</note>. The Syriac: <note>original Syriac: מנא מתחזיא לכון</note>. In <margin>Chapter x. 36.</margin> *Luke*: "Which, then, of these three seems to you <note>original Greek: δοκεῖ σοι (dokei soi)</note> to have been a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?" The Syriac: <note>original Syriac: מנו הכיל מן הלין תלתא מתחזיא לך דהוא קריבא להו דנפל באידי גיסא (Manno hakeil men halein tlata meth-hazya lak...)</note>. It is certain, therefore, that the word <note>original Syriac: אתחזי (eth-hazi)</note> is often the same as the Greek <note>original Greek: δοκέω (dokeo)</note> *to seem*. Therefore, the words <note>original Syriac: מתחזיא הוא בית צלותא (meth-hazya hwa beit tzlota)</note> respond to the Greek <note>original Greek: ἐδόκει προσευχὴ εἶναι (edokei proseuche einai)</note>, *it seemed to be a house of prayer*, which are found in the very ancient Manuscript of *Beza*, and seem to have been accepted by the common Interpreter <note>The Vulgate translator</note>. However, the most learned men, *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant Hebraist</note> and *Heinsius* <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a leading scholar of the Dutch Renaissance</note>, object; they do not want the word <note>original Greek: ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto)</note> to be explained here as *it seemed* (as if it signified the same as *it appeared*), but they urge that it be explained as: *it was according to accepted custom*, or *it was accustomed to be*. Nor can it be denied that the circumstances of the text favor them to some extent. For what necessity would *Paul* and those with him have had to guess, or to merely suspect, that some Synagogue...

However, regarding the points cited from *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant Old Testament scholar.</note> and *Heinsius* <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous scholar of the Dutch Renaissance.</note>, what I previously rejected, I reject even now for the same reasons. I do not clearly perceive, however, what reasons led them to this conclusion. For why, in those places called *Proseuchae*, should *Moses* and the *Prophets* not be read aloud just as they are in *Synagogues*? I admit that *Proseucha* signifies "prayer," and <term>metonymically<note>A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, like using "prayer" to mean "a house where one prays."</note></term> denotes an *oratory*; but what is more common than for a thing to be named after its most significant part? Among the Hebrews, a synagogue is called both a *House of Prayer* <note>Hebrew: בית תפלה (*Beit Tefilah*)</note> and a *House of Assembly* <note>Hebrew: בית הכנסת (*Beit HaKnesset*)</note>; yet it would be foolish to conclude from this that no reading of the *Law* and the *Prophets* is celebrated there.

Nor does it help *Heinsius* that the Syriac Translator <note>The *Peshitta*, an ancient Syriac version of the Bible.</note> translates *proseuchē* as *House of Prayer* <note>Syriac: בית צלותא (*Beit Tzlota*)</note> and *synagōgē* as *Synagogue* <note>Syriac: כנושתא (*Knushtha* or "Assembly")</note>, because the Syriac Translator had to adapt his version to the Greek expressions; this in no way prejudices the meaning of the Hebrew or Greek words among the people by whom they were used.
