What then? Did *Onias* mean to say this: that the Jews had Temples for themselves in all those places, in which sacrifices were offered at altars and the ceremonies of the *carnal Law* <note>A term used by early modern scholars to describe the physical rituals and animal sacrifices of the Old Testament Law, as opposed to spiritual worship.</note> prescribed by *Moses* were observed? Truly, I can hardly believe that the Jews commonly broke out into such excess, which is contrary to the universal practice of the nation. *Onias* built a Temple in *Egypt*, almost equal to the one in *Jerusalem*, in which Priests and Levites performed their duties, as *Josephus* relates. <margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 7, Chapter 30.</margin> But that was an entirely new and unheard-of deed. Therefore, I believe it is not absurd to understand this writing of *Onias* as referring to *Synagogues*, which appeared as certain minor Temples, about which *Onias* likely spoke with greater boasting to *Ptolemy* and *Cleopatra*, so that he might more <margin>Compare also Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 14, Chapter 17.</margin> easily draw them into supporting his wishes. We shall describe it in full, because it is very relevant to the matter we are discussing. *Josephus* is at the point of reporting the edict of *Emperor Augustus*, by which the privileges of the Jewish nation are confirmed in the cities of the *Roman Empire*. <margin>Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 16, Chapter 10.</margin> This, in truth, is its tenor: "It has seemed good to me and my council, with the sworn opinion of the Roman people, that the Jews may use their own customs and their ancestral law, just as they used them under Hyrcanus, the high priest of the Most High God; and that their sacred things <note>Greek: "τά τε ἱερὰ" (*ta te hiera*)</note> shall be inviolable and shall be sent to Jerusalem, and be delivered to the receivers of Jerusalem." **Gelenius** [translates]: *It pleases me, by common [oath...]*

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the term "sacred place" (hieron) was used to refer to synagogues in historical documents. ### CHAPTER 4. ON SYNAGOGUES.

...the decree of the sworn Senate [states], *that the Jews may use their own rites and laws, just as they used them in the time of Hyrcanus <note>Hyrcanus II was a High Priest and ruler of Judea in the 1st century BCE.</note>, the High Priest of the Most High God,* and that the *right of asylum shall remain* to their SHRINES; *and that they be permitted to send dedicated money to Jerusalem through certain men.* At first glance, it might seem that [Josephus] interpreted "the sacred things" <note>original Greek: "τὰ ἱερὰ" (*ta hiera*)</note> here as "Temples" <note>original Latin: "Templa"</note>, and thus understood the meaning of the edict to be that the shrines of the Jews enjoyed the right of asylum. But, if he held that opinion, he wandered entirely from the true sense and intent of the edict. For if you take "the sacred things" <note>original Greek: "τὰ ἱερὰ" (*ta hiera*)</note> here to mean "shrines" or "Temples," to what, I ask, will you refer the relative word "them" <note>original Greek: "αὐτὰ" (*auta*)</note>, which can be traced back to nothing other than "the sacred things"? Furthermore, I do not know on what basis it could be believed that the Synagogues of the Jews enjoyed the *right of asylum*? <note>The "right of asylum" was a legal status where a sacred place offered protection from arrest or violence to those within its walls.</note> I certainly do not accept that until I see it established by certain arguments. I would rather believe that *Gelenius* <note>Sigismund Gelenius was a 16th-century scholar known for his Latin translations of Greek classics like Josephus.</note>, who in his translations usually expresses the mind of *Josephus* more than his exact words, translated the text more loosely here because sacred money was usually kept in the Synagogues. 

You, however, should rather conceive the meaning of the edict thus: *It is my pleasure that the Jews enjoy their rites according to their ancestral Law, and that their sacred things be safe, and that they be sent to Jerusalem and delivered to the treasurers of Jerusalem.* By "the sacred things" <note>original Greek: "τὰ ἱερὰ" (*ta hiera*)</note>, however, we must understand the money or the *sacred* tax which every Jew, wherever he might be, was bound to pay to God as long as the Republic stood, and to transmit to the Temple in Jerusalem; which money in this same edict and in those following comes under the name of "the sacred funds" <note>original Greek: "τῶν ἱερῶν χρημάτων" (*tōn hierōn chrēmatōn*)</note>. From the beginning of this Chapter, it is clear enough that a controversy arose concerning these sacred funds. For they were accused by the Greeks because they exported the money. 

There is, however, something that relates more closely to our subject in this Rescript <note>An official written answer or decree by a Roman Emperor.</note> of Caesar. It goes on as follows: *If anyone is caught stealing the sacred books, or the sacred money, either from a sabbateion or a men's hall, let him be held as a committer of sacrilege* <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν δὲ εἷς φωραθῇ κλέπτων τὰς ἱερὰς βίβλους, ἢ τὰ ἱερὰ χρήματα, ἔκτε σαββατείου ἔκτε ἀνδρῶνός, εἶναι αὐτὸν ἱερόσυλον" (*Ean de eis phōrathē kleptōn tas hieras biblous, ē ta hiera chrēmata, ekte sabbateiou ekte andrōnos, einai auton hierosylon*)</note>. What *Josephus* expresses with the double term *sabbateion* <note>a place for the Sabbath</note> and *andrōn* <note>a men's hall or meeting room</note>, *Gelenius*, looking to the sense, translates as *religious places*. Rightly so, indeed. I think, however, that these words should be considered as having distinct meanings. *Sabbateion* seems to denote the Synagogue, in which men and women were accustomed to meet together on the Sabbaths (from which it takes its name);

### 134 ON THE DISTINCTION OF SYNAGOGUES. BOOK 1. PART 1.

...and to the Greeks, **Synagogues** <note>original Greek: "Συναγωγάς"</note>: Other names as well, by which **Philo** and **Josephus** denote the places of sacred assemblies, are not to be neglected. It is used in the **broader** sense when the word simultaneously includes the meaning of an **Academy** or **Public School**, in which the Teachers <note>or Doctors of the Law</note> dispute concerning the meaning of the Divine Law; and in the **stricter** sense for **Oratories** alone, in which the people gather on Sabbaths and Feast days to celebrate sacred rites.

### 135
-> CHAPTER 5. AND OF SCHOOLS &c. <-

...that **Schools** or **Gymnasia** <note>In this context, *Gymnasia* refers to places of intellectual training and study of the Law, rather than athletic facilities.</note> are included, especially in those places that did not have **Schools** distinct from **Synagogues**, and in which the **Synagogue** was used for combined **Scholastic** and **Ecclesiastical** purposes—that is, for **teaching**, **disputing**, and **praying**. We may believe that in the **Villages** and **Smaller** towns of the land of Canaan, as well as in the cities of the Roman Empire that supported Jewish citizens, it was generally arranged such that they shared a single Sanctuary consecrated for these various religious exercises. And certainly, many names by which **Philo** and **Josephus** designate the **Sacred Buildings** of the Jews must be referred entirely to this **Double** use and double kind of **Sacred Buildings**. Indeed, the Jews of this time alternate the words **Synagogue** and **School** in daily speech, and they very frequently and familiarly call the **Synagogue** itself a **School** (in German, *Shul* <note>original Hebrew: שול</note>). For this reason, even **Buxtorf** <note>Johannes Buxtorf the Elder (1564–1629), a celebrated scholar of Hebrew and Jewish tradition.</note> himself, when treating **Synagogues** and adapting himself to the language of the Jews, confuses these terms throughout; <margin>Synag. Jud. Cap. x.</margin> *In common usage, however,* he says, *the words Synagogue and School are used promiscuously and indifferently, which we have also often followed in this book.*

However, I would prefer to believe that Christ, as long as he performed his public ministry, was active more in **Synagogues** than in **Schools**, where **Synagogues** were distinct from **Schools**, even though he always conducted himself in the **Synagogues** before the people as a **Teacher** of the highest authority. But where **Synagogues** were merged with **Schools**, I believe he adapted himself to the customs of his time and mixed **Scholastic** manners with **Ecclesiastical** ones. This seems likely because Christ was ordinarily accustomed to preach in the most crowded assembly of people, and indeed on **Sabbath** days, when a great multitude of people flocked to the **Proseuchae** <note>From the Greek *proseuche*, meaning a "house of prayer."</note>. <margin>Luke IV. 16.</margin> Thus we read in the Gospel of **Luke**: *He came therefore to Nazareth, where he had been brought up; and he entered, according to his custom, on the Sabbath day into the synagogue* <note>original Greek: "καὶ εἰσῆλθε κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τῶν σαββάτων εἰς τὴν συναγωγήν"</note>. That Christ taught the people in this **Nazarene synagogue** and indeed on the **Sabbath** day, that was **Ecclesiastical** <note>pertaining to the formal religious service</note>; but that while teaching, after reading the text, he sat down, that smacked of the custom of the **Schools**, unless I am mistaken. Nor would I truly believe that in the more celebrated **Academies**, such freedom of teaching prevailed that Christ would have been allowed to occupy the **Chair** of any **Doctor** <note>A formal teaching seat or "Cathedra" belonging to a recognized scholar of the Law.</note> and deliver a speech from it. In the **Synagogues**, however, that freedom of teaching and speaking to the people flourished, which Christ enjoyed...

# CONCERNING THE DISTINCTION OF THE SYNAGOGUE, BOOK 1, PART 1.

...we read that it was seen, but in the established and more celebrated *Academies*, certain *Doctors* held the chairs with *Interpreters*, who spoke in their name and authority. Disciples, wise men, and any learned men were permitted to raise doubts in debate and seek their resolution. And indeed, if by the command of those Doctors others occasionally ascended the chairs—those who were associates of the same benches, or promoted to such dignity by their authority, or who greatly excelled in the brilliance of their teaching—they certainly burned with such envy toward Christ that we may easily presume they would not have easily lent their *Chair* to Christ. As for the idea that Christ was accustomed to raise questions in the Synagogues and debate them with great agitation of soul—as the Jews generally have as a custom—neither the gravity, nor the meekness, nor the modesty, nor the authority of Christ, nor the nature of his office would have permitted it. <margin>Chapter 2:46</margin> A youth of twelve years did this, as *Luke* reports <note>original: "Lucas"; referring to the finding of the boy Jesus in the Temple</note>. But when Christ was to be manifested as the supreme Prophet to Israel, it was more suited to his purpose to teach calmly than to dispute heatedly. Whatever I have written about him elsewhere, I wish it to be understood in such a way that it can be reconciled with what I now hand down; and it will be easily reconciled by a fair-minded reader.

Regarding Paul, however, the matter might seem more clear; about whom <margin>Acts 17:17</margin> it is written thus in the *Acts of the Apostles*: <note>original Greek: Διελέγετο μὲν οὖν ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ</note> HE REASONED *therefore* IN THE SYNAGOGUE, *with the Jews and the devout*, and IN THE MARKETPLACE *daily with whoever happened to be there*. To "reason" <note>original Greek: Τὸ διαλέγεσθαι</note>, I confess, can be taken in a sense so broad that it signifies nothing other than to speak, to make words, to discourse, or to discuss; <margin>Acts 20:9</margin> for which reason it is sometimes simply translated by the Dutch <note>original: "Interpretibus Belgis"; the author is likely referring to the Dutch Authorized Version or similar early modern translations.</note> as *to speak*. Yet, who would deny that "to reason" <note>original Greek: διαλέγεσθαι</note> most often signifies that mode of speaking in which one converses and disputes with another, often with alternating turns of speaking? In this sense it is used in the Gospel of Mark, where it is said of the disciples of Christ: <margin>Mark 9:34</margin> <note>original Greek: πρὸς ἀλλήλους διελέχθησαν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ</note> *they had disputed with one another on the way*. <margin>verse 33</margin> Indeed, "to reason" <note>original Greek: Διαλέγεσθαι</note> here is the same as "to debate" <note>original Greek: διαλογίζεσθαι</note>, as is clear from the question of Christ: <note>original Greek: Τί ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς διελογίζεσθε</note> "What were you debating among yourselves on the way?" The Dutch in this place: **He dealt with the Jews.** <note>original Dutch: "Hy handelde met de Joden"</note> In the margin they have: **He disputed.** <note>original Dutch: "Hy disputeerde"</note> Because, however, the act of Disputing is more suited to *Schools* than to *Synagogues*, strictly so called, perhaps...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 136 regarding the nature of the places where the Apostle Paul taught. # CHAPTER 5. AND CONCERNING SCHOOLS, etc.

We would not err if we took the word *Synagogue* so broadly here that it simultaneously includes *public schools* joined to the Synagogues. And the same may perhaps be observed elsewhere. I do not deny, however, that the word *to reason* <note>original Greek: "διαλέγεσθαι" (dialegesthai)</note> can and sometimes should be explained as referring to the *sermons* or *discourses* held by Paul in the so-called *Synagogues*. This is because Paul’s discourses were primarily directed at convincing the Jews of certain truths through logical arguments—which is, in essence, *to dispute*. Yet, that *Paul* taught and *disputed* not only in *Synagogues* strictly so-called, but also in *Schools*, is most clearly evident from the subsequent history describing Paul’s stay at *Ephesus*: <margin>Chapter 19:8</margin> "He separated the disciples, daily DISPUTING in the school of a certain Tyrannus" <note>original Greek: "Ἀφώρισε τοὺς μαθητάς, καθ' ἡμέραν διαλεγόμενος ἐν τῇ σχολῇ Τυράννου τινός"</note>. Without a doubt, the "School" here is a *House of Study* <note>original Hebrew: "Beit Midrash" (בית מדרש)</note>, a *house of debate and reasoning* <note>original Greek: "οἶκος συζητήσεως & διαλογισμοῦ"</note>. However, *Luke* <note>the author of the Acts of the Apostles</note> used the Greek word *scholē* (school) because by that era it had already been introduced into the Hebrew language. It is found in the *Midrashim* <note>ancient Jewish commentaries on scripture</note> and is written as *estola* or *askola*. <margin>a grammar school</margin> The most learned *Cohen de Lara* <note>David Cohen de Lara, a 17th-century scholar of Rabbinic language</note> explains that term as a *House of the Book* <note>original Hebrew: "Beit Sefer" (בית ספר), usually referring to a primary school for children</note>. But the Syriac translator did not neglect the use of this word, which was quite frequent at that time, in his version; it is phrased in this manner: "And daily he debated with them in the school of a man whose name was Turno" <note>original Syriac: "ובלשון ממלל הוא עמהון באסכולא דגברא דשמה טורנוס"</note>. Excellent indeed. For *Tyrannus* here is a proper name, the same as *Turnus*, which is common enough among the *Talmudic* writers, as *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius, a noted Protestant Hebraist</note> observed before us. Thus you have Paul here separating himself with the *disciples* (who among the Hebrews are called *Talmidim*, meaning *scholars and learned men*) and debating in the *School of a certain Turnus*. But what we have said so far is not quite enough to fully understand the distinction between *Schools and Synagogues* among the Jews; therefore, it would not be entirely out of place to discuss the condition of the *Schools* a bit more clearly, though briefly.

*Schools* or *Academies* in the institutions of Jewish Law and Religion are usually called, as already anticipated, *Houses of Disquisition* <note>original Hebrew: "Batei Midrashot" (בתי מדרשות)</note>, and they are distinguished by this name from the *Houses of Sacred Assembly* <note>original Hebrew: "Batei Kenesiyot" (בתי כנסיות)</note>, so properly called. These latter are the prototypes for *Christian Churches or Oratories*, which are the main subject of our treatise. *Midrash* <note>Hebrew: מדרש</note> indeed signifies "disquisition" or "inquiry."

or a "disputation" from *darash* <term>to seek, to inquire</term>, to weigh and judge a matter most accurately; a meaning of the word that was transferred to the investigation of the sense of Holy Scripture. One place in particular
<margin>Ezra 7:10</margin>
stands out in the Book of Ezra, which undoubtedly provided the occasion for this word to be used so frequently in this sense. Thus it is written there concerning Ezra: *And Ezra prepared his heart* TO SEEK THE LAW OF GOD <note>original Hebrew: "Ve-Ezra hekhin levavo lidrosh et torat Yehovah"; the author notes the root "darash" here means seeking or investigating</note> (for the text must be translated thus, if you simply consider the most familiar meaning of the word *darash*) *and to do it.* The Belgians <note>This refers to the Dutch "Statenvertaling" or States Translation of the Bible</note> translate this: **To seek the law of the Lord.** In their margin, however, they noted nothing further. But what does it mean, *to seek the Law of Jehovah*? Without a doubt, it means to judge, compare, and accurately weigh the text of the Law; then to inquire into the genuine meaning of the Law, and to explain it carefully to others. The illustrious Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist</note> says: In historical matters, the term *darash* is *to investigate minutely* <note>original Greek: "πολυπραγμονεῖν" (polypragmonein)</note>.
<margin>In the Lexicon at the word "darash", Luke 1:3.</margin>
To the Rabbis, *Midrash* is the consideration of the Holy text, or a sermon or reading regarding the holy text; and *darash* for them is to studiously extract the core meaning, or to explain diligently with words. Whether he [Cocceius] referred to this specific place, I do not know. However, the exposition of Alting <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a German philologist and theologian</note> is well-known:
<margin>History of Academic Promotion, p. 219.</margin>
*darash* indicates a broad explanation, such as is observed in sermons to the people, where everything is related to practice—for which purpose he [Ezra] seems to have immediately added the words *to do it.* I do not know, however, if this observation is not too subtle. It is closer to the truth to say that *darash* here denotes the review of the text and the investigation of the true sense of the Law. That later Jews accepted *darash* in the sense Alting describes is well established. Moreover, since in the diligent investigation of truth or meaning it often happens that we propose our doubts to others, weigh their opinions, and debate with combined arguments to seek the truth (which mostly lies in obscurity), hence *darash* <term>to seek</term> among the
<margin>Schindler in the Lexicon at this word.</margin>
Chaldeans, Syrians, and Arabs was transferred from the notion of seeking to that of investigating and debating. Thus the Syrian [Syriac version] uses this word
<margin>Acts 6:9</margin>
throughout the New Testament. We will give one example from the Acts of the Apostles: *But there arose some from the Synagogue called that of the Freedmen, etc.* DISPUTING WITH STEPHEN <note>original Greek: "συζητοῦντες τῷ Στεφάνῳ" (syzetountes to Stephano)</note>. The Syrian [Syriac]: *And they were disputing [root "drsh"] with Stephen.* Among the Jews, however, in their own language, the word *darash* began to be commonly used for any more profound or exquisite speech or dissertation on Scripture

They commonly adopt this [suffix], even though it often adds almost nothing to the <term>force</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνεργείας (energeias), meaning active power or impact</note> of the meaning. In my view, *Rabbana* <note>original Hebrew: רבנא</note> is a plural form with an Aramaic suffix of the same type, and carries the same weight as *Rabbenu* [Our Teacher]. It is pronounced *Rabbanan* <note>original Hebrew: רבנן</note>, if I am not mistaken, in place of *Rabbannana*, where the final letter has been absorbed, as almost always occurs in the writings of the Talmudists. Furthermore, the *Gloss* describes the *Beth Rabbanan* as the *Beth Midrash* or "House of Disquisition," and notes it is consecrated to the study of the *Mishnah* and *Gemara* <note>the core components of the Talmud; the Mishnah is the legal code and the Gemara is the subsequent commentary</note>; in which, truly, there is no difficulty.

Undoubtedly, however, the *Academy* is called *Beth Rabbanan* ("House of the Teachers") because the Teachers spend a great part of their lives in it, moving about and staying within it; unless someone prefers to see *Beth Rabbanan* as a shortened way of saying "The House of the Study of Teachers." # ON THE DISTINCTION OF THE SYNAGOGUE, BOOK I, PART I.

Scholars translate the term as the *Scholarly House of Assembly*. The Gloss <note>A standard commentary, likely on the Talmud</note> explains the word in this way: <note>original Hebrew: מקום שתלמידי חכמים מוועדין שם ללמוד תורה</note> *A place in which the disciples of the wise meet together to learn the Law.* In other places, it is called the <term>House of Doctrine</term> <note>original Aramaic: בית אולפנא (Beth Ulpana)</note>, both in the Paraphrase of *Onkelos* and that of *Jonathan* <note>The Targums: Aramaic translations and expansions of the Hebrew Bible</note>. Onkelos indeed, regarding what is said in the Mosaic text <margin>Exodus 33:7</margin> as the *tent of meeting* <note>original Hebrew: אהל מועד (Ohel Moed)</note>, which was pitched by Moses outside the camp, twice called it in one and the same verse the *Tabernacle of the House of Doctrine*. *Jonathan* likewise, when explaining the conversion of *Jethro*, the father-in-law of *Moses*, according to the mind <margin>Exodus 18:7</margin> of the Talmudists, changed what is said in the text, *and they came into the tent*, to: *And they came to the Tabernacle of the House of Doctrine*, that is, into the Lecture Hall <margin>Selden has explained the passage from Jonathan at length in his book on the Sanhedrin, book II, chapter II, section IV.</margin> of *Moses*, in which he was accustomed to render judgment and to teach. *Onkelos*, however, here simply has: *And they went up into the Tabernacle.*

Other passages also occur elsewhere. Another very common name is the <term>Session</term> <note>original Hebrew: ישיבה (Yeshivah), commonly referring to a rabbinic academy</note>. *Elias Levita* <note>A 15th-16th century Hebrew grammarian</note> writes: <note>original Hebrew: ישיבה קורין למקום שש שם מרביצי תורה לתלמידי רבים</note> *A place in which there are those who teach the Law to many disciples, they are accustomed to call a* <margin>Tishbi, under the entry "Yeshivah"</margin> *Session.* That which *Elias* has here, <note>original Hebrew: מרביצי תורה (Marbitzei Torah)</note> *those who make the law lie down*, was translated by *Philippus Aquinas*—who often repeats the words of *Elias*—as *Doctors of the Law*. And he is entirely <margin>At the entry "Rabatz"</margin> correct, because elsewhere the same *Elias* observes that the title *Those who make the Law lie down* is quite familiarly attributed among his people to the Doctors of the Academies. Thus he says: *So they are accustomed to call the masters of the Academy who enjoy many disciples, whom they imbue with Talmudic discipline.* He adds: *And especially in Spain, they were accustomed to call those (Doctors)* <margin>Menachot, folio 22, 2.</margin> *by this name, One who makes the Law lie down.* It is from this that / *Harbitza* / as noted by the lexicographers, also signifies an Academy. *Elias* wonders, and not without reason, how it happened <margin>Buxtorf, Castell <note>Famous 17th-century Hebraists</note></margin> that the word *Harbitz*, which properly pertains to the "lying down" or "couching" of beasts, was transferred to the Law. And indeed, the reason for that method seems a little obscure. Yet it is not entirely foreign to derive it from the idea that the Teachers provide a pleasant rest for the law and, as it were, delightful pastures in the minds of the disciples, <margin>Colossians 3:16</margin> just as the *Word of God* is said among us to *dwell* <note>original Greek: ἐνοικεῖν (enoikein)</note> within.

### CHAPTER 5. AND THE SCHOOLS, etc.

Certainly, where that *word* finds a mind so disposed that it receives it gladly, fosters it, and thinks and meditates upon it frequently, then it seems not inconveniently said *to lie down* and *to hide* *in the soul of man*, as if in a desired pasture. <margin>Chapter III. 6.</margin> I had also thought regarding this, whether <term>מרביצן</term> <note>original Hebrew: *marbitzan*, "one who causes to lie down" or "a teacher"</note> might not be translated as "those who water" and compared with the Pauline phrase <term>ποτίζειν</term> <note>original Greek: *potizein*, "to water" or "give drink," referencing 1 Corinthians 3:6</note> in the Epistle to the Corinthians. For surely <term>רבץ</term> <note>the root *r-v-ts*</note> in the *Piel* grammatical form denotes *to sprinkle with water*, and indeed even *to irrigate*; from which comes <term>תרביצא</term> <note>original Aramaic: *tarbitza*</note>, meaning both a *triclinium* <note>a Roman-style dining room where guests reclined</note> and a *garden*. But there was an obstacle: the word <term>מרביצים</term> <note>original Hebrew: *marbitzim*</note> is inflected in the *Hiphil* form, and the added word <term>תורה</term> <note>Torah/Law</note> does not correspond to this "watering" meaning.

Furthermore, what the Hebrews express through <term>ישיבה</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Yeshivah*, "session" or "academy"</note> and the verb <term>ישב</term> <note>to sit</note>, the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers</note> express—by changing the letter <term>ש</term> <note>Shin</note> into <term>ת</term> <note>Tav</note>, as frequently happens in their language—through <term>מתיבא</term> <note>Metiva</note> and <term>מתיבתא</term> <note>Metivta</note>, a most rich phrase: <term>בית מתיבתא מדרשא דישראל</term> — *The House of the Session of the Doctrine of Israel*, which appears in the Chaldaic Paraphrase <note>the Targum</note> of the Song of Solomon 2:4. The reason for the name is undoubtedly to be sought not so much from the *session of the Disciples* (of which we shall speak later) as from that of the *Teachers*. <margin>Chapter VII.</margin> It was the duty of those teaching not only to sit, but the *Teachers* and *Learned Elders* in the Lecture Halls and Judicial Courts constituted a certain *Synedrium* <note>a formal assembly or council</note> and sat together to settle controversies of Jewish Law. <margin>Cholin, folio 137, column 2.</margin>

Observe also that an Academy is called <term>סדרא</term> <note>original Aramaic: *Sidra*, meaning "order" or "arrangement"</note> among the Talmudists; hence <term>ריש סדרא</term> <note>Resh Sidra</note>, the *Head of the Academy*. I derive the explanation of this name from the *order of those sitting* in the Gymnasium <note>school</note> of Disciples: for <term>סדר</term> <note>Seder</note> denotes *order* or a *rank*. For exactly the same reason, they called the *Academy* <term>כרם</term> <note>original Hebrew: *Kerem*</note> or <term>כרמא</term> <note>Kerma</note>, a *vineyard*, because just as a vineyard is gracefully arranged in rows, so it was exactly arranged with the *benches of the Learned* in the Academies. <margin>Jerusalem Talmud, Beracoth, chapter IV, folio VII, column 4.</margin> Philippus Aquinas <note>A 17th-century scholar and lexicographer</note> explains <term>כרם</term> (*vineyard*) through the phrase <term>תלמידי חכמים שהיו עשוין שורות שורות ככרם</term> — *Learned Men, who like a vineyard are arranged in rows or lines*. These words are transcribed from the *Babylonian Gemara, tractate Jevamoth*, or the *Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Beracoth*. Mention is made there of the *School of Jamnia* <note>Yavne, the center of Jewish learning after the fall of Jerusalem</note>, specifically decorated with this title, to the explanation of which is added <term>ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ</term> <note>original Greek: "as an aside" or "in passing"</note>: <term>וכרם היה שם אלא אלו תלמידי חכמים שהיו עשוים שורות שורות ככרם</term> — *Was there truly a vineyard there?* <margin>In the Gloss on Jevamoth, chapter VIII, folio 42. 2. Hebraic Hours on Mark 6:40. In the lexicon at this word.</margin> (Buxtorfius <note>Johannes Buxtorf, a famous Christian Hebraist</note> translates: *An Academy was there: Or; I do not say that an Academy or School was there*. Neither translation is correct, if I judge rightly: since a difficulty is raised here over the word *vineyard*, which must be observed in this objection—

CHAPTER 6. Concerning SCHOOLS & ORATORIES etc. 145

### CHAPTER VI.

*A discussion on the Schools and Domestic Oratories and their use among the Teachers of the Jewish Nation. The true meaning of the words aliyah <note>original Hebrew: עליה, an upper room</note> / hyperōon <note>original Greek: ὑπερῷον, upper room</note>, anōgeon <note>original Greek: ἀνώγεον, upper room</note>, Cœnaculum <note>original Latin: a dining room or upper chamber</note>, and Chalcidicum <note>original Latin: a type of monumental hall or portico</note>, which pertain to this subject, is investigated. The use of these kinds of sacred upper chambers is shown from the writings of the Old and New Testaments as far as is sufficient, not omitting the opinion of the distinguished De Dieu <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch Protestant minister and orientalist</note> concerning the upper room in which the Apostles were gathered on the Feast of Pentecost. The windows of these upper chambers and their use are also discussed; finally, private gymnasia <note>used here in the classical sense of places for training the mind</note> belonging to several people are described.*

Among the Jewish people, the practice and system of religion was such that students of wisdom and others of a more fortunate status or more holy life set aside a part of their own houses specifically for exercises of piety and learning. This was located in the **upper parts of the house**, closest, it seems, to the roof, with windows open toward that quarter of the heavens in which the Temple was located; it was furthermore furnished with those supports which the study of piety or letters required. They would go there, not only as often as they—alone, with God and conscience as witnesses—cultivated a connection with the Divine through more private prayers or applied themselves to solemn meditations on divine matters, but also when they wished to converse with others about the Divine Law and debate its meanings, and to devote time to other sacred exercises. You have here a brief sketch of the *Schools*, or if you prefer, the *domestic houses of prayer* <note>original Latin: Proseucharum domesticarum</note>. What we have said must now be proven and illustrated.

To pave the way for this digression, we shall not skip over an ancient and well-known story—one already excerpted long ago by most learned men—which will nevertheless lead us to a knowledge of these upper chambers; for the rest, we care little. The words of **Rabbi Gedaliah**: *Rabbi Abbuya was the father of Elisha Acher* <note>original Hebrew: ר' אבויא אבו של אלישע אחר היה. Elisha ben Abuyah, known as "Acher" (the Other), was a famous 2nd-century scholar who became a notorious apostate</note>.

# CHAPTER 6. ON DOMESTIC ORATORIES.

*A strange tradition: When the son of Rabban Gamaliel* <note>Rabban Gamaliel II was the head of the Jewish academy at Yavne and a primary leader of the Jewish people in the late 1st century CE</note> *fell ill, he sent two scholars of wisdom to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa* <note>A first-century miracle worker famous for the efficacy of his prayers</note> *to plead for divine mercy on his behalf. After he saw them,* **HE ASCENDED INTO HIS UPPER ROOM** <note>original Greek: anebē eis to hyperōon autou</note>, *and prayed to God for him. But when he descended, he said: "Go, for the fever has already left him." They replied to him: "Are you one of the number of the Prophets?" He answered them: "I am indeed neither a prophet nor the son of any prophet, but I have been taught this by tradition: if my prayer is fluent in my mouth, then it is certain to me that he (for whom I pour out prayers) is accepted by God; but if the matter be otherwise, I know that he is lost." They, being confident, carefully noted that hour, and when they returned to Rabban Gamaliel, he said to them: "By the Temple service! You have erred neither by excess nor by defect of time, but it happened exactly so: for at that very hour the fever left him and he asked us for water to drink."*

The most learned *Selden* <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note> explained this passage excellently; but even before him, the illustrious *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius, a prominent Dutch theologian</note> had touched upon it, raising a suspicion concerning an error by *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a renowned Renaissance scholar</note>.

From these testimonies, it is not obscure to conclude certain things which we have previously touched upon. # ON SCHOOLS, Book I, PART I.

<margin>
Of Notes and Observations, chapter 3, section 2, pi. On forms. p. 138.
</margin>
I would say that *supper rooms* of this kind were situated on the upper floor of a *house*. This is quite clear not only from the testimonies already cited—in which the Teachers are said to have **ascended** into them—but also from the very word <term>aliyah <note>original Hebrew: עליה</note></term>, which is derived from the word "to ascend" <note>original Hebrew: עלה, alah</note>. This is translated by the Greeks as <term>hyperōon <note>original Greek: ὑπερῷον, meaning "upper room"</note></term>. An erudite dissertation by John Gregory <note>A 17th-century English orientalist and scholar</note> exists concerning the power and genuine meaning of both these terms. Gregory observes that Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop</note> teaches that *hyperōon* descends from the Lacedæmonian <note>Spartan</note> word *ōa* <note>original Greek: ᾠα</note>, as they were accustomed to call the "elevated parts of buildings" <note>original Greek: τὰ μετέωρα τῶν οἰκημάτων</note> the highest sections of the houses. He adds: *Moschopulus* <note>A Byzantine grammarian</note> says that the *hyperōon* is "a room built under another" <note>original Greek: οἴκημα τὸ ὑφ᾽ ἑτέρῳ ᾠκοδομημένον</note>, which among the Athenians is called a *dieres* <note>original Greek: Δίηρες</note>, or a **chamber built upon a chamber**. He interprets *hyperōon* through *dieres*, just as *Hesychius* <note>A 5th-century Greek lexicographer</note> interprets *dieres* as *hyperōon*, and "staircase and upper room" as <term>anōgeōn <note>original Greek: ἀνώγεων, literally "above the earth"</note></term>. In my copy, it is read thus: *hyperōon, hyperōon, anōgaion* room; *hyperōa, anōgaia*. This is correct. For the learned advise that it can be written both ways, as *anōgeōn* and *anōgaion*, unless perhaps *anōgaion* and *anagaion* <note>meaning "on the ground"</note> are confused. Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> writes: *Anōgeon* is a room. *Anagaion* and *katagaion* <note>underground</note> are written with a diphthong and a small 'o' <note>omicron</note>. *Anōgeon* is a **supper room situated in the upper part of the house**, whereas *anagaion* and *katagaion* are written with the diphthong *ei* and a small *o*.

<margin>
On this word *anagaion*.
</margin>
Let us also add the rest of what *Suidas* says: "Although the rules of grammar might dictate that the word *anōgeōn* be written quickly with a great 'o' <note>omega</note> and a smooth 'e' <note>epsilon</note>, nevertheless, that hunter of words and accurate master of the art of correct writing, **Master Coprogenius** <note>likely a reference to the scholar Constantine Porphyrogenitus, though "Coprogenius" is a mocking pun on his name</note>, who observed the accurate and correct method of exchanging these letters, handed down that this should be written with a smooth 'e' and a small 'o'." The word descends, as they believe, from *anō* (above) and *gaia* or *gē* (earth), because it signifies a chamber higher than the ground. It is called a **supper room** (*coenaculum*) by the Roman writers. To be sure, in ancient times the Romans were accustomed to **dine** (*coenare*) in the lower parts of their dwellings; but afterward, when they raised their houses to a greater height, they deemed it more dignified and magnificent to hold their dinners in some upper part of the building.

<margin>
In addition to Gregory, see Stuckius, *Antiquitates Convivales*, book II, chapter XI.
</margin>

### CHAPTER 6. AND ON DOMESTIC ORATORIES. 149

...you would wrongly conclude that the Hebrews dined on a flat, ground-level floor. In truth, the place in which Christ celebrated the Passover with his disciples is called in the Gospels an **upstairs room** <note>original Greek: ἀνώγεον, anōgeōn</note>; which *Erasmus* rendered as **dining room** <note>original Latin: triclinium</note>; *Beza* as **supper room** <note>original Latin: coenaculum</note>; and the Belgians as **upper hall** <note>original Dutch: Opperzale</note>. *Beza*, in his annotations,

<margin>Mark 14:15. Luke 22:12.</margin>
adds that **the Jews were accustomed to dine in that part of the house**. This is utterly rejected by the recently praised *Gregory*, because he believes the sacramental supper must be entirely distinguished from common and vulgar reclining. Indeed, *Gregory* even censures these words: **That the Jews were accustomed to have supper rooms of this kind, both for the reception of pilgrims and especially for the Passover.** "I do not wonder at the error," he says, "however great it may be; for since the sense of the **upper room** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑπερῷον, to hyperōon</note> was not correctly understood, it could hardly have happened otherwise than that they should err; but it was very badly done that they destined the same place for both uses, not to say profanely." I hesitate, however, whether we should yield to **Gregory** on this point. For why do we not interpret the **upstairs room** <note>original Latin: anōgeōn</note> here as a place in which the citizens of Jerusalem—as was their duty—received pilgrims with hospitality? For who is

<margin>in the place cited.</margin>
ignorant that **supper rooms** were destined for guest-lodgings? *Stuckius* will provide the testimonies. Indeed, who would believe that the **Passover** feast was celebrated by them anywhere else than in that part of the **house** where the Jews were accustomed to **dine**? But you may say: were the supper rooms, or the **upstairs upper rooms** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀνώγεον ὑπερῷον</note>, rooms consecrated for sacred exercises? Some were, indeed, but not all. For who could persuade us that the houses of all Jews were equipped with such supper rooms? And, if that were granted, who would assert that the houses of the Jews were only of two **stories**? Certainly, it seems altogether likely that **Paul spoke words to the faithful at Troas in a chamber on the third story**. For so it is read concerning **Eutychus**, who

<margin>Acts 20:9.</margin>
undoubtedly was present for Paul's oration: **he fell down from the third story** <note>original Greek: ἔπεσεν ἀπὸ τοῦ τριστέγου κάτω</note>. Therefore, if there was some **upstairs room** <note>original Latin: anōgeōn</note> on the second story, who could deny there was another, more sacred, on the third? Or if someone should refuse that, let them at least concede that the same story contained several chambers, among which nothing prevents one from being destined for sacred exercises and others for different uses. By another name, the **upper room** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑπερῷον</note> or **supper room** is sometimes called **chalcidicum** by Latin authors, even though the *Chalcidicum*, as described by *Isidore*, seems to differ from our **upper room** <note>original Greek: ὑπερῷῳ</note>. Nevertheless, I have found this noted by most learned men. *Turnebus* writes: **I also seem to have observed that the Chalcidicum**

<margin>Adversaria, Book 18, Chapter 34.</margin>
**is used for a supper room; for what Homer wrote;**

Salmasius, intending to explain the meaning of the word **upper room** <note>original Greek: ὑπερῷον, hyperōon</note>, wrote in the same vein: "There is no doubt that the *Chalcidicum* signified the **upper room** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑπερῷον</note>." Vossius suggested another passage from Arnobius: *"Your gods are described as dining and drinking in golden Chalcidica, and finally occupying themselves with stringed instruments and the melody of voices."* And it is certainly consistent with what has been said that the sacred dining room we are discussing was called a **Triclinium** <note>original Hebrew: טרקליין; a term borrowed from the Greco-Roman world referring to a dining room with three couches</note> by Hebrew writers. For Vossius has proved that **Triclinium** is used not only for the couches of the diners themselves, but also for the dining place of the house or the supper room.

<margin>
1 Kings 17:19. 2 Kings 4:10, verse 33.
</margin>

The chamber that the woman of Zarephath prepared for Elijah when he stayed with her seems to have been of this kind. For when her son had died, Elijah is said to have carried him away **into the upper chamber where he was staying** <note>original Hebrew: אל העליה אשר הוא יושב שם, el ha-aliyah asher hu yoshev sham</note>. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> renders this: **Into the upper room in which he sat** <note>original Greek: Εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον ἐν ᾧ αὐτὸς ἐκάθητο</note>. You may easily understand what kind of chamber this was, and with what instruments or furnishings it was equipped, from the things later narrated concerning Elisha. For when he frequently stayed at the house of the Shunammite woman—a woman of considerable means—she was so moved by the holiness of this Teacher that she urged her husband to build a supper room of this sort for Elisha's benefit: *"Let us make, I pray, a small **upper room with a wall**"* <note>original Hebrew: עלית קיר קטנה, aliyat kir ketannah</note>, *"and let us set there for him a bed, and a table, and a chair, and a lampstand."* <note>original Hebrew: ונשים לו שם מטה ושלחן וכסא ומנורה</note> The Septuagint again uses the word **upper room** <note>original Greek: ὑπερῷον</note>. It is clear enough that this chamber was intended for the prayers, sacred meditations, and studies of a most holy man; therefore, in the following verses, Elisha is read to have ascended into this inner sanctuary, and there, with the doors closed, he conversed alone with God.

<margin>
Daniel 6:10.
</margin>

Truly, no more distinguished or famous model of the Sacred Chamber occurs than that of Daniel; who, when King Darius had forbidden all petitions to be made to God or man for a space of thirty days except to himself alone, is read to have ascended in his usual manner **into his upper room** <note>original Aramaic/Hebrew: בעליתה, be-aliteh</note>, which was **facing Jerusalem** <note>original Hebrew: נגד ירושלם</note>, and equipped with **OPEN WINDOWS** <note>original Hebrew: כוין פתיחן</note>. Here, finally, you have the exact form and sketch of private oratories. It is a chamber, I say, located in a part of the house...

<margin>According to the common division of chapter 3. For the Hebrew text lacks [these] divisions.</margin>

Another passage, consistent with this, from the history of *Tobit*, was suggested by *John Gregory* <note>John Gregory (1607–1646) was an English orientalist and scholar known for his works on biblical archaeology.</note>. In that narrative, *Sarah*, the daughter of *Raguel*, overwhelmed by troubles, is introduced as having prayed to *God* in the upper room of her father's house, which was equipped with windows. These are the words as found in the edition of *Paul Fagius* <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549) was a German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew.</note>, which is the only one I currently possess; "And I prayed and said: Blessed be the Lord our God, and blessed be His great name, etc." <note>original Hebrew: ואתפלל ותאמר ברוך יהוה אלהינו וברוך שמו הגדול וגו'</note> *Then she went and fell prostrate* BEFORE THE WINDOW, *praying and saying: Blessed be Jehovah our God, and blessed be His great name.* Gregory reports that in other Hebrew copies it is written, (<term>she ascended</term> <note>original Hebrew: עלתה, altah</note>) *she ascended* <term>to her father's house</term> <note>original Hebrew: אביה, abiah</note> *to the upper room of her father*. The Pharisees displayed a singular piety by pouring out prayers <term>in the synagogues</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς</note>, in the Synagogues or *Public Oratories*. # ON SCHOOLS Book I. Part I.
<page-num>152</page-num>
<header>ON SCHOOLS Book I. Part I.</header>

...simply translates *dōma* <note>original Greek: δῶμα, meaning a house or, more specifically, a roof</note> as "upper parts." *Jerome*, *Erasmus*, *Price*, and others approve of this interpretation; they believe that *dōma* here means the same as the *upper room* <note>original Greek: τὸ ὑπερῷον (*to hyperōon*)</note> mentioned in other places. It is called *dōma*, they argue, because this bedchamber was located closest to the roof. However, <margin>II Samuel 11:13. II Kings 23:12.</margin> *Gregory* <note>Likely John Gregory, mentioned on the previous page</note> resists this, both because the *dōma* is distinguished elsewhere from the *upper room*, and because in this passage Peter is not said to have *gone up into the dōma*, but *onto the dōma*, which is equivalent to saying *onto the roof*. He judges, therefore, that this house of Simon the Tanner, being less spacious, lacked such a sacred upper room <note>original Latin: coenaculo</note>, and for that reason Peter, seeking a solitary place for retreat, climbed onto the roof itself. This opinion is not to be despised.

But the clearest evidence is found in what is reported in this same book of the *Acts of the Apostles* concerning the assembly of the first believers. <margin>Acts 1:13.</margin> *And when they had entered, after they had seen Christ carried into heaven, they went up into the upper room, where Peter and James were staying*, they ascended into the UPPER ROOM <note>original Latin: COENACULUM</note>, *where Peter and James were constantly remaining*, etc. The believers, one hundred and twenty in number, were gathered in a certain *upper room* <note>original Greek: ὑπερῴῳ (*hyperōō*)</note>, persevering, as the sacred text says, *with one accord in prayer and supplication*, continuing harmoniously in prayers and petitions. To what kind of house or what man did this upper room belong? For it must have been large and venerable to hold one hundred and twenty men. Here again, the opinions of the interpreters are divided. One scholar suspects it was in the house of *John the Evangelist*, *son of Zebedee*; another, that it was the house of *Mary*, mother of *John*, surnamed *Mark*: others generally think it probable that this <margin>Cave, On the Religion of Ancient Christians, book I, Chapter VI.</margin> is the same upper room in which Christ celebrated his final <term>Passover</term> <note>original Latin: θανάσιμον (*thanasimon*) Pascha, literally "mortal" or "final" Passover</note>, which is an opinion I now see is favored above the others by the most learned Mr. *Cave* <note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English church historian</note>.

But indeed, *Louis de Dieu* <note>A Dutch Protestant theologian and orientalist (1590–1642)</note> contends with great effort alongside the illustrious *Cloppenburg* <note>Johannes Cloppenburg (1592–1652), a Dutch theologian</note> that this upper room was <margin>See the Latin Critical Collections of Cloppenburg's Works, Part I, p. 350.</margin> one of the chambers of the Temple; a view from which I have already declared above that I am not entirely alienated. Among the greatest arguments of the most learned *de Dieu* is that *Luke*, speaking in his <margin>Mark 14:15.</margin> Gospel of this same retreat of the disciples, said that they returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and constantly celebrated God in the Temple: *and they were continually in the Temple praising and blessing God*; and *they were CONTINUALLY in the Temple praising* <margin>Chapter 24, verses 52, 53.</margin> *and celebrating God*. Observe, he says, the phrase *they were continually* <note>original Greek: ἦσαν διὰ παντὸς (*ēsan dia pantos*)</note>, whereas in the other place [Acts] it says *they were remaining* <note>original Greek: ἦσαν καταμένοντες (*ēsan katamenontes*)</note>. <margin>Volume II, Explanation of Ezekiel, Part II, book III, chapter XXVI. Selden, On the Sanhedrin, book II, chapter XVI, section II.</margin>

> The use of *exedrae* <note>hallways or meeting rooms with seating</note>, he says, is described by Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect of the 1st century BCE</note> in his descriptions of Greek gymnasiums. Spacious halls are established within three porticos, containing seats in which Philosophers, Rhetoricians, and others who take pleasure in studies can sit and dispute. Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note> thinks an *exedra* refers to a seating area where men are accustomed to sit together; though Cicero indicates it is a place where, having placed a couch, they might rest at midday. Regarding the seating, perhaps for that reason the Hebrews call the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and court of ancient Israel</note> an *exedra* <note>original Hebrew: *Lishkah*, meaning a chamber or hall</note>, because those seventy-two noble men sitting around would give judgment to the people and consult on the more difficult business to be conducted.

Yet there were many such chambers <note>original Hebrew: *lishkot*</note> in the Temple. I will not hide, therefore, that despite whatever *Gregory* might argue against it, I still lean toward the opinion of the distinguished *de Dieu*. Certainly, what aids the hypothesis of the illustrious *de Dieu* is that *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> calls these very Temple chambers *upper rooms* <note>original Greek: *hyperōa*</note>. For he certainly gives this name to the chamber in which *Ezra* sat with the other Princes of the Jewish Nation to investigate and judge the cases of forbidden marriages. He says it thus:
<margin>Antiquities, book XV, chapter V. Collected with Ezra chapter X:6.</margin>

Behold, an upper room of the Temple! Truly, whatever the truth of this matter may be, the opinion of the illustrious *de Dieu* deserves to be carefully weighed, and if not for its solidity, at least it should be praised for its ingenious invention and the beautiful appearance it presents.

These **seats** were protected by **lattices** <note>original Latin: *cancelli*; railings or screens</note>, outside of which other listeners from the common people—who took pleasure in hearing the disputes or sermons of the Teachers—were allowed to stand. 

To establish a **School** of more celebrated note (as the character of the Jewish Republic before its destruction by the Romans is depicted in the **Talmud** and **Jewish Histories**), these necessary **Persons** were generally required: 

1. The **Teacher** <note>original Latin: *Doctor*</note>, promoted to that dignity by the authority of the **Sanhedrin** <note>The supreme legal and religious council of ancient Israel</note>; 
2. The **Interpreter**, himself of lesser wisdom and status, who explained the Teacher's **words** to the listeners <note>The Interpreter, or *Meturgeman*, would repeat the softly spoken words of the sage in a loud, accessible voice for the crowd</note>; 
3. The **Colleagues**, who raised doubts to him and who sat in the **Sanhedrin** or the **judicial court** (though I would have this understood only regarding the most famous **Gymnasiums** <note>The author uses the Greek/Latin term for advanced schools</note>); 
4. The **Students**, who devoted their efforts to his discipline; 
5. And the **Ministers of the Academy**, who looked after the needs of the **School** and performed other necessary duties for the Teacher and disciples. 

The method of teaching was such: the **Colleagues** (learned men) and the **Studious Youths** would raise a **question** on this or that argument; the **Teacher**, through an **Interpreter**, would respond at length to it; or even, the **Teacher** himself would expand upon a **question** he had raised, and in its exposition, wander into any similar arguments. Let these things be said briefly as a sketch of the **ancient Schools**, each of which will now be illustrated more diligently—even if, admittedly, every difficulty in every part of this subject has not yet been removed for us. Nevertheless, let us see how far it is possible for us to proceed.

# Book I, Part I: ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS

First, it seems certain from the records of the *Talmudists* <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> that every *Sanhedrin* <note>A council or court of justice</note> had its own *lecture hall*, in which it explained the divine *Law*; the duty of teaching and explaining in that *lecture hall* was primarily performed by the Prince or President of the Senate, who for that reason was honored both as the *Rector of the Academy* and as the *President of the Senate*. Let us consider the words of *Maimonides* <note>The 12th-century philosopher and jurist Moses Maimonides, often called Rambam</note>, which we believe contain the proof of our opinion. He writes:

<margin>
Tractate Sanhedrin, chapter III, § 1.
</margin>
*How much time during the day did the Judges spend examining and deciding cases? The minor Sanhedrin and the three-man court sat from the end of the morning prayer until the end of the sixth hour of the day; however, the Great Senate of seventy-one men sat from the time of the morning sacrifice until the time of the evening sacrifice. But on Sabbaths and festival days, they sat in the Academy (the house of inquiry/study), which was on the Temple Mount.* <note>The original Latin translates the Hebrew "Temple Mount" as "Court of the Gentiles."</note> This definition by Maimonides is based on the

<margin>

This indeed seemed to be required by logic, though I will not hide the fact that this doubt occupied me for some time. For anyone who examines the *Talmudic* institutions or the histories of the succession of famous Doctors among them might doubt whether the very same place designated for judgment was not also designated for academic discussions. Certainly, the same person who was called the <term>Nasi</term> <note>Prince</note> in the Sanhedrins is called by another name, the <term>Rosh HaYeshiva</term> <note>Head of the Academy</note>, and in almost every case, the <term>Beth Midrash</term> <note>House of Disputation or Study</note> is attributed to them. Again, the *Rector* of the Academy is even today honored with the title <term>Av Beit Din</term> <note>Father of the Court</note>, even though the Jews now enjoy no Sanhedrins except for the *Academies* in which they teach the law. In the courts, the Senators sat according to their rank in a noble area in a semi-circle; two scribes stood at the extreme ends of this semi-circle, who recorded the opinions of those acquitting and those condemning. A fixed and decorous order was observed in asking for votes: in capital cases from the lowest to the highest, and in other matters from the opposite direction. # ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS BOOK 1. PART 1.

Proof from the Torah <note>original Hebrew: *Torah*</note> is not fitting for one to sit in the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and legislative council of ancient Israel</note>. One time, a practical matter arose among them, and they did not know how to bring a proof from the Torah, except for one elder who was babbling against him <note>Simeon ben Shetach</note>. He said to him, "Give me time, and tomorrow I will answer you." He gave him time. He went and sat by himself, and when he saw that he did not know how to bring proof from the Torah, the next day he was ashamed to come and sit in the Sanhedrin. Simeon ben Shetach then stood up and placed one of the students in his place and seated him there. He said to them, "The Sanhedrin cannot have fewer than seventy-one members." And he did this every single day until they were all removed, and the Sanhedrin of Israel sat according to its own judgment. And on that day when the Sanhedrin of the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect that often disagreed with the Pharisees on the interpretation of the Law</note> was removed and the Sanhedrin of Israel was established, they made it a festival day.

*The twenty-eighth day of the month of Tevet. The assembly of the Synagogue (or of the Great Sanhedrin) for the cause of the Jews. The reason for the festival is this: The Sadducees had once occupied the seats of the Great Sanhedrin, while King Jannaeus <note>Alexander Jannaeus, the Hasmonean King (r. 103–76 BCE)</note> and Queen Salome <note>Salome Alexandra (r. 76–67 BCE)</note> presided.*

<margin>Maimonides, Laws of the Sanhedrin, Chapter 2, Section 3.</margin>

*In these councils, where there is a vacancy, according to the words of Maimonides:* "And they do not seat a King of Israel in the Sanhedrin, because it is forbidden to disagree with him or to rebel against his word" <note>original Hebrew: ואין מושיבין מלך ישראל בסנהדרין שאסור לחלוק עליו ולמרות את דברו</note>. *Indeed, no one from the Israelites <note>Here referring to the Pharisaic tradition</note> sat with them as a member of the Sanhedrin except for Simeon ben Shetach. They used to ask for legal answers and definitions, yet no probable reason was ever brought forward from the Law. But Simeon, the son of Shetach, said to them: "Anyone who can confirm his opinion with probable reasons drawn from the Law is worthy to be a member of this illustrious Council; but anyone who does not know how to fortify his opinion with proofs from the Law is by no means worthy to be counted among the members of the Sanhedrin."*

*It happened, however, that they debated a certain case among themselves, and yet they did not know how to bring proof from the Law, except for a single Elder, who was boldly throwing out many arguments to the contrary. Eventually, he said to him (Rabbi Joshua <note>The text here attributes the speech to "R. Josua," likely Joshua ben Perachiah, though the narrative primarily concerns his student Simeon ben Shetach</note>), "Grant me time, and by tomorrow my answer will be ready." He (Rabbi Joshua) granted him time. He went away, therefore, and deliberated alone with himself about what he should answer. But after he saw that he was not sufficient to produce a proof from the Law to be brought forward the next day, shame prevented him from coming into the Senate and occupying his usual seat. Therefore, Rabbi Simeon, the son of Shetach, ordered one of the legal candidates to occupy his place, on this pretext: that the Great Sanhedrin cannot consist of fewer than seventy-one Senators. He observed this same method of acting toward the rest of them as well, until all those men of the Sadducean faction were removed from the Sanhedrin, and the Sanhedrin sat according to...*

### Chapter 7. Concerning the ACADEMIES.

...settled into its own system. On that day, when all the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect that often disagreed with the Pharisees on the interpretation of the Law</note> were moved out of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and legislative council of ancient Israel</note>, and the Sanhedrin once again consisted solely of Israelites—that is, of Senators belonging to the Pharisaic sect—they established a festival day. Consequently, questions were asked and debates were held within the Sanhedrins themselves whenever the Senators encountered difficult cases. Indeed, I believe we need not look elsewhere for the reason why three rows of Candidates <note>Students or junior scholars in training</note> sat on lower benches in the Sanhedrins of Twenty-Three <note>The smaller local courts composed of twenty-three judges</note> (if this tradition is to be believed, which I will not dispute now). It was so they might diligently observe various judicial cases and thus gradually become accustomed to legal judgments. I should also mention that if the Senators were stuck or if their votes were insufficient, some of these Candidates were joined to the Senators to help define a legal opinion alongside them. To this point also belongs the fact that, according to the Rules of the Talmudists <note>Scholars who compiled the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>, no one was admitted among the Senators of the Sanhedrin who was not equally fit for teaching the law as he was for pronouncing judgment.

I have no doubt, therefore, that debating and disputing took place within the Sanhedrins; however, a clear distinction between the **Courts of Judgment** and the **Academies** <note>Schools of higher learning</note> remained quite notable while the **Hebrew Republic** was standing and flourishing. But when jurisdiction was cut short or taken away from the Jews by the Romans and their Republic was overturned, I admit that the Sanhedrins and the Academic Lecture Halls became confused and blended together. I believe we should understand that most famous passage, which has long since been cited from the decrees of the Talmudists by various scholars of this discipline, as referring to those settings:

*The tradition is that the entire people were accustomed to rise whenever the* **Prince** *entered, and did not sit back down until he had said to them, "Be seated." When the* **Father of the Sanhedrin** *entered, they made a path on both sides (so says* Selden; *more accurately: they made two rows of people rising, according to the illustrious* Wagenseil) *until he had sat down in his place. # BOOK I. PART I. CONCERNING PUBLIC SCHOOLS

<margin>In the place cited</margin>
Furthermore, it pertains to their singular honor and majesty that the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> write of the supreme reverence publicly shown to them, with which they were usually received whenever they entered **CERTAIN ASSEMBLIES, WHETHER JUDICIAL OR SACRED**. I, however, as I have already suggested, think this statement should be understood entirely as referring to the Academies or the Sanhedrins <note>The supreme councils or high courts</note> of later times, and not to just any judicial courts from the era when the Republic was flourishing. For the things related in this text and those following (which you will see excerpted by the illustrious Cocceius) concern the fact that the people sat on the ground; that the children of the Senators assisted their parents; and that *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Nathan* conspired to present a more difficult subject of discourse to *Rabbi Simeon, son of Gamaliel*, the Prince of the Senate and the Academy (who first defined the degrees of honor to be shown to himself and other Senators). In my judgment, these details sufficiently argue that the discussion here concerns the Academies or the lecture halls of the Jewish Doctors as they existed once the Republic had already been diminished or overthrown; for indeed, that very *Simeon, son of Gamaliel*, died in his term as Prince just before the destruction of Jerusalem.

<margin>On the Sotah, chapter VII, page 816.</margin>
For this reason, the illustrious Wagenfeil also interpreted the word <term>Nasi <gloss>Prince or President</gloss></term> in this passage as <term>Aichmalotarch <gloss>original: "Aichmalotarcham"; the Leader of the Captives or Exilarch</gloss></term>. That a public Academy or School should be attributed to the supreme Sanhedrin is not a recent fiction. For it is hardly possible that when they speak of the ancient Rulers of their Republic—almost all of whom they consider both Judges and Doctors—they would not also mention such Schools or Academies. This will become clear from the following discussion on the origin of the Synagogue. The only thing to consider now was whether the smaller Sanhedrins also possessed such <term>Houses of Disputation <gloss>original Hebrew: "Batei Midrashot"</gloss></term> for public use.

<margin>Book II on the Sanhedrin, chapter X, section II.</margin>
*Seldenus* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note> does not think this should be doubted. Nor do we doubt it much ourselves, because since the Talmudists count three hundred and ninety-four, or even more, Synagogues in Jerusalem (as observed above), they add to them an equal number of <term>Houses of Judgment <gloss>original Hebrew: "Batei Dinin"</gloss></term> and **Houses of Disputation**.

<margin>Prolegomena, Chapter IV.</margin>
But what was the reason for such a great association between the Academies and the judicial Courts? I have no explanation other than this: that after the destruction of the Jewish Republic, the judicial Courts were transformed into Academies. It appears from their chronicles that after the overthrow of Jerusalem, the Sanhedrins remained intact in the land of **Canaan**. However, their jurisdiction was taken away from them. ...since the faculty of teaching was granted to the same people to whom jurisdiction was entrusted. If these words of the Most Learned Man <note>Refers to John Selden, mentioned on the previous page</note> are to be understood regarding that interval of time following the destruction of the Jewish Republic by the Romans, then I subscribe to them entirely. But if, as it seems, they are to be applied to all times of the Republic, even when it was flourishing, then I confess I hesitate at them. Jewish writers sometimes speak of this topic so ambiguously that I have often been pulled now in this direction, now in that, before I could satisfy my mind in defining it. For they are accustomed to speak of the <term>Sanhedrins <gloss>councils of elders</gloss></term>, as they were when the Republic flourished, in the same way that the Sanhedrins truly behaved after the Republic was overturned. I, however, would by no means believe, not even based on the plausible-sounding sayings of the <term>Talmudists <gloss>scholars of Jewish law</gloss></term>, that while the Republic of the Jewish Nation flourished, the Sanhedrins conducted themselves in the manner of *Schools*, as I have already declared. Furthermore, the form of these *Schools* is not obscure in itself, and you will understand it well from those things which we will soon intersperse in the treatment of *Doctors and the Mode of Teaching*. Indeed, how great is the **holiness of the Schools**, seeing as it even exceeds the **holiness of the Synagogues**; how much reverence must be shown to them! For instance, *one must not sleep in them*; *nothing but sacred matters are to be meditated upon in them*; *one is not to offer a blessing to someone sneezing*, and many similar rules. You will find these handed down in an accessible style by <term>Maimonides <gloss>a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</gloss></term>.

In these **Academies**, the highest power of teaching and the principal exercise of that power belonged to the **Rector of the Academy or Prince** <note>The Hebrew title is *Nasi*</note>, whom it behooved to be so practiced in all the minutiae of traditions that he could answer promptly to all proposed questions and continually clear up any difficulties thrown his way and discourse upon them. ### CHAPTER 7. OR CONCERNING ACADEMIES.
<meta>catchword: To Men,</meta>

*Our Masters say:* FROM THE DAYS OF MOSES UNTIL RABBAN GAMALIEL <note>Rabban Gamaliel the Elder was a leading authority in the Sanhedrin in the early 1st century and is mentioned in the Book of Acts as the teacher of Paul the Apostle.</note>, THEY DID NOT LEARN THE LAW EXCEPT STANDING; but FROM THE TIME RABBAN GAMALIEL DIED, a sickness <note>original: "morbus," likely referring to a decline in physical stamina or spiritual vigor</note> descended into the world, AND THEY LEARNED THE LAW SITTING; and this is that which they say: *From the time Rabban Gamaliel died, the Glory of the Law ceased.* <margin>Sotah, Chapter 9, § 15.</margin> These final words appear in the *Mishna Sotah* <note>A tractate of the Mishna, the first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note>. Regarding this "sickness" which they say <margin>Lightfoot on Matthew 13:2.</margin> invaded the world from the time of Gamaliel, you should understand it to mean that the bodies of the disciples were so weakened that they were no longer <margin>Alting, *Shiloh*, Book 4, Chapter 3.</margin> capable of enduring such standings. But I truly doubt whether sufficient faith should be placed in this tradition. For the more I weigh it, the more it seems to me to be of the genre of exaggerations <note>original Greek: τῶν ὑπερβολῶν (tōn hyperbolōn), meaning rhetorical overstatements</note>. In the history of the New <margin>Wagenseil on Sotah.</margin> Testament, both [postures] are predicated of the Lord's listeners: both that they sat and that they stood. You have an example of standing in the *Gospel of Matthew* in these words: *On that day, Jesus went out of the house,* <margin>Chapter 13:2.</margin> AND SAT BY THE SEA, *and a great crowd was gathered to him, so that he entered into a ship and sat; and the whole crowd stood on the shore* <note>original: ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ πλοῖον ἐμβάντα καθῆσθαι· καὶ πᾶς ὁ ὄχλος ἐπὶ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν εἱστήκει</note>. The same is found in Mark. <margin>Chapter 4:1.</margin> No other example of standing is brought forward from the writings of the New Testament that I know of. But who does not see that this case is entirely singular? For since Christ sat in a boat—a place surely not very elevated—it could hardly have happened that the listeners, who occupied the nearby shore, would have understood his words unless they received them while standing on their feet. Otherwise, it seems to be established from the whole of Scripture that the disciples sat on lower benches, or lay upon mats at the feet of the Teachers, who sat in a higher chair. There is a very clear testimony of this in *Mark*, who specifically relates that Christ taught the sitting crowd. *And a crowd sat around him* <margin>Chapter 3:32.</margin>—so the text of Mark has it <note>original: Καὶ ἐκάθητο... ὄχλος περὶ αὐτόν</note>. Yet surely this was done before the death of Gamaliel; nor is it likely that the listeners of Christ the Lord showed less reverence to their Teacher than was customary in that time. Nor do I doubt that this very custom of the disciples sitting can be clearly proven from the SITTING OF CHRIST in the midst <margin>Luke 2:46.</margin> of the Teachers <note>original: ἐν μέσῳ τῶν διδασκάλων</note>, *listening to them and questioning them* <note>original: ἀκούοντος αὐτῶν καὶ ἐπερωτῶντος αὐτοὺς</note>. I know there are some among the most learned...

## ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS Book I. PART I.

To those men who believe that Christ the Lord appeared in this assembly of Teachers not as a *disciple*, but as a *Teacher* <note>original: "Doctorem," referring to the learned Jewish elders in the Temple</note>: truly, they do not gain my agreement. For although I would not wish to detract in any way from the supreme progress made by Christ at such a tender age, I find it quite difficult to believe that a twelve-year-old youth, unknown (as it seems) to the **Teachers** and appearing in the *School* by chance, would have been received by them as a **Teacher**. To *listen* was the role of the **Teacher**, and to *ask questions* was the role of the disciple. Indeed, **Christ** questioned the **Teachers** as a disciple, and *heard their responses*, and, as occasion allowed, he examined and debated them—an activity that was permitted to any student of truth in the Jewish Schools. Therefore, he sat as a *disciple*, not as a *Teacher*. Nor am I easily persuaded that anything else is meant by what Paul says in his 
<margin>Acts 22:3.</margin>
defense before the people of Jerusalem: *brought up at the feet of Gamaliel* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἀνατεθραμμένον παρὰ τοὺς πόδας Γαμαλιήλ"</note>. For what can be understood more simply by that expression than that Paul the 
<margin>Observations, book III, chapter II.</margin>
Apostle *sat down at the feet of Gamaliel as a disciple*? To be sure, the **most learned Petit** <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar known for his work on ancient laws.</note> argues at length to the contrary; he thinks that these words indicate only that *Paul was nourished in the house of Gamaliel*, and thus lay down at the same table at his feet. What shall I say? To me, the speech seems much clearer and 
<margin>On the Sotah, chapter IX, p. 994.</margin>
simpler if I take it to refer to his instruction. The most excellent **Wagenseil** <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist who wrote a famous commentary on the Mishnaic tractate Sotah.</note>, who generally grants to **Petit** the truth of this Talmudic tradition regarding the *standing of disciples until the death of Gamaliel*, prefers to think that this is a modest self-extenuation by Paul. In this view, *Paul does not arrogantly boast that he was a companion and intimate of Gamaliel, sharing all things sacred and profane with him, but rather humbly and submissively confesses that he sat cast down as if at the feet of a great Teacher, gathering his food in that way.* Nevertheless, it is certain that **Petit** less successfully resolved another difficulty that is easily raised against this opinion. This difficulty comes from a fairly common phrase: *to cover oneself in the dust of the feet of the wise men*, which is taken from the aphorism of **Jose, son of Joezer**, a **Teacher** of ancient times. Thus we read in the *Pirke* <note>Referring to the Pirke Avoth, or "Ethics of the Fathers," a collection of ethical teachings from the Mishna.</note>:
<margin>Pirke Avoth, chapter I, § IV.</margin>
*Let your house be a house of meeting for the Wise, and COVER YOURSELF IN THE DUST OF THEIR FEET, and drink in their words with thirst.* <note>original Hebrew: "יהי ביתך בית ועד לחכמים והוי מתאבק בעפר רגליהם והוי שותה בצמא את דבריהם"</note> What does it mean here, "to cover oneself in the dust of the feet of the wise—"

### CHAPTER 7. Or, ON ACADEMIES.

...of the wise, than to fall upon the very soil which the Teachers sprinkle with the dust of their feet; or to sit at the feet of the Teachers, who are placed in a higher chair, and in this way receive their words?

<margin>Luke 10:39.</margin>
It is almost exactly as is preached concerning *Mary*: <note>original Greek: "παρακαθίσασα παρὰ τοὺς πόδας τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ἤκουε τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ"</note> *sitting at the feet of Jesus, she heard his word*. What does *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar of ancient law.</note> say about this phrase? He claims that the word *dust* <note>original Hebrew: "אבק" (abaq)</note> is equivalent in its meaning to *wrestling*. He suggests that this metaphor indicates that *even in times of relaxation and play, one must not let go of any wisdom and learning which they have acquired from constant association with the wise*. However, *Petit* proves this meaning of the word *dust* with no actual example. Furthermore, there is no reason in the words themselves to suggest this explanation. Indeed, what is more, it is a very crude and unpolished metaphor to compare *relaxation from work* with *wrestling matches*. The celebrated *Wagenzeil* <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist.</note> thinks instead that this expression recommends *humility* to the students. But that does not contradict our opinion. It was a mark of humility to *sit on the ground* before one's instructors, and to adopt that posture while learning.

<margin>Review of the Three Sects by Nicolaus Serarius, chapter 5.</margin>
We therefore embrace with both arms the opinion of *Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of the Renaissance.</note>, who interprets this phrase as referring to disciples *lying down on the ground*, and he illustrates this from other sources as well.

<margin>In the Lexicon at the word "dust" (abaq).</margin>
We have seen *Buxtorf* <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a famous scholar of Hebrew and Jewish tradition.</note> concede to the same side. But the most learned *Alting* <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a Dutch philologist and theologian.</note> confirms this explanation of *Scaliger* by the authority of the Masters, even if he himself does not entirely say goodbye to this Talmudic tradition for that reason.

<margin>In "Shiloh," book 3, chapters 6, 5, and vs. book 3. Genesis 49:10.</margin>
However, if you compare the things he has learnedly gathered for the explanation of the phrase <note>original Hebrew: "מבין רגליו" (mibein raglav)</note> *from between his feet*—which is part of the prophecy of the Patriarch *Jacob* concerning *Shiloh*—you will observe that it is not possible to satisfy so many passages of Scripture as he has cited if you suppose that the disciples anciently stood. For even if you imagine the Teacher sitting in a Chair, if you nonetheless conceive of the disciples standing, how could you say that the <note>original Hebrew: "מחוקק" (mechokek)</note> *Lawgiver* or Teacher is *between the feet* of the disciples? How much more easily is the whole matter understood if you establish that the disciples sat or lay upon the ground, and that the Teachers had their chairs placed between the disciples' feet? Truly, as far as I am concerned, I believe that the author of the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians* (who carries the name of *Ambrose* <note>This refers to "Ambrosiaster," an anonymous 4th-century author whose works were long attributed to St. Ambrose.</note>) hit the nail on the head when he recorded these words:

<margin>Commentary on 1 Corinthians 14.</margin>
> *This is the tradition of the Synagogue: that they dispute while sitting; the seniors in dignity in Chairs, those following on benches, and the newest on the pavement upon mats.*
