Yom Tov ben Abraham, in his marginal notes to the text of *Maimonides*, defends this latter part of *Maimonides's* teaching against Rabbi *Abraham ben David* <note>Also known as the Ra'avad (c. 1125–1198), a famous critic and contemporary of Maimonides.</note>, who, as is his usual habit, had found fault with it. The objection of Rabbi *Abraham* is this: **"This is a new thing; for behold Rav, who acted as the Interpreter for Rabbi Shila, changed and added to his words, because he was greater than him."** <note>original: "דבר זה חדש הוא וכי רב שעמד תורגמן לרבי שילא שנתן והוסיף מפני שהיה גדול ממנו". This refers to a famous incident in the Talmud (Yoma 20b) where the great scholar Rav served as an interpreter but, due to his superior knowledge, corrected the teacher.</note> But *Yom Tov* observes quite correctly regarding this critic’s annotation that the case brought as an objection is entirely singular; therefore, this very opposition serves more to confirm the opinion of *Maimonides* than to weaken it. For *Maimonides* transmits the common and fixed law in his Definitions, not caring much for what was done on this or that unique occasion contrary to the common customs of the School.

That it was indeed among the customs of the School that the *Interpreter* be lower in rank than the *Teacher* explaining the lesson, and that he was not permitted to depart from the *Teacher's* views, you may clearly gather from those things which are taught in the *Sotah* <note>A tractate of the Babylonian Talmud (Sotah 40a).</note> concerning the rare gentleness of the celebrated Teachers Rabbi *Abba* of Acco and Rabbi *Abbahu*. The former is praised for this reason:

**"that when he himself had stated a certain reasoning in teaching, and the Interpreter had pronounced a different reasoning, he nevertheless did not become angry."** <note>original: "דאיתו אמ' חדא טעמא ואמר אמוריה חד טעמא ולא קפיד".</note> What of it? Surely Rabbi *Abba* would have achieved nothing worthy of praise if it had been lawful for the Interpreter to dissent from the Teacher while preaching. 

Truly, the remarkable gentleness of the latter [Rabbi Abbahu] is commended for this reason: **"When the wife of the interpreter of Rabbi Abbahu said to the wife of Rabbi Abbahu: 'That man of ours (my husband) has no need at all for that man of yours (your husband); and as for the fact that he bows and rises before him, he does it only out of respect for the government.' The wife went and reported this to Rabbi Abbahu; but he replied: 'What does it matter to you? Through me and through him the Most High is praised, etc.'"** <note>original: "ואמרה ליה דביתהו דאמוריה דר' אבהו...". This story illustrates Abbahu's humility; even when told his interpreter claimed to be the superior scholar, he remained unbothered as long as God was being honored.</note> It is clear from this example that Interpreters were generally lower in dignity than the Teachers who were preaching. For Rabban Gamaliel the Second, who acted as the President of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme rabbinic court and legislative body</note> after the overthrow of the Jewish State, did not get along very well with *Rabbi Joshua*, the son of Hananiah, who was called the *Father* of the same Senate <note>The 'Av Beit Din', or the second-highest ranking member of the court</note>. "But," said Gamaliel, "it has been reported to me that you do disagree. We determine that there are four *major parts of the Synagogue* that concern our purpose—that is, the sacred instruments of its ministry, which are called in the Jerusalem Talmud the "vessels of the house of assembly" <note>original: "כלי בית הכנסת" (Klei Beit HaKnesset)</note>:

I. The **Ark**, in which the *Book of the Law* <note>The Torah scroll</note> is kept.

IV. The **Lamps**, by which the Synagogues are lit.

# CHAPTER 8. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

<meta>catchword: Synagogue-</meta>

<margin>Shulchan Aruch, chapter 150, section 5.</margin>
Regarding the gates: **“They do not open the entrance of the synagogue except on the side opposite to the direction in which they pray in that city. Thus, if they pray toward the west, they should open it to the east, so that they may bow from the entrance toward the Ark, which is in the direction they face during prayer.”** <note>original Hebrew: "אין פותחין פתח בית הכנסת אלא כנגד הצד שמתפללין בו באותה העיר באם מתפללין למערב יפתחוהו למזרח כדי שישתחוו מן הפתח נגד הארון שהוא ברוח שמתפללין נגדו"</note> By the word **Ark** <note>original Hebrew: "ארון" (Aron)</note>, as is clear, we must here understand the *box or chest* in which the *Scrolls of the Law* <note>original Latin: "Volumina Legis"</note> and their accessories and ornaments are preserved. Elsewhere, it is called the **Sanctuary** <note>original Hebrew: "היכל" (Heikhal)</note> or the **Chest** <note>original Hebrew: "תיבה" (Teivah)</note>.

<margin>Shulchan Aruch, Title 153, section 2.</margin>
We can learn both of these names from another certain Rule: **“The inhabitants of a city who sell a synagogue may use its price to acquire for themselves a Chest—that is, the Sanctuary in which they place the Scroll of the Law—or a table upon which they stand the Scroll of the Law.”** <note>original Hebrew: "בני העיר שמכרו בית הכנסת יכולין ליקח בדמיו תיבה דהיינו היכל שמניחין בו ספר תורה או לוח שמעמדין עליו ספר תורה"</note>

<margin>Chapter 4, section 1. On the Sanhedrin, book 3, chapter 16, section 1.</margin>
It is explained in this place <term>incidentally</term> <note>original Greek: "παρεγκυκλῶς" (parengkyklos), meaning 'in passing' or 'by way of a circuitous explanation'</note> what is to be understood by the term *Chest* <note>original Hebrew: "תיבה" (Teivah)</note> in the text of the *Megillah* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning the Scroll of Esther</note>, the words of which are repeated in the earlier part of this Rule.

<margin>Notes on the Arba’ah Turim: in this place.</margin>
The word **Chest** <note>original: "תיבה" (Teivah)</note>, says Rabbi Joseph Karo <note>A famous 16th-century legal scholar and author of the Shulchan Aruch</note>, is the **Sanctuary** <note>original: "היכל" (Heikhal)</note>, *that sacred shrine of the synagogue* (as elsewhere the term *Heikhal* was most elegantly translated by John Selden) in which the *Scroll of the Law is stored*. He adds, however, that this word also signifies the *table upon which the Scroll of the Law is placed*. Truly, as he himself notes elsewhere, the disciples of Rabbi Jonah <note>A prominent 13th-century Spanish rabbi</note> are the authorities for this meaning of the word *Teivah* where it is taken for a *table* or *reading desk*: **“The disciples of Rabbi Jonah explained that it is the table upon which they stand the Scroll of the Law throughout the year which is called a Chest.”** <note>original Hebrew: "ופי’ תלמידי הר’ יונה שהוא שלחן שמעמידין בו ספר תורה כל השנה נקרא תיבה"</note>

<margin>John 12:6. Drusius, book 2, Question 74. Waser, On Ancient Hebrew Coins, book 1, chapter 19. Megillah, folio 36, column 2, after the middle.</margin>
*The disciples of Rabbi Jonah say, indeed, that the reading desk, upon which the Scroll of the Law is kept throughout the whole year, is called a* **Chest** <note>original: "תיבה" (Teivah)</note>. Yet upon what foundation this was done by them, I do not know. For it certainly cannot be denied that the more common use of the word *Teivah* among the Hebrews is for an *ark* or *chest*. For this reason, it is compared by other authors with the Greek <term>glossokomon</term> <note>original Greek: "γλωσσόκομον", a case or casket, originally for the mouthpieces of flutes, later used for money boxes</note> (in the Megillah it is written as *gluskama* <note>original Hebrew: "גלוסקמא"</note>—and is used for a *bag*, *small compartment*, or *repository*), which signifies an *ark*, *chest*, or *purse*. Nor would I think that where mention is made of the synagogue in the writings of the Jews, it can ever be more appropriately explained than as a *Book Ark*. And thus I approve of how Constantinus l’Empereur <note>A prominent 17th-century Dutch scholar of Hebrew</note> interpreted this word in his work on Benjamin [of Tudela] while he was describing the Synagogue of Ezekiel.

<margin>In the Itinerary, page 78.</margin>
The words of Benjamin are: **“And in the courtyard of the synagogue is the Ark.”** <note>original Hebrew: "ובחצר הכנסת התיבה" (U-ve-chatzer ha-knesset ha-teivah)</note>

The synagogue is a repository for sacred books. For as our same Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> later says: **“And there is a certain large and holy house there, full of books, where books from both the First and Second Temple are preserved; whoever lacks children consecrates their books there.”** <note>original Hebrew: "ושם בית גדול של הקדש והוא מלא ספרים ומבית ראשון ומבית שני יש שם ספרים וכל שאין לו בן יקדיש ספרו לשם" / original Latin: "Ibidem sancta quædam magnaque domus, libris plena, est, ubi etiam cum e prima tum e secunda æde libri servantur; quicunque verò liberis carent, ibi libros suos consecrant."</note> This passage is praised elsewhere by *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel, a 15th-century statesman and philosopher.</note>.

Furthermore, although a doubt was once cast upon me from another source as to whether the phrase **“passing before the chest”** <note>original Hebrew: "עבור לפני התיבה" (Avoor Lifnei Ha-Teivah)</note> might not denote a *pulpit* or *reading desk* in that famous expression, **“to go around before the Ark,”** I am now most thoroughly persuaded and entirely certain that the ordinary meaning of the word holds in this case no less than in other similar ones; thus, **“to pass before the Ark”** or **“to go down before the Ark”** <note>original Hebrew: "ירד לפני התיבה" (Yarad Lifnei Ha-Teivah)</note> means to come forward or proceed before the Ark—that is, the Book-Chest—to recite the prayers, as is still the custom among the Jews today.

But we shall speak of this more distinctly later, when we interpret this phrase more clearly and certainly than in the past. In the Tractate *Megilla*, you may find the word **Chest** <note>original Aramaic: "תיבותא" (Teivota)</note> used in exactly the same sense in these words: <margin>folio 26, column 2.</margin> **“And Rabba said: From a broken larger Ark, one may make a smaller Ark; but to make a chair <note>The author uses the Latin "pulpitum" here, referring to a seat or lower-status platform.</note> is forbidden.”** <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: "ואמר רבא האי תיבותא דאיפגם מעבדי' תיבה זוטרתי; שרי כורסיא אסור" / original Latin: "Et dixit Rabba; Ex Arcâ ruptâ majore licet facere Arcam minorem; at verò pulpitum facere, vetitum est."</note> What is written as **Chest** <note>original Aramaic: "תיבותא"</note> in the text of the Gemara, *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> explained as **Ark** <note>original Hebrew: "ארון" (Aron)</note>. The words of *Maimonides* will soon be brought forward when we deal with the platform. Nor is the word **Chest** <note>original Hebrew: "תיבה" (Teivah)</note> understood otherwise in the Tractate *Taanith*: <margin>Tractate Taanith, chapter 2, section 1.</margin> **“What is the procedure for observing fast-days? They bring out the Ark into the city square and place burnt ashes upon the Ark, as well as on the head of the Prince and on the head of the Father of the Court, etc.”** <note>original Hebrew: "סדר תעניות כיצד מוציאין את התיבה לרחובה של עיר ונותנין אפר מקלה על גבי התיבה ובראש הנשיא ובראש אב בית דין וכו'" / original Latin: "Qua jejuniorum celebrandorum ratio est? Producunt arcam in plateam Civitatis, & ponunt cinerem adustionis super Arcâ: nec non in capite Principis, & in capite Patris Senatus."</note> For what is the **Chest** here? <margin>On this passage.</margin> Let *Bartenora* <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah.</note> say: **“The Ark in which the Scroll of the Law is placed.”** <note>original Hebrew: "הארון שס"ת מונח בו"</note> Of a related, though broader, meaning is the name **Ark** <note>original Hebrew: "ארון" (Aron)</note>; for it denotes, if I am not mistaken, any box or case in which sacred books are stored. So it is in the <margin>On Megilla, Chapter 43.</margin> definitions of *Rabbi Asher*: **“A chest in which they place the Law of Moses or a Fifth Part of it <note>A "Chumash," or one of the five individual books of the Torah.</note> is to be considered a sacred instrument.”** <note>original Hebrew: "ארגז שנותנים בו ספר תורה או חומש תשמיש קדושה היא" / original Latin: "Capsa, in quâ reponunt Legem Mosis aut Quintanam ejus Partem, pro instrumento sacro habenda est."</note> Likewise, <margin>Chapter 54, section 3.</margin> the word occurs in the *Orach Chaim* <note>The section of the Shulchan Aruch dealing with daily ritual law.</note>, where the sacred instruments of the synagogue are enumerated. ### CHAPTER 8. OF SYNAGOGUES. 177

The word *kamtrin* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: קמטרין</note> is explained as a "chest" <note>original Hebrew: ארגז (*argaz*)</note> by Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note>. The words of the tractate *Megillah* <note>A volume of the Talmud concerning the festival of Purim and the reading of the Scroll of Esther.</note> state: **“And Raba said: The wraps for the Five Books of Moses and the chests for the sacred books are to be considered as holy vessels, and therefore they must be hidden away <note>The Hebrew term *genizah* refers to the practice of storing away worn-out sacred texts rather than destroying them.</note>.”** In explaining the word *kamtrin*, Rabbi Solomon says: **“By *kamtrin*, understand a chest, which they call a shrine <note>original: אשקרייניי (*escrin* in Old French / *scrinium* in Latin), a term for a box or case for scrolls.</note>; if I am not mistaken, this is how that foreign word should be rendered, a meaning which is frequent in the Translation of Jonathan son of Uziel.”** <note>The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Prophets.</note>

But, as I have said, *kamtrin* and *argaz* can be taken here to mean any box in which the Book of the Law is stored in the Synagogue. Other common names, already listed, are *Aron* <note>Ark</note>, *Teivah* <note>Chest</note>, and *Heichal* <note>Palace/Temple</note>. The first two terms directly describe the book-chest itself, while the latter more generally denotes the entire holy sanctuary—often large and majestic, as you may see in the Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam—which was built for the sake of housing this repository.

<margin>
On the Female Habit, chapter 11, near the end.
</margin>
Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD.</note> called this sacred synagogue vessel an *Armarium* <note>A Latin term for a cupboard, closet, or chest.</note>. His words are: **“I know that the Scripture of Enoch, which assigned this order to the angels, is not received by some, because it is not admitted into the Jewish *Armarium*.”** This is correct, in my opinion. For to Latin writers, *Armarium* denotes a place where books are stored.

<margin>
Page 213.
</margin>
I learned this from Lotichius <note>Peter Lotichius, a classical scholar.</note>, whose comments on Petronius <note>A Roman novelist.</note> are as follows: **“An *armarium* is a place where books are stored; just as an *armamentarium* is where arms are kept.”** Furthermore, he cites the authority of Perrottus <note>Niccolò Perotti, a Renaissance humanist.</note>, whose words serve us excellently: **“To this,”** he says, **“*armaria* are inserted into the walls of houses, as are *armamentaria*, no less usefully than elegantly. *Armaria* are properly the places in which books are stored.”** Indeed, those Synagogue repositories are also commonly built into the very walls of the synagogues themselves. Nor would you inappropriately use the word *Arca* <note>Chest/Ark</note> here; for with that word, Livy <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian.</note> designated the compartment in which the books of Numa Pompilius were stored and preserved.

# ON THE STRUCTURE [OF THE SYNAGOGUE] BOOK I. PART I. 178

...[it was reported] by Jews who had come to believe, and they described it to us in great detail. Furthermore, there is a report that the book of the Acts of the Apostles was likewise translated from the Greek tongue into Hebrew and is kept there in the treasuries <note>original Greek: *gazophylakiois*; repositories for books or wealth</note>. *And again, it has been reported by others that the Gospel of John, having been translated from the Greek language into Hebrew, was brought into the treasuries of the Jews, specifically those in Tiberias <note>A city on the Sea of Galilee, a major center of Jewish learning in late antiquity</note>, and was stored there in hidden places, as certain men who converted from the Jewish nation to Christ have accurately told us. Indeed, a rumor also persists that the book of the Acts of the Apostles was similarly translated from Greek into Hebrew and is preserved there in the chests.* However, whoever compares the following passages of Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his writings against heresies</note>, and what he subsequently writes concerning the treasury of the late Patriarch Hillel, will see that **Epiphanius** is speaking of the **private cabinets of scholars**, and not of the **Arks** of the Synagogue, which are our present subject.

<margin>
Chrysostom, Oration III against the Jews. Greek edition, volume VII, page 344.

On the other hand, **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople</note> makes explicit mention of these Arks in his orations against the Jews, particularly in the third. It is permitted to excerpt some portions: *For do not say this to me, that the Law and the books of the Prophets are kept there. Is this not enough to make the place holy?* <note>original Greek: "Μὴ γάρ μοι τοῦτο εἴπῃς..."</note> Again: *Altogether, if you believe that because the Law and the books of the Prophets are kept there, the place is holy.* But, what is especially worthy of observation is that **Chrysostom** gives to that Synagogue chest the same name, *kibotos* <note>original Greek: κιβωτὸς</note> or **Ark**, or *Aron* <note>original Hebrew: ארון</note>, by which the Jews designate it even today. His excellent words are: *Otherwise, what kind of* **ARK** *is now among the Jews, where there is no mercy seat <note>original Greek: ἱλαστήριον (*hilasterion*); the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant</note>, no divine oracle, no tablets of the Covenant, no Holy of Holies... nor the other things which once made that Ark revered. To me, the Ark which the Jews now possess seems no better than the little chests sold in the marketplace; indeed, it is even worse.* (The Latin translator notes: *perhaps he read 'anointing' <note>original Greek: χρῖσμα (*chrisma*)</note> instead of 'oracle', but poorly.*)

Furthermore, this Ark or chest of the Synagogue must be built and placed on that side of the Synagogue which faces that quarter of the sky in which the Temple was once situated <note>Jerusalem</note>. If any Synagogue is built to the east of the land of Canaan, its **Ark** must be placed on the side...

### CHAPTER 8. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...the side that faces the West; if, conversely, a Sacred House of Prayer <note>Latin: *Oratorium Sacrum*</note> is built in the West, as frequently happens in these regions, it is necessary that the chest for the sacred books be placed on the eastern wall, with the door directly opposite it to the west.

<margin>Commentary on Megillah <note>A Talmudic tractate regarding the Scroll of Esther and synagogue rules</note>, chapter 3, section 36, verse 28, paragraph 6.</margin>
**They do not place the entrances of synagogues except toward the East, for thus we find in the Temple that its entrance was toward the East, as it is said: "And those who camp before the Tabernacle toward the front, before the Tent of Meeting toward the East" <note>Numbers 3:38</note>. This, however, was in those days when they prayed toward the West; but we bow toward the East, toward the land of Canaan.** <note>original Hebrew: *Ein potchin pitchai batei knesiyot ela l'mizrach...*</note>

<margin>The same words are found in Maimonides <note>The 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>, Laws of Prayer <note>Hebrew: *Hilcoth Tephilla*</note>, chapter 11, paragraph 2.</margin>
*They do not make the doors of the Synagogue except toward the East, because so we read of the Temple, that its door was toward the East, as it is said: "And those camping before the Tabernacle toward the East: before the Tent of Assembly toward the East." This truly was in those days, when they prayed toward the West: But it is necessary for us to bow ourselves toward the East toward the land of Canaan.* This statute rests upon a general Rule <note>Latin: *Canone generali*</note>, which you have in the Rituals:

<margin>Orach Chaiim <note>The "Path of Life," a standard code of Jewish law</note>, chapter 94, paragraphs 1 and 2.</margin>
**When one stands to pray, if he is standing outside the land of Israel, he should turn his face toward the land of Israel and direct his mind also toward Jerusalem, the Sanctuary, and the Holy of Holies. If he is standing in the land of Israel, he should turn his face toward Jerusalem and focus also on the Sanctuary and the Holy of Holies. If he is standing in Jerusalem, he should look toward the Sanctuary and simultaneously direct his mind to the Holy of Holies. If he is standing behind the Mercy Seat, he should turn his face toward the Mercy Seat.** <note>original Hebrew: *B'kumo l'hitpallel im hayah omed b'chutz la'aretz...*</note>

*When someone stands to pray, if he stands outside the land of Israel, let him turn his face toward the land of Israel, and also direct his mind toward Jerusalem, and the Sanctuary, and the Holy of Holies. # OF THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

**"The King is commanded to write for himself one copy of the Divine Law, which they correct from the Book of the Court-Office, according to the decision of the Great Sanhedrin."** <note>original Hebrew: אותו מספר העזרה על פי בית דין הגדול; original Latin: Regi præceptum est sibi scribere unum Legis Divinæ exemplar, quod corrigunt ex Libro Atrii, secundum sententiam Synedrii Magni.</note> It does not seem absurd to suggest that a most corrected copy of the Divine Law was kept by the Priests in the Court <note>The "Azarah," or inner courtyard of the Temple</note> of the Temple for the use of those making copies. Yet who could establish this with solid arguments? The most noble de Voysin <note>Joseph de Voysin, a 17th-century French Hebraist</note> described Maimonides' words regarding "the book of the Court" <note>original Hebrew: אותו וספר העזרה</note> as "The Book of Ezra" <note>original Hebrew: ספר העזרא</note> and translated it as the *Book or copy of Ezra*. However, the reading in my own Codex contradicts this; in it is written *Azarah* <note>meaning "court"</note> and not *Ezra* <note>the proper name of the scribe</note>. Furthermore, it would then have had to be written as *Sefer Ezra* without the "the" <note>the Hebrew letter 'He'</note> prefixed to it, which is not used with proper names. But, in whatever way this passage of Maimonides is understood, the ancient Jews did not conceive of any "Library Ark" existing outside the Ark of the Covenant. Rather, they believed that a certain small chest—which they call a *tabula* <note>tablet</note>, *glossokomon* <note>Greek for a case or box</note>, and *capsa* or *scriniolum* <note>small chest or case</note>—was attached to the Ark of the Covenant as a kind of appendix, so that the sacred writings produced in addition to the Ten Commandments might be stored within it.

**"Take this book of the Law and place it in the box at the right side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, and let it be there as a witness among you."** <note>original Aramaic: סבו ית ספרא דאוריתא הדא ותשוון יתיה בקופסא מן צטר ימינא דארון קימא דיי אלהכון ויהי תמן לכון לסהיד</note>

Thus, the Ark of the Covenant alone was regarded as the repository for the Sacred Books, and specifically for the Law of Moses. Following this example, the Volumes of the Law of Moses are placed in the Armoires <note>Arks</note> of the Synagogue with their additions and ornaments (which we shall discuss later), and from there, when the Law is to be read, they are brought out with solemn ceremony in the sight of the people. For they do not commonly store the Books of the Prophets in these chests, but only the Mosaic Writings.

## BOOK I, PART I.

**The King is commanded to write for himself one copy of the Divine Law, which they corrected from the Book of the Court, according to the judgment of the Great Sanhedrin.** <note>original Hebrew: אותו מספר העזרה על פי בית דין הגדול; original Latin: Regi præceptum est sibi scribere unum Legis Divinæ exemplar, quod corrigunt ex Libro Atrii, secundum sententiam Synedrii Magni.</note> Nor does it seem absurd that a very accurate copy of the Divine Law was kept in the Court of the Temple by the Priests, for the use of scribes. The most noble **de Voisin** <note>Joseph de Voisin (1610–1685), a French theologian and Hebraist.</note> described the words of Maimonides regarding the **Book of the Court** <note>original Hebrew: ספר העזרה (Sefer ha-Azarah)</note> and translated them as the **Book or Copy of Ezra**. But, in whatever way this passage of Maimonides is understood, the ancient Jews did not conceive of any library chest outside the Ark of the Covenant. Rather, they believed that a certain small box, which they call a <term>glossokomon</term> <note>original Greek: γλωσσόκομον; a case for keeping reeds or scrolls</note> or a <term>capsa</term> <note>original Hebrew: קופסא; a small chest or box</note>, was attached to the Ark of the Covenant as a kind of appendix, so that those

<margin>

</margin>

sacred writings which were written in addition to the Ten Commandments might be stored within it. Concerning this box, Jonathan Ben Uzziel <note>A famous translator of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic (Targum).</note> speaks in his paraphrase of Deuteronomy 31:26: **"Take this book of the Law and place it in a chest, at the right side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, and let it be there among you as a witness."** <note>original Aramaic: סבו ית ספרא דאוריתא הדא ותשוון יתיה בקופסא מן צטר ימינא דארון קימא דיי אלהכון ויהי תמן לכון לסהיד; original Latin: Reponite librum Legis hunc & locate eum in capsâ, ad latus dextrum arcæ fœderis Domini Dei vestri, & fit illic inter vos in testimonium.</note> Thus, the Ark of the Covenant alone was regarded as the repository for the Sacred Books, and especially for the *Law of Moses*. Following this example, the Volumes of the Law of Moses, along with their attachments and ornaments (which we will discuss later), are stored in the Cabinets of the Synagogue. From there, when the Law is to be read, they are brought out in a solemn procession before the eyes of the people. ### CHAPTER 8. OF SYNAGOGUES.
<meta>catchword: use</meta>

...should ascend, he who is to read the Divine Law, or deliver a serious sermon to the people, so that his words may be heard by all. When they set up the Ark <note>The *Aron Kodesh*, or cabinet for Torah scrolls</note>, in which the Book of the Law is usually kept, they place it in the center, so that the back of that Ark faces toward the Temple <note>referring to the site of the Great Temple in Jerusalem</note>, and the front faces toward the people.

<margin>§ II.</margin>
The latter words of this text might perhaps cause some difficulty, because the word **Sanctuary** <note>original Hebrew: היכל, *Hekhal*</note> in this text by Maimonides <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, a preeminent 12th-century Jewish scholar</note> appears to have an ambiguous meaning. For in the preceding paragraph, he had used the word **Sanctuary** <note>original Hebrew: היכל</note> for the small shrine of the Synagogue, in these words: **"And they build in it a Sanctuary in which they place the scroll of the Law, etc."** <note>original Hebrew: ובונין בו היכל שמניחין בו ספר תורה וכו'</note> But by the word **Sanctuary** in this later text, it seems entirely necessary to understand the Temple of Jerusalem, toward whose direction the back of the library Ark was supposed to be pointed, so that its front would face the people, as will be observed in the following paragraph, which will be cited next.

<margin>§ IV.</margin>
Unless perhaps Maimonides understands by the word **Ark** <note>original Hebrew: תיבה, *Tevah*</note> something separate from the sacred shrine—specifically, a mobile Ark that is placed between the **Sanctuary** <note>original Hebrew: היכל</note> and the **Platform** <note>original Hebrew: בימה, *Bimah*</note>, and before which the *Minister of the Synagogue* <note>The *Chazzan* or prayer leader</note> stands to pour out prayers.

<margin>In David's Journey p. 15. Romans 14:10. 2 Corinthians 5:10. Diogenes Laertius on Solon, book 1, page 37.</margin>
I do not deny, reader, that the passage is in some way obscure to me. However, I think no one doubts that the Hebrew word **Platform** <note>original Hebrew: בימה, *Bimah*</note> used by Maimonides is the same as the Greek *bema* <note>original Greek: βῆμα</note>, derived from the verb **to step** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ βαίνω</note>. Cohen de Lara <note>David Cohen de Lara, a 17th-century Sephardic scholar and lexicographer</note> states: **"The *Bimah* is like a seat of judgment"** <note>original Hebrew: בימה כי כסא המשפט</note>; **"The *Bimah* is the seat of justice occupied by a judge."** Thus, as seen on page 15, the word *bema* is used frequently by all sorts of authors, even the Sacred ones <note>The New Testament, as in the "Judgment Seat (Bema) of Christ"</note>. Among the laws of Solon <note>The famous lawgiver of ancient Athens</note> was this: **"That he who was notorious for shameful conduct and crimes was to be barred from the platform and public speakers' rostrums."** <note>original Greek: Τὸν ἡταιρηκότα εἰπεῖν τοῦ βήματὸς</note>. This is to be noted because the word **Bamah** <note>original Hebrew: בימה, written here with the same letters as Bimah</note>, though written with the same letters, pronounced in nearly the same way, and having a similar meaning among the Hebrews (for it denotes a high place, whether a Temple or an altar), contributed nothing to the origin of the word **Bimah** <note>original Hebrew: בימה</note> used here by Maimonides; though I have no doubt that the Greek word *bomos* <note>original Greek: βωμὸς</note>, which is used for an *altar*, but also for a Temple by some authors, and is likewise derived by Eustathius from **to step** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ βαίνω</note>, descends directly from this very word **Bamah** <note>original Hebrew: בימה</note>.

<margin>Tractate Sotah, chapter 7, § 8.</margin>
The Talmudists <note>The ancient compilers of Jewish law and tradition</note> use this same concept to designate the **Platform** <note>original Latin: Suggestum</note> built for a King or Priest who is about to read the Law. The words are: **"They prepared for him a wooden platform in the Courtyard, and he sat upon it."** <note>original Hebrew: עושין לו בימה של עץ בעזרה והוא יושב עליה</note> This passage...

For in the preceding paragraph, he had used the word *Heikhal* to refer to the shrine of the synagogue, with these words: *And they build in it a Sanctuary or Cabinet, in which they place the book of the Law, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: ובונין בו היכל שמניחין בו ספר תורה וכו׳</note> But by *Heikhal* in this later passage, it seems that the Temple of Jerusalem is entirely intended; the back of the library Ark had to be directed toward that location, so that its front would face the people, as will be observed in the following paragraph, which I will cite next.

<margin>§ IV.</margin>
Unless perhaps Maimonides understands the *Tevah* <note>original Hebrew: תיבה; literally "box" or "chest," often used for the Ark in the synagogue</note> to be a certain mobile Ark separate from the sacred shrine, which is placed between the *Bimah* <note>original Hebrew: בימה; the raised speaker's platform</note> and the *Heikhal*, and before which the Minister of the Synagogue stands to offer prayers. I do not deny, reader, that the passage is somewhat obscure to me. However, I believe no one would doubt that the Hebrew word *Bimah* used by Maimonides is the same as the Greek *Bema* <note>original Greek: βῆμα</note>, which comes from the word *to step* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ βαίνω</note>.

<margin>In Ir David p. 25.</margin>
Cohen de Lara <note>A 17th-century Sephardic scholar and lexicographer</note> says: *Bimah* means the seat of judgment. <note>original Hebrew: בימה פי׳ כסא המשפט</note> *The Bema is the seat of judgment occupied by a Judge.*

<margin>Romans 14:10; 2 Corinthians 5:10.</margin>
This is how the word *Bema* <note>original Greek: τὸ βῆμα</note> is frequently understood by all authors, including the Sacred writers <note>The New Testament uses this term for the "Judgment Seat" of God or Christ</note>.

<margin>Diogenes Laertius, Life of Solon, Book 1, p. 37.</margin>
Among the laws of Solon <note>the famous Athenian lawmaker</note> was this: *He who was notorious for wickedness and vice should be barred from the tribunal and the public platforms.* <note>original Greek: Τὸν ἡταιρηκότα εἰπεῖν ἐν βήματι</note> This is noted because the word *Bamah* <note>original Hebrew: במה</note>—though written with the same letters, pronounced almost the same way, and having the same meaning among the Hebrews (denoting a high place, whether a Temple or an altar)—nevertheless contributed nothing to the origin of the word *Bimah* used here by Maimonides. I have no doubt, however, that the Greek *Bomos* <note>original Greek: βωμὸς</note>, which is used for an altar and sometimes for a Temple, and is likewise derived by Eustathius from the word *to step*, descends directly from this Hebrew *Bamah*.

<margin>Sota, Chapter 7, § 8.</margin>
The Talmudic writers apply this same notion to designate the platform built for a King or Priest when they are about to read the Law. The words are: *They prepared for him a wooden platform in the Court, and he sat upon it.* <note>original Hebrew: עושין לו בימה של עץ בעזרה והוא יושב עליה</note> This place...

For the Legislator <note>Moses</note> had not determined this doubtful point.

Furthermore, Moses, in the history of this Precept, makes no mention at all of a platform; nevertheless, Josephus and the Talmudists rightly concluded that it is inherent in the power of the Law. For the Law could not be read with profit in the assemblies of the whole Nation unless the one reciting the Law held an elevated position. Elevated, I say.

</margin>

Ezra and the other Levites intended only that their address could be understood by the greatest multitude of people.

# CHAPTER 8. ON SYNAGOGUES.

...he noted: "The explanation of the place in the synagogue upon which they read from the Torah." <note>original Hebrew: פירו' המקום בבית הכנסת שעליו קורין בתורה</note> A place in the synagogue upon which they read the Law. Whether Maimonides <note>A preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note> uses this term elsewhere in the same sense was at one time a matter of doubt. His words are as follows:

<margin>Laws of the Torah Scroll, chapter 10, section 4 <note>original Latin/Hebrew: Hilcoth Sepher Tora cap. x. §. iv.</note></margin>
> The case prepared for the scroll of the Law and in which it is placed, as well as the wrappings, the Ark, and the **TOWER** <note>original Hebrew: מגדל, *Migdal*</note> in which they place the scroll of the Law—even if the scroll is inside its own case—and likewise the chair (or pulpit) designed for the scroll of the Law to be placed upon, and upon which it has been placed: all these are holy utensils. It is forbidden to throw them away; rather, when they are worn out or broken, they are to be hidden away <note>original Greek: ἀποκρύπτονται, *apokryptontai*; indicating a *Genizah* or storage for sacred scraps</note>. However, regarding the **platforms** <note>original Greek: τὰ βήματα, *ta bemata*</note> upon which the representative of the congregation stands while holding the scroll, and the boards upon which they write for a child to learn, these possess no inherent holiness. Silver and gold pomegranates <note>Decorative finials for the Torah rollers</note> and similar items made for the scroll of the Law as ornaments are considered holy utensils, and it is forbidden to put them to secular use unless they are sold to purchase a scroll of the Law or a Pentateuch <note>The Five Books of Moses; original Latin: *pars ejus quintana*</note> with the proceeds.

<margin>The Way of Knowledge, chapter 270, section 13 <note>original Latin: Jore Dea. cap. CCLXX. XIII. §. XII.</note></margin>
You can find these same words in the *Yoreh Deah* <note>A major code of Jewish Law</note>. I was, I say, kept in suspense as to whether Maimonides meant by "Tower" <term>Migdal</term> that fixed pulpit in the synagogue where the volume of the Law is stored, or something else, because I saw "Tower" <term>Migdal</term> distinguished here from "Chair" <term>Kisse</term>. <margin>Laws of the Torah Scroll, chapter 10, section 4 <note>original Latin/Hebrew: Hilcoth Sepher Tora cap. x. §. iv.</note></margin>

The **Tower** <note>original Hebrew: *Migdal*</note> is the high bench that is upon the platform <note>original Hebrew: *Bimah*</note> where the cantor <note>original Hebrew: *Chazzan*</note> places the scroll of the Law when he reads from it; it is a biblical term from Ezra: *And Ezra the scribe stood upon a tower of wood.* <note>Nehemiah 8:4</note> The **Chair** <note>original Hebrew: *Kisse*</note> is the *kursaya* mentioned in the Gemara, for there are places where they designate one specific chair to place the scroll of the Law upon during the day."

### ON STRUCTURE, BOOK I, PART I.

The Court of Israel was higher [than the Court of the Women] by two and a half cubits. It extended, as I have already stated, through the entire length of the Court of the Priests and the Court of Israel (according to the testimony, I say, of the Talmudists <note>The "Talmudists" refers to the ancient Jewish rabbis whose legal discussions and traditions are recorded in the Talmud.</note>) which was completed in one hundred and thirty-five cubits. <margin>f Tractate Middoth, chapter 2, section 6. In the middle. Abarbanel's Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 43, page 212, column 1.</margin> f Let us note the words from the Body of Jewish Traditions that serve to prove these points:

> <note>original Hebrew: עזרת ישראל היתה אורך מאה ושלשים וחמש על רוחב א' עשרה וכן עזרת כהנים היתה אורך מאה ושלשים וחמש על רוחב א' עשרה וראשי פסיפסין מבדילין בין עזרת ישראל ועזרת כהנים רבי אליעזר בן יעקב אומר מעלה היתה שם וגבוהה אמה ודוכן נתון עליה ובה שלש מעלות של חצי אמה נמצאת עזרת הכהנים גבוהה מעזרת ישראל שתי אמות ומחצה</note> *The Court of the Israelites was one hundred and thirty-five cubits in length and eleven cubits in width. And likewise, the Court of the Priests was one hundred and thirty-five cubits long and eleven cubits wide. The ends of the wooden beams <note>Referring to decorative or boundary markers between the courts.</note> distinguished the Court of the Priests from the Court of the Israelites. Rabbi Eliezer, the son of Jacob, says: there was one step there, one cubit high, and upon it was placed a platform <note>original Hebrew: דוכן, *duchan*</note> elevated by three steps, each of which was half a cubit; so that the Court of the Priests was two and a half cubits higher than the Court of the Israelites.*

On that platform stood <margin>a. Maimonides, Laws of the Temple Utensils, chapter 7; Laws of the Chosen House, chapter 7.</margin> a. the Levites <margin>b. Tractate Sotah, folio 28, column 2.</margin> (elsewhere it is said that b. the Priests also stood there to bless the people, though at other times <margin>c. Tractate Tamid, chapter 7, section 2.</margin> c. the steps of the Porch are assigned to them) chanting their prescribed songs, with their faces turned toward the altar. Perhaps the platforms of the synagogues, in imitation of these Temple platforms, were of a wider and longer structure, capable of holding many people at once. <margin>Nehemiah 8:4.</margin> Of this same form, one must believe, was the **wooden tower** <note>original Hebrew: מגדל עץ, *migdal etz*</note> or wooden platform on which Ezra is said to have stood. It was after this platform, as the closest model, that the pulpits <note>original Latin: *Cathedræ*, literally 'chairs' or 'seats of authority'.</note> of the synagogues were fashioned. For it is not right to think that it was so narrow that it held only Ezra, or that Ezra alone stood upon that platform—an image we might easily form from the examples of pulpits found in our own churches. For it was quite remarkable in its width as well as its height. <margin>f Commentary on this passage.</margin> f Aben-Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a major medieval biblical commentator.</note> certainly teaches that this platform was of the same form <note>original Hebrew: כאשר אנחנו עושים פה בבתי כנסיות</note> *as those we are accustomed to construct here in our synagogues,* as he says. Indeed, in the synagogues since the most ancient times, the platforms have been quite wide, as I have said, so that they might hold several people at once...

### CHAPTER 8. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<sig>A a 3</sig>

<margin>Nehemiah 9:4</margin>
...the <term>Teachers</term> <note>original Latin: Doctores; referring to those authorized to interpret and teach the Law.</note> were [seated]. It also seems to me that what follows in the text should be understood in this way:

> *And Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani stood upon the platform of the Levites and cried out with a loud voice to the Lord their God.*

I believe that they all stood together, yet in such a way that only one prayed at a time, while the others stood beside him and also took their turn praying to God. I see, however, that the Belgian Translators <note>Likely referring to the scholars of the Dutch "Statenvertaling" or contemporary Reformed theologians in the Netherlands.</note> dislike this idea more than anything else. But I freely grant, I say, that not everyone who stood on this platform spoke to the people at once—as that would hardly suit the maintenance of order in the Church—yet I see no absurdity in several <term>Teachers</term> standing together on one platform, each speaking in his own place and time, either to God or to the people. Indeed, I believe the present text teaches this most clearly, and the rituals of the Ancient <term>Hebrews</term> confirm the same. 

To say, however, that many platforms were erected here, <margin>Chapter 8:1</margin> and that the people were divided into many parts, is something that, in my opinion, contradicts the historical text. For it is clear from the text that all the people were gathered in one place, forming only one <term>assembly</term> <note>original Hebrew: קהל (Kahal); original Greek: ἐκκλησία (Ekklesia)</note>. Only *one* <term>wooden platform</term> <note>original: מגדל עץ (Migdal Etz), literally "wooden tower."</note> was erected, and we cannot conceive how the people, gathered in one place, could have been divided into distinct parts and listened to distinct <term>Teachers</term> without significant <term>confusion</term> <note>original Greek: συγχύσει (synchysei)</note>. 

Our opinion is also confirmed by the fact that in the narrative itself it is expressly said that *Ezra stood on a wooden platform*, <margin>Nehemiah 8:4</margin> *and Matatiah, Shema, Ananiah, and the other Levites and experts in the Law stood beside him* <note>original Hebrew: ויעמד אצלו (va-ya'amod etzlo), meaning "and he stood next to him."</note>. What? Do you think <term>Ezra</term> alone stood in an elevated place, while the others stood in a lower one? Certainly not; rather, they stood at the side of <term>Ezra</term> on the same platform for the same purpose, each in his own place and order, as is clearly established here. 

I will therefore say briefly how I have conceived it in my mind, and how those things that were done in this place ought to be understood according to the customs of the <term>Hebrews</term>. A <term>wooden platform</term> was constructed, in my judgment quite wide, on which several <term>Teachers</term> stood together. Once the assembly was gathered, <term>Ezra</term> brought out the book of the <term>Law</term>, and after the blessings were performed, he read a portion of it before the entire assembly of the people in a clear voice,

<summary>This page argues that Ezra and the Levites stood together on a single, large wooden platform to address the gathered assembly, rather than being scattered across multiple platforms, which would have caused confusion.</summary>

to all who understood the reading. In my judgment, however, the person who *read* was not the same person who *interpreted* what was read, nor did he illustrate the text with a more extensive commentary. For as much as we can gather from this historical narrative, the person who stood in the middle of the <term>platform</term> <note>original Latin: suggestu; a raised pulpit or stage.</note> read the text, while those who stood at his side interpreted what was read, so that each person spoke and commented in his own proper place. In this way, Ezra himself, while reading, did not explain the portion he had just read; rather, the other <term>Teachers</term> and <term>Scribes</term> <note>original Greek: γραμματεῖς (grammateis); professional scholars and copyists of the Law.</note> who were standing closest to his side performed that task. We seem to be able to conclude this from the fact that *Ezra* is said to have *read*, while the Levites <gloss>made the people understand the law</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: מבינין את העם לתורה (mevinin et ha-am la-torah)</note> and attend to it so that they might comprehend it. For this is the force of that <term>relationship</term> <note>original Greek: σχέσις (schesis); the connection or arrangement between the roles.</note>. Thus, there was one person who read <gloss>distinctly and clearly</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: מפורש (meforash)</note>, another who <gloss>gave the sense to what was read</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: שום שכל (shum sechel)</note>, and finally the people who heard the reading and understood it—three distinct actions which are specifically affirmed regarding the persons of that assembly. *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note>, who is quite skilled in ancient customs, explains the word "understanding," which is said here of the Levites, in this way: <gloss>that they were translating the words of the Law for the people.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: שהיו מתרגמן לעם דברי תורה</note> Indeed, in the Ancient Church, the interpreter was a different person from the reader. Let these remarks now suffice concerning the *Platforms of the Synagogues*.

### CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES

...there is indeed no obscure mention among the Hebrew authors. <margin>Maimonides</margin> <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter 11, § 4.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: כיצד העם יושבים בבתי כנסיות הזקנים יושבים ופניהן כלפי העם ואחוריהם כלפי ההיכל וכל העם יושבים שורה לפני שורה ופני של שורה לאחורי השורה שלפני עד שיהיו פני כל העם כלפי הקדש וכלפי הזקני׳ וכלפי התיבה</note> **How do the people sit in the houses of the synagogue? The elders sit with their faces toward the people and their backs toward the Sanctuary <term>Hechal</term> <note>The "Hechal" or Sanctuary refers to the ornamental chamber or cabinet where the Torah scrolls are kept, often called the Ark.</note>; and all the people sit row after row, the face of one row toward the back of the row in front of it, so that the faces of all the people are toward the Sanctuary, the Elders, and the Ark <term>Tevah</term> <note>The "Tevah" is the box or chest containing the scrolls of the Law.</note>.**

We see here the entire logic of the benches and their distinction between those occupied by the **Elders** and those occupied by the rest of the common people. However, in the two synagogues of Amsterdam—which are the only ones I have seen—this precept of Maimonides is by no means observed. In the synagogue of the Portuguese <note>The Sephardic Jewish community in Amsterdam.</note>, the seats of the **Elders** are placed on the northern side of the synagogue; the chair of the **Prefect** of the synagogue is joined to the <term>platform</term> <note>original Latin: suggestui; the raised pulpit or bimah from which the service is led.</note> so that he faces it, with his face toward the **Ark**. In the house of prayer <note>original Latin: Proseuchâ; a Greek term for a place of prayer, here referring to the synagogue.</note> of the Germans <note>The Ashkenazi Jewish community in Amsterdam.</note>, if I remember correctly, five seats for the **Elders** are joined to the platform in this same location and position; the other **Elders** sit near the **Ark**. The same difference can be observed in the **benches of the people**, which are not arranged in distinct rows facing the **Ark**, but are placed along the transverse sides of the synagogue.

The seats of the **Elders**, wherever they may be placed, are undoubtedly the **chief seats in the synagogues** of which Christ speaks in **Matthew**: <margin>Chapter 23:6.</margin> **"They love,"** (he says of the Pharisees) **"the chief seats in the synagogues."** <note>original Greek: τὰς πρωτοκαθεδρίας ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς (tas protokathedrias en tais synagogais)</note> That is, they vehemently strive for that dignity, so that they might occupy the first place in the synagogues. The word **chief seat** <note>original Greek: πρωτοκαθεדρία (protokathedria)</note> agrees, if I am not mistaken, in meaning with the word **presidency** <note>original Greek: προεδρία (proedria)</note>, by which the honored seats in the theaters for the **Presidents of the Athenian Judges** are designated. <margin>The Acharnians, Act 1, Scene 1.</margin> Aristophanes says:
> **Now every man pushes himself toward the front seat.**
> <note>original Greek: Εἰς τὴν προεδρίαν πᾶς ἀנὴר ὠסίζεται.</note>

A little earlier, he had called this the **first bench** <note>original Greek: τὸ Πρῶτον ξύλον (to proton xylon)</note>, regarding which Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian and rhetorician.</note> says: **"For the first bench is the seat of honor, especially for the judges."** Concerning that magnificent Alexandrian synagogue, where almost all the parts...

For in this text, it is not only said that chairs (<term>cathedræ</term>) were assigned to the Elders and Leaders of the Jewish People, but also to the individual men of each trade. Since this order was observed in the Synagogue of Alexandria, it was undoubtedly not neglected in other more noble synagogues, even if they were inferior to the Alexandrian one in ornament and size. From the Epistle of Saint James, it seems we must conclude that the first Christians—who were very inclined to preserve Jewish customs—observed these or similar distinctions of seating in their churches with too much anxiety and scrupulosity. # CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES

If there should enter into your synagogue—about which we will speak below (God willing)—a man wearing a gold ring and splendid clothing; and there should also enter a poor man in filthy clothing; and you look upon him who wears the splendid clothing and say to him: "You sit here in a fine place"; but you say to the poor man: "You stand over there, or sit here under my footstool." He adds: *Have you not made a distinction among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?* <note>original Latin: "male ratiocinantes"; referencing James 2:2-4</note> It is clear from the context of these words that the Apostle James is speaking of the place where the first Christians were accustomed to gather. In that place, he assumes there were distinct benches (<term>subsellia</term> <note>tiered seating or benches used in public buildings</note>), some more honorable and dignified than others. The more dignified seats were usually designated for the wealthy, who recommended themselves by the splendor of their clothing or the dignity of their office; less honorable places, whether standing room or seats, were assigned to the poor, who displayed no outward beauty or brilliance. This followed, essentially, the established custom of the Synagogues among the Jewish people. James, however, rebukes this practice, because in the assemblies of Christians it is right for there to be more and more certain evidence of brotherhood—that is, of unity, equality, and simplicity—than in the Synagogues. But Philo also provides testimony regarding this variety and distinction of seating in the Synagogue, where he describes the "Philosophers" or "Monks" <note>Philo is likely describing the Therapeutae, an ascetic Jewish sect in Egypt</note> of his own nation and their institutions and customs:

<margin>On the Contemplative Life, page 691.</margin>
"On the seventh day," he says, "they come together as if into a common assembly, and they sit down in order according to their age, with a proper posture, keeping their hands inside their garments—the right hand between the chest and the beard, and the left hand tucked down by the flank." <note>original Greek: "Ταῖς δ᾽ ἑβδόμαις... συνέρχονται καθάπερ εἰς κοινὸν σύλλογον..."</note> On the seventh day, they indeed meet in a common gathering, and **THEY SIT ACCORDING TO THE ORDER OF THEIR AGE**, in decent attire, keeping their hands under their cloaks, the right between the breast and the chin, the left pressed to the side. This passage of Philo is noted elsewhere by Eusebius.

<margin>On the Preparation for the Gospel, Book 8, Chapter 12.</margin>
Indeed, that which follows in this text concerning another distinction of seating in the Synagogue must by no means be overlooked. We mean the fact that women in the Synagogues (which is observed even today in Jewish Oratories, and was in no way neglected in the Temple of old for very weighty reasons) occupied seats distinct from the men. Regarding those matters pertaining to the Temple, I remember writing elsewhere; now I shall only touch upon those things that relate to the Synagogues.

Thus, after a few intervening words, Philo continues: "This common sanctuary in which they gather on the seventh day is a double enclosure, one part being assigned for the men’s quarters, and the other for the women's quarters; for women also, by custom..." <note>original Greek: "Τὸ δὲ κοινὸν τοῦτο σεμνεῖον... διπλοῦς ἐστι περίβολος..."</note>

<header>ON THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.</header>
<meta>catchword: Can-</meta>

...they listen together, possessing the same zeal and the same purpose. The wall between the houses is built up from the ground to a height of three or four cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note>, in the manner of a breastwork. The space from there up to the roof is left open for two reasons: first, so that the modesty becoming to the female nature might be preserved; and second, so that the women, sitting within earshot, might easily grasp what is said, as nothing obstructs the voice of the speaker.

This shared <term>σεμνεῖον</term> <note>original Greek: "semneion," meaning a sacred shrine or room for study and prayer</note> or Sanctuary, in which they gather every seventh day, is enclosed by a double partition, separating the assemblies of **men and women**. For following the custom, the women also listen at the same time, at least those who follow the same way of life. However, a middle wall rises from the floor to a height of three or four cubits, like a low parapet, while the upper portion remains open to the ceiling. From this, a double benefit arises: the modesty of the female sex is respected, and the words of the **Teacher** are heard easily without any obstacles to interrupt his voice. 

Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who described the practices of Jewish groups like the Essenes and Therapeutae.</note> has already explained for what purposes this distinction of **Seating for Men and Women** was introduced into the Synagogues. It was granted for the sake of decency, for which no opportunity—not even the slightest—should be given for it to be offended in places held sacred to God.

IV. A word must be added concerning the <term>נרות</term> <note>Hebrew: "Nerot," meaning lamps or candles.</note> **LAMPS** of the *Synagogue*. By these we mean the lamps—whether cast with greater or lesser craftsmanship—that are hung in the Synagogues or fixed to its walls, or even the candelabra which illuminate the Synagogue building where it is most convenient. 

Their use, unless I am mistaken, is derived from both necessity and religious custom <note>The original Latin uses "superstitione," which in this period's scholarly writing often referred to any ritualistic practice the author viewed as non-essential or overly formal.</note>. From necessity, certainly, because in the evening *liturgy* <note>original Greek: "leitourgia," referring here to the evening service.</note> of the Sabbath and the **Festivals**, they simply cannot do without them. From religious custom, however, because they are accustomed to honor the Sabbaths and feast days by lighting lights, either as a sign of joy (which light represents), or in honor of the **Law**, which is characterized by the name of **Light** in the Scriptures, or following the example of the **Sanctuary**, which was formerly illuminated by lamps, or for whatever other reasons religious devotion easily invents. This commandment concerning the Sabbath Lamps applies to private homes as much as to Synagogues. Regarding these kinds of Jewish Sabbath lights in private homes, one should consider the verses of *Persius* <note>A Roman satirist (34–62 CE) who often mocked the customs of various ethnic groups in Rome.</note>, which have not been understood with equal success by everyone:

<margin>
Persius, Satires
book 5, line 180.
</margin>
> *The days of Herod have come, and the* **LAMPS**
> *Arranged on the greasy window-sill have vomited a thick cloud,*
> *Bearing violets, and embracing the red dish...*

> ->The tail of a tuna swims <note>This refers to a humble meal of fish.</note>, the tall jar swells with wine:
> You move your lips in silence, and turn pale at the circumcised Sabbaths.<-

<margin>Commentary on this passage. Various readings, chapter XVIII.</margin>
Regarding the first words of this verse, it was observed by the Ancient Interpreter <note>Specifically, the "Scholiast," an ancient commentator on classical texts.</note> that the Jews, when celebrating the birthday of **Herod** and observing their Sabbaths, were accustomed to place lighted lamps, crowned with violets, in the windows of their houses. However, the Scholiast was undoubtedly mistaken in this by explaining these "days of Herod" as actual birthdays of Herod celebrated by the Jews, as *Theodore Marcilius* and *Petit* have correctly observed. Indeed, one can most conveniently understand "Herod’s days" as the festival days observed with the greatest religious devotion by every Jew; *Persius* <note>Aulus Persius Flaccus (34–62 CE), a Roman poet known for his difficult and satirical style.</note> calls them "Herod’s days" because Herod Agrippa, who was very well known to the Romans, could easily be presented as a type and example of the entire Jewish Nation. But it is truly clear from the words of *Persius* that the Jews, and many of those Romans captivated by Jewish sacred rites, were already then accustomed to that same practice which still clings to them: to light the Sabbath Lamps at the setting of the sun on Friday, to recline on well-prepared couches, to have cups full of wine nearby, and to recite their own blessings over each thing.

<margin>Seneca, Letter 95, page 604.</margin>
Thus it was the custom among the Jews; and many of the Romans imitated them, whom *Persius* mocks. Indeed, even *Seneca* <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE – 65 CE), a Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> criticized these customs in clear words, attacking superstitions and behaviors of men devoid of reason:
> Let us forbid anyone from LIGHTING A LAMP ON THE SABBATHS: since the Gods do not need light, and men certainly do not take pleasure in the soot.

<margin>Tractate Shabbat, chapter II, sections 1, 2, 3, etc. Maimonides, Laws of the Sabbath, chapter V, section 1 and following. Orach Chaim, Title 261, 263, 264, 265, 275, and following. Kol Bo, chapter XXXI.</margin>
Truly, regarding this ritual of lighting **Lamps** in private homes, especially at the beginning of the Sabbath and other Festivals, many precepts are found in the Hebrew statutes, both in the *Talmudic* Code and from there in *Maimonides* and the Ritual Books. For example, the precepts of *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> begin thus: 
<gloss>The lighting of the lamp on the Sabbath is not a matter of choice, such that if one wants he lights and if he does not want he does not light; nor is it a commandment that one is not obligated to pursue until he must perform it (such as the blending of courtyards <note>The Eruv, a legal enclosure allowing carrying on the Sabbath.</note> or washing hands for a meal). Rather, it is an obligation. And both men and women are obligated to have a lamp lit in their homes on the Sabbath. Even if a man has nothing to eat, he must beg at the doors to get oil and light the lamp, for this is included in the "Delight of the Sabbath" <note>original Hebrew: עונג שבת "Oneg Shabbat," the commandment to enjoy the Sabbath day.</note>. And he is obligated to bless before the lighting: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to light the lamp of the Sabbath," in the same way he blesses over all things that are obligatory according to the words of the Scribes.</gloss> / *The lighting of the Sabbath lamp is not placed in the choice of each person, so that, if he wishes, he may light it, and if he does not wish, he may not light it; nor is it a precept...*

...precept, the observation of which one is not bound to follow merely as a matter of study; such rituals include the Mixing of Courtyards <term>Eruv Chatzerot: a legal mechanism that allows Jews to carry items in shared areas on the Sabbath</term> or the Washing of hands before taking food. ### CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 12, Chapter 11.</margin>
<margin>Maimonides, *Laws of Megillah and Hanukkah*, Chapter 3, Section 2. *Gemara Shabbat*, Folio 11, Column 2.</margin>
<margin>1 Maccabees Chapter 4, verse 50.</margin>
<margin>Drusius, *Notes on the First Book of Maccabees*.</margin>
It must not be overlooked, however, that this religious practice <note>The author uses the Latin "superstitio," which in a 17th-century scholarly context often refers to a specific religious rite or ceremony rather than "superstition" in the modern sense.</note> of *lighted lamps* held a place especially in that *Festival* which, as *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> testifies, was called *Phota* <note>Greek: φῶτα, meaning "Lights."</note>. This festival fell during those eight days of the *Encaenia* <term>Encaenia: The Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah, celebrating the rededication of the Second Temple.</term>, in which the Jews are accustomed to commemorate the restoration of the Temple worship by Judas Maccabeus after the madness of Antiochus Epiphanes. Those *eight days*, I say, which were designated for celebrating the *Dedication of the Temple*, beginning from the twenty-fifth day of the month of *Casleu* <note>The Hebrew month of Kislev, usually occurring in November or December.</note>, are "days of joy and praise" <note>Original Hebrew: ימי שמחה והלל (*yemei simcha ve-hallel*)</note>, "and they light lamps in them during the evening time, at the doors of the houses, every night of those eight nights, so that the miracle may be recognized and made public." These are the words of *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note> describing this festival, drawn from the Talmudic Code. Its origin, however, is doubtlessly to be traced back—not to a certain divine miracle involving the multiplication of oil, about which the Hebrew authors tell stories from that time <note>The author refers to the miracle of the oil lasting eight days, which he treats with historical skepticism.</note>—nor perhaps even to the singular joy which the Jewish nation indulged in then due to the unexpected and sudden restoration of sacred and civil affairs, as *Josephus* would have it (though we do not entirely exclude that), but rather from the fact that the lampstands of the Temple, restored and refilled with oil in those days, illuminated the Temple with their light. This was indeed a most brilliant sign of the restored religion and Temple worship. This is suggested by the text in the *First Book of Maccabees*, which narrates this restoration of sacred worship: "And they offered incense upon the altar, and they lit the lamps that were upon the lampstand, and they gave light in the temple." <note>Original Greek: Καὶ ἐθυμίασαν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον, καὶ ἐξῆψαν τοὺς λύχνους, τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς λυχνίας, καὶ ἐφαίνοσαν ἐν τῷ ναῷ</note>. *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar of the Bible and Semitic languages.</note> certainly noted correctly regarding this passage (and so it seems to us): "they lit the lamps" <note>Original Greek: ἐξῆψαν τοὺς λύχνους; original Hebrew: וידליקו הנרות</note>; "and from here comes the name *Lights* and the *kindling of lamps*." A few words, but sound ones. Indeed, if you wish to know more about this festival, consult *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>.

<margin>Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, Book 3, Chapter 13, Sections 9 and 10.</margin>

Indeed, these very *private lamps* will easily lead us to the *public* ones. For it would not be fitting for the *House of the Synagogue* to lack sacred lights at the time when the chambers of private individuals were illuminated by them. which might be considered in any way profaned. ## CHAPTER X.

*A review of various utensils used for either sacred worship or for decorating the Synagogue: 1. The sacred Books with their attachments. 2. Trumpets and horns. 3. The Curtain of the Scroll Cabinet. 4. Charity boxes, etc. Concerning the Sacred Books, their form, requirements, and ornaments are mentioned, such as the pomegranates <gloss>Hebrew: רמונים (*rimmonim*), the decorative finials on the scroll poles</gloss>, the linens <gloss>Hebrew: מטפחות (*mitpachot*), the cloths used to wrap or protect the scrolls</gloss>, and the case <gloss>Hebrew: תיק (*tik*)</gloss>. On the Eve of the Sabbath, noting the differences in the blasts and instruments, and the rules to be observed regarding them; as well as the location where these instruments are stored. A few details are added regarding the curtain of the holy cabinet, etc.*

Having described the larger parts of the Synagogue according to our plan, we proceed to point out rather than fully explain its smaller instruments or *minor Utensils*, which are used for religious practice or the beauty of the Synagogue. Under this category, four items will primarily come to our attention: 1. *The Sacred Books with their attachments*. 2. *The Horn*. 3. *The Curtain of the Sacred Cabinet*. 4. *The Charity Boxes*.

1. **THE SACRED BOOKS**, especially the five *Books of the Law* <note>The Torah, or Pentateuch, the most sacred object in Jewish worship.</note>, undoubtedly deserve the first place in the list of *sacred utensils*, because their use in the Synagogue is paramount. # On STRUCTURE Book I. Part I.

<margin>
Buxtorf, 
*Jewish Synagogue*, 
chapter XIV.
</margin>
It is right to understand these Books of the Law, according to the customs of the Jewish Nation, as **Scrolls** (Hebrew: <gloss>מגלות (*megillot*)</gloss>), consisting of calfskin parchment <note>original: "membranis vitulinis"; this refers to vellum, a high-quality writing surface made from the skin of young calves</note> sewn together in length to the extent of several cubits. These are written with a character that is polished but somewhat thick, and they are attached at both ends to two **turned wooden rollers**, by which they can be lifted and carried. Here, a great opportunity would present itself for inquiring into and explaining the type of parchment used, its preparation, its eventual length, and the laws of writing that must be scrupulously observed regarding them; and finally, the reverence that is owed to a Scroll thus properly prepared—if we either thought it convenient to spread our focus so widely across every single subject, or if most eminent men before us had not already exhausted this labor.

<margin>
Preface to the *Dagger of Faith* by Raymond Martin, Folio 85 and following.
Maimonides, 
*Laws of Phylacteries*, etc., chapter VII, etc.
Alfasi, 
*Laws of the Book of the Law*. 
*Yoreh De'ah*, Section CCLXX and following.
</margin>
Indeed, *Joseph de Voysin* has recounted from *Maimonides* <note>Maimonides (1138–1204) was a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and jurist whose codification of Jewish law is still authoritative.</note> all the conditions that are required in a **Book of the Law** intended for public reading; and *Wilhelm Schickard*, drawing from the *Tractate of the Scribes* <term>Codex Sopherim: A minor tractate of the Talmud that details the rules for writing and reading the Torah</term>, *Alfasi*, and *Maimonides*, has so studiously followed all other matters that lead to a full understanding of these customs. Later, through the very diligent work of the most illustrious man, *Johann Benedict Carpzov*, these details were so learnedly supplemented that we have almost nothing of great importance to add. However, the teachings that the later Doctors—*Alfasi, Maimonides, Rabbi Jacob, and Rabbi Joseph Karo* <note>Rabbi Joseph Karo (1488–1575) was the author of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the foundational code of Jewish law.</note>—have handed down regarding these precepts for writing a scroll are taken from the aforementioned *Tractate of the Scribes*, the first part of which encompasses all these minutiae.

> In that tractate, I say, it is taught: on what parchment, how it is prepared, from which animals it is made, and by whom the Book of the Law must be written; what space should be left between lines and letters; how many letters in a line, how many lines on a page; by what space the books are to be distinguished from one another; which poorly written parts can be erased without profaning the book; which words must be divided into two; which divided words must be joined into one; which are written with one letter and read with another; which are written with a certain letter and read without it; which are written without a certain letter and yet read with it; which letters should be written large, small, suspended, or twisted; which words should be dotted above; which are to be written and not read; which are not to be written and yet read; and which are written one way and read another. <note>This list refers to the complex Masoretic traditions of *Keri* (what is read) and *Ketiv* (what is written), ensuring the text is preserved exactly as received even when the spelling seems irregular.</note>

*Exercises*, 
volume II, 
Exercise XII, 
chapter VI.
</margin>

### CHAPTER 10. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...those things which are so necessarily required in the book of the law for public reading that if even one of them is missing, the scroll must be considered **unfit** for public use. <margin>Laws of Phylacteries, chapter 10, § 1.</margin> These are the words of Maimonides on the matter: <note>original Hebrew: "נמצאת למד שעשרים דברים הן שכל אחד מהן פוסל ספר תורה ואם נעשה בו אחד הרי הוא כחומש מן החומשין שלמדין בהן התינוקות ואין בו קדושת ספר תורה ואין קורין בו ברבים."</note> *“We have learned that there are twenty things, each of which invalidates a Scroll of the Law; and if even one of them occurs in it, it is like a single volume of the Five Books from which children are taught, and it does not possess the sanctity of a Scroll of the Law, and they do not read from it in public.”* 

*We have received that there are twenty things, each of which renders the Book of the Law profane [unfit for ritual]: if any of these should befall it, it becomes like a fifth part of the Pentateuch* <note>De Voysin translates this as "It becomes like the Pentateuch," but that does not seem to be Maimonides' meaning. The word <gloss>חומש (*chumash*)</gloss> does not denote the whole Pentateuch here, but rather a "fifth part" of the Pentateuch—a single book whose sanctity was far below the sanctity of the entire volume of the Law, which contains all five books of Moses in one continuous scroll</note> *from which children are instructed; it lacks the sanctity of a book of the law, and they do not read from it in public.* 

Lest we seem to say nothing at all, we shall briefly present the sum of these **twenty** conditions in English words alone, referring the curious reader to the work of *Voysin*, praised above, who translated and illustrated them. Therefore, a scroll is <gloss>פסול (*passul*)</gloss> or "profane" [unfit] if:

I. *It is written on the <margin>In the place cited above.</margin> skin of an unclean animal.* <note>Jewish law requires materials for sacred objects to come from "kosher" species like cows or goats.</note>

II. *It is written on the skin of a clean animal that was not ritually prepared.*

III. *It is written on skin not specifically prepared for the purpose of being a scroll of the law.*

IV. *It is written on the wrong side of the skin. That is, on the "membrana" [flesh side] where the "pergameno" [hair side] should be used, and vice versa.*

V. *It is written <margin>See Buxtorf under the word דוכסוסטוס</margin> partly on flesh-side parchment and partly on hair-side parchment.*

VI. *It is written on <term>Duchsostos</term>.* <note>original: "δυξεςῳ" (duchsostos); this refers to the inner layer of a hide that has been split into two sheets.</note>

VII. *It is written without the use of a guide-line or ruler.*

VIII. *It is not written with permanent ink.*

IX. *It is written in other languages.* <note>A ritual Torah scroll must be in Hebrew.</note>

X. *It is written by a heretic or similar profane person.*

XI. *The Divine Names are written without holy intention.* <note>A scribe must mentally sanctify themselves before writing the names of God.</note>

XII. *If even one letter is missing.*

XIII. *If even one letter is redundant [extra].*

XIV. *If one letter touches another.*

XV. *If the shape of any letter is corrupted so it cannot be read clearly, or if it resembles another letter, or if the writing is torn, perforated, or stained.*

XVI. *If a letter is separated too far from another so that one word looks like two, or if words are too close so that two words appear as one.*

XVII. *If the format of the Sections is changed.*

XVIII. *If the format of the Songs is changed.* <note>Certain poetic portions of the Torah, like the Song of the Sea, must be written in a specific "brickwork" layout.</note>

XIX. *If the rest of the text is written in the style of a Song.*

XX. *If the sheets are sewn together with anything other than the sinews of a clean animal.*

The Hebrews judged these twenty conditions to be of the utmost necessity for a Volume of the Divine Law, which...
