### OF THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

...which would serve the uses of the Synagogue. The accuracy and precision in the sacred Books is more to be praised or wondered at! Certainly Christ the Lord most rightly depicted this kind of men, <margin>Matthew 23:24</margin> as *straining out a gnat, but swallowing a camel* <note>original Greek: διυλίζον τὸν κώνωπα, τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνον</note>: although certainly one would not disapprove of even the most anxious care and most fastidious precision concerning the text of Holy Scripture, upon which the supreme importance of our happiness depends, in such great perversity and sluggishness of the human race.

But we should not overlook the ornaments of these Books. Among those are included <term>matpachot</term> <note>Hebrew: מטפחות; wrappers or cloths</note> *wrappers*, which are linen cloths, stretched out more in length like bandages than extended in width, with which the sacred Book is wrapped. <margin>Orach Chaiim Title 154 § 4</margin> Concerning these, it is thus stated in the statutes of the Hebrews: *The linen wrappers of a Book of the Law which have worn out may be used to make shrouds for a "commanded corpse,"* <note>Referring to a "met mitzvah," a deceased person with no one to bury them, whose burial is a high religious priority.</note> *and this is considered to be their* <gloss>hiding</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀπόκρυψις (apokrypsis); referring to the practice of Genizah or ritual concealment.</note>. The same Rule is found in the definitions of Rabbenu Ascher, and in Maimonides. Mention is also made of the <term>tiq</term> <note>Hebrew: תיק; a case or chest</note> *case*, in which the Book of the Law is stored, in the same statutes, as well as the silver or gold apparatus with which the Book of the Law is adorned. <margin>Laws of the Scroll, chapter 10 § 3</margin> Rather than the passage cited above from Maimonides, let us describe only a part of the Rule of Rabbenu Ascher: <margin>Laws of Tefillin etc. chapter 10</margin> *Holy utensils, such as a case for books, <term>Tefillin</term>* <note>Phylacteries; small leather boxes containing scripture worn during prayer.</note> *and <term>Mezuzot</term>* <note>Scripture scrolls fixed to doorposts.</note> *and the Book of the Law, and the straps of the* <gloss>phylacteries</gloss> <note>original Greek: τῶν φυλακτηρίων</note>, *are hidden away.* <margin>To the Tractate Megilla, Rule 40.</margin> *The hiding of a Book of the Law is described in the following way in* <margin>Definition 43.</margin> *the later sections: A Book of the Law which is worn out by age is hidden in the grave of a student of Hebrew Law who repeats the traditions, and specifically in an earthen vessel.* These Rules mean that these holy Utensils should never be discarded in such a way that they could ever be applied to profane uses. The same is read in the <term>Yoreh Deah</term> <note>One of the four core sections of the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law.</note>. 

But other ornaments of the manuscript Pentateuchs are also mentioned there, which are added for the sake of beauty: thus it is in the text: <margin>Title 282 § 12, § 16</margin> *Silver or gold apples* <note>original Latin: "poma"; these are likely the "rimmonim" or pomegranate-shaped finials placed on the wooden rollers (etz chayim) of the scroll.</note> *which they make for the Book of the Law for beauty are holy utensils, and it is forbidden to put them to profane use, unless to buy with them a Book of the Law or a Pentateuch...*

### CHAPTER 10. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...[they are cast out], they are sacred instruments, which it is a sin to alienate <note>To "alienate" here means to sell or transfer ownership of a holy object for non-sacred use.</note>, unless a book of the law or its "fifth part" <note>The "fifth part" refers to a single book of the Torah (Pentateuch), as the Torah is divided into five books.</note> are purchased with their price. Maimonides had used the term <term>rimmonim</term> <note>Hebrew: רמונים</note> *pomegranates* <note>Decorative silver finials placed on the wooden rollers of the Torah scroll, often shaped like pomegranates.</note>. These Pentateuchs were usually stored in the Synagogue itself, as we have already understood from *Chrysostom*, in the **Ark**, specifically made for this use. If, however, the Synagogue lacked such an Ark, they were brought in from elsewhere. 11. Among the *Utensils* & *Instruments* of divine Worship celebrated in Synagogues, I include TRUMPETS & HORNS. I will assume, when about to discuss these, that my reader is sufficiently instructed from the Mosaic law regarding the difference between *Trumpets* (<term>chatzotzrot</term> <note>Hebrew: חצוצרות</note>) & *horns* (<term>shofrot</term> <note>Hebrew: שופרות</note>). <margin>Josephus, Antiquities book 3, chapter 12.</margin> The horn was formed from a ram’s horn, the Trumpet from metal, which you will find clearly described by *Josephus*, who has recently been worthily illustrated in this part by the most learned Englishmen. To the matter: that Synagogues were equipped with trumpets was noted long ago by *Lightfoot*, who also briefly indicated some of their uses. <margin>On Matthew chapter 6:2.</margin> Although this is not entirely false, he seems to have taken *trumpet* in a broader sense for an instrument fit for making a blast, and confused it with the *horn*, which has happened to other writers as well. But that is of little importance. Let us observe therefore after him: 1. That the *Trumpet* (or rather the horn) had a notable use in *Excommunication*. He proved this by citing a passage from the *Code Sanhedrin* <note>A volume of the Talmud dealing with the legal system and courts.</note>, in which among the <term>keli dayyanin</term> <note>Hebrew: כלי דיינן</note> *instruments of the Judges* there is also included the <term>shofra</term> <note>Hebrew: שופרא</note> *horn*. Let us relate the full text: <margin>Sanhedrin Folio 7, Column 1.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: אמר אלעזר מנין לדיין שלא יפסיע על ראשי עם קדש שני לא תעלה במעלות וסמיך ליה ואלה המשפטים אשר תשים אשר תלמדם מיבעי ליה אר' ירמיה ואי תימא ר' חייא בר אבא אלו כלי הדיינין כי הא דרב הונא כי הוה נפיק לדינא אמר הבי אפיקו לי מאני חנותא ומאי נינהו חוטרי וסנדלי שיפורי ורצועי</note> *Eleazar said: From where is it known that a judge should not step over the heads of the holy people? From "You shall not go up by steps" followed by "And these are the judgments which you shall set [before them]." It should have said "which you shall teach them." Rabbi Jeremiah said (and some say Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba): These are the tools of the judges, like that of Rav Huna, who when he went out to judgment said: "Bring out for me the tools of the shop." And what are they? Rods, sandals, horns, and straps.*

"If someone passes behind a synagogue building, or if his house is adjacent to the synagogue, and he hears the sound of the <term>Shofar</term> <note>original: שופר; a ram's horn used as a ritual trumpet</note> or the voice of the <term>Megillah</term> <note>original: מגילה; literally "scroll," usually referring to the Scroll of Esther, but here used generally for liturgical readings</note>, if he directed his heart [with intent] toward it, he has fulfilled his duty; but if not, he has not fulfilled it. For although both this man and that man heard the sound of the horn, one performed the act with a focused mind, while the other did not." 

And concerning this blowing of the **Shofar**, or **ram’s horn**, which must be performed in the synagogues during this festival of the New Year (indeed, this duty is performed to this very day, and for that purpose the **Shofar** is kept in the homes of the synagogue ministers), as well as the manner of sounding it and the qualifications of the blower, many things are found in *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Jewish scholar</note> and the authors of the Rituals, which are passed over here because we are not capable of describing everything. Only this must be observed: if this festival should fall on the **Sabbath**, the sounding of this **Shofar** would not be permitted, except in those places where the **Great Council** <note>The Sanhedrin, the supreme judicial and religious assembly of seventy elders</note> of 70 men was gathered. This is indeed handed down in the words cited by *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English Hebraist whose work is being critiqued here</note> from the tractate *Rosh Hashanah* <note>The section of the Talmud dealing with the New Year</note>, the meaning of which was not clearly enough expressed or well understood by him. # CONCERNING THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

On this solemn Fast, the trumpet <note>original Greek: σάλπιγγי (salpingi); usually referring to the straight metal trumpet</note> is not sounded, but rather the same Horn <note>original Latin: buccina; referring to the shofar or ram's horn</note> by which the New Year is inaugurated. And thus far indeed concerning the use of Trumpets and Horns in the Synagogue. Let it now be permitted to add that these Trumpets and Horns were preserved and hidden away in a certain secret place, which was in the roof of the Minister of the Synagogue <note>The *Chazzan*, an official or beadle who managed the synagogue's daily affairs</note>. This very thing is related in the *Code of Jewish Law*:

<margin>Tractate Shabbat, folio 35, Column 2, near the end.</margin>

Rabbi Jose Bar Chanina said: "I have heard that if someone comes to light the Sabbath lamp after the six blasts of the horn have been completed (otherwise this was to be done at the sound of the third blast), he is permitted to light it. For the Sages granted a certain measure of time to the Minister of the Synagogue to carry his horn back to his home and store it there." <note>original Hebrew: א"ר יוסי בר חנינא: שמעתי שאם בא להדלי' אחר שש תקיעו' מדליק שהרי נתנו חכמים שיעור לחזן הכנסת להולי' שופרו לביתו</note>

It was not permitted to carry a trumpet or horn from one place to another on the Sabbath <note>referring to the prohibition of carrying objects between public and private domains on the day of rest</note>; from which Rabbi Jose concludes that only after the six blasts are finished is the Minister of the Synagogue granted enough time before the start of the Sabbath to carry his horn back to his house and store it there again. For, as should be noted here, the sounding of the trumpet on the eve of the Sabbath was performed on a certain high roof of the City. Thus says Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the 11th-century commentator</note>: **"There was a unique roof in a high place of the city, and in its center this sounding was raised."** <note>original Hebrew: שהיה גג מיוחד בגובה העיר ובאמצעיה לתקוע שם</note> From this roof, Rabbi Jose wanted the trumpet to be carried back to the house of the Minister of the Synagogue after the six trumpet sounds were finished. But for other Sages, it was handed down thus:

> There was a hidden place for the Minister of the Synagogue at the top of his roof, where he would put away his horn, because they may not carry either the horn or the trumpets (on the Sabbath) to another place. But as for the external tradition, by which it is permitted to carry away the horn, but forbidden to carry only the trumpet from one place to another, Rabbi Joseph established that it holds no difficulty. # CHAPTER 10. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

...is obligated to nourish. The Ram’s Horn <note>original Latin: *Buccina*; referring to the *shofar*</note>, since it is curved, could also be used to draw water and provide a drink for children (which could not be done with a Trumpet <note>original Latin: *tuba*; the straight metal *chatzotzerah*</note>, as it is straight); for this reason, it was permitted for a private individual to carry it on the Sabbath. 3. Let us indicate in a single word another sacred ornament of the Synagogue, namely the most splendid VEIL <note>The *Parochet*, the curtain covering the Ark</note>, which is usually hung before the *Book Ark*. Thus it is written in the *Path of Life* <note>original: *Orach Chaiim*, a major code of Jewish law</note>: "The curtain which they hang before the shrine <note>original: *Heichal*</note> of the Synagogue possesses holiness, and therefore it must be hidden away <note>original Greek: ἀποκρύπτεσθαι (*apokryptesthai*); referring to the *Genizah*, a storage area for worn-out sacred texts and objects</note> should it become unfit for use <note>original Greek: ἀδόκιμον (*adokimon*)</note>." The reason for the holiness of this veil is further explained in the decisions of *Rabbenu Asher* <note>A prominent 13th-century German-Spanish rabbi and legalist</note>: "From a larger Pulpit <note>Original Hebrew: *Bimah* or *Kise*; the raised platform for reading</note> one is permitted to make a smaller one, but it is not permitted to make a step for the pulpit from it. And likewise, from a larger VEIL one may make a smaller one, or even a case for a Book of the Law <note>The Torah Scroll</note>, but it is not permitted to make a case for a volume of the Pentateuch <note>original: *Chumash*, referring to a bound book of the five parts of the Torah rather than a scroll</note> from it." There is no doubt that this *veil* is hung before the Book-Shrine in imitation of the *Veil* or the second curtain <note>original Greek: δευτέρῳ καταπετάσματι (*deutero katapetasma*)</note>, which was suspended in the Temple before the Holy of Holies and formerly covered the ancient Ark. For the Jews endeavored, as much as possible, to make the Synagogue as similar to the Temple as they could.

4. We must by no means overlook the ALMS BOXES or CHARITY CHESTS, which may be found within the Synagogues or at their entrances, so that those about to pray may have the opportunity to exercise their liberality toward the poor and thereby more easily earn divine grace. The *Charity Box* is usually called the *Kuppah* <note>original Hebrew: קופה</note>; hence there are "Collectors of the Box" <note>original Hebrew: *Gabbai ha-Kuppah*</note> among the Jews, who are distinct from the "Collectors of the Bowl" <note>original Hebrew: *Gabbai Tamchui*; referring to a collection of food for the immediate needs of the poor</note>. Indeed, that box of which Maimonides speaks was carried around by those very Collectors to gather alms, which were to be cast into it immediately. Sometimes these alms were also collected in a certain *Purse* or small bag, called by Maimonides, using a Talmudic phrase, the "Alms Purse" <note>original Hebrew: *Arneki shel Tzedakah*</note>. I see, however, that *Prideaux* <note>Humphrey Prideaux (1648–1724), an English theologian and orientalist</note> has rendered this as "Charity Chest." This does not create a difference in meaning; it is certain...

Where this regulation took its origin is clear enough from the testimonies already cited. First, they judged that so much reverence was due to their Houses of Prayer that they should stand out above the other structures of the City. For it surely adds to the honor of the divine House that it be higher and more excellent in structure than any human buildings. Then also, since, as has already been observed by us several times, they consider their Synagogues as the Temple... <note>The text breaks off here; the author is comparing the synagogue to the Holy Temple in Jerusalem</note>

<page-num>215</page-num>

### CHAPTER II. ON SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>On the Syrian Goddess. See Spencer's *On the Laws of the Hebrews*, Book 1, Chapter VI, Section 1.</margin>
Since they strove to make the synagogues as similar to the Temple as possible, it is not surprising that they assigned them a visible height. For the *Temple*, as was the custom among many nations, was built on a mountain whose peak was sufficiently elevated. Indeed, other nations building temples and sanctuaries in high places imagined themselves to be closer to heaven, and therefore believed that prayers would be more easily heard from "near at hand" <note>original Greek: *anchothen*</note>, as the writer *Lucian* <note>Lucian of Samosata was a 2nd-century satirist who wrote about religious customs</note> says. Whether the same opinion occupied the minds of the Hebrews is a reasonable question. It is certainly true that from the time they entered the land of Canaan, they felt a desire to worship God on the highest slopes and mountains. I do not doubt, however, that later it also occupied their minds that it was essential to the honor and splendor of the Temple for it to stand out above any buildings adjacent to it. In the prophecies, it was said that *the mountain of the house of the Lord would be elevated above the mountains*. <note>A reference to Isaiah 2:2 and Micah 4:1</note> And it is quite clear that Mount *Acra*, which according to the testimony of the historian *Josephus* was once higher than Mount *Moriah*, was leveled during the time of the Maccabees, with its peak removed *so that the Temple might also stand above it.* <note>original Greek: "hōs hyperphainoto kai tautē to hieron"</note> But we remember writing about that more extensively elsewhere.

<margin>Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book VI, Chapter VI (or Book V, Chapter XIV).</margin>
<margin>Lightfoot's *Hebrew Hours* on Matthew 4:23. Tosephot to the Tractate *Berachot*, folio 2, column 1, at the end.</margin>
11. Truly, besides the fact that Synagogues were to be built in the high places of every city where the Jews were self-governing, it also happened quite often in the past that they were established *outside the cities*, either *by rivers* or near tombs. The scholar *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and Hebraist who specialized in using Rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament</note> has already observed before us that some synagogues were formerly built outside cities *in the fields*. He cited two passages for that purpose from the *Tosephot* <note>Medieval analytical commentaries on the Talmud</note> and *Rabbenu Asher* regarding the Tractate *Berachot*. We shall display those testimonies in full from the Hebrew text:

**He recites two blessings before it** (the recitation of the *Shema* <note>The central "Hear O Israel" prayer</note>), **etc. There were seven blessings in total, corresponding to the verse: "Seven times a day I praise You."** <margin>Psalm 119:164.</margin> **But the prayer beginning "May our eyes behold" is not counted among these, because the Masters ordained this blessing specifically to wait for their companions in the Synagogue. This was specifically for their synagogues that stood in the field, where they were in danger from harmful spirits** <note>original Hebrew: "mazzikim" - often interpreted as demons or spirits that haunt desolate places</note>; **but in our synagogues, one does not need to wait for their companions except at night.**

# On STRUCTURE Book I. PART I.

## CHAPTER II. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...that not *all* Synagogues were once in the *fields*, but only *certain* ones. However, regarding the reasons why Synagogues were often not built in *cities*, I have these three. 1. Because Jews in exile were often not permitted to have Synagogues within the cities themselves. 2. Because a location *outside the cities* was considered more convenient for establishing Synagogues. 3. Because that same location *outside the cities* was often regarded as *holier*. Each of these must be discussed briefly.

1. Since the Jews were quite *hated* and *loathed* by other peoples, it does not seem likely that all nations granted them the power to build Synagogues in their cities. For it is possible that in certain parts of the empire, the Jews suffered the same fate that later befell the Pagans, whose superstition—after the Christian Religion prevailed throughout the world—was banished to the *villages* <note>original: *pagos*, from which the word 'pagan' is derived, originally meaning a rural dweller</note>. But I do not have at hand right now clear and explicit testimonies to support this hypothesis of mine; except that this very reason also seems to have existed for why the Jews *did not have a Synagogue in the City of Rome itself, but outside of it*.

2. The location for building Synagogues *outside the City* was often much more *convenient* than in the City itself. The reason for convenience can be sought from the fact that outside the cities the *view of the sky* was much more open, the place itself quieter, removed from crowds and therefore more suitable for religious exercises, and also because of the *water* or rather the *rivers*, near which Synagogues were most conveniently built, because Jews were required to *wash their hands* before prayers. We assume this now as something certain and known, because we undertake to prove it in the following sections. They preferred Synagogues built near *rivers* rather than near other water reservoirs because rivers provide purer water. To this point, I believe we should refer to what is read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the *Synagogue* which is said to have been outside Philippi: <margin>Acts 16:13.</margin> *And we went out on the Sabbath day outside the city by a river, where a place of prayer was customary* <note>original Greek: ἔξω τῆς πόλεως παρὰ ποταμὸν, οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι</note> OUTSIDE THE CITY BY THE RIVER, *where by accepted custom there was a Place of Prayer* <note>The author uses the term *Proseucha*, a Greek word often used specifically for Jewish places of prayer located outdoors or near water</note>. I remember dealing with this evidence in the preceding parts of Book 1. Let it now be permitted to recall that part of Book 1, Chapter IV, that *the Synagogue was said by accepted custom to be at the river*. What was the reason for that location? <margin>Annotations on Philippians, Number 32.</margin> The most venerable Dutch Interpreters think that Philip—

<margin>Genesis 24:62, 63.</margin>
> Jews perhaps sought the origin of this ritual (of building Synagogues by rivers) from the deed of their Father Isaac, who is said to have gone out into the field, and indeed to a well or spring, <term>to meditate</term> <note>original Hebrew: לשוח (*lashuach*), often interpreted as 'to pray'</note> or to pray, according to the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> interpreter, whom Pagninus <note>Santes Pagnino, a Dominican philologist</note> follows. From this, the rite seems to have arisen, so that Houses of Prayer were erected outside cities in the fields, and usually by rivers, springs, torrents, and other streams of water. Whether indeed this rite gained strength from the superstition of the Gentiles, who worshipped not only God by the torrents, but the torrents themselves as gods, I would not dare to say. 

<margin>Isaiah 57:6.</margin>
The distinguished *de Dieu* thinks that the idolaters rather imitated the *Jews*. Who is to say that the *Jews* of later times did not imitate the *Gentiles* <note>Non-Jewish people, particularly Greeks and Romans</note>, even if they did not fully cross over into their superstition? For it is certain that they borrowed many things from the *Gentiles*. We shall have occasion to observe the testimony of *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Church Father</note> regarding the Samaritan *Synagogue*, which was outside the city, in the course of our dissertation.

Indeed, it is clearly evident from the very constitutions of the Jewish people that they were greatly inclined to pray at *cemeteries* during fixed times of *fasting*. <margin>Maimonides, Laws of Fasts, chapter IV, § XVII.</margin> There is a clear passage on this in Maimonides: <note>original Hebrew: שבע תעניות האלו כל מקום שגוזרין אותם שם אחר שמתפללין יוצאין כל העם לבית הקברות ובוכין ומתחננין שם וכו׳</note> *On these seven fasts, in every place where they decree their observance, after they have poured out their prayers, the entire people goes out to the cemeteries, and there they weep and supplicate.* But what is the reason for this custom, whether of founding *synagogues* or of praying—specifically during *fasts*—at *cemeteries*? <margin>Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book XVIII, ch. 1. We have no doubt that *Synagogues* were originally erected at the tombs of eminent men to commend their memory to posterity. # ON THE STRUCTURE Book I. Part I.

2. A more serious and certain reason for this custom is sought from the fact that, over time, the opinion grew strong among them that the **souls** of the deceased wander around those tombs in which their corpses are hidden, and that through their intercession, help from God may be more easily obtained. Thus it is read in *Sota*: <margin>Gemara for chapter VII in Wagenseil’s Excerpts, § VI, p. 715.</margin> <margin>In the text of Numbers 13:23.</margin> **Rava says that it is taught that Caleb withdrew himself from the counsel of the Spies, and went and prostrated himself upon the graves of the Patriarchs, saying to them: "O Patriarchs of the world, seek mercy for me, that I may be delivered from the counsel of the Spies."** <note>original Hebrew: אמר רבא מלמד שפירש כלב מעצת מרגלים והלך ונשתטח על קברי אבות אמר להם אבות העולם בקשו עלי רחמים שאנצל מעצת מרגלים</note> In the same Tractate, a question is recorded by Rabbi Chama: why was the burial place of *Moses* hidden? <margin>Gemara for chapter I in Excerpts, § III, p. 128.</margin> It is answered, however, that God knew the Israelites were to be carried away into exile, and therefore He wished to take away from them the opportunity of coming **to the burial place of Moses** <note>original Hebrew: אל לקבורתו של משה</note> and there, with tears and supplications, pouring out these groans for their own salvation: **O Moses our Teacher, we beseech you, intercede for us!** <note>original Hebrew: משה רבינו עמוד בתפלה בעדנו</note> Regarding this text, *Wagenseil* <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist and scholar</note> discusses most learnedly. He cites, among other things, a passage from *Schalscheleth Hakkabbala* <term>Schalscheleth Hakkabbala: "The Chain of Tradition," a historical work by Gedaliah ibn Yahya</term>, <margin>p. 85.</margin> in which it is explained how the *Spirits* of the dead come to the knowledge of these prayers: **When the world is in distress and people go to pray in the cemetery, the soul is stirred by the spirit, and the spirit goes and stirs the higher soul, and they pray to the Holy One, Blessed be He, on behalf of the living.** <note>original Hebrew: כשהעולם שרוי בצער והולכים להתפלל בבית הקברות הנפש מתעורר על הרוח והוא הולך והתעורר על הנשמה ומתפללים אל הית' בעד החיים</note> His version of it is: *When some public calamity threatens, if the people retreat to the place of the tombs and pray there, then the awakened "nutritive power"* <note>original Greek: δύναμις θρεπτικὴ (dynamis threptikē)</note> *betakes itself to the "sensing power," and this, going away, awakens the mind, and thus they intercede with God for the living.* Ridiculous. But even more inept is what he recites from *Abarbanel* <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a Jewish statesman and philosopher</note>, as cited by the distinguished *Pococke* <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English Orientalist</note>, <margin>Miscellaneous Notes on the Gate of Moses, p. 121.</margin> who thinks that divine grace is derived to the living through the *bones of the dead*. ### CHAPTER II. ON SYNAGOGUES.

"What is the difference between them? The difference between them concerns the graves of the Gentiles." <note>original Hebrew: מאי בינייהו איכא בינייהו קברי גוים</note> *Why are prayers made at burial grounds?* Two rabbis, Rabbi Levi the son of Chamma and Rabbi Chama the son of Chanina, differ on this. One says, "*We are like the dead in your presence*"; the other says, "*It is done for this reason: so that the deceased may pour out prayers on our behalf*." What is the hinge of this controversy? The primary dispute is concerning the graves of "those outside" <note>original Greek: τῶν ἔξω—referring to non-Jews or Gentiles</note>. Specifically, **Rabbi Levi**, the son of Chamma, did not want graves to be visited on Fast Days for the purpose of obtaining help from God through the <term>intercession of the saints: The idea that holy people can pray to God on behalf of the living</term>, but only to stir up humility in the souls of the supplicants and to place their present condition vividly before their eyes—namely, that they are not far removed from the state of the dead. He supported this with the argument that on a Fast Day, Jews do not only visit the burial grounds of Israelites, but also those of the Gentiles if the former are not available. Yet it is not probable that they would wish to ask for help from the hands of the Gentiles. *Maimonides* <note>A preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>, in the passage cited above, continues:

<margin>Laws of Fasts, Chapter 6, Section 17.</margin>
"And they weep and supplicate there (at the graves), as if to say: 'Behold, you are all like the dead, just like these, if you do not turn from your ways.'" <note>original Hebrew: ובוכין ומתחננין שם כלומר הרי אתם כאלו אם לא תשובו מדרכיכם</note> Certainly, if some among the Jews hold this view, as **Rabbi Levi** and **Chamma** do, I do not doubt that the opinion of Rabbi Chama the son of Chanina was much more widely accepted. For in ancient times, the opinion dominated everywhere—and even today it is not yet fully rooted out—that *the souls of the deceased frequently hover around their graves and sleeping-places*. For this reason, as a most learned man says, *the Gentiles built their temples, from almost the earliest memory of their history, over the small coffins or sleeping-places of their Heroes*.

<margin>Spencer, *On the Laws of the Hebrews*, Book III, Chapter I, Dissertation VI, Section 5.</margin>
<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book II, Chapter VI.</margin>
<margin>See Germanus on that passage of Virgil, *Aeneid* Book VI, line 177: "And the altar of the tomb."</margin>
<margin>Cyril, *Against Julian*, page 342.</margin>
<margin>Maimonides, *Laws of Idolatry*, Chapter 1, Section 3; Chapter 65, 4.</margin>
This was proven at length by **Eusebius** in the chapter titled: *That what they call their holy temples of the Gods are actually the tombs of the dead.* <note>original Greek: Περὶ τοῦ νεκρῶν εἶναι τάφους, τὰ καλέמהνα αὐτῶν ἱερὰ τῶν Θεῶν</note> And **Cyril of Alexandria** indicates with many examples that the most famous temples of the Gentiles were actually graves or monuments to the dead. **Dionysius Vossius** noted the same in his brilliant *Observations on Maimonides' Tractate on Idolatry*. Perhaps it is to this that the passage in *Isaiah* refers, where a certain kind of idolater is described as "dwelling in graves" <note>original Hebrew: שבת בקברים</note> and "spending the night in secret places" <note>original Hebrew: לון בנצורים</note>. It is therefore not entirely far from the truth that it was primarily from this popular opinion about the dead that *Oratories and Synagogues were built near their burial mounds*.

...ments? Why did they establish a <term>Place of Prayer: Oratory; a small structure or room set aside for private worship</term> here? It seems to me they were moved by this: that they did not wish the memory of these celebrated men of their nation to perish.

2. A weightier and more certain reason for this custom is sought from this: that over time, the opinion grew among them that the souls of the deceased wander around those mounds where their bodies are hidden, and that through their intercession it is easier to obtain help from God. Thus we read in the tractate *Sota*: <margin>Gemara for Chapter VII in the Excerpts of Wagenseil, Section VI, p. 715.</margin> <margin>Regarding the text of Numbers 13:23.</margin> "Rava said: This teaches that **Caleb** <note>One of the biblical spies sent by Moses to scout the Land of Canaan; traditional Jewish sources say he visited the graves of the Patriarchs in Hebron</note> separated himself from the counsel of the Spies and went and prostrated himself upon the graves of the Patriarchs. In the same tractate, it is recorded that **Rabbi Chama** asked: why was the burial place of **Moses** hidden? <margin>Gemara for Chapter I in the Excerpts, Section III, p. 328.</margin> It is answered that God knew the Israelites were destined to be led into exile, and thus He wished to take away from them the opportunity of coming **to the burial place of Moses** <note>original Hebrew: learning. <margin>p. 85.</margin> He cites, among other things, a passage from the *Chain of Tradition* <note>original title: Schalscheleth Hakkabbala, a 16th-century historical and theological work</note>, in which it is explained how the spirits of the deceased come to the knowledge of these prayers: "When the world is in distress and people go to pray at the cemetery, the <term>Nefesh: the mind, and thus they intercede with God for the living.* This is a ridiculous explanation.

But even more foolish is what he recites from **Abarbanel** <note>Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), a famous Jewish statesman, philosopher, and Bible commentator</note>, as cited by the famous **Pococke** <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English scholar of Oriental languages</note>, who thinks that divine grace is derived for the living through the bones of the dead. <margin>Miscellaneous Notes to the Gate of Moses, p. 121.</margin> It will be more useful to note the testimony of the tractate *Taanith*, as we ourselves observed before these observations of Wagenseil were suggested to us: <margin>Gemara Taanith, folio XVI, column I.</margin> "Why do they go out to the cemetery? Rabbi Levi bar Chama and Rabbi Chama bar Chanina disagree on this. ### CHAPTER XII.

*The discussion continues regarding the circumstances to be considered in the building of synagogues; thus, it examines the Libraries, Guest Houses, and Trees adjacent to the Synagogue. Regarding the <term>circumstances: the Greek term *peristatika*, referring to the surrounding conditions or environment</term> that concern the building of a synagogue, it will not be useless to record, 3. that LIBRARIES were sometimes joined to *Synagogues*. Thus, for instance, **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler from Spain who documented Jewish communities across Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note> says expressly of the Synagogue of Ezekiel: "In that same place is a certain holy and great house, full of books, where books from both the first and the second Temple are preserved; and whoever lacks children consecrates his books there." <note>original Hebrew: ושם בית גדול הקדש והוא מלא ספרי ומבית ראשון ומבית שני יש שם ספרים וכל שאין לו בן יקדיש ספרו לשם</note>. To the Academies and Schools, which themselves were formerly joined with *Synagogues* to constitute a single <term>Gymnasium: used here in the classical sense of a place for study and mental exercise</term>, libraries of this kind were typically united. A modern example is provided by the Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam, which has a *Gymnasium* with an adjacent *Library* attached to it. Otherwise, Synagogues can be content with their own <term>chests: *thecas*, likely referring to the Torah arks or scroll containers</term>, which we spoke of previously. 5. It is not without use, while we are occupied with the buildings <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς προσευχητοῖς — in the places of prayer</note> of the synagogue, to also turn our mind to whether any synagogues ever lacked roofs. One must conclude that they did lack them, if faith is to be given to **Epiphanius**, who describes many prayer-houses of the Jews and Samaritans in such a way as if they were merely level areas and open spaces under the sky without a roof, in which it was possible to look directly at the heavens and stretch out one's palms to the air. **Epiphanius** had said, when describing the heresy of the *Massalians* <note>A 4th-century sect also known as the Euchites, meaning "those who pray."</note>, that they build certain houses for themselves—namely wide places, in the manner of forums, which they call *Proseuchas* <note>original Greek: προσευχὰς — places of prayer</note>; for the illustration of which he adds these following words: <note>original Greek: καὶ ἦσαν μὲν τὸ παλαιὸν προσευχῶν τόποι... — and there were of old places of prayer...</note> “And there were of old places of prayer both among the Jews outside the city and among the Samaritans, as we also find in the Acts of the Apostles, where the seller of purple, Lydia, met with those around Saint Paul, just as the Divine Scripture narrates. For it says, it seemed to be a place of prayer. And the Apostles approached and taught the women who had gathered at that time. But there is also a place of prayer in Shechem <note>original Greek: Σικίμοις — Shechem, a city in Samaria.</note>, in what is now called Neapolis, outside the city in the plain, about two miles away, theater-like; it is constructed in this way in the open air and under the sky by the Samaritans, who imitate the Jews in all things.” **AND THERE WERE OF OLD PLACES OF PRAYER BOTH FOR THE** **JEWS AND THE SAMARITANS OUTSIDE THE CITY,** *just as it is clear also from the Acts of the Apostles, where the merchant of purple, Lydia, is said to have met Paul: concerning which the Scripture narrates thus;* <margin>Acts 16:13</margin> **It seemed,** *it says*, **to be a place of prayer: and the Apostles approached and taught the women gathering during that time. # ON STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

<margin>

Let him enjoy that opinion, provided it is enough to prove it from suitable authors. As for this testimony of **Epiphanius**, I admit on his authority that among the Jews and Samaritans of old there were sometimes such **PLACES OF PRAYER** <note>original Greek: τόπος προσευχῆς</note> outside the cities. I admit this more willingly because it fits well with what we previously shared regarding the "Synagogues of the Fields"; furthermore, I easily assume that the Jews, being more devoted to religion, sought to imitate their forefather **Isaac** in that zeal. Additionally, the condition of certain locations might not have allowed for the construction of a more magnificent synagogue building. 

However, I still hesitate whether the word **proseucha** <note>original Greek: προσευχή — a place of prayer</note> designated only these types of prayer sites as distinct from the larger buildings to which the name "synagogue" would have been reserved. The writers of the New Testament stand in the way, along with **Philo** and **Josephus**. The former use the word **synagogue** <note>original Greek: συναγωγῆς</note> everywhere in the broadest sense for all **Places of Public Assembly**, whether destined for prayers and the reading of the Law or for instruction. The latter [Philo and Josephus], as we have proved with very clear testimonies, also apply the name *Proseucha* to the most grand synagogues. Therefore, I do not easily abandon the opinion defended above: that the word *Proseucha* once enjoyed the widest meaning and was applied without distinction to any Place of Jewish Assembly. In the Roman language, if I am not mistaken, we would call such a place as Epiphanius describes a **chapel** <note>original Latin: *sacellum*</note>. For thus **Festus** says of it: *Chapels are called places sacred to the gods without a roof.*

From this ritual of the Jews and Samaritans praying in the open air <note>original Greek: ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ — under the sky</note> without a roof, as Epiphanius states, you might not ineptly conclude that this famous opinion of the Pagans concerning the Jews gained strength: that the Jews worshipped the heavens themselves. Hence, in **Juvenal**, they are said to adore **NOTHING BUT THE CLOUDS AND THE DIVINITY OF THE SKY**; and in **Petronius**, they are said to "call upon the highest ears of the sky" <note>original Latin: *summas cilli* (meaning *caeli*, "of the sky") *advocare auriculas*</note>.

This is because *killos* <note>original Greek: κίλλος</note>, according to Pollux, signifies a "donkey" among the Dorians. For Petronius had said:

### CHAPTER 12. ON SYNAGOGUES.

It appears they were in common use, and that the widely accepted opinion of the Gentiles <note>The term "Gentiles" here refers to non-Jewish Greeks and Romans of the classical period.</note> concerning them owed its origin and progress to several other causes. For even if I set aside the fact that it was well known to them that the Jews **admitted no images into their cities or temples**, as Tacitus testifies, and that from this the Gentiles could easily have fallen into the error that the Jews worshipped the **nature of things** and the most excellent part of nature, the **sky**, three things deserve to be observed:

1. That the greatest part of the Jewish Temple, to which the Gentiles paid particular attention, lacked a roof; thus, when the Jews entered it to worship, a large portion of them stood in the open air <note>original: "sub dio" — literally "under the day/sky."</note>.

<margin>
Tacitus, *Histories*, Book 5, chapter 5. See there also the commentary by Lipsius.
</margin>

<margin>
Dio Cassius, *History*, book 37.
</margin>

Dio Cassius writes: *And for Him* <note>Referring to the God of the Jews, of whom he had been speaking.</note> *they built a temple, the largest and most beautiful, except for the fact that it was* **wide open and without any roof.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ αὐτῷ νεών τε μέγισον καὶ περικαλλέςατον, πλὴν καθ᾿ ὅσον ἀχανής τε καὶ ἀνώροφος ἦν ἐξεποίησαν.</note> They therefore saw the Jews praying in the **Temple** in the open air and lifting their eyes toward the heights above; it is certainly likely that they paid more attention to this ceremony of the Temple than to other Sacred Places, because whatever might have been lacking in the exercise of religion celebrated in other places was supplied in the **Temple**, the common sanctuary of the entire nation.

<margin>
Daniel 4:25. Matthew 3:2; 21:25. Luke 15:12. Martial, book 11, Epigram 95.
</margin>

2. That the Jews, during that time in which they maintained commerce with the Greeks and Romans, were accustomed to call **God** by the name <term>Heaven</term> <note>original Aramaic/Hebrew: שמיא (*shamaya*).</note>; examples of this are already found in **Daniel** and the writings of the New Testament. 

3. That the Jews truly swore by **heaven itself**, which certainly does not seem to have been unknown to the Gentiles, to whom that most holy oath of theirs by *Anchialus* was not unfamiliar. <note>The Roman poet Martial mocked the Jewish oath "by Anchialus," which scholars believe was a Latin corruption of the Hebrew phrase *Ani chai El* (As I live, by God) or *Ani chai olam* (אני חי עולם — As I live, the Eternal One).</note>

<margin>
Matthew 5:34; 23:22.
</margin>

Christ the Lord rebukes this: *But I say to you, do not swear at all; not by heaven,* etc. <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, μὴ ὀμόσαι ὅλως; μὴ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ.</note> and it is certainly certain that the Jews in common conversation swore as frequently as possible (a vice which the **Essenes** <note>A Jewish sect known for their asceticism and refusal to take oaths.</note> sought to correct by abstaining from oaths altogether); and they also very easily broke the faith of their oaths as they then stood—two things which are elsewhere not infrequently joined together. However, when the Jews swore by **heaven** quite frequently in the presence of the Gentiles, it was easy for them to adopt this erroneous opinion about them: that they worshipped the **sky** itself.

I do not know, however, whether beyond that ancient custom...

The reason for building synagogues in fields might be sought in the fact that synagogues were once commonly planted with *trees*. ### CHAPTER 12. OF SYNAGOGUES.
<meta>catchword: tatis (the beginning of the word "plantatis" or "planted").</meta>

-> <-

It is not at all fitting for the reverence that is owed to a more sacred place. One might certainly understand the term *Fruit-seller* <note>original Latin: *Pomarium*</note> in relation to a *House of Prayer* <note>original Greek-derived term: *Proseucha*</note> as simply a merchant belonging to the Jewish people and religion, or perhaps as someone who performed a specific duty in the House of Prayer, serving as its minister or caretaker. Certainly, until a greater light shines upon me, I would rather conclude this than grant *Scaliger* and *Drusius* <note>Joseph Scaliger and Johannes Drusius were prominent 16th-century scholars of Hebrew and biblical history.</note> their hypothesis. I am surprised, however, that *Scaliger*—neither in those passages nor elsewhere, as far as I can tell—explains the causes or origin of that Jewish custom by which they plant their *Houses of Prayer* or *Synagogues* with trees. I long to know these reasons and have not yet found them; indeed, it is difficult to grasp the truth while groping in the dark. 

It was cautioned by a specific divine command that the Jews should not, <margin>Deuteronomy 16:21</margin> following the example of the Gentiles devoted to idolatry, *plant trees near the divine altar*. The reasons for this were recently investigated with great genius <margin>Book II, *On Hebrew Laws*, chapter 16</margin> and learning by the renowned Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), a scholar who studied how ancient Jewish laws compared to the rituals of neighboring cultures.</note>. Therefore, no grove was present at the *Divine Temple*, once built on Mount Moriah; no trees were planted in it, except by wicked kings. 

Why was the same rule not observed by them regarding *Synagogues*, which the Jews otherwise take care to build in the image of the Temple? Or did they wish to make it publicly known by this sign that they held their Synagogues to be entirely distinct from the Temple? Or did they desire the courtyards of the Synagogues to be covered by the shade of shrubs solely for the sake of pleasantness and coolness? It would not be absurd to think so, as long as nothing better or more certain is available. 

Yet I will not hide that this also came to mind: whether this custom might have flowed from that very ancient habit where *Synagogues* were built outside cities, in the fields, near *rivers and springs* where shrubs are frequent; and whether it was sought from that very example of *Isaac* which we mentioned above—namely, so that *Synagogues* or *Houses of Prayer*, surrounded by trees, might appear more like those open spaces of the field which are especially suitable for pouring out prayers. Or perhaps those trees of the synagogues often served to protect them, adorn them, and distinguish them from other buildings? Or did the Jews perhaps look to the example of *Abraham*, who is read to have <margin>Genesis 21:33</margin> *planted trees* in the place where he *invoked* the name of God? ### CHAPTER 12. OF SYNAGOGUES.

Among the leaders, there must be consensus; otherwise, if one says one thing and another says something else, and because of this division of minds daily prayers cease and no orderly judgment is observed, then truth and peace will fail in the city, and even in the whole Kingdom that follows their factions. It seems to me, indeed, that care should be taken so that all the fathers of families who bear their own burden in paying taxes should gather in one place, and that they should bind themselves by an oath that each will set forth his opinion for the glory of God and the greatest benefit of the society. They must follow the votes of the majority, whether in choosing the leaders of the assembly, in appointing the ministers of the synagogue, in organizing the alms-chest, in appointing the collectors of alms, or in building or tearing down parts of the house of the synagogue, adding or subtracting, and so forth. The sum of the matter is that whatever pertains to the needs of the assembly should be done according to the decision of the majority. 

But if a part smaller in number refuses to submit and observe all these things we have written, the majority—or those elected to office by the majority—has the power to constrain and compel them in any way possible, whether in a court of the Israelites or even in a court of the gentiles, until they say: "We consent." If, however, it is necessary to spend money in this matter, those who constitute the smaller part shall bear their portion of those expenses. But he who refuses to give his opinion according to the formula of that oath, his vote is null. Thus, the votes of the majority, who have taken the oath upon themselves, are followed. We see from these words what that "compulsion" is of which Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides, a famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legalist</note> speaks.

### CHAPTER 12. ON SYNAGOGUES.

...left for the next day. The historian *Josephus*, indeed, determined this number by a fellowship of men, at a minimum of ten: <margin>The Jewish War, book VII, chapter XVII.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ὥστ’ ὥσπεר ἡ φρατρία περὶ ἑκάστην γίνεται θυסי́αν, οὐκ ἔλασσον א̓νדρῶן δέκα</note> *So that a sort of kinship (a fellowship) is formed around each sacrifice, which shall NOT BE FEWER THAN TEN MEN IN NUMBER.* Similarly, regarding the <margin>The Jewish War, book II, chapter VII.</margin> *Essenes* <note>An ascetic Jewish sect of the Second Temple period.</note>: <note>original Greek: Δέκα γοῦן συγκαθεζομένων οὐκ ἂן λαλήσειέ τις א̓κόןτων τῶן ἐןνέα</note> *WHEN TEN OF THEM SIT TOGETHER, no one speaks if the other nine are unwilling.* Therefore, the assembly of the *Essenes* consisted of ten men, without whose collective judgment no one from the group was permitted to speak. Since, therefore, the number of ten men was so commonly used to form a gathering, it is not at all surprising that the same custom also prevailed in sacred matters.

Indeed, in the Volume *Sanhedrin* <note>A tractate of the Talmud dealing with legal procedure and councils.</note>, even a Roman Emperor is introduced disputing with *Rabbi Gamaliel*, showing that he is not at all ignorant of this: <margin>Gemara on chapter VI, Excerpt by Cocceius, § XIII.</margin> <note>original Hebrew: אמר ליה קיסר לרבן גמליאל אמריתו כל בי עשרה שכינתא שריא</note> *The Caesar said to Rabbi Gamaliel: "You say that the Divine Presence [Shekhinah] is present in a gathering of ten men; how many deities are there then?"* <note>The Emperor is mocking the idea: if God is present with every group of ten, he suggests there must be many gods.</note> We heard *Maimonides* declaring earlier that no sacred action—the reading of the Law and the Prophets, public prayers, or the recitation of formulas dedicated to sanctifying God—takes place without a quorum of ten men. According to the *Definitions of Rabbenu Asher*, ten men are required to read the book of *Megilla* <note>The Scroll of Esther, read during the festival of Purim.</note> correctly. I would also think it refers to this that in the *Reading of the Law*, no fewer than ten verses are read, as found in *Maimonides*; <margin>Laws of Prayer, chapter XIII, § XIII.</margin> for the reason, I say, that consideration was given to the assembly, which was deemed complete if ten adult and free men were present. And these are indeed the most certain proofs from which it becomes manifest that in any complete assembly, a count of at least ten was required.

But what is the reason for this ancient custom? That Jewish explanation derived from the *Spies of the land of Canaan* <note>Referring to the ten scouts who brought a bad report of the Promised Land; the Talmud derives the definition of a "congregation" from this group.</note> is rejected as being too thin and weak. Furthermore, it is easily proven that the word <term>edah</term> <note>A Hebrew word meaning "congregation" or "community."</note> in that context does not designate those ten Spies of the land of Canaan, but rather the greater part of the entire Jewish people. What then? It is clear that the *Number Ten* is the most perfect of all numbers, for no one can climb higher in counting except by repeating the numbers already named. -># ON THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.<-

...and it was perhaps for this reason—that ten leaders were decided upon as the requirement for a full society of men—that this view does not seem unlikely.
<margin>chapter v. §. 1. A. m. iv.</margin>
This is why the Jews, in the *Pirke Avoth* <note>original Hebrew: "Ethics of the Fathers," a collection of ethical teachings from the Mishnaic period.</note>, so greatly extol the number ten and recount almost all its prerogatives one by one above other numbers. We notice, furthermore, in the reading of Holy Scripture, that the *number ten* is sometimes used to represent a *large multitude*, just like the number seven. Take, if you please, these words in that
<margin>Lev. xxvi. 26.</margin>
sense: <note>original Hebrew: ואפו עשר נשים לחמכם בתנור</note> *And ten women shall bake your bread in one oven.* This does not mean *ten* precisely,
<margin>chapter vi. 9.</margin>
but *many*, of any number. Observe at the same time a passage from Amos: <note>original Hebrew: והיה אם יותרו עשרה אנשים בבית אחד ומתו</note> *And it shall come to pass, if there remain TEN MEN in one house, they shall die.* Kimchi <note>Rabbi David Kimchi, a famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note> remarks: <note>original Hebrew: אינו דוקא אלא רוצה לומר רבים</note> *It is not precisely (ten), but rather he wishes to say MANY.* Add to this the history narrated in the
<margin>chapter iv. 2.</margin>
Book of Ruth concerning the *transfer of the right of the <term>Goel</term>* <note>The "Goel" is the next-of-kin or "Kinsman-Redeemer" responsible for legal and family obligations.</note> *and nearest Protector* of Ruth to Boaz. Here are the words as they are read there: <note>original Hebrew: ויקח עשרה אנשים מזקני העיר ויאמר שבו פה וגו׳</note> *And he took TEN MEN from the elders of the City, and said to them: Sit down here, etc.* Clearly, there was some business to be performed in a public *gathering* or *assembly* of men. Boaz therefore summons ten men to form a gathering, before whom the entire matter might be transacted. I believe this is the most ancient record establishing that the *number ten* was required to constitute an assembly. But was this a civil matter? Was it a civil assembly? Indeed, it was; but it happens not infrequently that religious customs imitate political ones. That which became standard practice in the *State*—namely, that a matter acted upon without *ten* witnesses present was not at all ratified—could easily be adopted by the *religious assembly* <note>original Latin: "Ecclesia," here referring to the Jewish congregation.</note>, since political and religious matters among the ancient Jews were not of a very different nature. If, however, none of these explanations are satisfactory, it remains to be said that the ancient Doctors required the necessity of the *number ten* in sacred gatherings because they thought that many men were required to perform the duties in the Synagogues with proper decorum. Just as they have passed down to us that a rightly constituted City ought to consist of a population of *one hundred and twenty* men, because the many duties to be performed in a City required that specific number of men. # CHAPTER 13. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...so that they might be exempt from secular matters among themselves and serve sacred things alone; the same should be said of the Schools destined for the public reading of the Law. Thus far, indeed, he [Maimonides] has spoken. This passage is taken from Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>. But truly, a more explicit testimony regarding this matter comes to us in the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>The "Set Table," the standard code of Jewish law compiled in the 16th century</note>:

<margin>
Laws of Prayer, chapter 11, § 21.
*Orach Chaim* <note>The "Way of Life," the section of the Shulchan Aruch dealing with daily ritual</note>, chapter 153, § 8.
</margin>

> <note>original Hebrew: בית סתם והקדישוהו אחר כך לבית הכנסת...</note> *If they simply built a house, and afterwards dedicated it as a House of the Synagogue, that house enjoys the full legal status of a Synagogue building:* **YET IT IS NOT SACRED UNTIL THEY HAVE POURED OUT PRAYERS WITHIN IT,** *not even if they built it under that name and title, specifically that it should be a House of the Synagogue. However, after they have prayed in it—even if they were only travelers who entered when the occasion arose—it is held as sacred, since it was already previously designated for public prayers.*

It is certainly possible to see clearly from this canon in what the Dedication of Synagogues consists. First, the Masters <note>The Rabbis</note> require that a building either be built under that name and title to serve public prayers, or at least, after it is built, it must be designated for those public prayers by those to whom this right belongs. When that is done, they then require in the second place that someone pour out his prayers in it, as in a house consecrated for this use, even if it is a traveler who does so. And then, finally, such Buildings are held to be sacred and enjoy all the prerogatives of a Sacred Building. Almost the same is read in the definitions of Rabbeinu Asher <note>Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), a prominent Talmudic scholar also known as the "Rosh"</note>:

<margin>
Canon 3. To the Tractate Megillah <note>The Talmudic volume concerning the reading of the Scroll of Esther and synagogue laws</note>, folio 11, column 1.
</margin>

> <note>original Hebrew: ואפי' אם בנה ב'י והקדישו אחר כך...</note> *Even if he indeed built a Building and afterwards dedicated it as a Synagogue Building, its status is that of a Synagogue Building. Yet it is not sacred until it serves such sacred uses;* not even if it was built from the beginning in the name of a Synagogue (for this end, title, and purpose).

This is surely the simplest method of consecrating, and most consistent with reason, if even the least amount is to be granted to superstition. However, how the Gentiles instituted the consecrations of Sacred Buildings may be learned from Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Neapolitan lawyer known for his work on ancient Roman customs</note>: The consecration of a Temple was performed *such that he who was to dedicate the Temple and the Building, holding the Doorpost, with a small fire lit, and having called upon the Deity to whom the Temple and Buildings are hallowed, removes himself from profane use and human law,*

<margin>
*Genialium Dierum* <note>Genial Days, a work on ancient customs</note>, book 6, chapter 14.
Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, book 3, chapter 14, § 5.
</margin>

But among the Hebrews, this Consecration achieves such an effect that a house of this kind, which has been destined for public prayers and has already been employed under that name and title, is held to be holy. Furthermore, the writers of rituals, frequently celebrated alongside the Talmudists, have abundantly handed down the various degrees of that holiness. In the *Shulchan Aruch* <note>The "Set Table," the definitive 16th-century code of Jewish law</note>, an entire Chapter is found on this matter, the title of which is: <note>original Hebrew: דיני קדושת בית הכנסת</note> *Statutes pertaining to the Sanctity of the Synagogue.* Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), a prominent Christian Hebraist</note> in his work *The Jewish Synagogue* did not neglect to represent some of these rules in a very brief compendium; which indeed could have sufficed, had we not already committed ourselves to a more fruitful treatment of these minor details. However, we cannot bring ourselves to pursue every single point that we read both in this Book and elsewhere, because many things are contained in them which are, by Hercules, not of great weight and are of the slightest consideration. We shall therefore do this: to spare our labor and diminish the weariness of reading, we will provide a summary of those canons contained in this chapter of the *Shulchan Aruch* (and perhaps nowhere more carefully), in the English language only, noting the Authors in the margin who will provide more to readers not satisfied with this mere taste.

When the King <note>Herod the Great, who reigned c. 37–4 BCE</note> noticed this, he commanded them to be of good cheer; for the old Temple would remain intact and would not be demolished until all the material necessary for the future fabric was gathered. To be sure, the Jews could never be led to love Herod—a man of a foreign and servile race in their eyes—no matter how many benefits or services he studied to bestow upon them. Furthermore, just as a synagogue was not to be demolished rashly, so too, once it was laid waste, neglected, or abandoned, it was not to be held with any less reverence.

<margin>Chapter *Bene Hair* [Sons of the City], which in some Codices is the fourth, in others the third. folio 26, column 1.</margin>
Now a word must be added concerning the **ALIENATION** <note>The transfer of ownership to another party</note> of Synagogues, which occurs either through **SALE** or **GIFT**. In order to correctly understand this matter, it must first be noted that the Jews distinguish their Synagogues into Synagogues of **FORTIFIED CITIES** <note>Hebrew: *Kerakhim*</note>, which may be called **PUBLIC**, and those of **VILLAGES** <note>Hebrew: *Kepharim*</note>, which we shall call **PRIVATE**. It was not permitted to sell the Public synagogues or the communal synagogues of fortified towns. The foundation of doctrine and debate regarding this argument is found in the Tractate *Megillah*, from which **Maimonides**, **Rabbi Jacob** <note>Jacob ben Asher, author of the Arba'ah Turim</note>, and almost all other compilers of rituals have extracted the relevant points. The chapter *Megillah* begins thus: <note>Original Hebrew: בני העיר שמכרו רחובה של עיר לוקחין בדמיו בית הכנסת בית הכנסת לוקחין תיבה וכו׳</note> *“The sons of the city (the community of Israelites living in a certain place) who sell the open square of the city, may buy a Synagogue with its price; those who sell a Synagogue, may buy an Ark <note>The chest where Torah scrolls are kept</note> with its price, etc.”*

Regarding those words, the **Gemara** <note>The part of the Talmud that provides rabbinical commentary and analysis</note> says: <note>Original Hebrew: בני העיר שמכרו רחובה של עיר אמ׳ רבה ברבר חנה אמר רבי יוחנן זו דברי רבי מנחם בר יוסי סתומתאה אבל חכמים אומרי׳ הרחוב אין בו משום קדושה ורבי מנחם בר יוסי מאי טעמי׳ הואיל והעם מתפללין בו</note> *“The inhabitants of the city, where they sell the square of the city: Rabba bar bar Channa said; Rabbi Yochanan said, these are the words of Rabbi Menachem bar Yose, the Canonical Doctor; but the Sages say, no sanctity at all resides in the square. What was the reasoning of Rabbi Menachem bar Yose? Because the people pray in it.”*

### Chapter 13. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Chapter 4, sections 1, 2.</margin>
Now, what argument did *Rabbi Menachem* put forward for his opinion? Specifically this: that the people pray in these places during *fast days and solemn assemblies* <note>The author uses the Latin "stationibus solennibus," referring to the 'Ma'amadot,' groups of laypeople who gathered for prayer while the priests performed sacrifices</note> (concerning which, see the Code *Taanith* <note>The Talmudic tractate 'Taanit' deals with the laws of fast days</note>). However, the Sages reply that this is a matter of *temporary circumstances* in the world. *Rabbi Menachem* believed that the very squares of the city should be considered *sacred* places because it sometimes happens that if the synagogues cannot contain the crowd, the people gather in the squares to pray.

2 Chronicles 32:6.
Ezra 10:9.
Nehemiah 8:2, 4.
</margin>
You can indeed find examples of this in the holy books. But in the *Gemara* <note>The Gemara is the portion of the Talmud containing rabbinic commentary and analysis</note> itself, it has already been determined that the opinions of the Sages differ from that of *Menachem*. <margin>
Hilchot Tefillah and Birkat Kohanim, chapter 11, § 21.

<note>original Hebrew: רחובה של עיר אע"פ שהעם מתפללין בו... "The city square, although the people pray in it..."</note> *Regarding the city square: although the people may pray in it on fasts and solemn assemblies because the crowd is too large for the synagogues to contain them, there is no inherent sanctity in it. This is because it only happens by chance that the square is used for such a purpose, and it was not properly established for set prayers. And so it is in houses and courtyards where people gather to offer prayers; there is no sanctity in them, since they did not establish those places solely for prayer, but pray in them only by chance, much like a man who pours out his prayers within his private home.* Therefore, the opinion of *Menachem* falls. <note>original Hebrew: הלכה כחכמים</note> *What has been pronounced by the Sages is here considered to be the law,* says *Bartenora* <note>Obadiah ben Abraham of Bertinoro, a 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note>. ...to sell a Synagogue? [This refers] to the ***Synagogue of Villages***, which they did not build except by the decision of *villagers only* <note>original Latin: "paganorum," here referring to inhabitants of a rural 'pagus' or village, rather than 'pagans' in a religious sense</note>, so that they might pour out prayers in it. Truly, the reason why it is not permitted to sell ***Synagogues of towns*** is given in the text: because people from the whole world are accustomed to gather there to pray, and there is a right of many over them. Let us learn what these things mean from the ***Tosafot*** <note>The 'Tosafot' are medieval commentaries on the Talmud that expand upon Rashi's explanations</note>:

"Since they come to it from the world [outside], it seems this should be explained as follows: since the majority of people are accustomed to go there to pray, even though they give nothing toward its building, nevertheless, since it was made with the intent of those many people, its sanctity becomes more severe and they are not able to sell it; and there is more to explain..." <note>original Hebrew: "כיון דמעלמא... ועוד יש לפר"</note>; *since they are accustomed to betake themselves to it from everywhere, they seem to be explained thus; since a great multitude of men is accustomed to frequent it for the sake of praying: for although they perhaps contributed nothing of their own to its construction, nonetheless, because a Synagogue of this kind was made for the sake of those many people, its sanctity must be judged to be more serious, and thus it is not permitted to sell it. Specifically, if a certain society of men had built a Synagogue or Academy in some city, it is always considered to be under the power of its owners in such a way that it was entirely within their rights to transfer it to others whenever they pleased. Therefore, what is proclaimed in these Canons <term>Canons</term><note>The established laws or rules of the Talmud.</note> regarding the *Synagogues of fortified cities* is only to be understood as referring to those Synagogues which truly belong to *those cities* and form a part of them. But not even all the doctors of law agree on this point. Indeed, *Rabbi Isaac of Vienna*, as found in the *Annotations to Rabbi Asher* <note>Rabbi Asher ben Jehiel, a prominent 13th-century German-Spanish rabbi.</note>, believes that any Synagogue can be sold provided it is established that it was built by the citizens at their own expense alone.

In the Observations on Rabbi Asher.
</margin>
*Let us review the text:* *But in the "Or Saruah"* <term>Or Saruah</term><note>original Hebrew: אור זרוע, "Light is Sown," a major legal code by Rabbi Isaac of Vienna.</note> *it is written that every Synagogue which is known to have been built by the city—having built it themselves and not having collected money from the world [outside]—may be sold by the authority of the seven good men of the city, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: אבל באור זרוע כתוב דכל בית הכנסת שידוע שבנו העיר בנו אות' ולא גבי זוזי מעלמא יש לה מכר על פי שבעה טובי העיר וכו'</note>. Let us also relate the rest, which follows: *And so, when a* **PRIVATE INDIVIDUAL BUILT A SYNAGOGUE**, *and gave it to the inhabitants of the City absolutely, also granting them the power of repairing the house and enlarging its building, so that neither he nor his heirs are able to prevent them, then indeed such a Synagogue is judged to be the property of the entire assembly, and it may be sold by the authority of the seven good men of the city. But if he gave it in such a way that the good men do not have the power to prevent him from entering it to pray, but rather it belongs to himself—so that they are not permitted to repair the house or add to the building, but only he or his heirs—it cannot be sold except by the authority of the community and his heirs.* <note>original Hebrew: וכן יחיד שבנה... ועל פי ורשיו</note>

# ON STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

<margin>
Luke 7:5. <note>“For he loves our nation, and has built us a synagogue.”</note>

On this passage.
*Orach Chayim* Title 153. § 14. <note>A section of the *Shulchan Aruch*, the foundational code of Jewish law, dealing with the sanctity of the synagogue.</note>
</margin>
...the **Seven Good Men of the City** <note>The *Zhivlei Ha'ir*, a council of seven community leaders authorized to act on behalf of the congregation in legal and financial matters.</note>. However, if a person gave it on the condition that the **Good Men** should have no power to prevent anyone from entering it for the sake of prayer, but reserved for themselves the right that no one—besides themselves and their heirs—shall have the power to restore the cracks in the house or promote its construction, then that **Synagogue** cannot be sold except by the decision of that congregation, or the donor, or his heirs. From these words, it is clear that **Synagogues** could be established by private individuals and, once established, could be given to the **Church** <note>The author uses the Latin *Ecclesia* (Church) to refer to the Jewish religious assembly or congregation.</note> either absolutely or with certain conditions. This seems to contribute somewhat to the illustration of **Gospel History**, in which the **Centurion of Capernaum** is said to have built a **Synagogue**, as was observed before us by **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English cleric and scholar who used rabbinic literature to explain the New Testament.</note>. Just as someone could donate an entire Synagogue to the congregation, so too could they give land or anything else that is among the necessities of a Synagogue.

Let us now discuss **under what conditions it was permissible for private individuals to alienate their Synagogues**. Specifically, if **private individuals** <note>original: *Paganis*. In this legal context, it refers to private citizens or non-members of the official communal structure, like the Roman Centurion mentioned.</note> had built a synagogue at their own expense, they were permitted to alienate it in two ways. Either it was legal for them to sell it privately to anyone, or it was sold through the **Elders** or the **Seven Good Men of the congregation** (the local Magistrate) **in a public assembly of the whole people**. If the former occurred, then attention had to be paid to these two conditions:

1. It was not permitted to sell the **Synagogue** for any use whatsoever, especially those that are base and ignoble.
2. It was also not permitted to convert the price of the sold **Synagogue** to uses other than sacred ones; and what is more, that price was to be used to acquire some other instrument of religion more sacred than a **Synagogue**.

However, if the **Synagogue** were sold **in a public assembly of the whole people** by the elders of that society, then it was sold so absolutely that the Synagogue building could be applied by any buyer even to the most base uses and services. Let us again prove these things we have said with domestic testimonies. Thus holds the **Mishnah** <note>The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions.</note>:

chapter III. § 1.
</margin>

> Just as it is permitted for them to sell a synagogue, so they may give it as a gift. For if the community did not receive some benefit from this gift, they would not have given it. Truly, they do not lease it for a fee, nor do they pawn it; and thus, where they demolish Synagogues to build them anew, it is lawful for them to sell, exchange, and give as a gift the bricks, the wood, and the dust (the earth) of them; yet it is forbidden to give these as a loan, because the sanctity is not removed from them except through the price of sale, or a benefit which stands in the place of a price.* We have nothing to add to these matters, which are clear enough.

# ON THE STRUCTURE BOOK I. PART I.

Were they instructed in the discipline of the Law of the Fatherland under the guidance of learned teachers? I would favor the latter view; both because the Jews record that a <note>original: "בית מדרש" (Beth Midrash)</note> **House of Study** was joined to every individual synagogue in Jerusalem, and because those learned men who are said to have disputed with Stephen <note>Referencing the trial of St. Stephen in Acts 6:9.</note> are far more probably established as having emerged from a *scholastic discipline* than simply from a *synagogue* in the general sense. Therefore, we may best understand the whole matter this way: that *Jews* of distinguished reputation, living in various regions of the world outside of Canaan, almost certainly took care that those who were from the same region, province, district, or famous city had some Academy established in their own name and at their own expense in Jerusalem. This was done both so they could send their sons there to be educated in the Language of the Fatherland and its traditions, and also so that those staying in Jerusalem for the sake of the holy rites might have a fixed and established place for practicing their religion. For the Temple could not accommodate all the individual synagogues. Appropriately, for the further illustration of this passage, <margin>In the place cited.</margin> *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist and clergyman.</note> produced from the Jerusalem Talmud this very *Synagogue of the Alexandrians*, which it seems the *Alexandrians are said to have built there in Jerusalem at their own expense*. Otherwise, no difficulty remains in this text, except for the obscurity regarding who those LIBERTINES were, whose *synagogue* is listed here first. If *Libertine* <note>original: "לִיבֶּרְטִינִי"</note> is to be understood here as a *Freedman*, properly so called—one who has been released from slavery into liberty, which none of us doubt (for we do not accept that this is the name of a *nation*, as it has seemed to some)—then the word, if I am not mistaken, carries a fourfold meaning. For by *Libertine* can be noted:
1. A *Jew* by origin and race who was sold into *slavery* to a Hebrew master in the land of Canaan, either by himself or by the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme rabbinic court.</note>, and was subsequently granted freedom by that same master. 
2. A *Jew* by origin and race who served a Gentile master (of which kind there were many in Italy and Rome) and was granted freedom by him. 
3. A *Gentile* by birth who, after performing service for a Hebrew master, was sent into freedom by him and, simultaneously with his manumission, was co-opted into Judaism as a <term>Proselyte of Righteousness</term> <note>A "Proselyte of Righteousness" (Ger Tzedek) is a full convert to Judaism who takes on all the obligations of the Law.</note> (both of which were performed through the rite of *Baptism* <note>Referring to ritual immersion or Mikvah.</note>).
4. Or a *Gentile* who, being subject to a Gentile master and manumitted by him, then embraced Judaism. To which class of *Libertines* should the *synagogue* in this text be attributed? The most learned men certainly vary—
