### CHAPTER 14. OF THE SYNAGOGUES.

...most illustrious and highly practiced men. *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a prominent English Hebraist.</note> understands the *Libertines* <note>Refers to the "Synagogue of the Libertines" mentioned in Acts 6:9.</note> to be of the first rank; *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>, who discusses this passage elsewhere with his usual learning, places them in the third; *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> however, considers them to be of the second and fourth ranks simultaneously. <margin>On the Law of Nature and Nations, Book II, Chapter V.</margin> The opinions of *Lightfoot* and *Selden* do not please me: I side with *Grotius*, whose judgment I increasingly find to be the most sound whenever he is not bound by accepted hypotheses. As for *Lightfoot*, who would believe that Jews who had surrendered themselves to slavery due to poverty, or were sold by the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme rabbinic court in ancient Israel.</note> because of theft—and whom *Lightfoot* himself calls the "dregs of the common people and a lice-ridden crowd"—would have had sufficient resources after their manumission <term>manumission|the act of a slave owner freeing their slaves</term> to build and maintain an Academy <note>original Latin: *Gymnasio*</note>? And if they did have the resources, what suitable cause would they have had for doing so in Jerusalem? For once they were restored to their former liberty and all their legal rights, there was no reason for them to separate themselves from the public synagogues of Jerusalem. Regarding *Selden*, I could hardly bring myself to believe that the Jews in the land of Canaan granted freedom to so many Gentile slaves and received them into their religion that these people could have borne the expenses of building and caring for an Academy; especially since the Jews—as *Lightfoot* observes—were quite reluctant to free <margin>See Maimonides, Laws of Idolatry, Chapter IX.</margin> Canaanite slaves. But even if there were a large enough number of these, what reason would there be for these freedmen to separate themselves from the common religious rites of Jerusalem, into which they had now been received, and withdraw into a synagogue peculiar to themselves? I admit they were inferior in certain prerogatives to Jews born of the true stock of Jacob, but surely that was no obstacle to their using the same rites in the same synagogues with other Jews. Indeed, the more they separated themselves, the more they made their own condition appear lower and more ignoble. Let us therefore think with *Grotius* that the term refers to *Jews* by origin who were enslaved to the service of Gentiles in *Italy* or *Rome* and granted liberty by them, and along with them, *Roman* or *Italian Freedmen* who had been initiated into Judaism as <term>proselytes of justice|converts who take on the full obligation of the Mosaic Law</term>. The following points support this view: 1. The very name **LIBERTINUS** used by *Luke* <note>The traditional author of the Book of Acts.</note>, which everyone knows is the common Roman word <note>original: *ΛΙΒΕΡΤΙΝΟΣ* (Libertinos)</note> by which *freedmen* were designated at that time; it seems Luke preserved it in the text so we would know which kind of *Libertines* should be understood here. For if Luke had simply wanted to translate the Hebrew word for *free* <note>original Hebrew: *חפשי* (chafshi)</note>, as *Selden* and *Lightfoot* contend, he undoubtedly would have used the Greek word for *freedman* <note>original Greek: *ἀπελεύθερος* (apeleutheros)</note>,

or some other similar power, but not specifically that Roman or Italian *Libertine* <note>The Latin word *libertinus* specifically refers to a person who has been freed from legal slavery.</note>. However, since these *manumitted* <term>manumitted|released from legal slavery</term> people were truly Romans and Italians—having either been born there or lived there for a long time—and since they were designated and known among the Romans and Italians by this name of *Libertines*, they retained this name even in the land of Canaan and in Jerusalem. They even placed it as a title over the Academy <note>original Latin: *Gymnasio*, referring to a place of study or a synagogue</note> which they built at their own expense. 

2. It should be observed that the *Libertines* are listed here alongside Alexandrians, Asians, Cyrenians, and Cilicians. It is well known that all of these were men of the Jewish nation, originating from places outside of Canaan <gloss>in the dispersion</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ (en tē diaspora)</note>, or at least living there because they or their ancestors had established their homes there. Yet, for the reasons mentioned above, they maintained their own Academies in Jerusalem. By probable reasoning, we suspect that the *Libertines*, listed with them, are of the same kind; that is, they were not *Jews* or *Manumitted Canaanites*, but people from foreign places—specifically Romans and Italians. Although they lived far away, they wished to demonstrate their love for their religion by this certain proof: ensuring that an Academy bearing their name was not lacking in Jerusalem. 

3. ### CHAPTER 14. OF SYNAGOGUES. 257

And indeed, this testimony of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who wrote extensively on the status of Jews in the Roman Empire.</note> is clear, from which we understand that the Jews who were assigned the *Transtiberine* <note>The area across the Tiber River in Rome, modern-day Trastevere, which was a historical center for the city's Jewish population.</note> region for their residence by Augustus were *Jewish Libertines* <term>Libertines|from the Latin *libertini*, meaning individuals who were formerly enslaved and then legally freed</term>, captured in various wars (both Civil and Foreign, which the Romans waged in the East) and then manumitted by their masters. <margin>Book on the Embassy to Gaius, page 785.</margin> "They were Romans," he says, "for the most part freedmen. For having been brought as captives to Italy, they were set free by those who had acquired them." <note>original Greek: Ῥωμαῖοι, ᾗ, inquit, ἦσαν οἱ πλείους ἀπελευθερωθέντες. αἰχμάλωτοι γὰρ ἀχθέντες εἰς Ἰταλίαν ὑπὸ τῶν κτησαμένων ἠλευθερώθησαν.</note> He calls them Romans because they had obtained the rights of Roman citizenship. If, therefore, there was such a great abundance of these Libertines in Rome under Augustus and Tiberius, why do we wonder that a *School* <note>original Latin: *Gymnasium*, here referring to a place of study or synagogue.</note> for these Libertines existed in Jerusalem? Nor is this contradicted by the objection raised by Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note>—that these Libertines of the Jewish race and religion were received into the sacred rites of the religion in Jerusalem as men of free-born status. This is true as long as it is granted that the name *Libertines* nevertheless stuck to them even among their own countrymen, because they were known by that name in Italy. Other matters in this passage from Luke <note>Referring to Acts 6:9.</note> are easily explained.

2. We also do not wish to overlook, while we are speaking of the *Private* synagogues of cities, the fact that a *part of the house* belonging to a private member of the congregation is sometimes consecrated as a *Synagogue* among the Jews. Thus we read in the *Orach Chaiim* <note>A major section of the Shulchan Aruch, the foundational code of Jewish law.</note>: <margin>in this place, section 17.</margin> "In whose house there was a synagogue for a long time, the congregation is not permitted to transfer it from there into another house." <note>original Hebrew: מי שהיה בביתו בית הכנסת ימים רבים אין הצבור רשאי לשנותו בבית אחר</note> Indeed, the houses of private individuals are often leased by the congregation for this purpose. <margin>section 16.</margin> Thus we read under the same title: "He who lent his house for a house of the synagogue, etc." <note>original Hebrew: מי שהשאיל ביתו לבית הכנסת וכו'</note> And it is also established that in such places of their exile where fewer Jews live, the same custom is still accepted among them. Indeed, this is not a trivial point. For from this, in my opinion, we can correctly explain a phrase quite familiar in the *Epistles of Paul* regarding the Church, which is AT THE HOUSE of this or THAT FAITHFUL person. <margin>chapter 16:3, 5.</margin> Thus he writes to the Romans: "Greet Priscilla and Aquila, and THE CHURCH WHICH IS AT THEIR HOUSE." <note>original Greek: καὶ τὴν κατ' οἶκον αὐτῶν ἐκκλησίαν</note> <margin>chapter 16:19.</margin> The same is repeated in the *First Epistle to the Corinthians*. Likewise to the *Colossians*: "Greet the Laodicean brothers and Nymphas, and THE CHURCH WHICH IS AT THEIR HOUSE." <margin>chapter 4:15.</note>

...that they did not have a synagogue. However, as far as we understand, there are two responses to this objection. 1. That we might say the word *Kepharim* <note>original Hebrew: כפרים, meaning villages</note> or *Villages* is sometimes used with greater emphasis and sometimes with less; that is, the word sometimes denotes *larger villages*, which are also called *Ayrot* <note>original Hebrew: עיירות, small cities</note> or *Communities*, and at other times it refers to *rural villas* located in the immediate outskirts of any City. 2. <margin>Chapter 1, sections 1, 11, 12.</margin> It is established in the Code *Megilla* <note>The tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud titled *Megillah*, which deals with the laws of the festival of Purim and the reading of the Scroll of Esther</note> that the reading of the *Megilla* (the small book of *Esther*) can and must take place at various times, depending on the different status of locations and communities. Towns which were walled from the time of Joshua, called *Krakhim* <note>original Hebrew: כרכים, fortified cities</note>, were required by decree to read the book of Esther on the fifteenth day of the month of Adar. The words are as follows: *Walled towns from the days of Joshua son of Nun read on the fifteenth.* <note>original Hebrew: כרכין חמוקפין חומה מימות יהושע בן נון קורין בחמשה עשר</note>. **TOWNS**, *walled from the times of Joshua Son of Nun, read on the fifteenth day*. Besides these towns, there are mentioned **LARGE CITIES** <note>Hebrew: *Ayrot Gedolot*</note> and **VILLAGES** <note>Hebrew: *Kepharim*</note>. *Large Cities* were those Jewish communities in which were found "ten men of leisure," as they were called <note>original Latin: *decem Otioſi*. These were community members supported by the public to be constantly available to ensure the required quorum of ten men for communal prayer and legal proceedings</note>, about whom more will be said later. It is determined in the *Megilla* that these enjoy this prerogative: they may read on the *fourteenth day*, that is, the day immediately preceding the fifteenth. *Large Cities read on the 14th day.* <note>original Hebrew: עיירות גדולות קורין בי"ד</note>. If, however, there were any other community lacking these *Ten* such *Men of Leisure*, they did not read the book of Esther except on the *day of the Synagogue Assembly* <note>original Hebrew: ביום הכניסה, *yom ha-knisah*</note>, that is, on *Monday* or *Thursday*. This was because on those days justice was administered and the Synagogue was frequented, of which more shortly. Suppose, for example, a Jewish community where the ten men of leisure were not found, and the ordinary time for reading the *Megilla* (the fourteenth day) fell on a *Tuesday* or *Wednesday*; it was the duty of that community not to read the *Megilla* on that fixed Tuesday or Wednesday, but to move the reading forward to the preceding *Monday*. This *Monday*, if the Wednesday were the 14th, would fall on the *twelfth day*; if the Tuesday were the 14th, it would fall on the *thirteenth day*. ...those not having their own **Synagogue** were required to gather in the **cities** <note>original Hebrew: עיירות (*Ayrot*), referring to small or medium-sized towns</note> so that they might complete the **Reading of the Megilla** <note>The Scroll of Esther, read during the holiday of Purim</note> in their **Synagogues**. Indeed, all smaller societies of **Jews**, being destitute of "idlers" <term>otiosi: Hebrew 'Batlanim'. These were ten men of leisure who were supported by the community to be available at all times for prayer services to ensure a quorum (minyan)</term>, are classified in this regard <margin>Chapter 1, section 5</margin> among the **Villages**, as you may easily see from **Maimonides** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and legal scholar</note>: **And every City that does not have ten Idlers is like a village, and they advance and read on the day of the Synagogue Assembly.** <note>original Hebrew: וכל עיר שאין בה עשרה בטלנים היא ככפר ומקדימין וקוראין ביום הכניסה</note> Regarding the **Villagers** who have neither **Synagogues** nor **Idlers**, the words are: **Megilla text:** **Villagers advance to the day of the Synagogue assembly.** <note>original Hebrew: כפרים מקדימין ליום הכניסה</note> This means that even if the appointed time for reading the **Megilla** fell on a **Wednesday** or a **Tuesday**, the villagers nevertheless advance the reading to **Monday**, when they are accustomed to travel to the cities. This is done so that no excessive hardship is created for them beyond the appointed times for going into the city <note>Monday and Thursday were traditional market days and days when the local courts sat, so villagers would already be in town</note>, since **those** who do not have their own **Synagogue** in the places where they live are not permitted to complete this reading there.

From this account, it is clear enough that **Villages** were not equipped with any **Synagogues**. If the villages had **Synagogues**, it would not be necessary for the villagers and rural folk to set out for the **Synagogues** of the cities on **Monday** and **Thursday** to perform the sacred rites there, much less would they travel to the cities to perform the **Reading** of the book of **Esther** in the **Synagogues** of the cities. For nothing would prevent them from being able to read the Book of **Esther** in their own **Synagogues** just as well as in the **Synagogues** of the cities. ### CHAPTER 14. ON SYNAGOGUES.

The **Sages** established that these things should be read by them, according to what is said: *In their appointed times.* <note>original Latin: "In temporibus suis"</note> And these are the times designated for that reading. In every region that was enclosed by a wall from the days of **Joshua, Son of Nun**, whether in the land of **Canaan** or outside of it—even if it is not enclosed by a wall today—they read on the fifteenth day of the **Month of Adar**. Such a region is called a **Walled Town** <note>original Hebrew: כרך (*Kerech*), a fortified or munitum town</note>. But in a district that was not surrounded by a wall in the days of **Joshua**, even if it is surrounded now, they read on the fourteenth day; such a district is called a **City** <note>original Hebrew: עיר (*Ir*)</note>.

<margin>Section V.</margin> **Even Susa the capital, although it was not surrounded by a wall in the days of Joshua son of Nun, they read there on the fifteenth day.** <note>original Hebrew: אף שושן הבירה על פי שלא היתה מוקפת חומה בימי יהושע בן נון קוראין בה בחמשה עשר</note> The **City of Susa**, although it was not fortified in the time of **Joshua**, nevertheless enjoys this privilege: the **Book of Esther** <note>original: "libellus Esther"</note> is read there on the fifteenth day because the sign of deliverance occurred there, etc.

<margin>Section VI.</margin> **The inhabitants of the villages, who do not gather in Synagogues except on Monday and Thursday, it was established for them that they should advance and read on the day of the Assembly.** <note>original Hebrew: בני הכפרים שאין מתקבצין בבתי כנסיות אלא בשני ובחמשי תקנו להם שיהו מקדימין וקוראין ביום הכניסה</note> **FOR THE SAKE OF THE RURAL INHABITANTS** <note>original Latin: "IN GRATIAM PAGANORUM"—the author uses "pagani" in the classical sense of rural villagers, not religious heathens</note>, **WHO DO NOT FREQUENT SYNAGOGUES EXCEPT ON THE SECOND AND FIFTH DAYS OF THE WEEK** <note>Monday and Thursday</note>, this statute was made: that they may advance the reading of this book and read it on the day of the **Synagogue assembly**. That is, on those very days—the second or fifth of the week—on which they are accustomed to frequent the **Synagogues** of the cities. Regarding the cities <note>original Hebrew: עיירות (*Ayrot*)</note> destitute of **Men of Leisure** <term>otiosi: Hebrew 'Batlanim'. Therefore, the **rural Jews**, who live in the cities of the villages, make the fourteenth day of the **Month of Adar** a day of joy and feasting, and a festive day. From this text, the **Jews** took the opportunity to form those precepts and constitutions which were related by us in the preceding pages and described from **Maimonides**. Specifically, in this text, there is mention of two kinds of places: **Susa** and the **Unwalled Towns**. **Susa** <note>original Hebrew: שושן (*Shushan*)</note> was a fortified city, the seat of the Emperor. ### CHAPTER 14. OF SYNAGOGUES.

Indeed, nowhere were secure locations more beneficial than on the seashores, where it is necessary for stored goods to be safe from plunderers and for the men guarding them to be safe from untimely waves; for this reason, the most famous fortifications and citadels of the Ancients were located by the sea.

In these various places, however, there existed a different celebration of the **Festival of Purim**. The Jews who lived in **Susa** <note>original: *Susan*, the capital of the Persian Empire where the events of the Book of Esther took place</note> observed this festival on the **fifteenth day**. Because **Susa** was a fortified city, this privilege was extended to the **fortified cities of the land of Canaan** <note>The Land of Israel</note>, and it was decreed that in all of them the **Festival of Purim** should be celebrated on the **fifteenth day of the month of Adar**. But why is this decree restricted to cities fortified from the times of **Joshua**? **Maimonides**, **Ascher**, and all the authors of the Rituals <note>The medieval codifiers of Jewish law</note> provide the reason: because many cities in the land of Canaan were destroyed at that time [of the Persian miracle], so that very few would have enjoyed this privilege if the status of cities fortified at *that* specific time had been taken into account. Thus, it seemed more prudent to grant this privilege to all those cities which could be believed from history to have been fortified since the time of **Joshua** <note>Joshua son of Nun, who led the Israelites into Canaan; this rule was established to ensure that cities in the Land of Israel were honored even if they were in ruins during the Persian period</note>.

Since the Ancient Jews understood by **unwalled places** <note>original Hebrew: *prazot* (פרוזות)</note> any locations in which mixed societies of men lived but which were not surrounded by a wall, it followed that all Jewish communities inhabiting places not surrounded by a wall should be able to read the **Book of Esther** <note>referred to here as the *libellum Esther*</note> **on the fourteenth day**, because they were considered to enjoy the same privilege as the **unwalled villages** <note>original Hebrew: *prazot*</note> in the lands of Media and Babylonia. And this is true to the extent that today, in any communities outside the land of Canaan, the **Megilla** <note>The Scroll of Esther</note> is read on the **14th day of the month of Adar**. However, this was not the conclusion reached by the ancient Sages. What, then, is the reason for this? Certainly, **Cities and towns** had **villages** <note>original Hebrew: *kepharim* (כפרים)</note> around them in their district; by these you should understand smaller societies of men living in the countryside within the district of a City or town, from whom the townspeople received their provisions. These **villagers**, having neither a **Synagogue** nor a **tribunal** <note>A local court of law</note> (for they lived in the district of a City or town), were accustomed to travel to the Town or City twice a week—that is, on **Monday and Thursday**—to display their wares and [await] judgments...

This reason for the name given by **Maimonides** pleases us more, because it is more general and better fits the nature of the word **Knesset** <note>meaning assembly</note>. For the **Synagogue** is called the **House of Assembly** <note>Hebrew: *Beit HaKnesset*</note>, from the same root **Kanas**, meaning "to gather."

Certainly, this difficulty can be removed in this way: by saying that the word **Village** <note>original Hebrew: *Kafar*</note> in the text of the *Megilla* <note>The Talmudic tractate concerning the Scroll of Esther and the festival of Purim</note> is taken more restrictively to mean smaller rural societies, such as those typically found in the districts of cities and towns. Concerning these, it is indeed true that they did not ordinarily enjoy the benefit of synagogues. However, as for the larger and more populous rural societies, they were very often equipped with synagogues.

Certainly, the word *Kafar* is explained in that more restrictive sense by Kimchi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note>, who says: "Houses outside the city for villagers and for those who cultivate the land." Philippus Aquinas <note>A 17th-century convert from Judaism to Christianity and scholar of Hebrew</note> says: "A few houses together outside the city."

Indeed, the word *Kafar* is clearly of the same meaning as the Latin word *tugurium* <note>a hut or cottage</note>. However, just as an entire city or society of men is eventually formed from many such rural huts, so the word *Kafar* also began over time to be applied to larger villages, which are otherwise called *Vici* <note>Latin for small towns or districts</note>, though this is not as frequent in the Biblical text as it is among the Chaldeans <note>The Aramaic translators of the Bible</note>. He says that Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian</note>, in the fifth book of his *Histories*, describes a **village-city** when he mentions "works of a long peace, destroyed, built not far from the camp in the manner of a municipality." **Bethsaida** was such a **village-city**, having recently acquired the appearance of a town; Luke here called them "cities" in a broader sense, as he also does in verse 12. Nor do the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> translate it in this way. # CHAPTER 14. ON SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>
Chapter 3, Article 4, Section 1.
</margin>
Regarding **THE SYNAGOGUES OF THE VILLAGES** <note>original Hebrew: *Batei Knesiyot shel Kfarim*</note>, one might ask: how could they exist if villages were once destitute of synagogues? Certainly, this difficulty can be resolved by saying that the word <term>Village <gloss>original Hebrew: *Kafar*</gloss></term> in the text of the *Megilla* <note>The Talmudic tractate concerning the Scroll of Esther</note> is used in a restricted sense to mean the smaller societies of country-dwellers—those typically found in the districts of *cities* and *towns*. Regarding these, it is indeed true that they ordinarily did not enjoy the benefit of having their own synagogues.

However, as for the *larger and more populous societies of country-dwellers*, those were quite frequently equipped with synagogues. Certainly, the word *Kafar* is explained in that more restricted sense by Kimchi <note>David Kimhi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval rabbi and Hebrew grammarian</note>: "Houses," he says, "outside the city for rural folk and tillers of the earth" <note>original Latin/Hebrew: *Domus extra Civitatem propaganis & cultoribus terræ*</note>. Philippus Aquinas <note>A 17th-century scholar and convert from Judaism who taught Hebrew in Paris</note> describes them as: "A few houses together outside the city." 

In every respect, the word *Kafar* has exactly the same meaning as the Latin word *tugurium* <note>A hut or cottage</note>. For just as the Latin word is derived from the word for "covering," so too is the Hebrew. The Dutch use a similar term: **Farmer’s hut** <note>original Dutch: *Boere-hutte*</note>. Truly, just as a whole city or society of men is eventually formed from many such rural huts, so over time the word *Kafar* began to be applied to **larger villages**, which are otherwise called *townships*, though this is not as frequent in the Biblical text as it is among the Chaldeans <note>The Aramaic translators/paraphrasers of the Bible</note>. 

For this reason, the Chaldean Translator rendered the phrase "unwalled cities" <note>original Hebrew: *Ari Prazot*</note> found in the *Book of Esther* as <term>Villages <gloss>original Aramaic: *Kufrana*</gloss></term>, as Elias <note>Elijah Levita, a famous Renaissance Hebrew scholar</note> records. <margin>In the book *Tishbi*.</margin> Certainly, the "Cities of the Villages" in the text of *Esther* denote quite large neighborhoods, even if they are not surrounded by a wall, where there is a frequent gathering of people. In Dutch, these are called **Village-towns** <note>original Dutch: *Dorpsteden*</note>. 

The term <term>Village-city <gloss>original Greek: *kōmopolis*</gloss></term> agrees entirely with this phrase. This word appears in the Gospel of *Mark*, <margin>Chapter 6:38.</margin> and nowhere else in the Holy Scriptures of the New Testament. It is said: "*Let us go into the neighboring village-towns*" <note>original Greek: *Ἄγωμεν εἰς τὰς ἐχομέναs κωμοπόλεις*</note>. The Dutch translate this as: **Market-towns** <note>original Dutch: *Blecken*</note>. But perhaps they would have rendered it better with the same word used in the Book of *Esther*: **Village-towns** <note>original Dutch: *Dorpsteden*</note>. 

There is a sufficiently elegant paraphrase of that passage by Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian</note>, which it would be a shame to leave untouched. He says that *Tacitus* <note>A famous Roman historian</note>, in the fifth book of his *Histories*, describes a *kōmopolis* when he mentions "works of a long peace, demolished, which had been built not far from the camp in the manner of a municipality." Such a "village-city" had been *Bethsaida*, which had recently acquired the appearance of a town; *Luke* called these "cities" here in a somewhat improper sense, as he also does in verse 12. Some of the Hebrew Masters believe that "unwalled cities" are these village-cities. There are those who disagree. Indeed, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> do not translate it that way. From the historian *Josephus*, it is established that there were "villages not falling short of the size of a city" <note>original Greek: *κώμας πόλεως μέγεθος οὐκ ἀποδεούσας*</note>. Our writers use the terms **city** <note>original Greek: *πόλιν* (polis)</note> and **village** <note>original Greek: *κώμην* (kōmē)</note> interchangeably. Thus, the Greek scholars Pollux and Harpocration <note>Julius Pollux and Harpocration were ancient lexicographers who studied Greek terminology</note> note that among the Greek poets, places that are actually **villages** are called **cities**, and they provide an example from Euboea, of which Euripides said: *In Euboea, there is a certain neighboring city of holy sites* <note>original Greek: *Eυβοεί ἀγναῖς ἐσί τις γείτων πόλις*</note>. I believe what Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian</note> teaches here is most true: that by the term **unwalled towns** <note>original Hebrew: *ערי פרזות* (arei perazot)</note> are designated **country-towns** <note>original Greek: *κωμοπόλεις* (kōmopoleis)</note>, or **villages**, which are settlements shaped like towns though they lack walls. Indeed, the Jews often called these latter ones **villages** <note>original Hebrew: *כפרים* (kefarim)</note>, which is also translated by the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> as **villages** <note>original Greek: *κώμας* (kōmas)</note>. Therefore, a **country-town** is a **village** <note>original Hebrew: *kafar*</note> in a broader sense. From this, it happened that this word *kafar* was so frequently joined in composition with the proper names of places or men that were celebrated in such a village, in almost the same way as occurs among the French with the word *ville* and formerly among the ancient Greeks with the word *polis*. # Concerning the ORIGIN Book I. Part 2.

That it is of ancient use and custom is clear from the Speech which *James* gave in the Council of Jerusalem: <margin>Acts 15:21</margin> *For Moses from ancient generations has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath;* <note>original Greek: "Μωσῆς γὰρ ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων κατὰ πόλιν τοὺς κηρύσσοντας αὐτὸν ἔχει, ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκόμενος"</note> for Moses has those from ANCIENT AGES, city by city, who proclaim him, since he is read every Sabbath in the Synagogues. The Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> punctuated this text with a very slight difference, and related the words *in the synagogues* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς"</note> to the preceding context rather than the following one, in this way: *For Moses from ancient times has in individual Cities those who preach him in the Synagogues: where he is read every Sabbath.* The Syriac version <note>Refers to the Peshitta, the ancient Syriac translation used by Eastern churches.</note> does the same; but, as I said, that difference in reading is of very little importance. The meaning remains the same: that Synagogues and their worship have long been established by use among the Hebrew People.

For the phrase *from ancient generations* <margin>Job 8:8, Malachi 3:4</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων"</note>—"from ancient ages"—which corresponds to the Hebrew *from the first generations* or *from former years* <note>original Hebrew: "מדורות ראשונים" (mi-dorot rishonim) or "משנים קדמוניות" (mi-shanim kadmoniyot)</note>, can signify nothing less than that Synagogues had already been accepted among the Jews for a long time, and that the reading of the Law practiced in them is of a sufficiently ancient custom. This is exactly what is signified, I say, by this phrase, although <margin>verse 8</margin> I am not unaware that a nearly similar <term>phrase <note>original Greek: "φράσιν" (phrasin), meaning a specific turn of phrase or wording.</note></term>, *from ancient days* <note>original Greek: "ἀφ’ ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων"</note>, which occurs in the speech of *Peter* mentioned a little earlier, should be interpreted with less emphasis. But that happens more rarely; therefore, it will not be <margin>Philo's *On the Embassy to Gaius*, page 801.</margin> necessary to delay us here any longer. 

Let us only observe that in a certain Letter of *Norbanus Flaccus*, Proconsul of Asia, *to the Ephesians*, a nearly similar <term>phrase</term> is found regarding the same subject in the works of *Philo*: *Caesar wrote to me that the Jews, according to their own ancient custom from age-old times, are to be thought of as gathering together to contribute money which they send to Jerusalem.* <note>original Greek: "Καῖσαρ μοι ἔγραψεν, Ἰουδαίους ἐξ αἴων ἰδίῳ ἀρχαίῳ ἐθισμῷ νομίζειν συναγομένους χρήματ' εἰσφέρειν, ἃ πέμπουσιν εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα."</note> Gelenius <note>Sigismund Gelenius (1497–1554), a scholar known for his influential translations of Philo and Josephus.</note> translates this as: *Caesar wrote to me that the Jews, wherever they are,* MAKE ASSEMBLIES ACCORDING TO THEIR ANCIENT CUSTOM, *and contribute money, which they send to Jerusalem.* Primarily, there is mention here of the *collection* of sacred coins, which were sent by the Jews of Ephesus to Jerusalem according to divine Law. At the same time, however, it is mentioned that they *gather together* <note>original Greek: "συνάγεσθαι"</note> for this purpose into assemblies, and both actions are traced back to an *ancient custom* <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀρχαίου ἐθισμοῦ"</note>, as if you were to say *from ancient days*, just as *James* does here. Nevertheless, a doubt remains as to what time these *ancient generations* or ancient ages take their beginning, if you look back to their first origin. For concerning this in the Holy Scriptures

<margin>Laws of Idolatry and Constellations, chapter 1, section 1.</margin> <note>Original: *Hilkhot Avodat Kokhavim ve-ha-Mazalot*. This refers to a section of Maimonides' *Mishneh Torah*, his comprehensive code of Jewish law.</note>
...who followed this treatise of *Maimonides* <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and jurist.</note> with a very brilliant commentary. We voluntarily overlook those things which we could describe at length from this and other authors. We will only give the reasons for which we think the Hebrew interpreters are in error in this passage.

<margin>Genesis 4, last verse.</margin>
1. The meaning of this version <note>referring to the interpretation that suggests profanation</note> destroys itself. For *to invoke the name of the Lord is not profane;* and therefore *it cannot be profaned by invoking the name of the Lord.* On the contrary, *to invoke the name of the Lord is a holy and praiseworthy work, and most fitting for a reasoning creature.* If you say that by the phrase *it was profaned by invoking the name of the Lord*, it is indicated that *the name of the Lord began to be invoked in a profane and unseemly manner toward God*, I believe I have solid reason to deny that such a sense can lie hidden in the power of these words. For one speaks quite obscurely and implicitly who, when he wants to say *men began to worship idols*, says *the divine name was profanely invoked*. As I said, that is an unusual and involved way of speaking, the like of which perhaps cannot be found in the Holy Scripture. For he who worships idols *does not invoke the name of the Lord*, and therefore does not profanate it *by invoking the name of the Lord*. If *Moses* had wanted to say that, he would have said it this way instead: *Then it was profaned by calling upon the names of other gods.* <note>Original Hebrew: אז הוחל לקרא בשם אלהים אחרים (*Az huchal likro be-shem Elohim acherim*).</note>

2. This was also quite rightly observed by *Dionysius Vossius* <note>A 17th-century Dutch scholar and translator known for his work on Maimonides.</note>: if this were the meaning of the words that the Hebrew interpreters choose—*in invoking*—then it would have been written in the Hebrew text with a *Bet* <note>the Hebrew prefix ב, meaning "in" or "with"</note> rather than a *Lamed* <note>the prefix ל, meaning "to" or "for"</note>, as in *to invoke*. For although I am not unaware that the letter *Lamed* joined to infinitives often has as much power as a *Bet*, as far as this passage is concerned, it would be said much more clearly and appropriately according to the sense the Jews attach to this place: *Then it was profaned* **in invoking** <note>Hebrew: *bi-kro*</note> *the Divine Name*, rather than **to invoke** <note>Hebrew: *li-kro*</note> *the Name of the Lord*. Nevertheless, I do not think it can be stubbornly denied that the word *huchal* <note>הוחל</note> can be translated as *it was profaned*.

<margin>Commentary on this passage.</margin>
Our colleague *Drusius* <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar of Hebrew and the Old Testament.</note> also did not deny that. But I believe that this meaning of the word is entirely unsuitable for this passage and its circumstances. Therefore, let the words be transposed, as we have already established: *Then it was begun to invoke the name of the Lord*; or, *then it was begun to be named by the name of Jehovah*, as *Aquila* <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note> has it: *Then he began to be called in the name of the Lord.* <note>Original Greek: Τότε ἤρξατο τοῦ καλεῖσθαι ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίε (*Tote ērxato tou kaleisthai en onomati kyriou*).</note>

The words of the Hebrew text certainly mean to say that the Divine Name was invoked at that time (whether rightly or profanely). Since, however, it is not *Onkelos's* habit to wander far from the text, but usually to stick very closely to the literal meaning, I would more easily believe that *Onkelos's* phrase, *to begin from invoking the Name of the Lord*, should be explained in a positive sense rather than a negative one.

For what is a Synagogue but an assembly of many into one to perform sacred rites? And what is the primary worship of Synagogues if not prayers, or the invocation of the Divine Name? I admit that the place where those faithful of the first centuries met is not mentioned in the text; nor is the time at which such fixed assemblies were celebrated. We pass, therefore, to that interval of time that flowed from the Flood up until the time of *Moses*. It is clear from the history of the Patriarchs that *Abraham*, while performing sacred rites, called upon the Divine name and publicly professed His worship. *Isaac* followed the praiseworthy example of his father. Yet it is not surprising that we read nothing about the public meetings of the faithful during that interval, nor the locations of those meetings, since it is established that the Church at that time was almost entirely confined to the families of the Patriarchs in *Canaan*. Therefore, the homes of the Patriarchs were themselves like schools and churches, in which they, as domestic teachers, provided guidance through their instruction and examples of piety.

<margin>Book on Abraham, page 275</margin>

in which it is said: **ויצא יצחק לשוח בשדה לפנות ערב** <note>original Hebrew: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening."</note> **AND ISAAC WENT OUT TO MEDITATE IN THE FIELD, BEFORE EVENING.** Onkelos <note>The author of the famous Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah.</note> and Iarchius <note>Rabbi Solomon ben Isaac, better known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> interpret this passage as referring to prayer. Therefore, according to them, the meaning of the passage is that Isaac went out in the afternoon hours towards evening to pray. I would not wish to overlook that what is called in this text **לפנות ערב** <note>original: "toward evening"</note> is read in *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher and codifier of law.</note>, as it is printed, as **לפנות היום** <note>original: "at the turning of the day"</note>—as *Schickard* and *Selden* <note>Wilhelm Schickard and John Selden, 17th-century Christian Hebraists.</note> also read it when they cite this very passage of *Maimonides*. However, *Selden* noted in the margin that in a manuscript copy of *Maimonides*, it is read as **לפנות ערב** <note>original: "toward evening"</note>, which is undoubtedly to be preferred. If *Maimonides* truly wrote **לפנות היום** <note>original: "at the turning of the day"</note>, then he seems to have understood the word **היום** <note>original: "day"</note> as the *inclination of the day* [towards sunset], in which sense it is sometimes accepted in Scripture. But this is a minor point. Regarding what they further add about *Jacob* as the author of the evening prayer, this seems to be extracted by them from the fact that *Jacob* is said **בערב** **TO HAVE COME IN THE EVENING** **FROM THE FIELD.** <note>Referring to Genesis 30:16.</note> Truly, as for the idea that *Jacob* meditated and prayed in the field after the example of his father, I confess the text does not sound clearly to that effect, but it is by no means absurd to suggest it is hinted at therein.

<margin>
Laws of the Recitation of the Shema, chapter I, § 4. <note>Reference to Maimonides' Mishneh Torah.</note>
</margin>

Beyond these things, there is also a tradition celebrated among the Hebrew people that *Jacob* and his sons, by their own example, began to teach their descendants 그at solemn profession of the *Unity of God*, which is part of the **קרית שמע** <term>Keriath Shema|The "Recitation of the Shema," the central declaration of Jewish faith.</term>—that is, the recitation of the *Shema*, or the section "Hear, O Israel" (about which, if it pleases God, we shall speak more fully in the following pages), to be repeated every morning and evening by every Israelite. Indeed, the Israelites wished the article of the *Unity of God* to be fixed so deeply in the souls of their people. But let us collect the entire text of *Maimonides* concerning this: **הקורא קרית שמע כשהוא** <note>original Hebrew follows:</note>

**"One who reads the Recitation of the Shema, when he**
**finishes the first verse, he says in a whisper: 'Blessed be the Name of His glorious Kingdom forever**
**and ever,' and then returns to reading as usual, 'And you shall love the Lord your God' until the end.**
**And why do we read it so? It is a tradition in our hands that at the hour when Jacob**
**our Father gathered his sons in Egypt at the time of his death, he commanded them and urged them regarding**
**the Unity of the Name <term>Yichud HaShem|The theological concept of the absolute oneness of God.</term> and the way of the Lord in which Abraham and Isaac his father had walked.**
**And he asked them and said to them: 'My sons, is there perhaps some defect <note>impurity or unworthiness</note> among you?**
**Anyone who does not stand with me in the Unity of the Name, as in the matter that Moses our Teacher said to us:**
**"Lest there be among you a man or woman, etc."?' They all answered and said: 'Hear, O Israel...'"**

### CHAPTER II.

*The opinions of Josephus, Philo, and even the later Masters are weighed; they seek the origin of the explanation of the Divine Law, practiced on Sabbath days, as far back as the Mosaic times and precepts. Evidence is unfolded from the Law of Moses regarding a <term>holy convocation</term> <note>original Hebrew: מקרא קדש (miqra qodesh)</note>, as they translate it (Lev. 23:3), and the sanctification of the seventh day (Exod. 20:8). Hugo Grotius <note>A famous 17th-century Dutch jurist and theologian who wrote extensively on law and scripture.</note> does not disagree that these were the intended references. However, it is proven that the origin of the Synagogues is not to be sought in either of those, both by explaining the phrase <term>holy convocation</term> and by clarifying the commandment regarding the sanctification of the Sabbath.*

There follows a period of time extending from Moses until the Babylonian Captivity. Indeed, to wish to search for Synagogues before the age of Moses might rightly seem a matter of excessive diligence and curiosity. But because there are many things here that present themselves to our investigation and judgment, it will be convenient to divide this entire time again into two spans: the first during the early stages of the Commonwealth, when it was governed without Kings; the second, which we shall begin from David and end at the Babylonian Captivity.

<margin>Book II, page 1072.</margin> Josephus, indeed, disputing against *Apion* <note>Referring to the work "Against Apion," where the Jewish historian Josephus defends Judaism against Hellenistic critics.</note> regarding the excellence of Moses over other Lawgivers, touches among other things upon this: that Moses commanded each of the Israelites to assemble on the *Sabbath* day to learn the Law. ### CHAPTER II.

*The opinions of Josephus, Philo, and even the later Masters <note>The "later Masters" refers to Rabbinic scholars and commentators of the post-biblical period.</note> are weighed, who seek the origin of the explanation of the Divine Law—practiced on Sabbath days—as far back as the times and commands of Moses. There follows a period of time that extends from Moses all the way to the Babylonian Captivity. Indeed, to wish to seek synagogues before the age of Moses might rightly be seen as a sign of excessive diligence and curiosity. It is true that there is something implicit in these words of *Maimonides* <note>The 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>. # CHAPTER 2. OF THE SYNAGOGUES.

...at these hours. This passage is famous and stands against the opinion of *Maimonides* <note>Moses Maimonides, the preeminent 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>, who does not attribute the very custom of establishing the reading on the second and fifth days of the week <note>Monday and Thursday</note> to *Ezra*, but rather attributes to him that specific change in the reading where the readers were required to read no fewer than ten verses. However, the testimony in the *Colbo* <note>A 14th-century legal compendium</note> is consistent with this passage:

<margin>Colbo chapter 20, at the beginning.</margin>
Thus <gloss>So</gloss> Ezra ordained for Israel that they should read from the Torah on the second and fifth days, so that they would not go three days without the Torah.

EZRA ORDAINED FOR THE ISRAELITES, *that* ON THE SECOND AND FIFTH DAYS OF THE WEEK THEY SHOULD READ THE DIVINE LAW, *lest they remain for three days without the Law.* If there is any support to be found for *Maimonides's* position, it must be sought in *Bava Kama* <note>A tractate of the Talmud concerning civil law</note>. Indeed, I have thought it worth the effort to investigate the nature of that evidence. It is said there *first in general terms*:

Ezra ordained ten regulations: that they read [the Torah] at the afternoon service on the Sabbath, and that they read on the second and fifth days, etc.

*Ezra ordained ten constitutions, namely, that they should read on the Sabbath toward evening, as well as on the second and fifth days of the week.* The other constitutions, which have nothing to do with this matter, are then listed. To these, the following words in the text of the *Gemara* <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis and commentary</note> succeed:

> Did Ezra institute that they should read on the second and fifth days? No, for it was already established from antiquity <note>original Greek: ἀπ' ἀρχῆς</note> by tradition based on the words: "And they went three days in the wilderness and found no water." <margin>Exodus 15:22.</margin> The mystical interpreters of Scripture explain *waters* as the *Law*, according to that which is said: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters." <note>Isaiah 55:1</note> Therefore, after they had gone for three days without the Law, they became exhausted. The Prophets who were among them arose and ordained for them that they should read from the Law on the Sabbath; then on the following first day of the week <note>Sunday</note> they should cease [reading]; then they should repeat the reading of the Law on the second day [Monday]; and cease on the third and fourth days; and read on the fifth [Thursday]; and cease on the eve of the Sabbath [Friday], so that they would not sleep for three days without the Law. Originally they ordained that one man should read three verses, or even three men should read three verses, corresponding to the Priests, Levites, and Israelites. But Ezra himself ordained that three men should read ten verses, corresponding to the ten idle men <note>The *Asara Batlanim*, ten men of leisure who were supported by the community to ensure a quorum for prayer was always available</note>.

On the contrary, it is clear to me thus far that the Legislator proposes the sum of the precept at its beginning: *Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy;* and then, he clearly and expressly explains what he understands by that "sanctification of the Sabbath" in the explanation <note>original Greek: ἐξήγησις (exegesis)</note> or narration of the precept that follows. Indeed, that explanation of the precept concerning the Sabbath contains the mandate regarding the cessation from labor, and the extent of that cessation and most religious rest, along with the foundation of the precept. Therefore, in my judgment, *to sanctify the Sabbath* primarily and directly, according to the mind of the Legislator, means *to do no work on the Sabbath:* which rest God willed to be a sign of sanctification, or the separation of the seventh day from the other days of the week; because while it was free for anyone to work on the other days, on this day it was entirely forbidden, unless an urgent or fatal case persuaded otherwise. For this reason, only that man among the Israelites who applied himself to daily and servile works without a specific divine appointment, or a case of most urgent necessity, violated this precept and was held to have violated it.

# ON THE ORIGIN, BOOK I. PART 2.

...and you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. <note>Leviticus 25:10</note> What, I ask, is this sanctification of the fiftieth year? It is surely its separation from other years through rest and certain other unique things to be performed in it. If, however, the sanctification of a year does not necessarily denote the separation of that year for the exercises of religious worship, there is no reason why the sanctification of a day should imply anything more. Therefore, to rest on the *Sabbath* was to *sanctify the Sabbath* <note>original Latin: *Sabbatum sanctificare*</note>. For that very act of resting (which was God’s dispensation under the Old Covenant) on the seventh day was to *worship God*, because God intended to foreshadow the most noble things through that rest. For that *rest* <note>original Latin: *quies*</note> denoted that God willed to sanctify the human sinner through the obedience of His Son, and that He willed to rest and be glorified in the sanctified sinner, as if in a certain new work of His grace and power. Therefore, the Israelite who did not rest on the seventh day, by that very act, denied all faith in the promises. He denied, I say, God’s purpose concerning the sanctification of the sinner. He denied that great work of grace—which God was laboring upon and had already been laboring upon since the time of fallen man for the sake of the sinner—was ever to be perfected and consumed, and that God would one day find rest in that work as one entirely perfected and finished. 

If you have perceived this secret, then you will simultaneously understand why God once valued the rest of the seventh day so highly that He commanded it to be observed most religiously; likewise, why He established that rest as part of the typical <note>In this context, "typical" refers to "typology," a method of biblical interpretation where persons or events in the Old Testament are seen as "types" or foreshadowing symbols of Christ and the New Testament.</note> worship under the dispensation of the Old Covenant; and also how the *Sabbath* could be <margin>Ezekiel 20:12, 20.</margin> a *sign between God and Israel*, that God is the sanctifier of Israel; and finally, why *rest*, after God has perfected and finished this great work of His, is now no longer, nor can be, a part of divine worship, and thus the *Sabbath* under the New Testament has been abolished. For when the body is present and shining from every side, its shadow must perish. And these things lead us to believe that in the letter of the precept concerning the sanctification of the seventh day, almost nothing else was contained or included than that the Israelites should cease from all work on that day.

<margin>Isaiah 58:13, 14.</margin>

*If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath,* <note>original Hebrew: אם תשיב משבת רגלך</note> that is, if you pull back your foot—which you have already moved as if to sin—on the Sabbath day, *from doing your own pleasure on my holy day* <note>original Hebrew: עשות חפצך ביום קדשי</note>, *so that you do not perform those things which serve the satisfaction of the flesh and your own lust; and if you call the Sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord honorable, and honor it, not following your own ways, nor finding your own pleasure, nor speaking your own words, then you shall delight in the Lord, and I will cause you to ride upon the high places of the earth, and cause you to eat the inheritance of Jacob your father, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken it.* 

The theme of these words is clear enough. The Jews were abusing the Sabbath, as they still tend to do today, by using it to pursue their own pleasures <note>The author uses the Latin *delicias*, which can mean luxury or self-indulgence</note>, profaning the leisure granted to them with the gravest sins and the exercise of lust. God rebukes this vice through the Prophet. He wants them to seek delights that are pleasing to God—that is, to find their delight in God Himself—and to honor the rest of the Sabbath with the devotion it deserves, especially since God, in turn, promises them exceptional rewards. 

Indeed, just as it was not at all permitted for the Jews to abuse the Sabbath by indulging their vices, I maintain that: 2. The very leisure <note>original Latin: *otium*</note> of the Sabbath, when used with right reason, strongly impelled them toward the kind of exercises they knew were acceptable to God. Commending oneself to God in prayer; recounting His virtues; meditating on His works; speaking with others about His ways; exhorting others to piety—these are exercises pleasing to God. These were just as permissible on the Sabbath as on other days. Since it was better to do these things than to do nothing—indeed, they had more free time to do them on that day than on others, as they were often hindered by the cares and business of this earthly life—they were, through this leisure, spontaneously incited to devote more time to these works of piety on this day than on any other. 

Finally, let us also add this: 3. Various circumstances invited and called them to these duties of religion in a singular way, especially on this day. God commanded that the sacrifices be increased on that day. Since external sacrifices were signs of divine worship, the Israelites seemed to be reminded by them that God [required] a greater... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

# ON ORIGINS Book I. Part 2.

...to demand His worship from them, more than on any other day. The Sabbath itself was given to the Israelites as a *sign*, that God *is and will be their God, and would sanctify them*. The Sabbath reminded them of the creation of the world and the subsequent rest of God; of the leading out of *Egypt*; and especially of a certain future and more noble rest of God from the great work of the *Redemption* of the human race, which God was already then setting in motion. Who would think it alien for a pious Israelite to meditate on these things on the Sabbath day, to be occupied in them, to speak of them, and to glorify God because of them? Indeed, who would not think that every diligent worshiper of the Divine name among the Jews was driven and incited by these circumstances to perform these duties of piety, if he wished to celebrate a rest pleasing to God?

This is our view; and to that extent we also concede that a pious Israelite, fixing his meditations on the words of the Law concerning <term>SANCTIFYING</term> <note>original Hebrew: קדש (qodesh)</note> the *Sabbath*, could, with good reason, come to believe that these sacred duties of Religion were also entirely included and commanded by those words—not, however, according to the literal word, but according to a *sublimer and higher sense*. For he had satisfied the legal requirements of the Jewish Republic <note>The author refers to the ancient Israelite state as a "Republic" (Respublica), a common term in early modern scholarship to describe its civil and legal structure</note> and the letter of the precept who had rested, even if he had perhaps merely been *idle*.

It was handled in almost the same way as the matter of sacrifices. An Israelite was not pleasing or acceptable to God if he offered a victim to God at the altar *without faith*. Nevertheless, he had satisfied the legal requirements of that Republic if he had brought the victim, ordained and prescribed by law, to the Priest, and had rightly performed the sacred rites to be carried out before its slaughter, even if he happened to have little or no faith in God. I have written about this more explicitly than I had intended, because of the importance of the argument. However, if you desire to know more about it,

read through what the most learned *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693), an English theologian whose work "De Legibus Hebraeorum" was a foundational text in the study of Jewish law</note> commented upon not so long ago with almost the same aim. Indeed, I would have easily avoided this dispute concerning the meaning of the words of the Divine Law—by which the *sanctifying of the Sabbath* is commanded—if I had been allowed to follow my own inclination and if the thread of the material had not led me there. For since this matter was sharply and fervently debated by many in the Churches of our homeland a few years ago; and since the learned men who opposed the sense of the words chosen and established by me simultaneously claimed that through this explanation the precept concerning the Sabbath is loosened...

# BOOK I, Part 2: On ORIGINS.

->BY APPOINTMENT I WILL BE PRESENT FOR YOU, to speak with you there.<-

The text continues: <note>original Hebrew: ונועדתי שמה לבני ישראל ונקדש בכבדי</note> And **THERE I WILL PRESENT MYSELF TO THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL**, and they shall be sanctified in my glory. The Hebrew word *ya'ad* <note>יעד</note> in its simple form (*Kal*) signifies to appoint a time for someone to meet; in the passive/reflexive form (*Niphal*—from which the meaning of the word *moed* <note>מועד; an appointed time or place</note> is derived), it signifies to present oneself to someone at an appointed time. Do you wish to see the power of the word *no'adti* <note>נועדתי; "I will meet"</note> expressed most precisely? You should translate it thus: *I will appoint a time for meeting there with you, and* **AT THE APPOINTED TIME**

<margin>Exodus 25:22</margin>
*I will meet you.* So God had spoken concerning the Ark: <note>original Hebrew: ונועדתי לך שם ודברתי אתך</note> And **I WILL MEET YOU THERE AT THE APPOINTED TIME**, and I will speak with you from above the Mercy Seat. The meaning

<margin>Psalm 48:5; Numbers 10:3</margin>
of this word is sufficiently familiar elsewhere. Therefore, the Tabernacle was called the <term>Tent of Meeting<note>Hebrew: *Ohel Moed*</note></term>, because God would meet there with Moses by appointment, and not, in truth, because the Israelites assembled there to pray or to learn the precepts of the Law. Since, however, this "Tent of Moses" shared the same name—*Ohel Moed*—with the Tabernacle of God (the structure of which was not yet finished at that time), one must not think that the reason for the name varies. For God met with Moses just as much in the tent that Moses had pitched outside the camp as He did later in the Tabernacle, which was constructed according to the prescription of Divine Law. This was rightly

<margin>Commentary on this place.</margin>
observed by <term>Aben Ezra<note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a major Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note></term>: <note>original Hebrew: ויקרא לאהלו אהל מועד כי השם נועד לו שם עד שנעשה המשכן</note> *But he calls his own tent the tent of meeting, because the Name [God] met with him there until the Tabernacle was prepared.* <term>Munsterus<note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and Hebrew scholar.</note></term> also on this passage says quite correctly:

<margin>In this place.</margin>
"Tabernacle of Testimony." Others prefer to read "Tabernacle of Assembly," or "of Constitution," because the Lord had constituted and agreed with Moses that He would be present there by a visible sign and give answers. Let it therefore now be established that this Tabernacle was called the Tent of Meeting because God was accustomed to present Himself there to His people. As for what is added—that everyone seeking the Lord went out to this tent—that is understood by some not as referring to fixed prayers or instructions for which this tent served, but regarding any questions and consultations of the sort that, in doubtful and uncertain cases, were frequently brought to Moses, and through Moses to God. Whatever the case, they divided the sentence into two parts, as if the passage should be translated: *Do not look to the Pythons, and* <note>original Hebrew: אל הידענים אל תבקשו</note> *do not ask of the soothsayers.* For this is how the Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> conceived the text: *Do not turn aside to magicians, nor inquire anything of soothsayers.* But it should be well noted that the words *to the soothsayers* do not belong to the following phrase, *do not seek*, but rather to the preceding one, *do not turn.* Therefore, if I may speak the truth, I think the words of the text, *do not seek to be defiled by them*, should rather be transposed in this way: *Do not seek to be polluted by them, or with them.* This is exactly what I believe **Onkelos** <note>The author of the famous Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah</note> wished to say in his paraphrase: *You shall not seek to be defiled by them,* even though in the London editions <note>Likely referring to the London Polyglot Bible</note> it is translated as: *Do not inquire of them, so that you are polluted in them.* Yet, what is strange is that in the version of **Uzielides** <note>Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, traditionally attributed to Jonathan ben Uzziel</note>, which contains the same words, they have placed: *Do not seek, so that you are polluted in them.* But it is hardly worth our while to pursue this matter so anxiously now. The Septuagint <note>LXX</note> translated the word *baqash* <note>בקש; to seek</note> once as "to be desired" <margin>Esther 2:6</margin> by design, but even there perhaps they did not "hit the nail on the head" <note>original Latin: rem acu tetigerunt; a needle-sharp precision</note>. It does not seem out of place, therefore, that the phrase *to seek the Lord* <note>original Hebrew: יהוה בקש</note> in this passage denotes *to commend oneself to God with singular zeal and repentance*, as it is used frequently enough in Holy Scripture. For what <margin>Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13</margin> prevents those who wished to testify to God of their true and serious repentance from approaching this Tabernacle more closely, and striving to reconcile themselves with God through Moses? Yet, we shall not for that reason turn this Tabernacle into a **Synagogue**, because this Tabernacle does not appear to have been consecrated for the <term>fixed prayers<note>Latin: statis precibus; prescribed liturgy at set times</note></term> of the entire Assembly or Church of the Israelites, which is what we require in a Synagogue.

### ON THE ORIGIN Book I. Part 2.

<margin>Exodus 20:24.</margin>
...He provided:
> In every place where I cause my name to be remembered, I will come to you and I will bless you. <note>original Hebrew: בכל המקום אשר אזכיר את שמי אבוא אליך וברכתיך</note>
> *IN EVERY PLACE where I have caused my name to be recorded, I WILL COME TO YOU, and I will bless you.* <note>original Latin: IN OMNI LOCO, ubi recordari fecero nominis mei, VENIAM AD TE, & benedicam tibi.</note>

A man of beyond doubt learned standing, <margin>On the Hebrew Laws, book II, chapter V.</margin> John Spencer <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an English theologian and Hebraist known for his pioneering work on comparative religion and Hebrew law.</note>, recently strove to shed some light on this text; for it is somewhat obscure. He observed that the word *zakar* <note>original Hebrew: זכר</note> was accepted in antiquity with the meaning not only of remembering and recollecting, but also of worshipping, performing a sacred duty, and (especially in the *Hiphil* <term>Hiphil: a specific Hebrew verb form that typically denotes causative action, here meaning "to cause to remember"</term>) of celebrating. He brings forward certain passages from the sacred Authors to confirm this. <margin>Isaiah 66:3, Amos 6:11, 1 Chronicles 16:4.</margin> He adds that if this opinion holds, it would support the view of those who believe the word *Sacer* <term>Sacer: the Latin word for 'sacred' or 'holy'</term> is derived from *zakar* (signifying memory or worship). But we leave that matter undecided. 

He continues, judging that this sense of the word in this text is to be preferred over other meanings, since it is easy and fits the passage perfectly; so that those words, *"In every place where I have set the memory of my name,"* should be understood according to him as: *“Wherever I shall present myself to be worshipped and celebrated.”* Yet what prevents us from declaring that this opinion is burdened by some difficulty? For while *zakar* certainly denotes *to commemorate, to praise*, and if you like, *to worship and to pray* (though this is rarer), it never means *to present oneself to be commemorated or worshipped in a certain place*. Truly, those two—*to worship* and *to present oneself to be worshipped*—differ greatly. 

Then also, the sense of these words—*where I shall present myself to be worshipped, there I will come to you*—is not very clear or fluid. For according to the mind of the famous Author, this would mean: *“Wherever I cause you to pour out your prayers to me, there I will present myself to be present with you.”* But in this way, God would indicate no specific place in these words where he wished to be worshipped by the Israelites; yet he seems to want to indicate such a place by this precept. For it remained obscure and doubtful until now where God wished to present himself for worship and be adored by the Israelites; whereas, as I have already noted, God seems in these words to designate and define the places of his worship with certain characteristics, so that the Israelites would not remain in doubt about where they should worship God. Others, therefore, preferred to conceive the intention of the Lawgiver in this way: *“Wherever you pray to me and celebrate my name, there I will come to you and bless you.”* And the Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible translation</note> seems to tend toward this, having already been criticized for that reason by Fagius <note>Paul Fagius (1504–1549), a German Renaissance scholar and Hebraist</note>: <margin>Exodus 20:24.</margin> *In every place where there shall be a memory of my name, I will come...* <note>original Latin: In omni loco, in quo memoria fuerit nominis mei, veniam</note>

The author critiques John Spencer's interpretation, arguing that the passage must define specific sacred spaces rather than general acts of prayer.</summary>

...is it? This, if I am not mistaken, is the sense: *Wherever I demonstrate my presence by certain proofs, there I will come to you and bless you.* Therefore, the words seem to be translated thus: *Wherever I celebrate* (or, make celebrated) *my name, there I will come to you.* The word <term>Hizkir <note>original: הזכיר. This is the causative form of the Hebrew root Z-K-R, meaning "to remember."</note></term> means *to be remembered* and *to cause to remember*, and consequently *to celebrate* or *to make celebrated*. From this, it is quite correctly used regarding men who worship God, but especially those who celebrate God and proclaim His praises. But God Himself can also celebrate Himself; God, I say, can Himself *make His own name celebrated in a certain place*. This happens when, in a specific place, He causes signs and proofs of His *presence* to exist, especially those of *His* glory or grace, because the signs of Divine Grace most effectively draw the sinner toward the reverence that must be shown to God in this or that place. To better understand this, it will be useful to observe that the ancients were accustomed to venerate God most in those places where God had *previously* appeared to them—that is, where He had given them some singular proof of His presence. Thus, we certainly read in the history of Abraham:

God altogether permits the building of uncultivated and crude altars when occasions are given; yet He adds that the established worship of Him must be performed in a certain place, which He Himself wishes to indicate and celebrate with the symbols of His presence.

# CHAPTER 3. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES

<margin>
John Spencer, *On the Rationale of the Laws of Moses*, book III, chapter III, section I.
</margin>
And certainly, since in the entire Law of *Moses* there exists no express commandment concerning the making of prayers—as has long been observed by others—who would wonder that in the statutes of that Law nothing is found concerning the Structure of *Synagogues*, which are primarily dedicated to prayers? To be sure, the ancient *Israelites* were not sluggish in pouring out prayers to God, since reason itself urges and impels every man toward them in times of greatest necessity. One may also find examples of those praying, as well as formulas for prayers and thanksgivings, within the Law. Sacrifices, too, were always regarded by them and by all other peoples as aids to prayer. Nevertheless, you will not easily encounter an express mandate concerning *prayers* themselves in the Law. Therefore, you would look there in vain for any precept concerning *Synagogues*.

Of the ORIGIN, Book I, Part 2.

### CHAPTER IV.

## *The opinion of the illustrious Hugo Grotius concerning the first origin of Synagogues is examined—an opinion built upon the precept found in Moses regarding the reading of the Law, which was to be repeated every seven years during the Feast of Tabernacles. Furthermore, the views of Cornelius Bertram <note>Cornelius Bertram (1531–1594) was a French Protestant theologian and professor of Hebrew who wrote extensively on the governance of the ancient Hebrew state.</note> on the same subject are investigated and refuted; it is argued that Synagogues do not owe their origin to the distribution of the Levites throughout the land of Canaan, though that distribution was ordained by a unique divine decree.*

<margin>Deuteronomy 31:11, 12.</margin>
However, it is not permitted to leave this field before we have examined the opinion of *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a world-renowned Dutch jurist and theologian. His "Annotations on the Old Testament" was a standard reference for scholars of this era.</note>. For he traces the first origin of *Synagogues* entirely from the *Mosaic* Law, and he does so not with doubtful or obscure words, but with clear and evident ones. A command was given by Moses—as he was repeating his statutes before Israel shortly before his death—that after *every passing seven-year period, the Israelites should appear before the face of the Lord in that place which God shall choose, and that the Priests, Levites, or Elders should read that law before all Israel, in their hearing; and they should gather the whole people to hear the reading of the law—men, women, children, and even foreigners—so that they might hear and learn and fear Jehovah, their God, and diligently observe all the commands of the law.* Regarding this command, *Grotius* noted: **THIS IS THE INSTITUTION OF SYNAGOGUES.** It would have been useful if that illustrious man had explained his mind here somewhat more clearly. For as the Law reads, you will not find even a word in it about *Synagogues* or their institution. The people are commanded to appear before the Lord *in the place which God shall choose*, that is, not in every place, but in a certain place where God would display the evident symbols of His gracious presence. For such a place was considered the location in which the Tabernacle was built, and later, the Temple; which no one, I believe, would deny. In *this place* the Israelites are commanded to appear, not in every place. Yet indeed, it is a certain right of Synagogues that they be built <note>original: *בכל מקום* (bekhol makom)</note> **in every place**, as was noted above from the religious laws <note>The author refers to the "canons" or established rabbinic rules governing where a synagogue could be established.</note>...

### CHAPTER 4. OF SYNAGOGUES.

...having been brought forward, it has been proven. Furthermore, Moses commands that this reading of the law be instituted after the passing of a *seven-year period*. However, the statute of the Synagogues is that the reading of the *Law and prayers* be celebrated in them at least every single week. Furthermore, there is no mention in this *Law* regarding prayers, which nevertheless constitute the greatest part of *Divine worship* as it is celebrated in Synagogues. Indeed, on the contrary, because Moses ordains a solemn reading of the Law here *every seventh year* so that the knowledge of the *Divine Law* might not perish among the Israelites, by that very fact—in my judgment, at least—*Moses* clearly presupposes <margin>See what was discussed above on page 111 and following.</margin> that up to this point the *Israelites* lacked other opportunities for learning the *Law*. 

For if the *Law* had already been read at that time in certain places ordained for that purpose; or, if *Moses* had supposed it would be the case that, after his death, the *Law* would be read in *Synagogues* scattered throughout the whole region in the land of *Canaan*, then the reason for a *seven-yearly reading of the Law* becomes null. For he who hears the *Law* read in a gathering every week, what necessity does he have to be gathered into the *Temple* for this purpose after the lapse of seven years, in recurring turns? Thus, no more certain evidence occurs to me in the *Law* by which I might prove that no *Synagogues* existed at that time, and that *Moses* did not even look toward them in his *Laws*, than this very point. 

This seems to me to be further confirmed by the fact that *Moses* bound every *head of a household* by a specific command to <margin>Deuteronomy 6:7</margin> *diligently instill the precepts of the Law into his sons*, whenever the opportunity was given at home. For even if domestic instructions <note>original: "κατηχήσεις" (katechēseis) — refers to the practice of oral instruction or "echoing" the faith from teacher to student.</note> are rightly joined with *public institutions*, I am not easily persuaded that *Moses* would have emphasized these *domestic instructions* so successfully if he had assumed there were public ones.

Yet, who would deny to *Grotius* that *Moses* foreshadowed the *Synagogues* with this precept? For that public *reading of the Law*, which <margin>See Heidegger, *Theology of the Jews*, Volume 2, Topic 6, § 27. <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698) was a Swiss theologian. His work "Theologia Judaeorum" examined Jewish customs and their relation to Christian theology.</note></margin> *Moses* ordains every *seven years* at the feast of *Tabernacles*, had much in common with the reading of the *Law* which was later established in the *Synagogues*. Indeed, there is no doubt that this command gave some occasion for the *reading of the Law* later ordained in the *Synagogues*. At least, it is significant that in their *Synagogues*, the *Jews* begin to read the *Law* every year at the feast of *Tabernacles*, and terminate the *reading of the Law* in that same *Feast*...

<margin>Chapter 10:5.</margin>
It may truly be possible that this place (the "land of Mizpah" <note>original Hebrew: ארץ המצפה, *eretz ha-Mizpah*</note> mentioned in the text of Joshua) is that same Mizpah where the Israelites were always accustomed to gather. Yet here, a very great number of Kings were subdued by Joshua. It is truly possible that Joshua built an altar there in memory of this great salvation. And for this reason, the Israelites gathered at **MIZPAH** rather than in any other place, whether they were to go out to war or if any other grave business had to be performed by them. <margin>1 Samuel 10:18.</margin>

For this is a matter of historical fact, and must therefore be proved from history. If history is lacking, the matter cannot be determined with certainty through conjecture. <header>CHAPTER 5. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.</header>

...was accustomed to come <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's "venire," meaning "to come."</note> to pray, why is there no mention of it in the History? Frequent opportunities arose where it could have been recorded. Why then was it neglected? Samuel, I admit, *prayed at Mizpah* for the people and with the people, and celebrated a fast with them. But it is not said that he prayed in any *Oratory* <note>A formal room or building set aside for prayer.</note>. He also offered
<margin>1 Samuel 7:5, 6, verse 9.</margin>
a *sacrifice to the Lord at Mizpah*. However, it is not said that it was offered on the altar that had long ago been built at *Mizpah*. But even if that were stated in the text, it would no more allow us to conclude that there was a Synagogue at *Mizpah* than at any other place that possessed an altar. For altars easily exist without synagogues. Yet a doubt remains as to whether there was any specific place at *Mizpah* in which the people gathered for the sake of either taking counsel or offering prayers; a question I feel it is my duty to resolve. Receive, then, the following points for the elucidation of this inquiry.

In my opinion, therefore (and I allow others to keep their own views), it does not seem that there was any *Building* at *Mizpah* specifically devoted and consecrated for the Council or the prayers of the people; *firstly* for this reason: that no house, unless it were immense, and no porches, unless they were most ample, could have contained such a multitude of men meeting in assembly. The gathering assembled at *Mizpah* in this case consisted of *four hundred thousand men*, as
<margin>Judges 20:2.</margin>
appears from the history. Who could conceive of such a *Building*, who of a structure so magnificent, who of porches so majestic at *Mizpah* that they could encompass so many men? And who, moreover, would believe that the writer of sacred history would make no mention of such a majestic edifice? By whom was this *Building* founded? At what cost? At what time? In that most turbulent state of the Jewish people? Truly, I do not think anyone will easily untie these knots for me. Perhaps one exception remains: that not all that multitude, but only the Leaders of that multitude were gathered into a certain place to deliberate on the most important matters. Indeed, some have thought those Leaders of the Council were indicated by the word <term>פנות</term> (*pinnoth*), meaning "corners."
