### CHAPTER 5. OF SYNAGOGUES. 323

...with the Benjaminites, and the Lord said: Judah shall go first. but after the <term>Jews<note>The author uses the Latin *Judæi*, though in this biblical context it refers to the allied tribes of Israel fighting Benjamin.</note></term> had been routed by the Benjaminites, it is repeated: And the Israelites went up, <note>original Hebrew: ויבכו לפני יהוה עד ערב</note> **and they wept before the Lord until evening.** <margin>[verse 23.]</margin> Again, when they had been defeated in a second battle: <margin>verse 26.</margin> And all the Israelites and all the people went up, <note>original Hebrew: ויבאו ביתאל</note> **AND THEY CAME TO THE HOUSE OF GOD**, and wept, and sat there before the Lord, and fasted that day until evening; and they offered burnt offerings and <term>peace offerings<note>Sacrifices intended to express gratitude or conclude a vow.</note></term> before the Lord. Certainly, it is clear from these testimonies that the people, intending to pray, perform sacrifices, and consult the mouth of the Lord, went up from Mizpah to the House of God. From this, it is gathered that Mizpah was still at that time a place for counsel, but <term>Shiloh<note>Latin: *Silunta*.</note></term>, where the Tabernacle was located, was considered the place sacred for prayers and sacrifices. At the very least, so far is it from there being any probable argument hidden in this history for some "Mizpatic Synagogue," that on the contrary, everything argues the opposite. For it is not read that the people prayed at Mizpah. On the contrary, it is read that the people, intending to pray, betook themselves elsewhere. What reason, therefore, remains from this history for concluding that Mizpah was a Synagogue? 

The place, indeed, into which the people ascended to pray, is called <note>original Hebrew: בית אל</note> **Bethel**, which may be translated: **The House of God**. Interpreters have raised doubts as to what place that might be. By some, it is thought to be Shiloh, or rather the Tabernacle of God built at Shiloh. By others, however, it is thought to be Bethel, a place sacred due to frequent Divine appearances, and for that reason sufficiently illustrious in the sacred history of the earliest times. We, along with those most excellent men to whose judgment it is right to grant much weight, incline toward the former opinion. I say, we think that by <note>original Hebrew: בית אל</note> **House of God**, the Tabernacle—which was still at that time erected at Shiloh—is entirely to be understood here. I will state, therefore, what seems to me the most excellent reason for this phrasing, by which the Israelites are declared to have *assembled* at *Mizpah* <term>to the Lord<note>original Hebrew: אל יהוה (*el YHWH*)</note></term>. For the entire difficulty resides in that phrase. Great and solemn conventions and gatherings of the people of God were not only summoned as if in the name of God Himself, but God was held and judged to have been present in them in a singular way. For it is not only a common perception of the populace, but also an explicit doctrine of the Word of God, that God is present in a peculiar and particular way at every established congregation that is organized in a public place for a public cause; even more so if that congregation is summoned in the name of God, and is indeed of the people of God, in whose midst God has professed that He wishes to dwell. 

Indeed, whatever is done publicly is judged to be done *before the Lord*, because even though nothing escapes God that is done in the most private places, the conscience of everyone teaches that those things in no way escape God which do not even escape men themselves. Let us prove what we have said from the Scriptures.

<margin>2 Samuel 6:3</margin>

We do not believe the sacred Historian would have shrouded these movements of the Ark in silence if it had truly been brought to this place.

For one can discern from the text that the sacrifices themselves were offered <note>original Hebrew: לפני יהוה (*lifnei YHWH*)</note> *before the Lord*.

The singular presence of the Lord moved the Israelites to offer sacrifices; however, the sacrifices were not themselves the *cause* of the divine presence.

Let us say, therefore, that this phrase <note>original Hebrew: לפני יהוה (*lifnei YHWH*)</note> *before the Lord* means nothing else here than that God is present in the assembly, which is gathered in God's name and represents God's cause.

### C H A P T E R  V I.

*A transition to another interval of time in the Judean Republic, namely when it was governed by Kings until the Babylonian captivity; the question is asked: did that period give rise to Synagogues? To this question, the answer is given that while Synagogues, specifically so-called, do not appear to have arisen during all that time, the Jewish people did not lack public instruction. However, before that first proposition—which denies Synagogues to this interval of time—is proven, a preliminary discussion is held regarding the nature and manner of public instruction. In particular, the public* **Schools of the Prophets** <term>Prophetarum Scholæ: Early Israelite communal groups where prophets trained and taught the public.</term> *are described, in which they were accustomed to preach before the common people, illustrated by various texts of Holy Scripture. It is then proven that such institutions were not entirely lacking even under the Judges, although they were very rare at that point in time. On this occasion, the meaning of a praiseworthy and obscure passage—II Chronicles 15:3, 4, 5—is sought, after examining the commentaries of Hebrew interpreters.*

# On ORIGINS Book I. Part 2.
->330<-

It is well attested that **David** gave new life to the Judean Republic, which before his time had been afflicted in various ways and through many reversals. Since he was renowned no less for his piety than for his bravery, you may rightly ask whether his era and reign did not give rise to **Synagogues**? It is equally well known that the affairs of the **Hebrews** were most flourishing under the rule of **Solomon**. You might then press the point: were **Synagogues** born in that golden age, or perhaps in the following centuries during which the Jewish people were subject to Kings descended from the family of **Jesse** <note>The father of King David; this refers to the Davidic dynasty</note>, up until the **Babylonian Captivity**? 

This is a sufficiently difficult and obscure question, and in defining it, I will not deny that I remained undecided for some time. However, after weighing the evidence that has come to my attention, it seemed best to answer the question as follows: *first*, we concede that throughout that entire interval of time there existed *some kind of public institution*, the manner and nature of which we shall explain according to our understanding; *second*, we shall argue with various reasons that it is not sufficiently clear that *Synagogues*, specifically so-called, were in *use* among the Judean nation during all this time; and finally, *third*, we shall weigh those arguments which have been either debated by learned men or could be debated to the contrary.

1. To anyone reading the Histories contained in the **Codex of Sacred Books** <note>The Bible</note>, it is not obscure that some kind of public institution flourished among the Judaic people. We conceive it to have been generally of this sort: if there was a **Prophet** among the people who had proven the certainty of his mission—whether through holiness of life, the power of his teaching, the frequency of his miracles, or the truth of his predictions (of which several are known to have existed among the Judean nation)—this man, being already abundantly instructed in the divine will, established a practice of **keeping a public school**. In this school, he nurtured and instructed certain disciples, his constant followers, both in the knowledge of Divine matters and in the precepts of holiness. On the **Sabbath**, the **New Moon**, and other feast days, he admitted into this school of his any other people who desired to be instructed in the word of God. ...succeeded the deceased; or how individual disciples, according as they excelled in wisdom or gifts, also had *their own Schools*, and through their own instruction commended themselves to the people, so that they might prepare disciples for themselves. Besides these things, it also seems that the *Levites*, as they increased in number over time and were not always abundantly supported from sacred offerings as was fitting, and were therefore reduced to poverty, frequently introduced themselves into the more honorable Jewish families throughout the entire region of Canaan, so that they might either procure the Divine blessing, which was believed to accompany them, or be the moderators of sacred worship to be performed for God in those families. 

Concerning both parts of my opinion, I wish to discourse distinctly from certain passages of Scripture that I have come across. The Orations of the most learned **Alting** <note>Jacob Alting (1618–1679), a prominent German-born professor of Hebrew at Groningen</note>, in which he follows the history of both the *Hebrew Academies* and the *Academic Promotions among the Hebrews*, would provide me with a great abundance of writing—as they are concise in speech and weighty in matter—if I wished to heap together here everything that I could. But my plan now is different. For I do not wish to report so much what the Hebrews think, as what they *rightly* think. Therefore, whoever wishes to know what origins and what progress they assign to *their Schools* and their *Promotions*, I recommend to him the aforementioned **Alting**. But what I understand by *Schools* will become clear from the following.

# ON THE ORIGIN Book I, Part 2.

THEY DO THEM. For they make sweet songs in their mouths; their heart follows after their own gain.
> And behold, you are to them as a lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice and can play well on an instrument; they hear your words, but they do not do them.

God assumes in this entire speech to the Prophet that the people were accustomed to come to Ezekiel at fixed times; to *sit* before him; to receive his rebukes with reverence; and to be solemnly instructed by him in the knowledge of the ways of God. The Prophet Ezekiel was therefore considered a public Teacher of the people, who, in his own home—as if in a certain public *School*—established assemblies. There, before a frequent congregation, he interpreted the Divine will with eloquent speech. Anyone who pays diligent attention to the words of the text I have cited will sense this meaning hidden within them. For those hypocrites of whom God speaks to the Prophet are said to come *to him* <note>original Hebrew: כמבוא עם</note> AS THE PEOPLE ARE ACCUSTOMED TO COME, that is, solemnly, and showing reverence toward the word of God and the Prophet; <note>original Hebrew: כמתי חברין</note> just as *students* of the truth are accustomed to come, according to the Chaldean <note>The "Chaldean" refers to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note> interpretation, which **Kimchius** <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), also known as Radak, was a preeminent medieval Jewish rabbi and grammarian</note> follows. Indeed, those same hypocrites are also said to *sit before his face* and to *hear his words*. From these things it is clear that such assemblies at the houses of the Prophets were fixed and solemn. For it was not just this or that individual man, either moved by a true affection toward God or by some specific desire of his own soul, who went to the Prophet and cursorily sought out the true sense of the Divine will; rather, an entire multitude of people gathered solemnly to the Prophet and *sat* before him, which was the custom of disciples before a Master. Ezekiel, moreover, did not fulfill his duty among the people with a few words, but preached among them with a composed oration. This is evident from the fact that those hypocrites are said to receive the words of the Prophet as a pleasant sound, by which an eloquent orator or a skilled flute-player charms the ears.

### CHAPTER 6. OF SYNAGOGUES. 333

<margin>Chapter 14:1.</margin>
<margin>Chapter 8:1.</margin>
To go to the Prophet here means to gather solemnly in his presence to receive his teaching and his corrections. For this must be compared with what was said in the preceding context: <note>original Hebrew: ויבואו אלי אנשים מזקני ישראל וישבו לפני</note> **And men from the Elders of Israel came to me, and THEY SAT BEFORE ME.** They came, therefore, to present themselves as the Prophet's disciples and to be instructed by his warnings. The same thing is reported elsewhere with no less significance: *And it happened in the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, that I was sitting in my house; and the Elders of Judah* <note>original Hebrew: ישבים לפני</note> **WERE SITTING BEFORE MY FACE.** Likewise: *And it happened in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, that men from the Elders of Israel came* <note>original Hebrew: לדרש את יהוה</note> *to seek (to consult) the Lord,* **AND THEY SAT BEFORE ME.** There is no doubt that occasionally various situations arose where the people sent the Elders as extraordinary messengers to consult the mouth of the Lord. However, that by no means excludes the regular and frequent assemblies which the people celebrated at the houses of the Prophets. For the homes of the Prophets are rightly compared to public workshops of knowledge and virtue, which any student of the Divine Name was permitted to enter.

<margin>2 Kings 4:23.</margin>
Furthermore, to prove and illustrate these points, much is contributed, if I am not mistaken, by what we read in the *Books of Kings* in the history of *Elisha* <note>Elisha was the successor to the prophet Elijah in the 9th century BCE</note>. He used to frequently visit the *Shunammite* lady, who, because of the kindness she showed the Prophet, received a male child through a singular divine blessing. But when that son died quite unexpectedly one day, the troubled and grieving mother immediately formed a plan to go to the Prophet *Elisha*, and therefore asked her husband for a servant and a donkey for that purpose. To which the history continues: *And he* (the husband) *said; why are you hurrying to him* **ON THIS DAY,** <note>original Hebrew: לא חדש ולא שבת</note> **WHICH IS NEITHER A NEW MOON, NOR A SABBATH.** This is indeed a simple narrative, but of great weight for our argument. For in that response from the husband to the wife, it is clearly presupposed that it was the custom of the people on Sabbath days and *New Moons* <note>The New Moon, or Rosh Chodesh, was a minor festival in the ancient Hebrew calendar often associated with religious gathering</note> to go to the Prophets and public Teachers, so that they might be instructed by them and imbued both with the knowledge of God and true piety.

Therefore, the houses of the Prophets were Schools, or, if you prefer, Synagogues, in which the people were accustomed to congregate in that state of affairs. You may see this observed everywhere by the Commentators on this passage.

### CHAPTER 6. OF SYNAGOGUES.

The interpretation of this passage will emerge in conformity with the explanation of the preceding testimonies in which this phrase was found. Indeed, I have no doubt that Isaiah looked back to this established custom of the instruction of the Prophets when he prophesied concerning Tyre <note>An ancient Phoenician port city famous for its commerce</note>. His words are: *And her merchandise and her gain shall be holiness to the Lord;* Isaiah 23:18. *it shall not be treasured up, nor laid away;* <note>original Hebrew: כי ליושבים לפני יהוה יהיה סחרה — literally: "for to those sitting before Jehovah shall be her profit"</note> *but* FOR THOSE WHO SIT BEFORE THE LORD *her merchandise shall go, that they may eat to satiety, and for durable clothing.* Who are these *sitting before the Lord*? They are the disciples of God, who were nurtured in the School of God; a phrase derived from the custom of sitting before Teachers and Prophets, which was most common in those centuries.

Even if we should think that these public Schools of the Prophets flourished most greatly after the times of David and Solomon, who could bring themselves to believe that there were none at all before then? A few indeed, I confess, but that there were some will become clear from what we shall say in the following Chapter. I would like to prove that they were few and rare from a notable passage in the Chronicles of the Kingdom of Israel. It is told there that it happened in the time of King Asa, that *Azariah, son of Oded*, stirred by God, spoke thus to Judah and Benjamin: <margin>2 Chronicles 15:3, 4.</margin> *Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; Jehovah is with you, when you are with him, and if you seek him, he will be found by you, and if you forsake him, he will forsake you.* AND FOR MANY DAYS (*there were, are,* or *will be*) ISRAEL, <note>original Hebrew: ללא אלהי אמת וללא כהן מורה וללא תורה</note> WITHOUT THE TRUE GOD, AND WITHOUT A TEACHING PRIEST, AND WITHOUT THE LAW. <note>original Hebrew: וישב בצר לו — "and he returned in his distress"</note> *And, WHEN THERE WAS DISTRESS UPON THEM, THEY RETURNED TO JEHOVAH THE GOD OF ISRAEL, AND SOUGHT HIM, AND HE WAS FOUND BY THEM. ### CHAPTER 6. ON SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>Isaiah 1:25.</margin>
...of the restoration <note>original Latin: *reductionis*</note> of the Israelites from Captivity: *And I will restore your judges as in the beginning*; for as long as they are in exile, they are considered to be deprived of their true and upright judges. I have already mentioned that Kimchi suggested this interpretation. As for the fact that this author cites Onkelos <note>a famous 2nd-century convert to Judaism and author of the standard Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> to confirm the hypothesis that the Scripture speaks of those who live among idolaters as if they themselves worshiped idols, the matter stands as follows. Moses, toward the end of his ministry, foretells to the Israelites their future defection from God and their abduction into the Babylonian Captivity (as I believe), and their idolatry and conversion during that captivity; in which speech these words occur:

<margin>Deuteronomy 4:27-28.</margin>
<margin>See on this passage Solomon Jarchi <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note></margin>
> *And you shall serve there gods, the work of human hands:* <note>original Hebrew: *Ve-avadtem sham elohim ma'aseh yedei adam*</note> which are rendered thus by Onkelos: *And you shall serve there the peoples, the worshipers of idols.* <note>original Aramaic: *Ve-tiflehun taman le-amemaya palchei ta'uta*</note>

The son of Uziel <note>Jonathan ben Uziel, the traditional author of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets</note> enters upon the same path of interpretation. Both undoubtedly sought to free their nation from the hatred that is weighed against them by these words. However, it should not be overlooked that the *Vulgate* translator <note>St. Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin in the 4th century</note> himself interprets this testimony, which we are discussing, as referring to a future time. For he says:

> *For many days Israel shall sit without the true God... and when they return in their distress to the Lord God of Israel, and seek Him, they shall find Him.*

The Greek Interpreters <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> seem to have been of the same mind, as they expressed certain words of this text in the future tense. Thus in the fourth verse:

<margin>Antiquities Book 8, Chapter 8.</margin>
> *And he will turn them to the Lord God of Israel, and he will be found by them.* <note>original Greek: *Kai epistrepsei autous epi Kyrion Theon Israel, kai eurethesetai autois*</note>

In the following verse, however, they retain the present tense: *And in that time there is no peace.* Indeed, Josephus also thought here of the future:

> (thus he introduces the Prophet, threatening the wicked) *a time will follow in which no true prophet shall be found in your crowd, nor a priest declaring what is right; but even the cities shall be overturned, and the nation shall be scattered over all the earth, living the life of a stranger and a wanderer;* <note>original Greek: *chrēsei... chronon ekeinon, en hō mēdeis alēthēs eurethēsetai prophētēs...*</note>

*there will follow such a time, in which neither a truthful prophet will be found among the people, nor a priest who is a cultivator of justice: and then both their cities must be subverted, and the Nation must be dispersed through all lands, leading a life in the manner of wanderers, with no fixed dwellings.* But I do not think that these Interpreters, and those who follow them, hold the truth. For certainly the Hebrew words, *and he returned* and *they sought him* <note>original Hebrew: *vayashev* and *vayevakshuhu*</note> as they are now punctuated in our text, absolutely demand a past-tense meaning. This is also the case with the words, *the days of old* <note>original Hebrew: *yamim rabbim*</note>.

### CHAPTER 6. ON SYNAGOGUES.

Regarding those who take this as referring to the past, the Illustrious **Beck** <note>Matthias Friedrich Beck (1649–1701), a German Orientalist known for his work on the Targums</note> shows that Rabbi **Solomon**, **Abendana**, and **Tremellius** <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a prominent Jewish convert and Hebraist who produced a widely used Latin translation of the Bible</note> are in agreement. Rightly so. However, the first two interpret the passage as describing the state of the *Kingdom of Judah* as it had been under *Rehoboam* and *Abijah*, as we shall soon see; but *Tremellius* applies it to the *Israelites* <note>Referring to the northern Ten Tribes of Israel as distinct from the southern Kingdom of Judah</note>. For he renders it thus: *For many days have passed for the Israelites without the true God.* His annotations prove this point more fully. But for my part, I see no basis in the text for this opinion. On the contrary, I see arguments occurring in the text that overthrow this interpretation. For: 1. There is mention not only of the Israelites’ rebellion, but also of their conversion from that rebellion. In *verse 4*, the Israelites are said to have *returned to Jehovah the God of Israel and sought Him when they were in distress.* When was this ever done by the Israelites of the ten tribes, in the period from the beginning of *Jeroboam* until this time of King *Asa*? I find no such conversion to God in their history. As for the fact that the Jews <note>The inhabitants of the southern Kingdom of Judah</note> repented under King *Asa*, I do not think this can be applied to them [the northern tribes]. *Tremellius*, sensing this difficulty, rendered the fourth verse in Latin as: *But if he had turned, when there was distress for him, to Jehovah, the God of Israel, to those seeking him, he would have been present.* However, the text does not use a conditional phrasing, but an absolute one. The text reads: *And when there was distress for him, he returned to the Lord, and was found by them.* It is not permitted for an Interpreter to change an absolute proposition into a conditional one. 2. The condition of this time is depicted in the text as one where there was no peace for the one *going out or returning*; there were violent commotions; *nation was crushed by nation*; and God pressed the inhabitants of these lands with every *distress*.

<margin>2 Chronicles 15:2</margin>
Who, indeed, among readers of sacred history could derive these <term>criteria</term> <note>original Greek: κριτήρια (*kritēria*) — identifying marks or standards of judgment</note> for the time of *Jeroboam’s* reign? It is well known that the *Jews* and *Israelites* were sometimes crushed against each other. It is also clear that the hearts of the *Kings of Judah* up to this time were not truly reconciled with the hearts of the

<margin>1 Kings 14:30</margin>
*Kings of Israel*. However, the troubles, commotions, distresses, and collisions of this time are described too emphatically for the words to fit the state of *Jeroboam’s* Kingdom exactly. 3. It must be observed that the time assigned to this troubled state of affairs is expressed as <term>many days</term> <note>original Hebrew: ימים רבים (*yamim rabbim*)</note>. In that description, a long period of time is noted, if there are no [restrictions] in the text...

What are these **many days**? Let Kimchi <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), also known as Radak, a preeminent medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian</note> answer, whose explanation of these words, though well-known, is nevertheless worthy of being recorded: **THESE ARE THE DAYS OF EXILE, WHICH WE ARE PASSING THROUGH AT THIS TIME** <note>original Hebrew: "ואלה הם ימי הגלות שאנחנו בו היום ואין לנו לא מלך ולא שר מישראל כי ברשות הגוים אנחנו וברשות מלכיהם ושריהם" (V'eleh hem yemei ha-galut...)</note>, **in which we have neither King nor Prince from Israel; rather, we are under the power of the nations and in the power of their Kings and Princes.** It is certainly clear that this long time of Israelite exile and servitude, which they are now enduring, is expressed by the phrase **many days**. From this, we may at least conclude that this expression, if not restricted by the context, signifies a long interval of time. However, from the time of the Israelites' rebellion under Jeroboam until the time <margin>1 Kings 15:10</margin> of King Asa, only twenty years had passed. Consider now whether those twenty years deserve to be called a **long time**, especially when the text suggests no argument for a restricted interpretation of this phrase. I, at least, believe that it indicates a longer interval of an age than that which is completed in the course of twenty years.

The same difficulty presses even more heavily upon *Rabbi Solomon* <note>Referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator</note> and, in the following century, *Abendana* <note>Likely Jacob Abendana (1630–1695), a Sephardic scholar and Hakham of the Spanish and Portuguese Jews in London</note>, who referred this situation to the times that had already elapsed from the third year of King Rehoboam until <margin>1 Kings 12; 2 Chronicles 12</margin> the beginning of Asa’s reign. Let us hear Abendana: **Rashi explained: "And for many days Israel was without the true God" until you [Asa] arrived; for it is written of Rehoboam: "And it came to pass when the kingdom of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he forsook the law of the Lord and all Israel with him," and of Abijah it is written: "He walked in all the sins of his father which he had done before him." And concerning this he said that there were many days for Israel that they had no true God and no teaching priest, because there was no one who asked a matter of Law from a priest, and therefore he did not teach until now.** <note>original Hebrew: "ורש"י פירש וימים רבים לישראל אלהי אמת עד שבאת אתה..."</note>

### CHAPTER 6. ON SYNAGOGUES.

->That now in their distress they returned to the Lord their God and sought him and he was found by them<- <note>Hebrew: שעתה בצר להם שבו אל ה' אלהיהם ויבקשהו וימצא להם (from 2 Chronicles 15:4)</note>

Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>Solomon ben Isaac (1040–1105), commonly known as Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator</note> indeed interprets the words thus: *And for many days Israel was without the true God, until you (Asa) came.* 
<margin>2 Chronicles 12:1</margin>
For it is written concerning Rehoboam: *And it happened, when Rehoboam had established the kingdom and had gained strength, that he forsook the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him.* 
<margin>1 Kings 15:3</margin>
Concerning *Abijah* <note>original: "Abia"</note> it is likewise recorded: *And he walked in all the sins of his father, which he had done before him.* And yet of him it is said that THERE WERE MANY DAYS FOR ISRAEL in which they had no *true God, and no teaching priest*. Because there was no one who consulted the Priest, the Priest consequently had no occasion for teaching; *until now, when they were pressed by distress, they returned to the Lord their God, and sought him, and he was found by them.* Against this interpretation, I have said that the previously cited reasoning carries even more weight than against the preceding one. For the time of which the Prophet Azariah speaks here cannot be thought to span from the third or fourth year of Rehoboam until the fifteenth year of King *Asa* (which Abendana <note>Jacob Abendana (1630–1685), a Sephardic rabbi and scholar in London known for his Latin translations of Jewish works</note> seems to claim, because 
<margin>2 Chronicles 15:10</margin>
this prophecy was delivered at that time), since the earlier years of *Asa’s* reign were spent in *peace* and security, as is clear from Sacred History. Therefore, whatever is proclaimed in our text concerning these *many days* does not fit those years. 
<margin>2 Chronicles 13:23</margin>
For the Prophet says that in these "many days" there was no peace. These years would therefore have to be thought of as spanning from the fourth year of Rehoboam until the beginning of *Asa’s* reign, which is roughly seventeen years. But should it really be said that *seventeen* years in this passage are referred to so absolutely as "years" or *many days*? To me, at least, it does not seem so. Furthermore, I would like attention to be paid to whether it can be applied with such great emphasis to this time that the Israelites were *without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without the law*? For although I grant with a generous hand that the people contaminated themselves at this time with the foul crime of idolatry, it must not be overlooked that during this interval of time, Divine worship still flourished in the Temple and the Priests, in some manner, performed their ministry. We may perceive this from the speech of *Abijah* to the Israelites who were guilty of defection under Jeroboam: 
<margin>2 Chronicles 13:9, 10, 11</margin>
*Have you not driven out the Priests of Jehovah, the sons of Aaron and the Levites, and made for yourselves priests like the peoples of these lands? — But as for us, Jehovah is our God, and* WE HAVE NOT FORSAKEN HIM; AND THE PRIESTS, *who minister to Jehovah, are the Sons of...*

### ON THE ORIGINS Book I, Part 2.

The descendants of Aaron and the Levites <note>The priestly class of ancient Israel</note> are assigned to their duties. AND THEY OFFER BURNT OFFERINGS TO JEHOVAH EVERY MORNING AND EVERY EVENING—*for we keep the charge of Jehovah our God* <note>original Hebrew: כִּי שֹׁמְרִים אֲנַחְנוּ אֶת מִשְׁמֶרֶת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ</note> for we observe the watch of Jehovah our God, and **YOU HAVE FORSAKEN HIM.** Many other statements of the same kind follow. I would not deny, indeed, when I weigh the histories of this time, that Abijah <note>The son of Rehoboam and king of Judah, also called Abia</note> spoke these words to the Israelites with a certain boastfulness. Yet, this much is easily granted to me from those words: that under the reign of Abijah, although it was by no means purged of idolaters, the Priests in the Temple had nonetheless not yet ceased to perform their duties. And this also favors our position: that Abijah, relying on the justice of his cause, courageously expected victory from God and carried it away from the enemy. Truly, that expectation of his would have been entirely in vain if, under his rule, all religion had utterly collapsed. Indeed, these were those <margin>2 Chronicles 12:12</margin> *good things* <note>original Hebrew: דְּבָרִים טוֹבִים; Latin: res bonæ</note> which the historian says were still surviving under the reign of Rehoboam. We conclude that regarding this interval of time, it cannot be said with any emphasis that the Israelites were then "without a teaching priest." 

I will add one more argument which confirms us in this same truth. Azariah the Prophet addresses the Jews, to whom he directed his speech, by the names of Judah and Benjamin. Thus he addressed the King: <margin>2 Chronicles 15:2</margin> *Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin* <note>original: Audite me Asa, וְכָל יְהוּדָה & omnis Jehuda & בִּנְיָמִן Benjamin</note>. Then, after a few words, he adds: *For many days Israel has been [without the true God]* <note>original Hebrew: יָמִים רַבִּים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל; Latin: Dies multi fuerunt Israeli</note>. If he had wished this to be understood regarding Judah and Benjamin—the two tribes he was speaking to—he would have said, in my opinion: *for many days there were for Judah and Benjamin.* 

But because it now appears that while he was speaking to Judah and Benjamin, he interjected the name "Israel" into his speech, this seems entirely to suggest one of two things: either this Prophet is speaking about the ten tribes <note>The Northern Kingdom of Israel, which broke away from the Southern Kingdom of Judah</note> who at this time were known by the name of "Israel" as distinct from the name of "Judah"; or, if his speech does not find the truth in those ten tribes, he is speaking of all the Israelites at a time when they were still all called and addressed by the name of "Israelites" or "Children of Israel." Since, however, we have already proven that these words of the Prophet cannot easily be applied to the state of the ten tribes of the Israelites—since they are not recorded to have converted back to God after their defection from Him—it remains for us to determine that these words...

### CHAPTER 6. ON SYNAGOGUES.

We believe that the words of the Prophet, which we have proved should be understood as referring to a past time, belong to an earlier age; namely, those years which passed after the death of *Joshua* or *Phinehas* <note>Phinehas was the grandson of Aaron and a High Priest</note> until the time of *Eli* or *Samuel*. The logic of our undertaking therefore requires that we briefly show that the characteristics <note>original Greek: κριτήρια</note> of those times are contained within the Prophet's speech.

The time which the Israelite nation spent under the Judges was nearly three hundred years. Other most learned and experienced men set a much higher number; for now we will be content with the minimum, nor will we pursue the matter more accurately at this moment, because our interpretation will remain consistent even if this number of years is contracted or extended. Let it only be held that the leadership and priesthood of *Eli* is excluded by us from this time frame. Nothing more is required to strengthen this hypothesis of ours, except to show piece by piece that those things said by the Prophet *Azariah* *concerning a certain past time* can be aptly applied to this period without any distortion. It is certain that this time is most excellently and significantly expressed by the phrase *many days* <note>original Hebrew: ימים רבים (yamim rabbim)</note>. One hundred, two hundred, or three hundred years are indeed truly *many years* <note>original Hebrew: ימים רבים</note>, a long span of time, which is the genuine meaning of this expression. *Indeed, during these many days Israel was without the true God.* This should be understood to mean that the Israelites *did not worship the true God during those many days*. Is this not true of that long period which the Jews lived through before, but also after, the times of *Eli*? Indeed, nothing is more certain. Let us weigh what is clearly written about this in the *Book of Judges*.

<margin>Chapter 2:10</margin>
There it is said that when *Joshua*, and the elders of that generation who had seen the miracles of the Lord with their own eyes, had met their fate, *there arose another generation of men after them, who did not know Jehovah, nor the work that He had done for Israel*. To which is immediately added:

<margin>verse 11</margin>
*And the children of Israel did what was evil in the eyes of Jehovah, and* **THEY WORSHIPPED THE BAALS** <note>The "Baales" or Baalim were local Canaanite deities whose worship often tempted the Israelites</note>; *And* **THEY ABANDONED JEHOVAH, THE GOD OF THEIR FATHERS, WHO HAD BROUGHT THEM OUT OF EGYPT, AND FOLLOWED OTHER GODS FROM THE GODS OF THE PEOPLES** *who were around them, and they bowed down to them, and provoked Jehovah to anger. And they abandoned Jehovah, and served Baal and Ashtaroth.* Consider whether this is not exactly what it means *to be without the true God*? And this is predicated not of just one part, but of the entire interval of this time, as will be clear to anyone consulting the text—

It appears we must conclude from the First Book of Samuel that the Priesthood was granted and entrusted to Eli by a certain singular occurrence. For how could it have happened that God committed the Priesthood to Eli, if those to whom it belonged by right <note>The right of the high priesthood usually descended through the line of Eleazar, but Eli was of the line of Ithamar</note> had not abandoned or profaned it? Therefore, since we suspect that during this long interval of time the High Priests—and following their example, the common priests—neglected their duties for a very significant reason, we rightly conclude that it is to this period that the following description applies: the Israelites *for a long time* were <note>original Hebrew: ללא כהן מורה (lo kohen moreh)</note> *without an instructing priest* <note>or "without a teaching priest"</note>.

...expressed it so clearly that scarcely any room was left for doubt. But how many useless questions have disputatious and idle minds not fashioned for themselves here? How many subtleties have they not devised? How many scruples and "cases of conscience," as they say, have they not thought up? He who has even lightly inspected the Talmudic Tractate <note>A reference to the vast body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> on this subject will marvel at the windings and cunning of human wit.

But, what I wish to say now is, if any Israelite had conceived a scruple in his mind regarding the practice of Religion, it was his duty to approach a Levite or a Priest and seek from him an interpretation of the law. It then fell to that man to answer the one asking about the law and to remove every scruple from him, if he were sufficient for the task. If he were not sufficient, he was to send the questioner to another man of his tribe—one wiser, more practiced, and of greater dignity than himself. 

I would indeed gladly grant that the Levites were scattered by God throughout the entire land of Canaan for this very reason: so that the Israelites might more easily approach them, be taught by them, and be instructed in the knowledge of the Divine will. For I observe that the Blessings of Moses and the Predictions of Jacob agree quite harmoniously; Jacob predicted the dispersion of this tribe of Levi, while Moses ascribed to them the prerogative of teaching. It seems to me that this double prophecy can be joined together in this way: the Levitical tribe was to be dispersed through the other tribes for the purpose of obtaining a greater opportunity for serving them. 

Thus, Baal Hatturim <note>Rabbi Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343), a prominent halakhic authority known for his commentary on the Torah</note> noted with no small judgment in these brief words: <note>original Hebrew: "יורו משפטיך ליעקוב שיפוצו בכל ישראל ללמוד תורה וכן אמר יעקוב ואפיצם בישראל"</note> *They shall teach your judgments to Jacob, since they shall be scattered among all the Israelites to teach the Law; and so Jacob said, "I will scatter them in Israel."* 

<margin>Genesis 49:7</margin>
For thus Jacob spoke of them: *And I will scatter them through Israel.* That such a prerogative of teaching, as we have now described, belongs to the Levites is, in our judgment, to be gathered from those testimonies which we have cited. For what less can be understood by those words, **THEY SHALL TEACH YOUR JUDGMENTS TO JACOB**, and your Law to Israel, than that the Israelites would often approach the Levites and ask them what is just and right? Would they not seek from them interpretations of the Law? Was it not the duty of the Levites to respond concerning the law and to free the Israelites from the weight of their scruples? What else do God’s words in Malachi mean: *The lips of the priests* <note>The author is referencing Malachi 2:7: "For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth."</note>

...“will keep knowledge, and they will SEEK THE LAW <note>original Hebrew: *yevakshu*; Latin: *requirent*</note> from their mouth?”
These words do not allow for a gentler or more lenient interpretation than that this duty was commanded to the Levites: that they, being instructed in the knowledge of the Divine Will, should give answers to those consulting them about the law. On these texts, all interpreters—both Jewish and Christian—teach this. But other testimonies must also be brought forward into the midst, by which the same point is confirmed. Let us note, therefore, the Mosaic Law concerning the Priests: 
<margin>Leviticus 10:10</margin>
*“And it shall be their duty to discern between the holy and the profane, and between the impure and the pure;* and to TEACH <note>original Hebrew: *le-horot*</note> the Children of Israel all those decrees <note>original Greek: *dogmata*</note> which the Lord commanded them through Moses.” The same constitution 
<margin>Chapter 44:23</margin>
concerning the Priests is repeated in Ezekiel: *“They shall teach my people what difference there is between the Holy and the profane, and they shall show them how the pure is to be discerned from the impure.”* You may find similar things elsewhere as well. 
<margin>Deuteronomy 24:8</margin>
We clearly see from these words what duty was imposed on the Levites by God. It fell to the **Levites** to teach the people. It was the people's part to hang upon their every word. However, the most simple method of teaching was this: that when Israelites consulted them on the meaning of the Law, they would faithfully explain the mind of the Lawgiver <note>That is, God</note>.

For it must be noticed that the words of both these constitutions correctly refer to the Priests. However, the Priests—being few in number at their first institution—were not to be separated from the Tabernacle <note>The portable dwelling place for the divine presence from the time of the Exodus</note> to preside over Schools and Academies and explain Divine precepts in such places. They remained at the Tabernacle, where their station had been assigned to them by God; though I am not unaware that in following times, as their number grew, the face of things changed. 

In the beginnings of their ministry, therefore, when they were no less bound to observe this Law than in later times, they had almost no other occasion for *teaching the people* than by religiously observing the Divine Laws in all their ministry—providing an example of their observance to others—and by clearly interpreting the Divine constitutions for Israelites who were asking questions or hesitating. But what is thus ascribed to the **Priests** in the Mosaic Laws, we—not without reason—attribute also to the **Levites**, since it is clear from other places in Scripture that they held the office of teaching in common with the Priests.

For any kind of cause or legal action did not necessarily demand an appeal to the Judges in Jerusalem; rather, many common matters could be settled in the cities and villages where Judges of a lower bench were appointed to administer justice—provided the case in question was defined in the Law, or could at least be determined from it through clear logical consequences. But if some more serious question was to be decided by the Judges, which was neither declared in the Law itself nor previously handled by that higher Tribunal of the Priest or Judge, they had to go up to the place *chosen by God*. There, the Priests and Judges who were present, constituting the Great Sanhedrin, were to be consulted; to deviate even slightly from their opinion, <italic>Doctrine</italic>, or <italic>Law</italic> was a capital offense.

<margin>1 Chronicles 12:32</margin>
However, the reader who is a student of the Divine Word will not take it poorly if I add a few thoughts to these meditations of mine, which are not foreign to the subject I have been occupied with so far. In the Book of Chronicles, there is a list of the famous men who defected from the Kingdom of Saul to David, and among them are the men of Issachar, marked with this title: <gloss>original Hebrew: ומבני יששכר יודעי בינה לעתים לדעת מה יעשה ישראל</gloss> *And of the children of Issachar, those who had understanding to discern prudently the opportune times, to know what Israel ought to do.* This is indeed a distinguished eulogy for the men of Issachar. Yet, it is doubtful how it should be understood. The <term>Chaldean Paraphrase<note>Also known as the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term>, which was published some years ago through the care of the most learned <term>Beck<note>Matthias Friedrich Beck (1649–1701), an Orientalist scholar who published the Targum on Chronicles.</note></term>, explains this passage as referring to chronological and astrological science, since the knowledge of distinguishing the times depends upon it. I will record only the first part of it: <gloss>original Aramaic: ומבני יששכר יודעי סוכלתנו לעדניא חכימין</gloss> *From the Issacharites there were those skilled in the science of times (Chronologists), and learned in fixing the beginnings of years and months.* But as for what is added in the text: <gloss>original Hebrew: וכל אחיהם על פיהם</gloss> *And all their brethren were at their command* (literally "at their mouth"), the same Paraphrast interpreted it thus: <gloss>original Aramaic: כל אחוהון עבדין פתגמי אוריתא וחכימים על מימר פומיהון</gloss> *All their kinsmen indeed performed the WORDS OF THE LAW, and were made wise BY THEIR INSTRUCTION.* Many of the Jewish interpreters, both ancient and more recent, follow this explanation. Nor can it be denied that it has some appearance of truth. Other most learned interpreters, however, think that here only secular prudence is hinted at—the wisdom by which one discerns what is best to do or not to do in the various cases of human life, and likewise in the various affairs of the State. <term>Jarchi<note>A common Latinized name for Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki), the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note></term> himself says: <gloss>original Hebrew: שיודעים לתת עצה לפי הענין של מעשה שצריך דוד להתעץ היאך יחזק המלכות מפני בני שאול</gloss> <margin>Commentary on this passage.</margin> *Who know how to give counsel according to the nature and circumstances of each case; the kind of men David needed to consult on how he might confirm his kingdom against the sons of Saul.* The <term>Belgic Interpreters<note>The Dutch translators of the "Statenvertaling" or Dutch Authorized Version of the Bible.</note></term> also [incline] toward this—

# ON ORIGINS Book I. Part 2.

"You stand from afar; you hide yourself, <note>original Hebrew: לעתות בצרה (le-ittot ba-tzarah)</note> *when **TIMES OF TROUBLE** are present*" [Psalm 10:1]. You might interpret the expression in this passage in the same way: *Those knowing prudence, when the time demanded it*. However, it is not inconsistent to also translate that word <note>original Hebrew: לעתים (le-ittim)</note> *the times* as: *according to what the various occasion of the times brings.* Moreover, the use of this prudence is determined more precisely by these words: <note>original Hebrew: לדעת מה יעשה ישראל (la-da'at mah ya'aseh Yisrael)</note> *to know what Israel ought to do.* <term>Kimchi<note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian, often cited by Christian scholars for his linguistic expertise.</note></term> says it should have been written, "to know what the King ought to do." But I do not see why our explanation requires this phrasing any more than Kimchi's does. For these words admit of an easy explanation. To know what Israel ought to do is to recognize what work needs to be done in the various circumstances of the <term>Commonwealth<note>The author uses "Respublica" to refer to the political organization of the Hebrew state.</note></term> and the Kingdom of Israel. Truly, everything leads us to think that *secular prudence* is described here. Queen Vashti, summoned by the King, had resisted his command; it was not clear what should be done in this matter. Therefore, the King consulted the men most skilled in law and ancient customs, who had been taught either by tradition or by writings what was done in the past, and what ought to be done now and at other times. These are <note>original Hebrew: יודעי העתים (yode'ei ha-ittim)</note> *those who know the times*; these are <note>original Hebrew: יודעי דת ודין (yode'ei dat va-din)</note> *those skilled in the laws and ancient customs.* These were men practiced and distinguished in the knowledge of every matter, but especially of histories, and thus fit for giving counsel in doubtful and complicated cases. If we say that these Issacharites were such men, perhaps we will not be far from the truth. But in whatever way this passage is explained, we gain from it the fact that the study of letters and wisdom was, as it were, revived and practiced by many under the Reign of Saul, which we supposed and established in the preceding sections.

# On ORIGINS Book I. Part 2.

And whether it is denied to the Princes, or to the entire people—which is more likely—there is absolutely no reason to conclude that the "instruction" mentioned in that context should be understood as the kind of institution that later flourished in the *Synagogues*. The opposite will become clear if we look more closely at this passage. Observe, therefore, that it mentions the institution of the <term>Torah<note>Hebrew: תורה; though often translated as "Law," it refers here to the systemic teaching and instruction of the divine word.</note></term> as being distinct from the institution of the Prophets. For after it was said: "there is no Law" <note>original Hebrew: אין תורה (*Ein Torah*)</note>, it is soon added: "her prophets also find no vision from the Lord." But what is that institution which was set in contrast to the Prophetic institution among the Jews? 

It is surely the *Sacerdotal and Levitical* <note>Relating to the Priests and the Levites, the two tribes responsible for religious duties and legal interpretation.</note> institution. In the mouths of the *Priests and Levites* was the Law <note>Hebrew: תורה (*Torah*)</note>; it was their duty to teach the people when they asked, to resolve doubtful cases, to illuminate obscure matters, to settle disputes according to the Law, and for the most part, to preside over judgments. These points were proven by us, unless I am mistaken, in the *preceding Dissertation*. This Law, this institution, is what the Prophet had his eyes fixed upon in this passage while lamenting the calamity of the people. The entire Commonwealth was in turmoil. Especially sad was the face of *Jerusalem*, of which the Prophet speaks here. Formerly, the *People of Jerusalem* rejoiced in *Kings, Princes, Priests, and Prophets*. For it is clear from the words of *Christ the Lord* himself that the Prophets resided chiefly in Jerusalem.

<margin>Luke 13:33</margin>
But now, destitute of all these things, the city remains in the greatest of evils. No Kings or Princes reside there. No institution of Priests flourishes there. No Prophets instruct the people with their visions. I believe this is the underlying sense of the words. And indeed, it should be observed for our purpose that the Prophet, when speaking of the destruction of the sacred places, mentions only the Temple, and no other holy building besides it. Behold the tears of the Prophet!

# CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES. 383

...even this very word, "sanctuaries" <note>Hebrew: מקדשים (*Miqdashim*)</note>, is used in the plural number to refer to the single Temple of Jerusalem. But since at least in this text the Prophet <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Lamentations, traditionally identified as Jeremiah.</note>, mourning the destruction of the *sacred places*, only mentions the *Sanctuary of Jerusalem*, who would not conclude from this that there were no other prominent Sacred Houses in Judea at that time? But as we have seen, he now records that only one <term>Sanctuary<note>Hebrew: מקדש (*Miqdash*), in the singular.</note></term> has been laid waste. He 
<margin>Chapter 2, verse 6.</margin>

In this text, the Prophet again pours out his laments over the destruction of the Sacred Places. Yet none are mentioned except for one *place of assembly* <note>Hebrew: מועד (*Mo'ed*)</note> in the singular number; no one can deny that this must be understood as the Temple of Jerusalem, serving as the common sanctuary for the entire Jewish Nation. The same must be understood by the *booth* <note>Latin: *tugurium*; Hebrew: *shakh*</note> *of the Israelite garden*, besides which you will find no others in these *Lamentations*. From this, I conclude that there were no other Sanctuaries in the land of Canaan at that age, as they could not have escaped the tears of the Prophet—who was searching everywhere for reasons to grieve—if they had been destroyed at the same time as the Temple.

*Secondly*, I would like it to be noted that in the *public fasts* which were celebrated before the time of the Babylonian Captivity, the entire population of the Jewish nation was summoned to the *Temple*, and not to *Synagogues*. This would not have seemed necessary if Synagogues had already been established at that time. Indeed, a *fast* can be celebrated just as well in *Synagogues* as in the *Temple*. But first, I will prove this hypothesis; then I will press the point. That *fasts* before the times of the Babylonian Captivity were celebrated in the *Temple alone* can, unless I am mistaken, be gathered from these words of *Jeremiah*:
<margin>Chapter 36, verses 9 and 10.</margin>

## ON THE ORIGIN BOOK 1, PART 2. 386

...or if he were held captive in foreign regions, then he would necessarily be prevented by that circumstance from visiting this Temple and performing the customary religious duties toward God within it. What counsel was given then? Naturally, the people, in whatever place they were, would *turn themselves toward that* quarter of the sky in which the Temple was built, and in offering their prayers, they would conceive in their minds the presence of that place from which their bodies were so distantly separated. This is truly *to pray* <note>original: דֶּרֶךְ הָעִיר וְהַבַּיִת (*derekh ha-ir ve-ha-bayit*)</note> *by way of the city and the house*, which may be translated: *toward the city and the Temple*.

But if no such circumstance detained the people, then it was their duty to betake themselves to this Temple and supplicate God there in person. Those who did so were said to *pray* <note>original: אֶל הַבַּיִת (*el ha-bayit*)</note> *at the house*, near the Temple or in the Temple. Indeed, the small word <note>Hebrew: אֶל (*el*), meaning "to" or "at"</note> (not to mention other examples easily found elsewhere) 
<margin>Verse 30.</margin> 
is used in that very context: *And you shall hear* (the prayers poured out to You) <note>original: אֶל מְקוֹם שִׁבְתְּךָ אֶל הַשָּׁמַיִם (*el meqom shivtekha el ha-shamayim*)</note> AT THE PLACE OF YOUR DWELLING, IN HEAVEN; *and you will hear and show yourself favorable*. What is called <note>original: אֶל הַשָּׁמַיִם (*el ha-shamayim*)</note> you should properly translate as *at heaven*, which is in heaven itself; an elegant mode of speaking often favored by the Sacred Writers.

As far as I can judge, Solomon, through this entire range of words, presents *the Temple alone* as a kind of *public house of prayer*. Jehoshaphat certainly repeated this privilege of the Temple, 
<margin>2 Chronicles 20:9.</margin> 
and he himself, praying to God in this Temple, said: *If any evil should come upon us* (this is a fragment of his words) *the sword, judgment, or pestilence or famine*; <note>original: נַעַמְדָה לִפְנֵי הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה וּלְפָנֶיךָ (*na'amdah lifnei ha-bayit ha-zeh u-lifnekha*)</note> *we will stand before this house and before You*. Here you see only the Temple proposed as a public <term>house of prayer<note>Greek: προσευκτήριον (*proseuktērion*), a term used for a place dedicated to prayer.</note></term>, nor do any other sacred places come into consideration besides it. Indeed, what is said here—*to stand before this house*—agrees with the phrase *at this house*, which has already been explained.

Moreover, since the *Gentiles* <note>Non-Jewish nations of the ancient world.</note>, whose ceremonies the Jewish people imitated with great zeal, were at that time proud of their temples everywhere—as is clear from sacred history—who would think that the Jews of that age were no more affected by the Religion of the Temple than by that of Synagogues? And that, after the most splendid Temple was built, they would have wished to diminish its value, splendor, and majesty by the construction of Synagogues? As far as I can see, this does not quite align with the character of the Jews of that time.

Fourthly, when we consider that from the reign of Rehoboam <note>The son of Solomon whose reign saw the kingdom split into Israel and Judah.</note> until the Babylonian Captivity, idolatry dominated the people—at some times more, at others less—and that the efforts of even the pious Kings were continually interrupted and disturbed, either by the perverse inclinations of the people or by the policies of succeeding Kings; how can we believe that the worship of *Synagogues* flourished at that time? Or that the Jewish people, in such a state of affairs, devoted themselves to establishing Synagogues? Even the buildings of the Temple itself were at times so neglected that they had to be repaired at great expense. On the contrary, the people were carried away with such monstrous zeal toward the *High Places* <note>original: *Excelsa*; these were local hilltop shrines or altars used for worship outside the central Temple in Jerusalem.</note> that the most pious Kings were almost unable to overthrow them. By *High Places*, however, you should understand not only the higher mountain peaks and summits, but also certain smaller *shrines* <note>original: *fana*</note> built upon them. This was the love and delight of the people, who were rivals of the superstitions of neighboring nations right up until the Babylonian Captivity. How well does it fit to imagine Synagogues being established in this state of affairs? Indeed, if we look a little more closely at the face of the Church during that interval, we will find it much more afflicted and foul than we would dare to think or believe without the explicit testimony of Sacred History, and more than we are commonly accustomed to believe.

<margin>2 Chronicles 17:6.</margin>
1. I would like it to be noted what Sacred History relates concerning *Jehoshaphat*, a most pious Prince. The words of the text: *And in the third year of his reign he sent his princes Ben-Hail, and Obadiah, and Zechariah, and Nathaneel, and Michaiah*, <note>Hebrew: ללמד בערי יהודה (*lilmod be-arei Yehudah*)</note> **TO TEACH IN THE CITIES OF JUDAH:** AND WITH THEM WERE THE LEVITES *Shemaiah, and Nethaniah, and Zebadiah, and Asahel, and Shemiramoth, and Jonathan, and Adonijah, and Tobijah, and Tob-Adonijah, Levites*; and with them *Elishama and Jehoram*, Priests: <note>Hebrew: וילמדו ביהודה ועמם ספר תורת יהוה (*va-yelamdu bi-Yehudah ve-immam sefer torat Yehovah*)</note> **AND THEY TAUGHT IN JUDAH, AND WITH THEM WAS THE BOOK OF THE LAW OF THE LORD;** and they went around all the cities of Judah, <note>Hebrew: וילמדו בעם (*va-yelamdu ba-am*)</note> **AND TAUGHT THE PEOPLE.** From every circumstance of this history, it is clear that this act of King *Jehoshaphat* was entirely unique. **1.** <note>original: Hebrew letter "א" (Aleph) used as a list marker.</note> Where we see King *Jehoshaphat* sending extraordinary legates into Judah—the *Priests and Levites to teach the people*—from this it seems altogether clear that the people at that time enjoyed almost no formal public instruction. But there is no place for that objection here. For King *Asa* did not prevent the public worship of the true God, nor did he destroy Synagogues, if any had existed during his reign. From where, then, came such deep ignorance among the people that an extraordinary remedy had to be prepared? # CHAPTER 9. ON SYNAGOGUES.

If copies of the Mosaic Law had been preserved and available elsewhere, why would these Teachers carry a copy of the Law of Moses with them? Furthermore, why would the author of this history record that detail so pointedly? The fact that these Priests and Levites, along with the Princes, are said to have traveled through all the cities of Judah, clearly reveals that this institution of teaching was not a continuous or permanent one. For otherwise, the King would have had to assign certain Teachers to every city who would devote themselves to educating the people on every occasion. However, from this text it appears that the Teachers chosen by the King toured the entire region of Judah, and it is not equally clear that others succeeded them in that place. Indeed, from this case—rare and notable as it was—one may conclude that the common people in that age enjoyed no such ordinary reading and exposition of the *Divine Law* <note>original: "Legis Divinæ"</note> as is now practiced in the Synagogues.

<margin>2 Kings 22:10</margin>
**2.** We may draw similar conclusions from the events narrated as having occurred under King *Josiah*. *Josiah*, likewise a pious Prince, had ordered the repair of the Temple, which had fallen into ruin in various parts and been profaned. While faithful men were occupied with this work, the Book of the Mosaic Law was found in the Temple by *Hilkiah* <note>The High Priest during Josiah's reign, c. 622 BCE.</note> the High Priest; this same book was handed to *Shaphan* <note>A royal scribe or secretary.</note> the scribe and read aloud to King *Josiah*. When the King perceived its meaning, not without astonishment, he first sent the High Priest Hilkiah and other men of proven faith as legates to consult *Huldah* the Prophetess regarding this discovery;

<margin>chapter 23: 1, 2</margin>
Then he ordered the Elders of all Judah and Jerusalem to be gathered in the Temple, and the decrees of the *Mosaic Law* <note>original: "Legis Moſaicæ"</note> to be read and explained to them. This history is certainly worthy of all our attention regarding the matter at hand. For what else could you conclude from it, other than that the use of the *Book of the Law* <note>original: "Libri Legis"; likely referring to a scroll of Deuteronomy or the entire Pentateuch.</note> was rare—indeed, exceedingly rare—at that time among the Jews, and even among the Priests themselves? Otherwise, why would the High Priest marvel at the Book of the Law being found? Why would King *Josiah* be stunned by its reading and its message? Why is God consulted in an extraordinary manner to explain the words of His own Law? Why also are the Elders and all the Jews gathered to hear the reading of this Law, and to renew a covenant with God based on the conditions written within it? Certainly, we can understand none of these things distinctly unless we suppose that the use of the Mosaic Law at that [time]...

### ON THE ORIGIN BOOK 1. PART 2. 398

[the au]thor, he wished to express future things through such *signs*, or through such voices and phrases, which were known and understood at that time in which he uttered this prophecy. For this is the custom of the Prophets. When they speak of future things, they are accustomed to express them in such words and phrases that are in common use at the time they publish their prophecies. Since I have disputed this in the preceding pages, I have no need to deal with it at greater length now. Imagine that at the time the Prophet wrote these things, *Synagogues* did not exist. Neither he, therefore, nor the people of that time, would have had any concept of Synagogues. Now, indeed, it is rare that the Holy Spirit would hand down future things in words used to designate things of which the people of that age have no idea; for in doing so, He would make the understanding of His word too difficult. Instead, He is more often accustomed to represent future things through such terms or emblems which are drawn from *matters* known and understood in the age in which He produces His word.

<margin>Malachi 1:11.</margin> 
Thus, when about to foretell that *prayer halls* <note>original: *oratoria*</note> were eventually to be built for God throughout the whole world, and that *Gentiles were to be chosen as Ministers of the Church*, He says *in every place a pure offering must be offered to God, and Priests must be taken from the Nations* <note>original: *Gentibus*</note>, etc. If, therefore, it is conceded—which seems to be conceded by the most learned *Burmann* <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian</note>—that by the "assemblies of God" <note>original Hebrew: מועדי אל (*moade el*)</note> the *Synagogues* of later times were designated (such as, for example, the Prayer Halls and Temples of Christians), then it will turn out entirely likely that *Synagogues* already existed at that time. For it seems that if they had not existed, the Prophet would have used another phrase by which he would have excited a easier concept in his readers of a thing unknown at that time.

Indeed, when we consider the *Psalm* <note>Psalm 74</note> diligently, it seems to us to deal entirely with a certain time of public calamity, and specifically with the most wretched state of the *Jewish Commonwealth*, when the people were led away into the Babylonian Captivity. In this Psalm, I say, the deplorable face of the Judean Republic and Church is *prophetically* depicted at that time when—the Temple having been turned to ashes by the command of the King of Babylon, and Judea having been laid waste by the Chaldeans—the nation sacred to God was deported into foreign regions. This will be very clear to anyone who compares the tenor and contents of this Psalm with the *Lamentations of Jeremiah and the actual outcome of events*. And this is also the opinion of *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French biblical scholar</note>, who moreover thinks that *Asaph* <note>The biblical figure to whom Psalm 74 is attributed</note>, who [composed] this lamen-

Asaph knew that sad events of this kind would one day befall the Jews. He therefore composed a lamentation, and a supplication attached to it, so that the people of that time might use this formula of dirges and relieve their sorrows with these tears. 

As for my saying that these hymns represent the fates of the Babylonian Captivity, I can hardly understand how the most Learned Men could be stuck on that point. ...of Nebuchadnezzar. But those first two, *Jeremiah* and *Ezekiel*, flourished only during the first years of the Babylonian Captivity; of *Daniel*, enough has already been said. Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note> says likewise: <margin>Commentary on this place.</margin> **מועדיך הוא בית המקדש אשר נאמר בו ונועדתי לך שם** *Your places of assembly; this is the Holy Temple, regarding which it was said;* <margin>Exodus 25:22.</margin> **ונועדתי לך שם** *and I will meet with you there.* It is permissible, therefore, to understand by **כל מועדי אל** *all the meeting places of God*, according to the most excellent Interpreters, the most august Temple with its splendid courts and magnificent structures of halls <note>original Latin: *exedrarum*, referring to side-rooms or outdoor seating areas in a classical or sacred complex</note>, as it was prepared by Solomon at vast expense. These were **כל מועדי אל בארץ** *the meeting places of God in the land of Canaan*, because in them God exhibited His presence to His people.

Yet, what forbids us from extending the emphasis of this expression even further, if it were possible to do so? Let us observe, therefore, that by **כל מועדי אל**, by the power of the Hebrew phrase, we should understand any *place* in which God either now exhibits Himself as *present* or formerly exhibited Himself as *present*, and which He decorated with some apparition of His own and the manifestation of His grace. If I am not mistaken, by **כל מועדי אל** the Hebrews most properly denote a *place*, not into which men gather, but in which God, as if by appointment, appears and gives clear evidence of His presence and grace. For the phrase, as was rightly noted by Jarchi, is taken from those words of God to Moses regarding the space of the Ark <margin>as cited above</margin> between the two Cherubim: **ונועדתי לך שם** *AND THERE I WILL COME TO*

...family, and whether every family—be they men or women—would have had their own specific place assigned to them? Since no one will easily grant this, it follows that what is stated here concerning the specific mourning of women can in no way be applied to the customs of the Synagogues. Therefore, it is permitted to explain what is said here—that every family and their women shall mourn **separately** <note>original Hebrew: *levad*</note>—either as being about the gravity of the grief (in which even the dearest friends separate from one another, choosing solitary places where they might pour out their tears without a witness), or as being about the personal reasons for lamenting that each mourner would have for themselves, or even that **for the sake of modesty** <note>original Hebrew: *mishum tzeniyut*—a Jewish legal and ethical concept regarding privacy and decency</note> women were to separate themselves from their husbands during mourning and seek out solitary retreats. Among the Hebrews, **assembly**, **congregation**, and **gatherings** <note>original Hebrew: *qahal*, *qehilah*, and *meqahalim*</note> denote any large multitude of men, or rather of some people, living or gathered in any place. This was proven above when we specifically dealt with the meaning of the word **assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *qahal*</note>. Nor do these words take on any other meaning in these passages. For Christ, who speaks in them, says that he will preach and celebrate the divine name in whatever place, before whatever listeners, and on whatever occasions. Christ did this in the Temple, in the Synagogues, on the mountain, on the shore, and in the deserts. He allowed no occasion for glorifying his Father to pass by. Therefore, the **assembly** <note>original Hebrew: *qahal*</note> is the **people** <note>original Hebrew: *am*</note> itself, found or gathered in any place whatsoever. In these and other sayings of this kind, there is nothing that supports the existence of [formal] Synagogues.

# CHAPTER II. OF SYNAGOGUES.

<margin>1 Kings 21:8, 9, 10, etc.</margin>
Finally, I will not hide a difficulty that occurred to me while I was occupied with these matters, arising from the history of the stolen vineyard and its murdered owner, **Naboth**. **Jezebel**, the most wicked wife of **Ahab**, had conceived in her mind the crime of forcing her husband into possession of Naboth's vineyard through the most unjust violence—a vineyard which Naboth had refused to surrender to Ahab because it had come down to him as an inheritance from his ancestors. She therefore sent letters to the Elders and Nobles of **Samaria**, and to the leaders and magistrates of the people, in which she commanded that a *Fast be proclaimed, and that Naboth be seated* <gloss>original Hebrew: *be-rosh ha-am*</gloss> **AT THE HEAD OF THE PEOPLE** <note>original Latin: *in primis populi*</note>. The subsequent context of the story indicates that these men carried out and managed this task diligently. This fast was celebrated in Samaria. But where exactly? For it seems clear that it was celebrated in a specific place ordained for that purpose, since everyone had a seat according to their dignity in that solemn act. This certainly seems to be indicated by the words: *and you shall seat Naboth at the head of the people*. Was there, then, a **Synagogue** in Samaria in which the people were accustomed to gather at the time of a Fast? I think not. For how can it be imagined that one existed where such great impiety reigned? You may then insist: where, then, was this Fast observed? I respond: either in some **public square** <term>original Latin: *foro*; the open marketplace or civic center</term> of the city, or in the **Temple** that had been built by Ahab in Samaria. In ancient times, when fixed places were not yet destined for the exercise of religion in such acts, Fasts seem to have been celebrated **in the public squares and streets**. I do not doubt that this was also observed in the **Fast of Mizpah** <note>original Latin: *Mispitico*; referring to the assembly called by Samuel in 1 Samuel 7</note>, about which we have spoken elsewhere.

# Chapter 12. CONCERNING SYNAGOGUES.

In the era of Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a Church Father known for his writings on heresies and biblical history</note>, it was believed that no synagogues had been built in Canaan. I do not wish, therefore, to hold tenaciously to this opinion <note>original Latin: *mordicus tenere*; literally "to hold with the teeth"</note>. Rather, I will have done better if I suspend my judgment until the whole matter has been more thoroughly investigated by me. In the meantime, it is permitted to observe the following points, which can be affirmed by us with some certainty.

1. It cannot be denied that many of the principal rites observed in today's synagogues draw their origin from the times of Ezra. Let us consider the words read in the Book of *Nehemiah*:

<margin>chapter 8, verse 1.</margin>

> *And all the people gathered, as one man, at the square that is before the Water Gate, and they told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses, which the Lord had commanded to Israel:* AND EZRA THE PRIEST BROUGHT THE LAW *before the assembly of men and women, and all who could hear with understanding, on the first day of the seventh month. And* HE READ FROM IT *at the square that is before the Water Gate from early morning until midday in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law.* AND EZRA *the scribe* <note>original Greek: *ὁ γραμματεὺς*</note> STOOD UPON A WOODEN TOWER <note>likely a raised wooden platform or pulpit</note> *which they had built for this purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah on his right hand; and on his left, Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam. And* EZRA OPENED THE BOOK *in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people; and when he opened it, all the people stood. And* EZRA BLESSED THE LORD, *the great God, and* ALL THE PEOPLE ANSWERED: AMEN, AMEN, *lifting up their hands, and they bowed their heads and* WORSHIPPED *the Lord with their faces toward the ground. ### On the ORIGIN Book 1, Part 2.

been written. Indeed, this dispute is not of great importance; however, I believe that when it is said <note>original Hebrew: *ויקראו בספר בתורת*</note> "*They read in that book, in the Law of God*," it is sufficiently indicated that Ezra read from the Law written by Moses, which the people had requested. Thus, it was not necessary to indicate this by some other rare and infrequent word. This is especially true because those oral traditions do not seem to have been widespread or to have held any authority at that time. Indeed, I hardly believe that the people who had returned from the Babylonian Captivity—whose affairs were quite disordered and who had almost forgotten the written Law—would have thought anything of unwritten traditions. These traditions were eventually fabricated by extravagant minds after the deaths of the Prophets and were covered by the cloak of venerable antiquity <note>The author suggests that "oral laws" were later inventions designed to look old and authoritative</note>. I therefore retain the **common version** of the text, in which there is no difficulty.

However, a learned man <note>likely referring to a contemporary scholar or commentator</note> has correctly interpreted that last phrase <note>original Hebrew: *ויבינו במקרא* / *wa-yavinu ba-miqra*</note>, which *Tremellius* <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a prominent Jewish-Italian convert and Hebraist who translated the Bible into Latin</note> had translated as: *they gave understanding through the scripture itself*. The *Dutch* <note>original: *Belgæ*; referring to the Dutch translation of the Bible</note> rendered it: **Thus they acted / so that one understood in the reading**; that is, *the listeners understood the Scripture.* For if the version of Tremellius and the Dutch were to prevail, the same thing would be said twice in a short history, and in such a way that the second mention would be less emphatic than the first. Furthermore, the word <term>בּין</term> <note>Hebrew root *B-Y-N*, meaning to understand or discern</note> is constructed here with the preposition <term>בּ</term> <note>the Hebrew letter *Beth*</note>, which usually signifies *to understand*, not *to make someone else understand*. 

We therefore conceive of two distinct groups mentioned in this verse: the *Teachers*, namely, and the *Listeners*. It is said of the *Teachers* that they *read* and *gave the meaning*; it is said of the *Listeners* that they *understood what was read*. There is still some doubt as to whether the same people who read the Law before the people also interpreted it or gave the meaning. 

Certainly, if we consider the *eighth* verse, it is clear that the *Levites*, whose names are even listed, instructed the people in the Law. Therefore, Ezra did not do this alone, but the Levites did so, having been taught by Ezra and standing at his side. Nor should it be imagined that only *Ezra* read here, even though that action is ascribed to him as the primary <unclear>legislator</unclear> <note>original Greek: *νόμῳ*</note> in the fourth verse. For those *Levites* who stood by him also read, as we 
<margin>Nehemiah 8</margin>
clearly gather from chapter 9, verses 3 and 4; each read in his own place and order, as was fitting. 

Truly, we must describe more distinctly from this text those features which the Synagogues of subsequent times held in common: 
α. Here you have a *wooden pulpit* <note>original: *suggestum ligneum*</note>, raised up high.
