2. Since Ezra was very well practiced in both the reading and the understanding of the Law, and since he ignited many other Priests, Levites, and indeed even Israelites of his age with a love for that study, it seems that from that time forward, many copies of the Holy Scripture were transcribed. These were bought and read more diligently by students of the divine law than had been done before the Jews were led away into Babylon. Codices <note>early book-style manuscripts, as opposed to scrolls</note> seem to have been rare, interpretation rare, and studies of the Divine Law lukewarm before these times of the Babylonian Captivity. But the people, according to the <margin>Deuteronomy 30:2</margin> Divine promise, having been purified through those afflictions and led by repentance for their sins, began to inquire more diligently into the Divine will. They began to value the word entrusted to them by God above all other nations, and to explore its meanings more anxiously than before. Hence it is that in the history of the *Maccabees* <note>Books of the Apocrypha detailing the Jewish rebellion against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE</note>, more frequent mention occurs of the *Sacred Books*. Therefore, it should not be doubted that from the time of Ezra onward, the Law was much more read and used by the people than before.

...[pie]ty, I believe. <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "pietate" (piety) or "necessitate" (necessity)</note> The experience of all ages has taught us that the sacred matters of Religion tend to be handled lukewarmly and negligently when their exercise is free and unhindered; on the contrary, where Religion is oppressed by force or confined within narrow bounds, it is then that the zeal for it flourishes most. This was almost exactly the case with the Jews. As long as they lived in Canaan <note>The Promised Land</note>, enjoying their own Prophets and Priests, they continually fell away from the worship of the true God into foul idolatry, from which they could be deterred by no promises or threats. Then they also began to handle the Word of God more diligently, and to examine and search out its meanings; as is evident from *Ezra*, who was most celebrated among the Captives for this very reason. From this study was born the public reading of the Divine Law, instituted among the Jews who returned from Captivity to Jerusalem, held in the square which was before the Temple, about which we were just now explaining a few things.

It is not clear to me, indeed, whether *Fasts* before the Captivity were formerly observed in other places besides the Temple, which was "a house of prayer and petition for your people, O God" <note>original Greek: *oikos proseuchēs kai deēseōs tō laō sou Theos*</note>,

Whether, however, the frequency of Fasts and the solemnity of their observation was such that they produced this effect while the first Temple still stood, is as uncertain as anything else. All public calamities into which the people of God fell, according to the predictions of their Prophets <note>original: *Vatum*, referring to the biblical seers</note>. Calamities, whether private or public, usually have the effect of stirring men to seek God and implore His help.

# ON THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE
## BOOK ONE.
### PART III.
### On the Correspondence of the Oratories of the Christian Church with the Synagogues of the Jews.
### CHAPTER I.

### CHAPTER II.

#### *Several reasons are brought forward to prove that the sacred houses of the early Christians were modeled after the pattern of the Jewish Synagogues; this point is further emphasized by a brief comparison established between the Names, Parts, and certain Accidental Features of Synagogues and Christian Oratories.*

<margin>Hebrews 10:15</margin>
It is now a matter for further inquiry whether the houses of assembly which the early Church possessed owe their origin to the **Synagogues of the Jews** and were modeled after their pattern. Here, indeed, one must answer with some <term>distinction</term> <note>original Greek: "διακρίσει" (diakrisei), meaning a careful discernment or nuanced judgment.</note>. Sound reason dictates that people of the same society and profession should often meet together in one place. Moreover, the laws of Christian society expressly require the same. Furthermore, since that same nature teaches men that specific places must be chosen for such meetings, nothing is more consistent with reason and the laws of Christian society than for members of this society to designate certain locations for the exercise of their <term>religious worship</term> <note>original Greek: "θρησκείας" (thrēskeias), referring to the outward rites and service of religion.</note>, and to make these places unique and sacred for their gatherings. 

Since humans also easily understand from the principles of natural science that a place consecrated to the exercise of Religion must be equipped with those **instruments** <note>In this context, "instruments" refers to the physical furnishings of a building, such as seating, reading desks, or ritual objects.</note> without which its sacred rites cannot be performed—and it is certain that the meeting houses of the early Christians had no other instruments than those which the exercise of that religion necessarily required—there is no great cause compelling us to derive the locations or the instruments of sacred Christian worship from any source other than that of common **REASON**. 

However, besides **REASON**, there are two other principles by which the exercise of Religion and its manner can be defined: namely, **COMMAND** and **EXAMPLE**. Formerly, indeed, it pleased God that many things which common reason teaches both concerning...

But besides these, many ceremonies are often transferred into any given religion from the example of another religion, wherever that *zeal for imitation* of the religious rites received from others may arise; whether from *emulation*, or from the perception of *utility* or *convenience* which is believed to exist either in the religion itself or in its ceremonies, or even from other principles. To this cause, beyond doubt, must be ascribed the fact that the superstitions of the Gentiles once agreed so much among themselves; and also that, as is well known, Christianity itself received various ceremonies and names into its sacred rites from <term>Paganism</term> <note>original Latin: "Gentilismo."</note>. For mortals are of such a nature that they are led more easily by examples than by Laws. Therefore, although we do not deny that the *Form of Divine Worship*, as it has been received in Christianity, is greatly in harmony with reason, it is nevertheless not improper to inquire whether a *Precept* exists by which the Christians of the earliest times were bound, or an *Example* which they followed in ordering and establishing the outward form and manner of their religion. And indeed, as far as PRECEPTS are concerned, we know of no command of Christ, nor even any *precepts of the Apostles regarding the building of Oratories and Places of Assembly*; much less regarding the *Form, Parts, and Instruments of such Places*. Christ permitted this to the judgment of the Apostles; the Apostles then followed their own judgment,

1. I would like it to be considered that *Synagogues* were extremely suitable and well-adapted for the practice of the Christian Religion. *Synagogues* are public or private places in which Jews are accustomed to gather both to praise God and pray, and to receive the *reading and interpretation of the Divine Law*. The most learned *Fuller* <note>Refers to Nicholas Fuller (1557–1626), an English scholar of Hebrew and sacred philology</note> proceeds to reason in almost the same way, discussing that *School* which a certain *Tyrannus* lent to *Paul at Ephesus*. "Therefore," he says, "concerning that place which he was forced to borrow from the outside due to pressing and sudden necessity, must we not think that at the first opportunity, once matters were settled to his satisfaction, he would have given diligent effort so that the Church or assembly of the godly might acquire its own place? Especially since, by birth as well as by education and discipline, as a Jew, he knew best the many advantages and the good order <note>original: "εὐταξίαν" (eutaxian), meaning orderly arrangement or discipline</note> of the Synagogues among his own people?"

### CHAPTER 2. RELATION TO SYNAGOGUES, ETC. 455

<margin>Concerning the Sanhedrin, Book 3, Chapter 15, Section 5 <note>A reference to John Selden's *De Synedriis veterum Ebraeorum* (1650), a foundational work on Jewish law and its influence on the Church.</note></margin>
<unclear>DEDICATED</unclear> THINGS OF THE CHURCH signified nothing at all beyond the **houses of prayer** <note>original: "εὐκτήρια Oratoria"</note> themselves, which could be converted to other uses at the whim of the owners from whom they were leased or permitted—provided no other obstacle stood in the way. Even if some formula of prayer or a *Mass* <note>original: "Miſſa." The author notes: "lest there be a dispute here regarding that name or the thing itself, as it was at that time."</note> was understood to be part of such a Dedication, certainly nothing else can be inferred from it except for the very first *use* of praying or celebrating the Mass in them. Just like the first inhabiting of any house, whether built, rented, or bought—even when done with blessings—this sort of Dedication is merely an "opening," not based on any notion of "consecrating" the building itself, nor of any other such kind. This is excellently confirmed by the most learned Dodwell, when explaining what it means to "dedicate a reading" in the works of Cyprian.
<margin>Cyprianic Dissertations, on Epistle 33 <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711) was a scholar who wrote extensively on the early Church father Cyprian.</note></margin>
His digression begins thus: "The word *dedicate* has the same value among the Africans as *to begin*, as Pamelius also observed before us." But he did not explain why it signifies this. *That meaning was clearly derived from the Dedication of sacred places*, IN WHICH THE VERY FIRST SACRED OFFICES HELD THE PLACE OF DEDICATION.
<margin>Athanasius, Apology to Constantius</margin>
He teaches that the word is to be understood in this sense in the accusation against *Athanasius*: that he had "dedicated" a magnificent Temple built by *Constantius* without the Emperor's order. In reality, he had simply celebrated a **Liturgy** <note>original: "Synaxin" — a Greek term for a formal Christian gathering or Eucharistic service.</note> and performed solemn rites there during the Easter festivities, because the smaller houses could not contain the multitude of the faithful. The simple administration of *sacred rites* in a recently built Temple was considered a "Dedication." Yet who does not know that from this very time—with increasing superstition and luxury—Christian Temples began to be titled and consecrated in the manner of the *Jewish* Temple, or rather that of the *Gentiles*? They were no longer dedicated to God and Christ the Lord alone, but to the *Virgin Mary, martyrs, and Holy Men*, and were inaugurated in their honor with various ceremonies. It is certain that these Dedications were established following the example of both *Jewish* and *Gentile Temples*; for just as the former was dedicated to the true God, so these latter ones were inscribed and named for false gods. However, we strongly doubt whether this ritual can be derived in any way from the Synagogues. For those, as far as we know, reject all such *titling* and solemn Dedications. It is true that the Jews held the Synagogues of illustrious men in the highest esteem, or were even accustomed to build Synagogues near their tombs and name them after those same holy men whose memory was preserved at such a place (as you find in *Benjamin* <note>Refers to Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented synagogues named after biblical figures.</note>

the **Christian Prayer Halls** <note>original: *Oratoria Christiana*</note> began to take on the appearance of later times. It is well established that Christians, even from ancient times, were accustomed—in whatever part of the world they lived—to pray toward the **East** <note>original: *Orientem*</note>, and, when they gained control over their own affairs, to establish the rear part of their **Prayer Halls** in the **East**, and the front part in the **West** <note>original: *Occidente*</note>. This arrangement of **Christian Houses** was entirely contrary to the layout of the **Temple** <note>The Great Temple in Jerusalem.</note>, which faced the **East** from its front part and the **West** from its rear, so that one entering it would pray toward the **West**. Certain learned men, weighing these facts, have thought 
<margin>See Durand <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), a French liturgical writer.</note> and Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential Jesuit theologian.</note> in Hospinian’s <note>Rudolf Hospinian (1547–1626), a Swiss Reformed theologian who wrote on the history of temples and rituals.</note> *On Temples*, book II, chapter 1.</margin> 
that **Christians** wished to oppose the **Jews** in this regard; seeing that the Jews turned toward the **West** in their prayers, the Christians, in their opinion, turned toward the **East** out of a hatred for **Jewish** superstition. But those men did not consider that the layout of the **Synagogues** was not the same as that of the **Temple**, and that the **Jews** did not always turn toward the same quarter of the sky when praying. Let us therefore call to mind that among the rules for building a **Synagogue**, its rear part must face the **Holy of Holies** <note>original: *Sanctum Sanctorum*</note>. Indeed, 
<margin>See book 1, Part 1, chapter VIII.</margin> 
all **Jews**, when about to worship God in prayer, were bound to turn toward that place. Therefore, if a **Synagogue** is built in the **East** <note>i.e., East of Jerusalem, such as in Babylon.</note>, its front part is placed in the **East** and its rear in the **West**; but if it is in the **West** <note>i.e., West of Jerusalem, such as in Europe.</note>, the front is placed in the **West** and the rear in the **East**. One that is built in the **South** has its rear directed toward the **North**; one in the **North** is directed toward the **South** region. Furthermore, since the greatest multitude of **Jews** lived outside the land of **Canaan** <note>The biblical land of Israel.</note> in those regions of the earth which had the land of **Canaan** and the **Temple** to their **East**, it is evident that, according to these ordinances, all those **Western Jews** were required to turn toward the **East** in their prayers just as much as **Christians**. Consequently, it is so far from being true that the **Christians** (the greatest part of whom inhabited the **West**) were contrary to the **Western Jews** in this ritual, that on the contrary, it is not unpleasant to observe here a friendly consensus between both sides in the external gesture of praying or the layout of the **Prayer Halls**. Yet, even though this is the case—that is, although all **Western Synagogues** had exactly the same orientation as the **Christian Prayer Halls**, and **Western Jews** turned toward the **East** in prayer just as the **Christians** did—who would nevertheless dare to say that the **Western Christians** received this custom from the **Jews**? Indeed, the ancient Church expected that this same Christ would one day come for the Last Judgment from the East, relying on the words of Christ in the Gospel of Matthew: *For just as the lightning* COMES OUT OF THE EAST <note>original Greek: ἐξέρχεται ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν; Latin: *egreditur ab oriente*</note>, *and shines* EVEN UNTO THE WEST <note>original Greek: κὴ φαίνεται ἕως δυσμῶν; Latin: *& apparet usque ad occidentem*</note>, *so also shall the coming of the Son of Man be.*

Since, therefore, the Ancients stood perpetually ready and waited for the arrival of Christ in the clouds of heaven for judgment, they thought it best that they should turn toward the East when they prayed.

<margin>1 Peter 2:9.</margin>
Furthermore, since the origin of *light* is in the East, and since the first Christians recognized that grace of the Holy Spirit by which they were called out of *darkness* into *light*, they wished to turn toward the *East* in prayer. They did this to declare through this symbol that they were Children of Light, having been converted from darkness to *light*. For this reason, those who were being initiated into the Christian religion through Baptism were turned around in a circle toward the *East*, away from the West—the direction toward which their faces had previously been inclined. This was done so they might be warned of the new 
<margin>Acts 14:15.</margin>
change in their status, as those who *had passed from darkness to light, and from vain and perishing things to the living God.*

For since the light is born in the *East*, and its rising floods the human mind with joy and refreshes the spirit, the *East* is held to be an emblem of those superior blessings which revive and lift up the soul.

<margin>Stromata, book 7, page 520.</margin>
Let us hear Clement of Alexandria: *“Because the East is the image of the day of birth, and from there the light increases, having first shone out of darkness; and so to those wallowing in ignorance, the day of the knowledge of truth has dawned like the sun. Therefore prayers are made toward the morning sunrise. This is also why the oldest of the temples looked toward the West, so that those standing opposite the faces of the statues might be taught to turn toward the East.”* <note>Original Greek: Ἐπεὶ δ' γενεθλίης ἡμέρας εἰκὼν ἡ ἀνατολὴ... On the contrary, it is not absurd to suggest that in this very rite, they were imitating the Jews. For since the Christian Religion was chiefly propagated in the *Western Regions* relative to the land of *Canaan* <note>Israel/Palestine</note>, and the Jews of those regions were accustomed to face the **East** in their prayers, and to turn the back part of their Oratories toward the East, why should we not say that the Christians—whose churches were first founded by Jews—patterned themselves after their example and customs in this rite? And was it not from there that it became a practice for Christians to also place the back part of their Oratories in the *East*?

# CHAPTER 3. WITH SYNAGOGUES etc.

*For it has indeed now truly come to pass, as it truly is, that the glory of this house is the latter, greater than the former?* <note>original Greek: "γέγονε γὰρ καὶ νῦν ὡς ἀληθῶς ἐστὶν, ἡ δόξα τοῦ οἴκου τούτου ἐσχάτη ὑπὲρ τὴν προτέραν;" — This is a reference to the biblical prophecy in Haggai 2:9.</note> Thus, that heavenly prediction which I mentioned above no longer exists merely in bare words, but is seen fulfilled in the work itself. FOR THE GLORY OF THIS POSTERIOR HOUSE HAS NOW INDEED BECOME GREATER THAN THE PRIOR ONE. Therefore, the Author compares this new "Temple" of the Tyrians with the Old Temple, and even prefers it to that one. Indeed, it is from this point that the Oratories of the Christians began to be divided into three parts: the **Portico**, the **Holy Place**, and the **Holy of Holies**, so that they might appear more similar to the Temple at Jerusalem.

By the **Portico** (<term>pronaon</term> <note>original: "πρόναον" — the space in front of a temple</note> or <term>nartheka</term> <note>original: "νάρθηκα" — a narthex or vestibule</note>), you should understand the **Vestibule** of the Temple with its courtyards, colonnades, and porches. In this area, the Penitents of the second degree—who were called the "hearers"—and the Catechumens <note>Students preparing for baptism but not yet fully admitted to the community.</note> used to stay. Furthermore, Jews and Pagans (<term>those foreign to the faith</term> <note>original Greek: "οἱ ἀλλότριοι τῆς πίστεως"</note>) were also admitted into the vestibule, so that they might at least be witnesses to the external magnificence of the Christians.

By the **Holy Place**, you should understand the <term>naon</term> <note>original: "ναὸν"</note> or <term>naun</term> <note>original: "ναὺν" — meaning a ship, from which we get the English word "nave."</note>, the nave or the heart of the Temple, into which the faithful of all ranks and dignities were admitted; however, the places for standing and sitting were distinct for men and women.

By the **Holy of Holies**, however, was signified the Place which was destined for the Clergy (the Priests, or Presbyters and Deacons). It was separated from the nave of the Temple by railings and curtains, and was set higher. It was called the <term>Bema</term> <note>original: "Βῆμα" — a raised platform or rostrum</note> and <term>Hierateion</term> <note>original: "ἱερατεῖον" — the sanctuary or place of the priests</note> among the Greeks; among the Latins, it was called the **Presbytery**. Here the altar was placed; here likewise the thrones for the Bishop and the Presbyters were prepared, in which they sat together.

But this ultimately resulted in great evil for the Church of Christ. For even if at first a not-unpleasant spectacle was presented to the believers—because the wealth of the world and its most beautiful ornaments were eagerly offered and consecrated to Christ, in whom seemed to reside the proof that the world was subject to Christ and the Church—experience has nevertheless taught that through this pomp which was brought into the Church, men were led away from the *simplicity that is in Christ Jesus*, and their eyes, by the contemplation of these external and earthly things, were turned away from a deeper consideration of the hidden majesty and true splendor of the Kingdom of God. *Jerome*, indeed, although he [spoke/wrote] rather immoderately against *Vigilantius* <note>Vigilantius was a 4th-century priest who criticized the cult of martyrs and the use of luxury in churches; Jerome was his fierce opponent.</note> on behalf of the *Basilicas of the Apostles*, (for with this word more than once

# BOOK 2: ON THE FORM OF GOVERNMENT

...often disagree so much with one another that they are not easily reconciled. It is easy to note the causes of this disagreement. *First*, the constitution of the *Ancient Synagogue* itself is quite difficult to investigate. Second, the *form* of government of the *Christian Church* is fiercely disputed among *Christian Doctors* <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to learned theologians and scholars of the church.</note> themselves, a controversy that remains undecided to this day. 

As a result, according to the different hypothesis each person adopts regarding the *Government of the early Christian Church*, they also construct for themselves a corresponding image of the *Government of the Synagogue*. Since human judgment often varies even in the clearest of matters, let everyone reflect on how easily it can happen here that those who set the same goal for themselves nevertheless rush toward it by different paths. 

However, since our purpose is—despite this difficulty which might have rightly deterred us from this work—to modestly attempt what we can contribute to the clarification of this subject, it will be very necessary for us to define the MODE OF GOVERNMENT of both the SYNAGOGUE and the ANCIENT CHURCH before we descend to the comparison of *Individual Offices* <note>The specific roles or titles held by leaders, such as elders, deacons, or overseers.</note>. Since truth is drawn out from the disputes of scholars (conducted honestly for the sake of seeking truth alone) much like fire is struck from flint, it will be a pleasure first of all to weigh the opinions of certain learned men who have dealt with this matter before us in the scales of right judgment. We shall select or reject from them what seems to agree more or less with the truth, so that finally we may have the means—having thoroughly examined everything that seems relevant to the best of our ability—to conclude something certain about the constitution of both the *Synagogue* and the *Ancient Church*, and in this way proceed properly to the treatment of *Individual* matters. 

Since, however, *Hugo Grotius*, a man illustrious by his own merit, is (as far as I know) easily the leader among the learned who have adopted and illustrated the hypothesis regarding the similarity of the *Government of the Synagogue* and the *Church*, it will be a good deed to hear him speaking in the first place and to dwell a little on his words.

### The Opinion of GROTIUS on the Form [of the Church], Book 2. 470

There are some who are **Hazzanim** <note>Greek: Ἀζανῖται, a transliteration of the Hebrew *Hazzanim*, meaning overseers or attendants</note>, others **outside-deacons**, others **sub-deacons**, others **Doorkeepers** <note>Latin: *Janitores*</note>, others **acolytes** of the Bishops, others **readers**, and others **psalmodists** <note>singers of psalms</note>. Even *Jerome* <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin</note> says that reading in the Church is the duty of Deacons. In the *Tractate Sukkah* <note>Original: "Massecha Succa," a volume of the Talmud concerning the Festival of Booths</note> we read: **AND THE HAZZAN OF THE SYNAGOGUE STANDS TO READ FROM THE TORAH.** <note>Hebrew: וחזן הכנס עומד לקרוא בתורה</note> And THE MINISTER or **assistant** <note>Greek: ὑπηρέτης (*hypērētēs*)</note> STANDS TO RECITE FROM THE LAW. *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century bishop and counter-heresy writer</note>, in the section concerning the **Ebionites** <note>An early sect of Jewish Christians</note>, when discussing **Joseph**, the Apostle of the Jews—whose rank was next after the first of the **patriarchs** <note>Greek: τῶν πατριαρχῶν</note>—says that many were moved from their positions in the Synagogue by him; he lists the offices of the Synagogue as follows: *Many of those wrongly appointed as Rulers of the Synagogue, and priests, and elders, and Hazzanim (who are interpreted among them as deacons or ministers), being purified and moved from their dignity, were held back by many.* <note>Greek quote from Epiphanius</note>. He states clearly that those who were called **Hazzanim** <note>Hebrew: חזנים</note> by the Hebrews were called in Greek either **deacons** <note>Greek: διακόνους</note> or **ministers**. For these terms carry the same meaning.

<margin>Book II. chapter XXVIII.</margin>
In the *Constitutions of Clement* <note>An early Christian collection of ecclesiastical law</note>: *Let them signify what they wish through the ministers, that is, through the deacons.* <note>Greek: Διὰ τῶν ὑπηρετῶν ἂ βέλονται σημαινέτωσαν, τοῦτέστι διὰ τῶν διακόνων</note>. *Ignatius* <note>An early 2nd-century Bishop of Antioch</note> in his *Epistle to the Trallians*: *It is necessary that those who are deacons of the mysteries of Jesus Christ please all in every way. For they are not deacons of food or drink, but ministers of the Church of God.* <note>Greek quote</note>. For this reason also *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor who wrote to Emperor Trajan about the Christians</note> calls the Deacons of the Christian church **female ministers** <note>Latin: *ministras*; likely referring to deaconesses he interrogated</note>. *Cyprian*: **But after the Lord's ascension, the Apostles appointed Deacons for themselves as Ministers of their Episcopacy and of the Church.** And *Optatus of Milevis* in more than one place places **Ministers** between the Laity and Deacons, understanding them to be those who were called **sub-deacons** <note>Greek: ὑποδιάκονοι</note>. Canon XVIII of the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council of the Church in 325 AD</note>: *Let the Deacons remain within their own measures, knowing that they are ministers of the Bishop.* <note>Greek quote</note>. Just as men were scarcely ever chosen for the Council of Elders unless they were already advanced in both age and wisdom, so the **ministry** or **Diaconate** was almost always entrusted to young men. *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note>: *The young men among those in the community, having been selected as the best with all care, serve the liturgical needs.* <note>Greek quote</note>.

Thus far *Grotius*, whose discourse I wished to present in full, both so that his entire opinion might be more clearly perceived and more easily judged, and also so that it might be seen without effort what I and others, who have exercised ourselves in this **arena of debate** <note>Latin: *palæstra*; literally a wrestling school</note>, owe to *Grotius*. We see, moreover, that *Grotius* repeats here the hypothesis previously laid down, and recognizes in the Synagogue a **RULER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>Latin: *ARCHISYNAGOGUM*</note>, distinct from the **ELDERS**; besides these, however, he recognizes in the same Synagogue certain **MINISTERS**, called **Hazzanim**, and from these he derives the Deacons of the First Christian Church, bringing forward arguments and authorities by which he [supports] this, his opinion...

# Chapter I. Of the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church.

...to strengthen and fortify his opinion. We must yet say with whom Grotius compares the *Ruler of the Synagogue* and the *Elders of the Synagogue* in the Christian Church. For so far we have heard him advising nothing concerning them. <margin>Grotius on 1 Timothy 3:1.</margin> Attend, therefore, to what he writes in the *Epistle of Paul to Timothy*: "If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a good work." *Overseeing* <note>Greek: ἐπισκοπῆς (*episkopēs*); Hebrew: <term>פקדה</term> (*pequdah*)</note> signifies an inspection of any kind. <margin>Numbers 4:16, Psalm 109:8, Acts 20:28.</margin> The INSPECTORS or PREFECTS of the Church are the ELDERS <note>Latin: *Presbyteri*</note>, WHO IN THE SYNAGOGUE are likewise called **Elders** <note>Hebrew: <term>זקנים</term> (*zeqenim*) or <term>קשישים</term> (*qashishim*)</note> or **Administrators** <note>Hebrew: <term>פרנסים</term> (*parnasim*)</note>. THE CHIEF OF THESE later began to be called the BISHOP <note>Greek: ὁ ἐπίσκοπος (*ho episkopos*)</note> *par excellence* <note>Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχὴν</note>, *as in the so-called Apostolic Canons, in the letters attributed to Ignatius, in Tertullian, and others.* This is "the angel" <note>Greek: ὁ ἄγγελος (*ho angelos*)</note> in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>; elsewhere in Paul he is "the one who presides" <note>Greek: ὁ προεστὼς (*ho proestōs*)</note> or "the one laboring in the word"; and similarly in Justin Martyr he is "the president." In the same way, the one who was the Chief in the Synagogue was called the Ruler of the Synagogue <note>Greek: ὁ Ἀρχισυνάγωγος (*ho Archisynagōgos*) or ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς (*archōn tēs synagōgēs*)</note>, or the "president" <note>Greek: ὁ πρόεδρος (*ho proedros*)</note> in Philo’s writings; in Hebrew he is the <margin>On Matthew 9:18.</margin> **Head of the Congregation** <note>Hebrew: <term>ראש הקהל</term> (*Rosh Ha-Qahal*)</note> and in Syriac the **Head of the Assembly** <note>Syriac: <term>ריש כנישתא</term> (*Reish Kanishtha*)</note>. But here, as we have said, "overseeing" <note>Greek: ἐπισκοπὴ (*episkopē*)</note> is the honor of the Elder; here the Syriac is **eldership** <note>Syriac: <term>קשישותא</term> (*qashishuta*)</note>. It is certainly clear from these words that *Grotius compares the Ruler of the Synagogue with the Bishop, and the Elders of the Synagogue with the Elders of the Christian Church.* This, I say, seems sufficiently clear. 

Yet what of that obscure and ambiguous phrasing where, speaking of the Elders of the Christian Church, he says: "The Chief OF THESE LATER began to be called the Bishop *par excellence*." What does this "later" mean? Is it therefore the case, according to *Grotius's* hypothesis, that in the first institution of the Elders of the *Christian Church*, no *Chief of Elders* was appointed? Not at all. What *Grotius* means is that this Chief of Elders—whom he supposes was indeed chosen from the beginning along with the others in the ordering of the Church—only later began to be called the *Bishop*; he acknowledges that this name was previously common to both himself and the other Elders. That *Grotius* truly felt this way can be gathered without difficulty from other parts of his commentary. Thus he says expressly on the Epistle to the *Philippians*: <margin>On verse 1, chapter 1.</margin> THE ONE WHO HELD THE PRIMACY IN THE ORDER OF ELDERS was called, by way of excellence, the Bishop <note>Greek: ὁ Ἐπίσκοπος</note>. *From this it happened that this name remained his by a certain proper right, just as the name of* ELDERS <note>Latin: *Senum*</note> *[remained] for the Primates of the Bishops in Africa. Moreover, the Chief of this Philippian presbytery seems to have been Epaphroditus himself.* He says as much on the Epistle to *Titus*. <margin>On verse 5, chapter 1.</margin> Permit me to add one more passage to those now cited, in which he discusses this same argument in the same vein...

Even though Grotius seems to express his mind clearly enough in these passages, there is still something about which I hesitate. Specifically, a significant doubt has arisen for me: whether what he writes concerning the whole Body or College of Elders—whose President was called the **Head of the Congregation** <note>Hebrew: <term>ראש הקהל</term> (*rosh ha-qahal*)</note>—is intended to be understood as a *Homogeneous* Body or College, or rather as a College of men of different types and ranks. A University <note>Latin: *Academia*</note>, for example, is governed by a College of men of the same type, all of whom perform the duty of teaching in it, even if the primary care of business is entrusted to one of them under the title of **Rector**, acting as a President. Political and Judicial Senates among us usually consist of men of *one type and rank*, even though they are directed here and there by some President, whether permanent or temporary. Therefore, I call such groups of men *homogeneous*. 

But our churches at this time are governed by a *heterogeneous* College of men—namely, of a different rank and type, consisting of Pastors and Lay Elders; who, although they constitute one body, remain distinct in name, office, and dignity. Indeed, even today's Jewish Synagogues are governed by men of different types, specifically by a certain TEACHER called a **Rab** <note>Hebrew: <term>רב</term> (*rab*)</note>, (about whom more will follow), and **PASTORS** <note>Hebrew: <term>פרנסים</term> (*parnasim*)</note>. To the former is generally committed the management of sacred matters, while the latter are entrusted with the care of "those things lying outside the church" or the **Jewish Civil Administration** <note>original Greek/Latin: *Politia Judaica*</note>; yet these two groups sometimes join into one body and share counsel with each other. And it is required that the **Rab** be a **promoted Teacher** <note>A formally authorized scholar</note>, which is not required of the **Pastors** <note>Hebrew: <term>parnasim</term></note>. ### CHAPTER I. On the Government of the Synagogue and the Church.

<sig>Ooo 3</sig>

...of the Synagogue is heterogeneous. Now, if you consider the words of *Grotius* regarding the *Government of the Ancient Synagogue* by several Elders together with a President or Chief of the College, it appears entirely that those words should be understood as referring to a *homogeneous College*—that is, a Senate of Elders who are all of nearly the same kind. Nevertheless, when we pay attention to the phrases which *Grotius* used in his commentaries on this matter, the opposite might seem to be the case. 

For *Grotius* seems to have taken those expressions of his—concerning the one Leader of the Synagogue who is called <term>Rabbi</term> <note>original Hebrew: רבי (*Rabbi*); literally "my master," a title for a teacher of Torah</note> or **MASTER**, and concerning the other Directors who are called <term>Parnassim</term> <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים (*Parnassim*); literally "sustainers" or "providers," referring to those who managed the communal and financial affairs of the synagogue</note> or **PASTORS**—both from the writings of *Benjamin of Tudela* <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented the customs of Jewish communities across Europe, Africa, and Asia</note> and from the *Government of the modern Synagogue*. 

Yet, the synagogues over which *Benjamin* says individual <term>Rabbis</term> <note>original Hebrew: רבים (*Rabbis*)</note> or **MASTERS** were placed were certainly not ruled by a homogeneous College of Teachers and Directors, but by *One Master*, whether acting alone or joined with Elders of a different order. Similarly, modern Synagogues are governed by Directors of different orders and duties. 

It is possible, however, that *Grotius*, in using these names, looked more to their true original meaning than to the way they are used in the modern Synagogue. Therefore, so that we may proceed in these matters distinctly and with certainty, as is our purpose, we shall first lay this foundation: *Grotius's hypothesis* regarding the *Government of the Ancient Synagogue* as a model for the *Government of the Church* is by no means to be admitted, unless it is understood to refer to Elders of the same kind and rank—that is, a homogeneous College of Elders. This is because it can be certainly and unassailably demonstrated that the first Christian Churches everywhere were ruled by Elders of the same kind. We shall therefore provide proof for this point, since so much depends upon it, and then we will express our opinion more freely regarding the remaining part of the *Grotian* hypothesis.

# GROTIUS'S Opinion on the Form [of Church Government], BOOK 2.

...that [authority] was acknowledged neither by the Elders nor by the whole Church. 7. Following the example of those Apostles and Apostolic men <note>Men who were students of the original Apostles, such as Polycarp or Ignatius</note>, other *Presiding Elders* over time also sought greater dignity and authority; and so it happened that those *Presidents* were soon distinguished from common Elders by name and rank, and the *Episcopacy* <note>The office or system of government by bishops</note> was introduced into the Christian Church. Anyone who accepts these hypotheses with me regarding the *Form of Government* of the early Church will, on the *one hand*, satisfy the records of Holy Scripture—specifically the Acts and the Apostolic Epistles, where we are taught about the governance of the early Church—and, on the *other hand*, will easily perceive how the *Episcopacy* was received and established in the Church so shortly after the death of the Apostles, or perhaps even before the departure of some; a matter which is otherwise the subject of great labor when comparing these two things. 

But I must now specifically prove the *first* and *third* of these hypotheses; I will discuss the others more fully in their proper place later. And so, here two opinions stand in our way, against which we must argue. The *first* is that of those who believe that *Bishops* were already from the beginning set *over* the Elders by the Apostles with unique authority and dignity, being distinct from them in rank, order, and office—a view from which Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian who sought a middle ground in church politics</note> is not far removed. The *second* is that of those who believe the Elders of the early Christian Church were divided into *Teachers* and *Rulers*, such as our own *Lay Elders* <note>original: "de Plebe Presbyteri", literally "Elders from the common people," referring to the Reformed practice of having non-ordained members help govern the church</note>. 

Both groups (especially the latter) deny a *homogeneous Council of Elders* <note>A "homogeneous" council implies that all elders held the same basic rank and office, rather than being split into different classes</note>, by which we maintain the early Churches were governed everywhere. But since, as I have already noted, the *first* of these controversies has been extensively and learnedly debated by many learned men, I may spare myself unnecessary labor here and briefly and clearly present only the summary of the arguments in favor of our opinion. On the *second* question, I may be more long-winded.

<margin>Acts 20:17</margin>

Regarding this, the text says: *But sending from Miletus to Ephesus, he called for the elders...* <note>original Greek: "μετεκαλέσατο τοὺς πρεσβυ[τέρους]" (metekalesato tous presbyterous). The author cuts off the word at the end of the page.</note>

Those who are not distinguished by name, and who are likewise not distinguished by office—by what reasoning, then, should they be distinguished by rank? Peter addresses all the Elders together, those who were ordained as a group in whatever churches they were in. To all of them, he attributes the duty of *oversight* <note>original Latin: ἐπισκοπεῖν (episkopein), from which "Episcopus" or "Bishop" is derived</note> and *shepherding* <note>original Latin: ποιμαίνειν (poimainein)</note>. Therefore, all Elders are Bishops; all are Pastors. And no other reason can be given why Paul mentions only two orders 
<margin>1 Timothy 3:1-2.</margin>
of Church Offices; one of *Bishops*, and the other of Deacons. Under the name of *Bishops*, he includes the Elders; since no marked distinction had a place among them at that age in which he was writing, it is not surprising that he took no account of the distinct notions of these names which subsequently became established through usage. This same point is clear from the prologue of the Epistle to the Philippians. The words are: *Paul and Timothy, servants 
<margin>Philippians 1:1.</margin>
of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the* **BISHOPS AND DEACONS** <note>original Greek: σὺν ἐπισκόποις καὶ Διακόνοις (syn episkopois kai Diakonois)</note>.

There were, therefore, several Bishops at Philippi; and besides these, there were no other officials of the Philippian Church than the Deacons. Furthermore, since there is no reason to doubt that every church had its own Elders, it is clear enough that the Elders are hidden here under the name of *Bishops*. Indeed, I would think it more worthy of notice that Elders are included by Paul under the name of *Bishops* than that Bishops are included under the name of *Elders*. For since the name of "Elder" <term>Presbyter: a title of dignity or age</term> is one of honor and status, it would not seem so strange if persons of different office and rank were included under one and the same common word of honor; however, those who are designated not only by one name of *honor*, but also by one name of *office* <note>meaning "Bishop" or "Overseer"</note>, cannot be presumed to have been greatly distinguished from one another. 

We see, indeed, how harmoniously the whole Scripture of the New Testament, when considered in its various parts and passages, agrees in this: that the first Church was ruled by *several Elders*, men of one and the same name and office, without any notable distinction of status. ### Opinion of GROTIUS on the Form [of Church Government], BOOK 2.

...to act, setting aside prejudices and passions. How can we bring our minds to believe that neither *Luke* in the *Acts* nor *Paul* or the other Apostles in any of their *Epistles* would have made even the slightest mention of any *Chief of the Elders* <note>original Latin: Presbyterorum Principis</note>, if indeed such a *Principate* or dignity, or a specific duty, or a unique title for one of the Elders had been instituted and known in their time? For they frequently had to speak—and did speak—concerning the *Churches* and the *Governance of the Churches*. The fact that they write frequently about all other offices, but remain entirely silent about this office of *Episcopacy* <note>original Latin: Episcopatus; referring to the office of a Bishop as distinct from an Elder</note>, as it was later called, is proof to us that at that time no such name for a duty or rank was yet in use.

Nor is it necessary here to repeat the lengthy exceptions that the patrons of the opposing view produce here and there, whether regarding this or earlier testimonies; for in a matter so clear, those exceptions can have no value or weight. They only attempt to take the light of so many arguments—which shines more strongly when united—and scatter it into various parts, breaking its force and brilliance once divided. *Jerome* <note>original Latin: Hieronymus; a 4th-century scholar and Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin</note>, who was most deeply well-versed in the reading of the Scriptures, saw this truth. He was not afraid to frequently and boldly urge and insist upon it, even at a time when the *Episcopal* dignity had already grown to its highest peak.

Lest I call other witnesses again (of whom I could call very many, because this same question has been sufficiently discussed by learned men), I will remain in this same Letter of Jerome. "*Wherever there is a Bishop*," he says in the course of it, "*whether at Rome or at Gubbio; whether at Constantinople or at Reggio; whether at Alexandria or at Tanis: he is of the same merit and of the same Priesthood. The power of riches and the humility of poverty do not make a Bishop either more sublime or inferior. For they are all successors of the Apostles.*" Jerome means that one Bishop is not greater than another in authority; rather, all are equally to be considered successors of the Apostles. This was entirely the opinion of the Ancient Church. Therefore, whoever wonders how it happened that *one* of the Elders in time became a prelate over the rest—even though the Apostles established all Elders as *equals* in name and office—let him consider within himself how it happened that one *Bishop* [became superior] to many, indeed, at last *one* over all... <note>The author is drawing a parallel: just as the Bishop became superior to the Elders for the sake of order, eventually one Bishop (like the Pope) sought to become superior to all other Bishops.</note>

### Opinion of GROTIUS on the Form of Government, BOOK 2.

...that he should be placed above everyone else, which was certainly not ordained by Christ and the Apostles in this way. For all agree—at least those who are not being foolish—that the first Church of Christianity knew neither *Archbishops*, *Metropolitans*, nor *Patriarchs* <note>These are higher-ranking titles in church hierarchy that developed centuries after the Apostles.</note>. I will not discuss more regarding this *first inquiry*, lest I seem to want to "re-cook the same cabbage so many times" <note>original: "crambem toties coctam recoquere." An ancient proverb referring to a boring repetition of an old argument.</note>. I pass therefore to the *second inquiry*, which is of the greatest utility and importance to the present matter. Specifically, I believe that from the testimonies noted above, it can be concluded in good faith not only that there were no *Bishops* in the Early Church who were superior in rank to *Presbyters*, but also that no *Presbyters* were known in that same Church who were distinguished from other men of their own order by their specific duties. 

We notice, certainly, that the Churches of our own Homeland <note>Refers to the Dutch Reformed context of the author.</note> are governed by *Presbyters* of two kinds: *Teachers* <term>Docentes: ministers or clergy who preach</term>, as they are called, and *Rulers* <term>Regentes: lay elders who assist in governance</term>. By *Teachers*, we mean *Ministers of the Gospel*, to whom the care of proclaiming the Divine Word and administering the Sacraments is especially committed. By *Rulers*, we mean men of respected dignity, chosen from the body of the Church, who are joined to the *Ministers of the Gospel* so that they may participate with them in all the business of taking sacred counsel for the benefit of the Church. Yet these *Ruling Presbyters* are quite notably distinct from the *Teachers* in various ways. For they do not have the power of teaching or of administering the sacraments. Nor are they supported financially by the Church. Nor do they preside over the Church forever, but when they have served in this office for a certain defined time, they make way for other successors. This, I say, is the condition of the *Ruling Presbyters* among us, who are distinguished enough from the *Teachers* in their rank and duty. However, I personally believe that no such *Presbyters* existed in the Ancient Apostolic Church.

### Chapter 2. On the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church.

...to govern the flock with the spiritual power granted by Christ to His ministers. This position will stand, I believe, as long as there are those who read the *Acts of the Apostles* and their *Epistles* without partiality <note>original: "προσωποληψίᾳ" (prosōpolēmpsia), meaning favoritism or "respect of persons"</note>. For do we seriously dare to assert and defend that the name of *Bishops* or the name of *Pastors* applies to these *Lay Presbyters*? If we do not dare, then the case for them is surely closed, since no other *Presbyters* were recognized and established by the Apostles in the Church besides those who are simultaneously *Pastors* and *Bishops*.

And yet, whoever holds this hypothesis must either admit these *Lay Presbyters* to the order of *Bishops*, or establish that the Apostle Paul passed over them when listing the offices of the Church, even though he does so here carefully and by design. What kind of *Presbyters* did the churches have after the time of the Apostles (as far as can be judged from ancient records)? In what way and in what form were they governed? Certainly, nothing is more certain, nothing better established in all ancient history, than that the *Presbyters*, as distinct from the so-called *Bishop*, constituted the most distinguished part of the *Clergy*. They were considered like the *Bishop*, or, if you prefer, like the *Ministers of the Divine Word* of our own time, as being entirely consecrated to caring for the *Church*. They were not admitted into the *clergy*—that is, into the order of sacred persons—except with the intention that they should persevere in it for their whole life, renouncing all other worldly cares, duties, and dignities. They had the power of *teaching in the Church* and in other public and private places (for it was considered a singular and rare thing if this power were denied to a *Presbyter*). They likewise had the power of administering the sacraments: of anointing the baptized on the forehead with chrism <note>consecrated oil</note> in the absence of the *Bishop*; of presiding over the Lord’s Supper and distributing its symbols; and of reciting blessings and prayers as the custom in such cases required. From this, they were considered as *Priests* <note>original: "Sacerdotes"</note>, men of the same order as the *Bishop*, who was himself a *Priest*. They lived off the sacred offerings no less than the *Bishop*. Indeed, what

For it must be noted: 
1. That not one but various eloquent texts exist in the Apostolic Writings from which it is clear that the age of the Apostles did not recognize *Bishops* as distinct from *Presbyters*. When, however, in the subsequent Church after almost half a century had passed, we encounter *Bishops* distinct from *Presbyters*, no other reason remains for us to reconcile this later custom with the texts that show us the constitution of the Apostolic Church, than to say that *Bishops* were born—gradually and imperceptibly, as they say—after the death of the Apostles. This happened either by human counsel or even because, since they were the presidents of the *Senate of Presbyters* <note>original: "Senatus Presbyterorum," the council of elders</note>, they continued the use and exercise of this dignity in the *Church*. 

If the *equality* <note>original: "ἡ ἰσότης"</note> of the Presbyters of the primitive Christian Church could not be so clearly and eloquently established from the first and undoubted monuments of *Church History*, namely, the *Acts* and the *Apostolic Epistles*, we would altogether desist from that hypothesis. But since those records suggest the contrary, we had to see how we might conceive a certain middle opinion, through which both those very monuments of the early Church and the practice of the subsequent Church might be reconciled with each other. But since those *Lay Presbyters* are no more found in the *Apostolic* [Writings]...

...writings than are found in the Churches of the following times, it is clear that this exception falls apart on its own. **2.** It must be carefully noted that these two things being compared nevertheless differ greatly from one another. Surely, it is easily perceived from our hypotheses in what ways those called *Bishops*, even if none appeared in the Apostolic Churches, could have been born in the Churches within a short interval of time. But it is not easily perceived in what ways it could happen that *Lay Presbyters* <note>non-ordained elders who govern but do not preach</note>—if we suppose them to have been instituted by the Apostles—could have undergone such a massive change in the Church, so that after a short lapse of time they emerged as entirely different men than they had been not long before. 

For as to that *former* point <note>the rise of the office of Bishop</note>, reason and experience demand that we believe those Councils of Presbyters <note>original: "Senatus illos Presbyterorum"</note> in the early Church had their own *Presiding Officers* <note>original: "Praesides"</note>, although they were men of the same office and name. For how could a Council be assembled, questions and doubts be submitted for deliberation, votes requested, collections organized, and decisions put into execution without a *President*? Furthermore, the simplicity, piety, and prudence of that age together suggest we should believe that the Presbyters chose the most suitable man to be the President of their Council <note>original: "Synedrii"</note>—one who excelled among the others either in age, or in learning and spiritual gifts, or in civic dignity (the prestige he perhaps held before his profession of Christianity). Since the office of this President continued throughout his entire life, who would wonder that his authority and dignity soon received great increases above the others, until at last he began to be considered superior in *order* to the other Presbyters? 

Now, let those who defend the opposite opinion show us that *Lay Presbyters* could have been so easily transformed <note>original Greek: "μεταμορφῶσθαι" (metamorphōsthai)</note> into *Clerical Presbyters* <note>ordained ministers</note> as we have shown that *Bishops*, distinct from Presbyters, could have arisen in the Church, and we will admit the exception they produced above. We would not have needed so many words in this response if we had accepted the assertion of *Jerome* <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> that Bishops were introduced into the Church—specifically the Church of *Alexandria* since the time of *Mark the Evangelist*—by a singular decree *for the sake of avoiding Schism.* 

<margin>Letter to Evagrius, on this matter.</margin>

But it pleased us to be generous in this disputation, so that we might satisfy even the most fastidious readers. Let it now be permitted to draw this logical conclusion <note>original Greek: "σύναξιν" (synaxin)</note> from what has been said: If no Churches which directly <note>original Greek: "ἀμέσως" (amesōs)</note> succeeded the Apostolic ones acknowledged such *Presbyters from the common people* <note>lay elders</note> as are honored in our Churches today...

This is the simple, clear, and least ambiguous sense of **Paul's** words. ### CHAPTER 3. Of the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church.

...flourished in the office of *Pastors* in the early Church. I do not deny even that certain extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit persisted in the Christian Church until the times of *Cyprian* <note>Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus (c. 210–258 AD), the Bishop of Carthage.</note> and beyond. However, regarding this extraordinary gift <note>original Latin: *charismate*</note> of Teachers, the matter seems more doubtful to me. For truly, if that were the case, in our judgment there would exist in the ancient records not just a few obscure accounts, but many very clear testimonies of it. For the Church would certainly have sought refuge with these *Teachers* in many doubtful cases; it would have elevated them, as the most worthy, to the honor of <term>the episcopate <note>original Greek: *τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς* (tēs episkopēs), referring to the office or rank of a Bishop.</note></term>; and it would have honored them with every other kind of distinction. What shall we also say concerning the testimony of *Possidius* <note>A 5th-century bishop and biographer of St. Augustine.</note>, that in the African Churches no one among the Presbyters was accustomed to *preach* except the Bishop? That point is, I confess, recorded regarding the age of *Augustine*; however, it is presented in such a way that it extends to preceding times and is simply promoted as the most ancient custom of those Churches. Certainly, this testimony of *Possidius* carried such weight with the most learned <margin>Regarding the 3rd Sermon of Augustine.</margin> *Sirmond* <note>Jacques Sirmond (1559–1651), a French Jesuit scholar and expert on Church history.</note> that he granted it full credit.

Therefore, I would prefer (deferring to the judgment of those more skilled) to understand by these *Teaching Presbyters* certain *ordinary Teachers* from the number of the *Presbyters*; not indeed those who *preached* the *Gospel* publicly in the Church, but those who, either in their own houses or in any other places, by the permission of the Bishop, opened schools in which they interpreted the doctrines of the Christian religion, both for the members of their own *lower-order clergy* and for any other Christians engaged in more advanced studies. Concerning *Origen* <note>A prolific 3rd-century theologian from Alexandria.</note>, *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note> writes thus: <term>To one [Heraclas], he entrusted the primary introduction of those who were just being instructed in the basic elements; but for himself, he reserved the hearing of those in a state of proficiency <note>original Greek: *Τῷ μὲν τὴν πρώτην τῶν ἄρτι στοιχειουμένων εἰσαγωγὴν ἐπιτρέψας ; αὐτῷ δὲ τὴν τῶν ἐν ἕξ. φυλάξας ἀκρόασιν ;* from Ecclesiastical History 6.15.</note></term>. <margin>Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 15.</margin> Indeed, he [Origen] mandated to him (*Heraclas*, whom he had taken as a colleague in the teaching office) *the instruction of those who were still being imbued with the first rudiments; but* FOR HIMSELF HE RESERVED THE TEACHING OF THE MORE ADVANCED. Thus, Deacons or Sub-deacons may have been employed in training the <term>Catechumens <note>Individuals receiving basic instruction in Christianity before baptism.</note></term> (although it is certain that Presbyters often did not think even this duty beneath them), while the Presbyters applied their efforts to teaching the exercises of the faithful, or the clergy themselves—the Deacons, Readers, and Sub-deacons. Certainly, that *Bishops*, and by their permission Presbyters, devoted themselves to the instruction of others—much like those Teachers today who are put in charge of educating youth—is not, I think, a new thing in the History of the Ancient Church.

At the very least, who is unaware that there were open Schools in *Alexandria* in which certain so-called Teachers <note>The original Latin *Doctores* refers here to formal instructors or professors of theology rather than medical doctors.</note> explained the mysteries of the Christian Religion? *Jerome* (who transcribed these accounts from *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History."</note>, and is cited here for the sake of brevity) had said regarding *Pantænus* that, *according to a certain ancient custom in Alexandria, from the time of Mark the Evangelist, there were always* ECCLESIASTICAL TEACHERS. Paul wants more stipend, subsidy, or nourishment to be granted to the Presbyters of the Church than to the widows, both because their families are more burdensome and because they deserve more on account of their labor. Paul does not divide external honor or veneration between Presbyters and widows. Therefore, we rightly conclude without any ambiguity that if *Paul* treats here of such *Presbyters* whom he wishes to be sustained by the Church, it follows that he in no way refers in these words to *Lay Presbyters*, such as our churches have received. This cannot be said of *our Lay Presbyters*, as is well known. He **PRESIDES**, therefore, and he ought to carry this through here as well, with diligence and by no means sluggishly. He [Theophylact] now continues: <note>original Greek: Προΐστασθαι δέ ἐστι... — The author is quoting Theophylact of Ohrid, an 11th-century archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> **TO PRESIDE, MOREOVER, IS TO HELP BOTH THROUGH WORDS AND THROUGH ONE’S OWN BODY THE ONE WHO STANDS IN NEED OF ASSISTANCE. Romans 1:11.
Ephesians 4:28.
1 Thessalonians 2:8.
</margin>

The same is also found in the *Second Book of Maccabees*. <note>original: "μεταδιδόναι" (metadidónai) — to give a share or distribute.</note> Therefore, when "to distribute" is used so very familiarly with this meaning, it seems we should not rashly depart from it. It has already been observed by the most learned men, and not overlooked by *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch prodigy and foundational figure in international law and biblical hermeneutics.</note>, that *Paul’s* use of this word is singular and emphatic, carrying the meaning of liberality in giving alms. <margin>2 Corinthians 8:2, 9:11, 13</margin> In this sense, it occurs once and again in *Paul’s* *Second Letter to the Corinthians*. The Belgians <note>Referring to the Dutch "Statenvertaling" or contemporary Dutch translations.</note> translate it: **Benevolence**. <margin>James 1:5</margin> *James* likewise approves of this use of the word where he says of *God* that he gives to all **SIMPLY** <note>original: "ἁπλῶς" (haplōs)</note>, or "liberally." The Belgians have: **generously**. Indeed, there is great elegance in this meaning. There is no other cause for liberality pleasing to *God* than pure and <gloss>unfeigned</gloss> *love of God and brothers*. Where there is charity and <gloss>unfeigned faith</gloss> <note>original: "πίστις ἀνυπόκριτος" (pistis anypokritos)</note>—a faith that is pure, candid, and simple—there one will find a liberal mind. Conversely, when someone communicates his gifts to the needy sparingly and with a tight hand, it arises <gloss>from hypocrisy</gloss> <note>original: "ἐξ ὑποκρίσεως" (ex hypokriseōs)</note>, which is the opposite of **simplicity**. In hypocrisy, there is a double will of giving and not giving. The man fights with himself over whether he wants to give or not; he debates within himself how much he ought to *give* to his brother, but how much he should *retain* for himself. He is eventually led by fleshly reasons to help his needy brother, yet in such a way that he does not expend as much as he ought; and even that which he does expend, he would rather retain for himself than impart to his brother, if the laws of external decency would allow it. I do not doubt, along with the <term>Famous Cocceius</term> <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology" and expertise in Hebrew.</note>, that *Paul* sought to temper this use of the Greek word to a similar way of speaking found in the Scriptures of the Old Testament. <margin>1 Chronicles 29:9</margin> For at the *end of the First Book of Chronicles*, the liberality of the leaders and the Jewish people, exercised in building the Temple, is described in the same style: *And the people rejoiced over their liberal* (or their?) *offering*; <note>original Hebrew: "כִּי בְלֵב שָׁלֵם הִתְנַדְּבוּ לַיהוָה" — For with a whole heart they offered willingly to the LORD.</note> **FOR WITH A WHOLE HEART** (which you might translate as; *in simplicity of heart*) **THEY CONTRIBUTED MUNIFICENTLY TO THE LORD**. From these things, I think it will be manifest to anyone that "simplicity" pertains to those who expend something of *their own* for the use of *God* and the *Church*. But if it is proved that by "the one who distributes" we are not to understand the <term>Deacons of the Church</term> <note>Official administrators of church charity; the author argues Paul is referring to private donors here instead.</note>, but any of the wealthier faithful who relieve the poverty of the *Church* with their own resources,

### Chapter 3. Governance of the Synagogue and the Church.

...we will have made much progress in the true understanding of this passage. Indeed, two things then become certain. First, it will be established that *the Apostle Paul*—despite what the authors of the opposing view use as the foundation for their hypothesis—is not here listing those kinds of <term>charismata</term> <note>Spiritual gifts or divine endowments.</note> or gifts of the Holy Spirit that pertain to the formal governance of the Church. Rather, he refers to any gifts whatsoever in which even the ordinary, rank-and-file faithful participated. Every kind of gift, I say, is enumerated here by *the Apostle Paul*, as much those that apply to *teachers* as to *students*, and those that suit the *leaders* as well as the other members of the Church. This is further confirmed by the final words of this <margin>Verse 8.</margin> sentence: **THE ONE WHO SHOWS MERCY, WITH CHEERFULNESS.** <note>original: "ὁ ἐλεῶν ἐν ἱλαρότητι" (ho eleōn en hilarotēti)</note> For whatever the authors of the opposing opinion may claim, it is simply not possible that "the one showing mercy" describes a specific class of Church officials.

Second, if the exposition we have provided is accepted, then it is highly probable that by **THE ONE WHO PRESIDES** <note>original: "τὸν προϊστάμενον" (ton proistamenon) — often translated as "the leader" or "the one who rules."</note> we should not understand the Elders of the Church. For who would believe that *the Apostle Paul* would observe so little order in listing the gifts of the Holy Spirit that, right after speaking of the gift of *liberality* in giving alms, he would suddenly begin speaking about the gift of governing the entire Church? Here, "the one who presides" is placed in the middle, between **THE DISTRIBUTING BELIEVER** <note>original: "τὸν μεταδιδόντα" (ton metadidonta)</note> (the wealthy man who pays out something of *his own* to the poor) and **THE ONE SHOWING MERCY** (who offers singular help and aid to the wretched according to his ability). Therefore, it is entirely fitting that we believe "the one who presides" designates someone with a similar kind of <term>giftedness</term> <note>original: "κεχαρισμένον" (kecharismenon) — one who has received a 'charisma' or grace.</note>.

Otherwise, what order or connection would there be in *Paul's* discourse? Why would the gift of Church *governance* be placed in the middle, between the gift of *liberality* and that of *commiseration*? For this reason, I gladly align myself with the opinion of *Theophylact* <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107) was a prominent Byzantine archbishop and biblical interpreter.</note>, that "the one who presides" designates those members of the Church who are present for and *in charge of* caring for the poor and needy, whether in their own name or the Church's. Only one thing is required to confirm this interpretation: we must prove that the word "presiding" can be conveniently explained in this sense. And here, indeed, I do not <margin>1 Thessalonians 5:12</margin> deny that the notion of "presiding" is used once by *Paul* to refer to the *Leaders* of the Church. However, the word "patroness" <note>original: "προστάτις" (prostatis) — the feminine form of the word for leader/president.</note>, which is of the same origin and meaning, differing only in *gender*, is used by our *Paul* in this very same *Epistle* in the sense we are <margin>Romans 16:2</margin> urging. "I commend to you," he says, "Phoebe our sister, **A SERVANT OF THE CHURCH AT CENCHREAE**." <note>original: "Διάκονον τῆς Ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἐν Κεγχρεαῖς" (Diakonon tēs Ekklēsias tēs en Kenchreais)</note>

### The Opinion of GROTIUS on the Form [of the Church], Book 2.

<margin>Commentary on this passage.</margin>
*“That you may receive her in the Lord, in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her in whatever business she has need of you, for she herself has been a* **PATRONESS** *of many, and of myself also.”* <note>original: "Ut eam excipiatis in Domino... καὶ γὰρ αὐτὴ προστάτις πολλῶν ἐγενήθη..." — Romans 16:2.</note> Beza translates this as: *For she has provided* **HOSPITALITY** *to many, and to me myself.* The Dutch translation uses: *A Patroness.* <note>original: "Een Voorstandster."</note> Therefore, in the judgment of these excellent interpreters, the word *prostatis* <note>A female patron or protector.</note> denotes here a woman who followed many acts of charity toward both Paul and other holy men. Let us hear Beza: *“It should be known that those called* **PROSTATAI** <note>Plural of prostates; a patron or protector.</note> *by a specific name were also called* **PROXENOI** <note>Official hosts for foreigners.</note>; *that is, those who were chosen by a city to receive guests and strangers into their home and into their protection. According to Eustathius, this signifies the 'leadership of strangers'.”* Thus, the Apostle signifies that the home of this Phoebe—a servant of the Church of Cenchreae—was open to traveling brothers as if it were a public hostel for the saints; these are the very virtues he requires in a widow.

Certainly, the term "the one presiding" <note>original: "ὁ προϊστάμενος" (ho proistamenos)</note>, by the force of the word and its origin, is the same as "a patron" <note>original: "προστάτης" (prostates)</note>. Therefore, I am entirely persuaded that Paul, in this text, understood by "the one who presides" those people who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, were led to offer and provide help to the needy and afflicted with singular love, care, and prudence. I consider this to be the genuine sense of this text; I was led to choose this interpretation not by necessity, but by reason.

For even if I were to concede that "the one presiding" in this passage should be understood as the **Governors of the Church**, who could then conclude from this that "Lay Elders" <note>Presbyteros Laicos: A term for elders who govern but do not preach/teach.</note> exist? You could only conclude that there are Elders who, above others, have received a singular **gift** from the Holy Spirit for prudently ruling and caring for the Church. Just as there were Elders who—during that singular <term>oikonomia</term> <note>The "economy" or divine administration of the early church's spiritual gifts.</note> of the abundant distribution of the various gifts of the Holy Spirit—were more fit for teaching, and others more suitable for exhorting, convicting, rebuking, and comforting, so too were there those better prepared by the Holy Spirit for governing the Church and offering help in various cases.

Each of the Elders contributed his own **gift** for the benefit of the Church. Yet, there was only one **order**, one **condition**, and one and the same **office**; the care and the counsel of these Elders were shared in common. If, indeed, a new order of "Presiding Elders" <note>original: "Presbyterorum προϊσταμένων" (Presbyterorum proistamenōn).</note> must be produced from these words, why should we not also invent other orders of Elders, such as "Exhorting Elders" as well as "Teaching Elders"? Therefore, let us hold to this: there was one order of Elders in the Early Church, upon whom in general it was incumbent...

### CHAPTER 3. On the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church.

...was bound to nourish the Church. To this end, each person contributed his own gift. One was more suited to teaching, another to exhortation. Another, in turn, was more capable in care and counsel. Yet all had the same right of teaching, exhorting, governing, and performing the other duties of Pastors. I recognize the Elders <note>original: *Presbyteros*</note> of the Early Church to be such men; and as for the person who understands the "leaders" <note>original: *προϊσταμένους* (proistamenous)</note> in this text in his own way, let him enjoy his own opinion, which is by no means contrary to mine, even if the former explanation is more pleasing to me.

<margin>Chapter 12, verse 28.</margin>
Let us see in the last place whether there is more support for this opinion in certain other words of Paul, which are read in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:
> *And indeed God has appointed some in the Church, first* **Apostles**, *second* **Prophets**, *third* **Teachers**; *then miracles, then gifts of healing, helps,* **Governments** <note>original: *κυβερνήσεις* (kyberneseis)</note>, *various kinds of tongues.*

Here again, very learned men believe that by "governments" Paul designated his "ruling elders" from the common people. We wish the following points to be weighed: 1. *The Apostle Paul is dealing here with the gifts of the Holy Spirit* <note>original: *χαρίσμασι* (charismata)</note> *and not with the ordinary offices of the Church, as is evident from the entire context of Paul's discourse. Indeed, he himself describes them as "gifts" in verse 31. To perform miracles* <note>original: *virtutes*</note>, *to heal the sick, to speak in various tongues, to predict the future, or to explain prophecies about future events, ought not to be considered ordinary offices of the Church, but extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit.* But you might say: are not the Apostleship and the office of Teacher <note>original: *Doctoratus*</note> functions of the Church? I grant, certainly, that the Apostleship and the office of Teacher—if you consider these words outside the circumstances of this text—can just as easily be called offices of the Church as gifts of the Holy Spirit; nevertheless, as they occur here, it is most certain that these names are placed by Paul more for the gifts than for the offices. When Paul says in this place that God "gave some to be Apostles," he means this: that God equipped certain men with such gifts as were required for the Apostleship, a most weighty duty. Again, when he says that God "gave some to be Teachers," he means to say that the Holy Spirit conferred on certain faithful people the fitness for teaching, just as he gave to others the power of publishing or explaining prophecies, to others the knowledge of tongues, and to others other things. Paul deals primarily with gifts, not with offices. Therefore, since the same Paul proclaims here that God has placed "governments" <note>original: *κυβερνήσεις* (kyberneseis)</note>, this (assuming for now that the word "government" here refers to the governance of the Church, such as that of the Elders) can be understood to mean that God...

# Opinion of GROTIUS on the Form, BOOK 2.

...the Spirit has bestowed this grace upon certain members of the Church, so that they might excel in prudence, counsel, and care for governing the Church. This will be the simple meaning of Paul, if one assumes, I mean to say, that the term *governance* <note>original: *κυϐερνησις* (kybernēsis)</note> is to be understood here as the administration of the Church. From this, no one can correctly conclude that there are ordinary Elders <note>original: *Presbyteros*</note> from the common people <note>that is, "lay elders" who do not preach</note> in the Church to whom the government of the Church is committed without the power of teaching and exhorting; this is because an argument drawn from the extraordinary graces of the Holy Spirit to the ordinary offices of the Church is not valid. 

The matter truly stood thus, as we have already often declared. The office of the Elders was once the same; marked by the same honors, and burdened by the same duties, if you consider the office in itself. However, as God worked in various ways by His Spirit in the early Church, He distributed various gifts to these same Elders. This one He furnished with the gift of teaching; on others He bestowed the virtues of exhorting, consoling, disputing, healing, and performing miracles, as well as the gifts of tongues; to others again He conferred the grace of *governance* <note>original: *κυϐερνησεως* (kybernēseōs)</note>, for which prudence and counsel are required. 

Each of the Elders—indeed, every member of the Church—employed these gifts of theirs for the benefit of the believers of the whole Church. If anyone, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, excelled in the gift of teaching and exhorting, he, having been chosen into the order of Elders, applied this gift of his to the building up of the Church; if someone else excelled in prudence and counsel, he was applied to the governing and caring for the Church. Moreover, that one should excel another was not due to the office—which was the same for all—but to the singular grace of the Holy Spirit, which was more illustriously visible in one than in another. 

2. It is doubtful and uncertain—perhaps more than anything else—whether Paul intends here to designate the governance of the Church by the word *governance*. Truly, Paul, in listing the *spiritual gifts* <note>original: *χαρισμασι* (charismata)</note> of the Holy Spirit, follows this order: descending from the greater and more excellent gifts to the lesser. The most excellent and first of all *gifts* was the grace of the Apostolate. The last and weakest of all was *kinds of tongues* <note>original: *γένη γλωσσῶν* (genē glōssōn)</note>, that is, the ability to express the feelings of one's mind in various languages. Paul emphasizes this point more because there were those in the Corinthian Church who were quite proud of this gift. Now it must be considered:

1. <note>original: the Hebrew letter Aleph (א) used as a list marker</note> Paul places this gift of *governance* in the penultimate <note>second to last</note> place in his list of various *spiritual gifts*. Yet truly, the gift of governing the Church ought to be considered among the greatest and most excellent gifts of the Spirit...
