### CHAPTER 3. On the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church.

...of the Holy Spirit. For to govern the Church there is need of wisdom <note>original: *σοφίᾳ* (sophia)</note> and prudence <note>original: *φρονήσει* (phronēsei)</note>, foresight, and counsel. Wisdom and prudence, just as they are the highest perfections of man, so at the same time they must be held as the most excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, Paul by the term "governance" <note>original: *τὴν κυβέρνησιν* (tēn kybernēsin)</note> had designated the gift of governing the Church, it seems he would have given it a more honorable place among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are recounted here by him in a distinct order. 

**2.** Paul places this gift of governance <note>original: *κυβερνήσεως* (kybernēseōs)</note> after the gift of "helps" <note>original: *ἀντιλήψεως* (antilypseōs)</note> in this list of his. "Helps," according to the mind of those interpreters against whom we are now disputing, denotes either the gift or the office of caring for and relieving the poor. Through these "helps," therefore, according to their hypothesis, the Deacons are to be understood. But since the office or gift of governing the Church is much more excellent than the gift or office of caring for the poor and providing them with help and assistance, it seems improper to understand the gift or office of governing the Church by "governance" here; for it is well established that Paul lists the gifts of the Spirit in this place in such an order that he places the more excellent ones before those that are less excellent. For this reason, other practiced interpreters of Scripture have moved away from this meaning of the word and have interpreted it far differently. Theophylact <note>A 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and influential Bible commentator.</note>, whose work we have just used not without profit, writes as follows:

> *Helps, governances* <note>original: *Ἀντιλήψεις, κυβερνήσεις* (Antilypseis, kybernēseis)</note>] *That is, the supporting of the weak, and the governing—that is, the managing—of the affairs of the brothers. For although these tasks belong to our own diligence, he says they are nonetheless gifts of God, persuading us to be grateful and to look toward Him and not to be puffed up.*

Therefore, "governance" in the view of Theophylact is the same as "ruling" <note>original: *πρόστασις* (prostasis)</note> in the Epistle to the Romans. If this interpretation of Theophylact finds a place, then the Apostle’s discourse will be consistent with itself. Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Hebraist known for using Talmudic literature to explain the New Testament.</note>, who himself exercised his talent here, understood "helps" to mean the companions of the Apostles, who were an assistance to them in baptizing believers, and, as he says, *were sent by them here and there to places which they themselves, occupied with other matters, could not reach.* He attempted, however, to explain the word "governance" from the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translators, who <margin>Proverbs 1:5; 11:14.</margin> are accustomed to translate the Hebrew word *tachbulot* <note>original: *תחבלות* — meaning "steering," "guidance," or "wise counsel."</note> through this Greek term,

# Grotius’s Opinion on the Form, Book 2

...which the Hebrew word *tachbulot* <gloss>notes as profound skill</gloss> <note>original: תחבולות. This Hebrew term refers to "guidance" or "wise counsel," often used in the context of steering a ship, which correlates to the Greek *kybernesis*.</note>. However, Lightfoot <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), an English churchman and Rabbinic scholar.</note> estimates that the Apostle, through this word "governance" <note>original: *κυβερνήσεως* (kybernēseōs)</note>, wished to designate that *gift* which he elsewhere calls the "discernment of spirits" <note>original: *διάκρισιν πνευμάτων* (diakrisin pneumatōn)</note>; for this gift requires skill, sagacity, and a sharpness of wit and judgment. Indeed, that Most Learned Man <margin>verses 8, 9, 10.</margin> thinks that the gifts of the *Holy Spirit* which *Paul* had recounted at the beginning of this same chapter should be compared in order with those he recounts in the words just described. If this comparison is established, the *gift* of the "discernment of spirits," mentioned there, will correspond to the *gift* of "governance," which occurs in this latest *list*.

Truly, that hypothesis has not been proven to us so far, because according to it, the *gift* of "prophecy" <note>original: *προφητείας* (prophēteias)</note> would have to be matched with the *gift* of "helps" <note>original: *ἀντιλήψεως* (antilypseōs)</note>; which, even if *Lightfoot* attempted it in some way, is not admitted by us. *Paul* indeed recounts *gifts* of the same kind at the beginning of this *chapter* as those he mentions at the *end*, and which therefore can and should be compared with one another; and yet it is not clear enough that *Paul* enumerates these *gifts* in the former place in precisely the same order as in the latter. In this latter list, he observes a most accurate order, as is evident from the particles "first," "second," "third" <note>original: *πρῶτον, δεύτερον, τρίτον*</note>. In the former list, however, he clearly does not neglect order; yet he is not as observant and studious of *it* as he is in this latter place.

But neither do we agree with Lightfoot that by "helps" <note>original: *ἀντιλήψεις* (antilēpseis)</note> in this text we should understand the *ministers of the Apostles*. It is not an absurd opinion, I confess. It is also certain that the Apostles everywhere had such ministers at hand. I think, however, there is something else that can be produced with greater evidence for a genuine explanation of this word. *Paul*, after he had recounted the gifts of the Holy Spirit in this latter place, soon repeats them in the *immediately following verses*; except that instead of the *eight* gifts he had numbered, he repeats *seven*; *perhaps with one repeated gift encompassing two* previously listed, or otherwise. So that the whole matter may become clearer, we represent them in a table as they are set against each other:

| Some indeed he placed <note>original: *Οὓς μὲν ἔθετο*</note> | vs. 29. Are all... <note>original: *Μὴ πάντες*</note> |
| First, Apostles. | ...Apostles? |
| Second, Prophets. | ...Prophets? |

From this diagram it is clear that the individual gifts listed in verse 28 are repeated by their own names, except for those of "helps" and "governments"; in place of those two, the gift of "interpretation" <note>original: *διερμηνείας* (diermēneias)</note> is substituted. However, the gifts or *offices* of "helps" and "governments" are distinct if you attend to the meanings of the *words*; nor do they seem capable of being explained by a single common *name*. It must therefore be said—for I do not see how this difficulty could be resolved by any other more convenient reasoning—that *Paul*, in this repeated *enumeration*, omitted one of those two mentioned *gifts*, and substituted the word "interpretation" for only *one* of them. 

Now, this gift of "interpretation" <note>original: *τῆς ἐρμηνείας* (tēs hermēneias)</note> will be much more appropriately referred to the gift of "helps" <note>original: *ἀντιλήψεως* (antilypseōs)</note> than to that of "governments" <note>original: *κυβερνήσεως* (kybernēseōs)</note>. For certainly those who *interpreted tongues* in the Church were an *aid* both to the Church and especially to those members or leaders of the Church who spoke in an *unknown language*; and therefore, by the highest right and most suitable expression, they are called "helps" <note>original: *ἀντιλήψεις* (antilypseis)</note> or *assistances*. Let "helps," therefore, no longer be regarded as referring to *Deacons*, but rather to *Interpreters of foreign languages*. 

Now we must come to the gift of "governments" <note>original: *κυβερνήσεως* (kybernēseōs)</note>. I have said that in this repeated list it seems to have been omitted by the Apostle, which makes it more difficult to explain. However, all things being rightly weighed, I affirm that <term>Lightfoot</term> <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English scholar of Rabbinic literature and the New Testament.</note> hit the nail on the head by comparing it with the gift of the "discernment of spirits" <note>original: *διακρίσεως τῶν πνευμάτων* (diakriseōs tōn pneumatōn)</note>, <margin>verse 9.</margin> which had been explicitly mentioned by *Paul* in the *first enumeration*. For even if we were to reject that part of the *Lightfootian* hypothesis—that *Paul* repeats the various gifts of the Holy Spirit in the final part of this *Chapter* in the same order *in which* he had listed them at the beginning—we nevertheless do not deny that he repeats those same types of gifts, though the order is changed in some. 

Reasoning favors this opinion. Since the notion of "governments" <note>original: *κυβερνήσεως* (kybernēseōs)</note> in the New Testament Scripture is so unusual that it is found only in this text, it is certainly safest to return to the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>original: *LXX Interpretes*. The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament, which the New Testament authors frequently used as their primary reference.</note> and from there retrieve its true meaning. <margin>
On the Rights of the Common People in Church Government.
</margin>

It remains for us to say a word to untie the knot tied by the ecclesiastical writers of the earliest times in favor of these "Lay Elders." To be sure, very learned men—among them **Blondel** <note>David Blondel (1591–1655), a French Protestant scholar who wrote extensively on church hierarchy.</note> in his published treatise on this argument—have observed that in the ancient monuments of the early Church, certain **Elders of the Churches** <note>original: *Ecclesiarum Seniores*</note> are mentioned who are distinct from the clergy; they contend that these can be compared to the Lay Elders of our own times.

<margin>

</margin>

For example: *“You Bishops, ELDERS, Deacons, and SENIORS, know about the four hundred bags of Lucella.”* Again: *“To the Clergy and SENIORS of the people of Cirta, eternal salvation in the Lord.”* Augustine uses a similar style in his letters: *“To the Clergy and SENIORS of the Church of Hippo.”* We omit other examples cited by other authors. Our response will be brief and clear.

1. We acknowledge that in certain ancient churches, this most praiseworthy custom prevailed, so that Bishops and Elders, in matters of weightier importance, did not neglect to employ the opinions and advice of respected men from among the common people. This is clear from the testimonies commonly produced on this matter. 

2. We concede that by this custom of certain ancient churches, the institution of **Lay Elders** <note>original: *Presbyterorum Laicorum*</note>, such as those received into our churches, is in some way proven and confirmed. For the fact that **Seniors are heard in doubtful cases**, and that testimony of actions is sought from them...

<header>Chapter 3. On the Governance of the Synagogue and Church.</header>

<margin>History, book 1, chapter 32.</margin>
That **those older by birth** <note>original: *majores natu*</note>, whose judgment is strengthened by experience, are consulted about more serious business—as is found in the song of **proclamation** <note>original: *indictionis*; likely referring to a formal declaration or ritual formula</note> in **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note>—cannot but be considered a fair and useful practice. But the hinge on which the matter turns is this: while there is no mention of such **Seniors** in **Scripture** (upon which the disagreeing parties will easily agree in this case), they were nonetheless in every way and manner most distinct from our **Lay Elders**. 1. These **Seniors**, specifically so-called among the Ancients, did not form part of the **clergy**—that is, the ecclesiastical order—but of the **people** <note>original: *plebs*, referring to the lay congregation</note>. They were not with the **Clergy**—that is, the **Bishops**, **Presbyters**, and **Deacons**—in the **presbyteries** <note>the councils of elders</note>, in the choir, or in the Councils, but remained with and among the people, and constituted a part of them, albeit a respected and distinguished one. 2. These **Seniors** are placed after **Deacons** for that reason, as is evident from the testimonies we have noted. 3. For this reason, the Ancients also took care that they were not called **PRESBYTERS** <note>original: πρεσβύτεροι (*presbyteroi*)</note>, lest anyone through ignorance should confuse them with the **Presbyters of the Church** mentioned in Scripture; instead, they were called **SENIORS** and **elders** <note>original: γέροντες (*gerontes*)</note>.

<margin>In the Code of Canons of the African Church, canon 100. See Forbes in the cited place.</margin>
4. The **Care of the Church** was not entrusted to them; indeed, it was no more their duty than that of any other member of the Church to admonish, exhort, or instruct the **people**, if not publicly, then at least **privately**. They had no part in excommunicating sinners or admitting penitents. To put it in a word: they were not part of the **Ecclesiastical Senate** <note>The author uses this term to describe the governing body of the church</note> to which the care and ministry of the Church were entrusted.

<margin>“And we have in the Church our own Senate, the assembly of Elders.” Jerome, Commentary on Isaiah, Book 2, on Chapter 3.</margin>
They were a respected part of the people, remote and distinct from the Clergy and its **Senate**, and performing no duties of the clergy or ecclesiastical ministry. This happened, I say—which reason teaches to be fair and good—so that the **Bishops** and **Presbyters of the Church** did not neglect to employ the counsel, aid, and testimony of these **Seniors** or distinguished men **from the people** <note>original: *de plebe*</note> in certain cases. Truly, in that ancient age of the Church, when there was greater integrity of mind, more ardent charity, and less ambition, a much greater commerce flourished between the **Clergy** and the **People** than afterwards. Therefore, lest anyone further confuse these **Seniors** with the **Apostolic Presbyters**, I will say in a single word: they were not **overseers** or **Rulers** of the **CHURCH**, but **SENIORS OF THE PEOPLE**. Be careful, therefore, not to believe that there is any mention of such **Seniors of the people** in the [writings] of the **Apostles**...

Written under the name of **Elders and the Church** <note>original Greek: Πρεσβυτέρων & Ἐκκλησίας; Latin: Presbyterorum Ecclesiæ</note>. ### CHAPTER IV.

#### *Grotius's hypothesis concerning the governance of the Synagogue and the Church is examined against the truths already proven; the extent to which it should be accepted or rejected is defined.*

The conclusion of our entire preceding dispute is this: that the Apostolic Churches were rightly governed by **Elders** of the same Order and Office. Regarding **Deacons**, there has been no dispute. If this conclusion is built upon solid principles, then we shall have at least one certain rule of judgment. By this rule, we can determine what truth or falsehood exists in the "Grotian hypothesis" <note>Referring to the theories of Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational figure in international law and theology who compared Christian church structure to Jewish synagogue models.</note> regarding the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church, as well as in the hypotheses of other learned men to be reviewed later. Therefore, let us now address this and discuss what in Grotius's work is more pleasing and what is less so.

*First, it seems doubtful and uncertain to me whether Grotius—in establishing the comparison between the governance of the Synagogue and the Church, and specifically in describing the governance of the Synagogue by drawing from **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler whose accounts provided Christians with information on Jewish communal life.</note> and more recent customs—is correct in frequently applying the terms **Leaders** <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים, *Parnasīm*, meaning community administrators or providers</note> and **Master** <note>original Hebrew: רב, *Rav*, or Rabbi</note> to those...*

I have already noted that the *Synagogues* of the present day are presided over everywhere by a certain *Prefect of the Synagogue*, known by the title <term>רב</term> **Master** <note>original Hebrew: *Rav*; the title for a Rabbi</note>, <term>מורנו</term> **Our Teacher** <note>original Hebrew: *Morenu*; a high-ranking honorific for a scholar</note>, or <term>חכם</term> **Sage** <note>original Hebrew: *Chakam*; often used by Sephardic communities for their religious leaders</note>. Besides him, however, there are certain prominent *Prefects* in the Synagogue called <term>פרנסים</term> **Pastors** <note>original Hebrew: *Parnasîm*; community leaders responsible for administrative and charitable needs</note>, <term>ממונים</term> **Overseers** <note>original Hebrew: *Memunîm*; officials or appointees</note>, or <term>זקנים</term> **Elders** <note>original Hebrew: *Zekenîm*</note>. These men lead and *rule* the Synagogue assembly of each place or nation with both their influence and power; they manage its interests before the *Magistrate* to whom they are subject, and they conduct the *public affairs* of the Jews like certain *consuls* and *praetors* <note>The author uses these Roman political titles to explain the civic and administrative roles of these Jewish leaders</note>. 

However, even if I were to suppose that the *Governance of the Apostolic Church* was formed after the *model of Synagogue Governance*, many things nevertheless stand in the way of my admitting that the *Governance of the Apostolic Church* was similar to the *Governance of the modern Synagogue*, or that it was fashioned after such a model. Whether Grotius actually endorsed this hypothesis remains, as I said, unclear.

There is one reason for my view, which is solid and certain: it is because the *Prefects of the modern Synagogue*—the **DOCTOR** <note>referring to the *Rav* or Rabbi</note> and the **PASTORS** <note>referring to the *Parnasîm*</note>—form a *College of Governors* made up of different kinds of officials. Yet, it has been proven in the preceding pages that the *Christian Churches* in their beginnings were governed by a **homogeneous Council of Presbyters** <note>original: *Concilio Presbyterorum homogeneo*; meaning a council where all members held the same basic rank or spiritual office</note>. That the Governors of the *modern Synagogue* constitute a College of men of *various orders and kinds* is clear for two reasons:

**1.** Because they are so distinguished by names peculiar to themselves in the modern Synagogue that the **Pastors** <note>Hebrew: *Parnasîm*</note> are never, so far as I know, called **Masters** <note>Hebrew: *Rav*</note>, and the **Master of the Sacred Rites of the Synagogue** is never simply included under the name of the **Pastors**, even though I would not deny that this latter name has a wider and more general meaning. By contrast, the Governors of the early Church were all addressed and honored by the single name and title of **Pastors**, **Bishops**, and **Presbyters**, **without distinction of rank** <note>original Greek: χωρὶς ἀξιώματος; meaning they were essentially equals in status</note>.

<page-num>515</page-num>

# CHAPTER 4. On the Governance of the Synagogue and the Church.

Who could endure to compare things of such diverse kinds and orders—distinguished so greatly both by their titles and their duties—with the **Bishop** and **Presbyters** <note>Ancient Greek: *presbyteros*; an elder or communal leader</note> of the Apostolic Church? For even those who wish to see the Bishop and Presbyter as most distinct in rank and dignity would not say they differ from one another as much, or in as many ways, as the *Master of the Synagogue* differs from its *Pastors*—to say nothing of the many other marks of dissimilarity I could bring forward here. If, therefore, **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch scholar who argued that Christian church structure was modeled after the Jewish synagogue</note> intended to compare the **Bishop** and **Presbyters** of the Early Church with the *Master* and *Pastors* of the *modern Synagogue*, he has undoubtedly wandered from the truth. But if he conceived in his mind that the *Ancient Synagogues* were often governed by a *Senate of Learned Men* of a single type and order (about which we shall discuss more extensively, **God granting** <note>original Greek: Θεῷ διδόντι</note>, in the following pages), then that opinion can easily be reconciled with Grotius’s words. In that case, we find nothing to criticize in the Grotian hypothesis; indeed, we shall labor to support and illuminate that view in its proper place to the best of our ability.

Secondly, I would wish it to be observed that Grotius—being, as it seems, too intent upon his **<term>Chazan</term>** <note>original Hebrew: חזן; often translated as "overseer" or "cantor"</note> or *Bishop of the modern Synagogue*, to whom nearly all the care of the Synagogue's sacred rites is demanded—tends to attribute more to the **Bishops** of the Apostolic Churches throughout his *Commentaries* than is right, elevating them too far above the **Presbyters**. We acknowledge that in the original Churches there was a certain *President of the Presbyters* who, due to age, the gravity of the office, and spiritual gifts, would soon become more conspicuous in dignity than the other Presbyters. However, we do not acknowledge that the **Bishop** and the **Presbyters** of the early Church were truly different in their kind or their *presbyterial office* from the very beginnings of their institution. Yet, as far as I can see, Grotius’s *Commentaries* lead us to that conclusion, even though Grotius himself may not unwillingly concede that the word *Bishop* <note>Latin: *Episcopus*; derived from the Greek *episkopos*, meaning "overseer"</note> originally had a more general meaning. What the true difference was between the *President* and the *common Presbyters*, we shall clearly teach in its proper place, investigating it from the Synagogue itself. Since the order of our treatment forbids us from anticipating other matters now—beyond what we said in the preceding *second chapter of this Book*—we shall not add more regarding Grotius’s example at this time. How much we disagree with Grotius will become manifest by the *end of this Book* and the *first part of the following Book*.

### Chapter V.

->The structure of the Synagogue, which the most learned Petit has reconstructed from the **Body of Civil Law**, is examined: in which case it is debated how various titles of dignity—such as those of **Patriarchs**, **Primates**, **Chiefs**, **Nobles**, **Rulers of the Synagogue**, **Fathers of the Synagogues**, **High Priests**, **Priests**, **Presbyters**, and **Elders**—are to be understood within the Roman Laws that deal with the Jews.<-

<margin>
Various Readings
book II. I.
</margin>
Setting Grotius aside, let us turn our attention to **Samuel Petit** <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643) was a French scholar known for his work on ancient law and Jewish antiquities</note>, himself a most learned man. Intending to explain certain obscure names from the **Pandects** <note>original Latin: *Juris Pandectis*; the *Digest*, a massive compendium of Roman legal opinions compiled under Emperor Justinian</note> by which the Hebrews, after the destruction of the Temple, expressed the more noble offices of their nation, he attributes almost as many distinct functions to the Synagogue as there are titles of dignity found in the Imperial Decrees. Mention is made in the Legal Codes of the names **Rulers of the Synagogue**, **Fathers of the Synagogues**, **High Priests**, **Priests**, **Presbyters**, etc., who are called the **Primates** <note>Leaders or chief men</note> of the Jews and are said to preside in their **Sanhedrins** <note>The supreme councils or assemblies of the Jewish people</note>. Furthermore, mention is made of the **Azanitae** <note>original Latin: *Azanitarum*; likely a Latinization of the Hebrew *Chazzanim*</note>, the ministers of the Synagogue, according to the interpretation of **Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century Bishop and Church Father known for his writings against heresies</note>.

The most learned Petit, however, as I have already said, entered into his reasoning as if these distinct names designated just as many distinct offices and duties within the Synagogues. He judges that the **RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>original Latin: *Archisynagogos*</note> presided over the ecclesiastical gatherings that meet in the Synagogues; but that the **FATHERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** held the second rank of dignity in the Synagogue and were the deputies of the Rulers. He draws a conjecture for this from the fact that in the Jerusalem Sanhedrin, the **Father of the Court** <note>original Hebrew: *Av Beit Din* (אב בית דין); the second-highest presiding member</note> was first after the **Prince** <note>original Hebrew: *Nasi* (נשיא); the president or highest official of the Sanhedrin</note>, as is established from the **Talmudists** <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note>.

By like reasoning, he says, we consider the Fathers of the Synagogues to be the first after the Rulers of the Synagogue. *And perhaps it is from this,* he adds, *that several people are named as "Rulers of the Synagogue" for a single congregation: not because there were actually several Rulers, but because in each Synagogue there was one Ruler, and another after him called the Father of the Synagogue, his deputy, who is adorned with the honor of that same name—just as among those same Jews, although there was only one High Priest, nevertheless his deputy was also [called] high...* <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "sum-", likely leading to "summus" or "highest priest".</note>

Furthermore, as for the **Presbyters**, he says, "*the Jews who are also called* **Elders** <note>original: *Seniores*</note> *in Law 15 of the Code concerning Jews and Worshippers of Heaven, it is our opinion that these were the most noble and wise among the Jews. Together with their* **Ruler of the Synagogue**, *the* **Father of the Synagogue**, *the* **High Priest**, *and the* **Priests**, *they presided over their synagogue. Thus, according to Petit, the governance of the synagogue involves the Ruler of the Synagogue, the Father of the Synagogue (his deputy), the High Priests, the Priests, and the Presbyters or Elders. We shall not concern ourselves with the **Azanitas**, the synagogue ministers, for now.

Who would deny that *Petit* has earned great favor among all cultivators of literature? With commendable industry, he has gathered into one place various laws scattered throughout the **Body of Roman Law**—a source less familiar to theologians—and labored to explain them with the talent and erudition with which he was so excellently equipped. Yet, firstly, I doubt whether the true form of the governance of the ancient synagogue can be defined with sufficient solidity and confidence from the books of Roman Law. Secondly, I am certain that *Petit*, in his interpretation of those titles for synagogue leaders which he encountered in the legal decrees, has often wandered quite far from the truth.

Regarding the *first point*: although the founders of Roman Law may have excelled in worldly wisdom and possessed minds adorned with a vast knowledge of various affairs, I can hardly persuade myself that they applied their minds so diligently to understanding the "internal discipline of that most contemptible sect"—or, to use Suetonius’s words <note>Suetonius (c. 69–122 AD) was a Roman historian; "discipline of idleness" refers to the Roman view of the Jewish Sabbath and religious life</note>, that "*discipline of idleness*" <note>original: *inertiae disciplinam*</note>—that they either understood it clearly or, if understood, wished to record it with precision in their edicts and decrees...

# Petit’s Opinion on the Form, Book 2

...RUM. For this reason, it does not seem necessary to work so hard at distinguishing so carefully between the remaining titles: *Archisynagogues, Fathers of the Synagogues, Teachers, Priests, and Elders*. However, it will be useful to review these individual titles of dignity as they appear in the Laws, and to offer our judgment on their use and meaning briefly and candidly.

<margin>See Morinus, *Biblical Exercises*, Book 1, Exercise 3, Chapters 1 and 2.</margin>

First, **Petit** <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643) was a French Protestant scholar and jurist noted for his work on the laws of Athens and Jewish history</note> discusses the **PATRIARCHS**, whom he says correspond with the **Aichmalotarchs** <note>From the Greek "Aichmalotarches," meaning "leader of the captives." This was the title for the Exilarch, the leader of the Jewish community in Babylon</note> (the *Heads of the Exile* <note>original Hebrew: "Rashei Galuyot"</note>), the Princes of the Jews in Captivity. In this, we do not disagree with him. Therefore, we will not repeat what he, as well as **Morinus, Hottinger, Alting, Vorstius, L’Empereur**, and recently **Tillemont and Pezron**, have written at great length regarding this supreme office. This was a prefecture that the Jews enjoyed—by the indulgence of the Roman Emperors—for several centuries after the destruction of their commonwealth. These Princes were the leaders of all the Sanhedrins and Synagogues of their province <note>original Greek: "eparchia"</note>, whether in the land of **Canaan** or in **Babylon**. Their authority was first in matters of **RELIGION**, where they held the highest judgment, and later also in **Civil and Criminal** matters, to the extent that the Roman Emperors did not restrict or instead tolerated the exercise of that power.

<margin>Laws 8 and 15 of the Theodosian Code, concerning Jews and Sky-worshippers, page 243.</margin>

And truly, for a time, those Emperors were most indulgent toward the **Patriarchs**, whom they call *Illustrious, Respectable, and Most Distinguished Men* <note>These were specific honorary ranks in the Roman administrative hierarchy: *Illustres*, *Spectabiles*, and *Clarissimi*</note>. This is clear from many other proofs, but especially from the remarkable testimony of **Origen** <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who lived in Caesarea</note> in his *Letter of Response to Africanus*: "And even now," he says <note>original Greek: "Καὶ νῦν γέ..."</note>, "with the Romans reigning and the Jews paying them the two-drachma tax, how much power the **Ethnarch** <note>A title meaning "leader of a nation"; Origen uses it here to refer to the Jewish Patriarch or Nasi</note> has among them by the permission of Caesar! So much so that he differs in no way from a king of the nation—as we who have experienced it know."

Origen continues: "Moreover, secret judgments are held according to the Law, and some are even sentenced to death; this happens neither with full legal freedom for this purpose, nor yet without the Emperor’s knowledge—and this we have learned and confirmed by spending a long time in the country of that nation." <note>This suggests that while the Romans officially reserved the right of capital punishment (the "power of the sword"), they turned a blind eye to the Jewish leadership exercising it internally</note>

### CHAPTER 5. The Government of the SYNAGOGUE is examined.

...I know from the one who reigns; something which we learned and were certainly persuaded of when we lived in the region of this people for a long time. There were two of the more distinguished Patriarchs: the one who ruled in Babylonia was called the **Head of the Exile** <note>original Hebrew: ראש הגלות (*Rosh Ha-Galut*); also known by the Greek-derived title Aichmalotarch, meaning "leader of the captives"</note>, and the one in Palestine was called the **Prince** <note>original Hebrew: נשיא (*Nasi*)</note>. However, be careful not to take this as if only the Prince of the Jews in the land of Canaan was called *Prince*, since in reality this title was common to both. This is seen in the Letter of Rabbi Abraham, Son of Maimonides <note>Abraham ben Moses ben Maimon (1186–1237), leader of the Jewish community in Egypt and son of the famous philosopher Maimonides</note>, to Rabbi Joseph, Son of Gershon:

<margin>See also Alting, *On Shiloh*, Book 1, Chapter 19.</margin>
**Whoever is appointed to be the Head of the Exile in Babylon, we call him Prince; and whoever is the Head of the Academy in the Land of Israel, we call him Prince, etc.** This is also established from the book *Scheveth Juda* <note>"The Scepter of Judah," a 16th-century chronicle of Jewish history and persecutions</note>, in which the inauguration rite of this Prince is described. There it is expressly stated: **He is indeed called PRINCE and HEAD OF THE EXILE.**

<margin>See Jerome, *Against Rufinus*, Epistle Part 2, page 72, column 1, Book 2, Exercise 3, Chapter 2.</margin>
It appears certain that the Synagogues of Egypt were under a specific Prefect who ruled them in the manner of a Patriarch. This is evident from what **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) based in Alexandria and Caesarea</note> mentions concerning the Patriarch **Huillo** <note>Likely referring to Hillel II or a similar figure; Origen frequently consulted Jewish scholars for his biblical commentaries</note>, whose assistance he admits to having used often in interpreting Scripture. Furthermore, this is supported by **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented communities across Europe, Asia, and Africa</note>, although he, as is well known, speaks of later times. His words are:
**And among them is Rabbi Nathanael, the Prince of Princes, Head of the Academy; and he is the head for all the communities of Egypt to establish rabbis and cantors.** <note>original Hebrew: חזנים (*Chazzanim*), the officials who lead the congregation in prayer</note>

**Nathanael** the Great Teacher, as the supreme Prince, presides over both [types of Synagogues]; he is the Head of the Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme legal and religious council of the Jewish people</term> and presides over all the Churches of Egypt for the purpose of appointing Masters and Ministers. However, I am not unaware that Origen elsewhere mentions only one Patriarch as the common **Ethnarch** <note>A Greek title meaning "ruler of a people" or "governor"</note> of the Jews.

After the **PATRIARCH**, the legal decrees mention the **PRIMATES** <note>A Latin term for "leading men" or "chiefs"</note>. ### CHAPTER 5. The Governance of the SYNAGOGUE is examined.

...do the words *Archipericita* <note>original: *Archipericita*; likely a Latinized Greek term for the head of a Jewish academy or school district</note> or *Presbyters* <note>Elders</note> mean? Is not the finger pointed here at the *Archisynagogues of the Jews*? But what does this also mean to you: **Perhaps even the Masters**? Certainly, what is more evident than that the Emperors understood very little of the difference between those titles—if there was any—or at least did not scrupulously distinguish these titles from one another in their usage within their Laws?

<margin>Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note>, *Sanhedrin*, chapter 1, § 11.</margin>
Next in order come the **Fathers of the Synagogues**, whom *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a scholar of ancient law</note> makes **Deputies of the Archisynagogues**, after the likeness of the *Father of the House of Judgment* <note>original: אב בית דין (*Ab Bet Din*); the vice-president of the Sanhedrin</note> in the *Sanhedrins*, and the *Deputy* <note>original: סגן (*Sagan*)</note> *of the High Priest in the Temple*. And in the Great Sanhedrin indeed, a certain *Father of the Sanhedrin* was subordinate to the President, who was called *Prince* <note>original: נשיא (*Nasi*)</note> and *Head* <note>original: ראש (*Rosh*)</note>; but in the *Synagogue* we have not so far encountered the kind of *Fathers of the Synagogue* that *Petit* suggests; nor is any other testimony produced by *Petit* from elsewhere by which he might defend these *Fathers of the Synagogues* of his. Therefore, we

<margin>Law 4. Theodosian Code <note>A compilation of Roman laws under the Christian emperors since 312</note>, on this title.</margin>
judged that by *Fathers of the Synagogues* in the *Decree of Constantine* we should understand either the *Presbyters* or *Elders* of the Synagogue themselves, called so elsewhere, or the *Archisynagogues* or *Heads of Academies* themselves, who in later centuries claimed for themselves the title *Fathers of the House of Judgment* <note>original: אבות בתי דינין (*Abot Batte Dinim*)</note>. Thus you frequently find in the titles of the Teachers of the Jewish Nation: *Father of the House of Judgment and Head of the Academy in the Holy Community* <note>original: אב בית דין וריש מתיבתא בקהله קדושה (*Ab Bet Din ve-Resh Metivta be-kehillah kedoshah*)</note>. Likewise: *Father of the Sanhedrin in the Holy Community* <note>original: אב בית דין דקהלה קדושה (*Ab Bet Din de-kehillah kedoshah*)</note>. *Father of the Sanhedrin*, I say. But the same phrase *Father of the House of Judgment* <note>original: אב בית דין (*Ab Bet Din*)</note> can be translated as: **Father of the Synagogue**. For *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist</note> was the first to observe on another occasion, and now almost all learned men grant, that *House of Judgment* <note>original: בית דין (*Bet Din*)</note> was often interpreted by Greek and Latin authors, both Sacred and secular, not only as *Sanhedrin*, but also as *Synagogue*. If we admit this interpretation of the title, then it must be said that in the *Decree of Constantine*, titles of the same meaning are confounded with one another; which we have supposed and defended above as not absurd to occur elsewhere in the Imperial Laws.

**Priests** follow next, namely *Hierei* <note>original: ἱερεῖς; Greek for priests</note>. And indeed, the Synagogue of old had Priests, just as the modern one does. To whom honor is deferred not only by reason of their lineage, so that they are the *first* to read the Mosaic Law in the Synagogue, but especially the duty is committed to them of *blessing* the assembly gathered in the *Synagogues* after the sacred rites are finished, *with hands uplifted* <note>original: בנשיות כפים (*bi-nesi'ut kapayim*); refers to the Priestly Blessing, or Nesiat Kapayim</note>;

...are not to be considered as IDLE and LAZY men; but as <term>ceasing from their own work and occupying themselves with the needs of the community</term> <note>original Hebrew: בטלן ממל אכתן ועוסקין בצרכי צבור (*batlan mim'lakhtan v'oseqin b'tzorkhei tzibur*)</note> to whom (*as those who were not entangled in worldly affairs*) it was LEISURE only to care for the matters of the Synagogue and to devote themselves to the study of the Law. # CHAPTER 6. On the Government of the Synagogue and Church, etc.

<margin>
Lightfoot, *Hebrew Hours on Mark 1:38*.
</margin>
This seems to be concluded from the fact that he was so careful in describing these *Idle Men* <note>original: *Otiosorum*; referring to the *Batlanim*, men at leisure for community service</note> to ensure they were not taken for *lazy* and *indolent* men. It is also evidenced by the fact that he elsewhere explained related material regarding the distinction between <term>fortified towns</term> <note>original Hebrew: כרכים (*krakhim*)</note>, <term>villages</term> <note>original Hebrew: כפרים (*kepharim*)</note>, and <term>towns</term> <note>original Hebrew: עיירות (*ayarot*)</note>, drawing not only from the *Talmudic* text but also from the *Glosses* <note>Interpretive commentaries</note> attached to it. I cannot easily persuade myself that he handled those topics without the related *Glosses* concerning the *Ten Idle Men* coming under his observation.

<margin>
Observations on the New Testament, p. 26, on Matthew 18:15.
</margin>
Recently, however, I noticed that *Jacques Cappel* <note>A noted 17th-century French Protestant scholar and Hebraist</note>, a most learned man, has moved toward an opinion hardly differing from that of *Lightfoot*. Cappel’s words are these: **"THESE TEN-MEN <note>Latin: *Decem-viri*</note>, WHO (MAIMONIDES) SAYS REPRESENT THE SYNAGOGUE, SEEM TO TEACH US ENTIRELY THAT EVERY SYNAGOGUE HAD TEN-MEN, ACCORDING TO WHOSE OPINION MATTERS PERTAINING TO THE SYNAGOGUE WERE CONDUCTED."**

<margin>
Talmud Tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 1, § 1.
</margin>
*This assembly dealt neither with civil nor capital cases. For the court that dealt with civil cases consisted of three men; the one for capital cases consisted of twenty-three men, as Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> teaches in the same place. It remains, therefore, that this TEN-MAN SENATE was ECCLESIASTICAL.* And this very explanation of the *Idle Men* did not seem so absurd to me when I first began to comment more freely on the sacred matters of the Synagogue; indeed, I not only approved of it, but later took pains to defend it when it was challenged. Now, removed from the heat of debate, I will not stir up a dispute long laid to rest. Instead, I will only briefly repeat the reasons which I have elsewhere produced to either justify or clarify *Lightfoot's* explanation, so that my reader may have the opportunity to judge this question skillfully and freely. Since I have no reason to force *Lightfoot’s* opinion on any soul—as I myself once followed it not as a certainty, but as a probability—it will be enough for me to have shown that it is not inconsistent with reason. If I achieve that, I shall be little concerned with the rest. For just as the ceremonies of ancient times are shrouded in much darkness, so undoubtedly, without rashness, nothing can be boldly defined in many such matters.

# THE OPINION OF LIGHTFOOT CONCERNING BOOK 2.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>
Lightfoot, *Hebrew Hours*, Book 2, ch. 1, sec. 1.
</margin>
<margin>Lightfoot, *Hebrew Hours*, p. 8.</margin>
<margin>
*Observations*, Part [?], p. 23.

</margin>
Here, several points are brought forward that serve to illustrate the opinion of Lightfoot and Cappel <note>Jacques Cappel, the French Hebraist mentioned on the previous page</note> concerning the **Ten Idle Men**, and to establish its probability. Specifically: 1. Benjamin of Tudela <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler from Spain who documented Jewish communities across the world</note> interpreted the "Ten Idle Men" as **Ten Learned Men**, who were free for teaching and legal judgments. 2. Not only in the Hebrew language, but also in others, it is customary for studious and learned men to be called "Idle" <note>In the sense of being "at leisure" from manual labor to pursue intellectual or civic duties</note>. 3. The <term>periphrasis</term> <note>A roundabout way of speaking or a descriptive phrase</note> used for these Idle Men—*those occupied with the needs of the community* <note>original Hebrew: עוסקים בצרכי צבור (*osekim be-tzorkhei tzibur*)</note>—fits Lightfoot's explanation perfectly.

<margin>p. 70.</margin>
1. It has been investigated and found that Benjamin of Tudela understood the word <term>Batlan</term> (*Otiosus* or "Idle Man") to mean a **LEARNED MAN**. Indeed, he interpreted the phrase "Ten Idle Men" as referring to the very Leaders of the Sanhedrins <note>The high councils or courts</note> and Schools. This is seen in his description of the city of Baghdad, as translated and illustrated by the most learned Constantine L'Empereur: *Furthermore, almost a thousand Jews dwell in Baghdad, who enjoy tranquility and peace, and even great glory under the power of the Great King. Among them are the wisest men,* **AND THE HEADS OF THE ACADEMIES WHO OCCUPY THEMSELVES WITH THE LAW OF MOSES** <note>original Hebrew: וראשי ישיבות מתעסקים בתורת משה (*ve-rashei yeshivot mitaskim be-torat Moshe*)</note>. *In that city, there are* **TEN ASSEMBLIES** (*Academies and Sanhedrins*). *The head of the High Sanhedrin is the teacher Samuel, son of Eli—the head, I say, of the most eminent Sanhedrin. The Deputy* (<term>Sagan</term>) *of the Levites is the head of the second; Master Daniel is the president of the third Sanhedrin; Master Eleazar, an associate, is president of the fourth; Master Eleazar, son of Tsema, the Steward of the Order (whose genealogy is traced back to the blessed Prophet Samuel), is the head or president of the fifth Sanhedrin; Master Hasdia, the glory of the scholars or associates, is president of the sixth Sanhedrin; Master Haggai is the prince of the seventh; Master Ezra of the eighth; the teacher Abraham, called Abou Tahir (Holy Father), is the head of the ninth Sanhedrin; and finally, Master Zaccheus, son of Buxtana, their general treasurer, is the president of the tenth Sanhedrin. He then adds the following, which you must not fail to notice, my reader:*

> These are the ones called "Idle Men," because they do not occupy themselves with any other matter except the needs of the community, and throughout all the days of the week, they act as judges for everyone. <note>original Hebrew: הם הנקראים בטלים שאין מתעסקים בדבר אחר אלא בצרכי צבור ובכל ימי השבוע הם דנין לכל</note>

### Chapter 7. On the Government of the Synagogue and the Church, etc.

...for all the people of the land, the Jews, except for the second day <note>Monday, a traditional day for Torah reading and court sessions</note> when they all come before Rabbi Samuel, the head of the "Pride of Jacob" Academy <note>original Hebrew: ישיבת גאון יעקוב (*Yeshivat Gaon Yaakov*)</note>, and he stands with the **ten idle men**, the heads of the academies, to judge all who come before them, etc.

**They are called "Idle,"** because they are not occupied with any worldly matter, but only with the necessary business of the people. **And they administer justice to all the Jews of that region** every day of the week, except for the second day, when everyone gathers before Master Samuel, the head of the Sanhedrin <note>The high council or assembly</note>—which bears the name "The Excellence of Jacob"—and he himself is present **with those ten idle men**, the heads of the Sanhedrins, so that he may administer justice to all who approach without distinction. It is certainly clear from this testimony that *Benjamin of Tudela* interprets "Idle Man" <note>original Latin: *Otiosus*; Hebrew: *Batlan*</note> as a man of letters, who is free for study for the benefit of the *commonwealth*. Furthermore, it is evident that he speaks not only of Idle Men in general, but specifically of the *Ten Idle Men*, by whom he understands the ten leaders of the Sanhedrins or the major schools of Baghdad. Who would now doubt that *Benjamin*, in speaking of the *Ten Idle Men*, was referring to the accepted expression used by the *Talmudists concerning the Ten Idle Men*? Nevertheless, the interpretation of this title which *Benjamin* provides differs greatly from that of *Jarchi* <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki), the preeminent medieval commentator</note> and more recent interpreters of the *Talmud*. From this, it seems necessary to conclude that in the time of Benjamin, various interpretations of this title were in use. For if a fixed and definite interpretation of the *Ten Idle Men* had existed in the time of *Benjamin*, what would have possessed Benjamin of Tudela to knowingly and willingly depart from the common authority of the Teachers without any necessity, fashioning some other explanation for that title which would be entirely new and unwelcome to his own people? If this is the case, I do not see why *Benjamin’s* reasoning should not be held in the same regard as *Jarchi’s* in the explanation of this title. For they were men of the same century—that is, the twelfth since the birth of Christ. Indeed, our man of Tudela was fond of inventing and believing fables. I admit it; but *Jarchi* was also a man of fables, if ever there was one. Yet who would believe that *Benjamin*, however inclined he might be toward fables and fictions, would wish to introduce new meanings for words into the Hebrew language for no benefit and to no thanks from his own people? I repeat, therefore, that in the age of Benjamin, not only did the interpretation of the title *Ten Idle Men* vary, but even then, the name was explained by some as referring to *learned and scholarly men, who are entirely devoted to [divine] matters...*

# Lightfoot's Opinion on Book 2.

...they were devoted and dedicated to Divine matters, whether in the Sanhedrins and Schools or in the Synagogues.

2. It should be observed that this very word **"Idle"** <note>original Latin: *Otiosus*; referring to the Hebrew *Batlan*</note> most appropriately—indeed, quite elegantly—carries the meaning that *Benjamin of Tudela* assigns to it. This is true whether you consider its use among Hebrew authors themselves or compare it with words of equal power in other languages. Indeed, among Hebrew authors, I have found that "Leisure" or "Cessation" <note>original Hebrew: בטלה (*batlah*)</note> is attributed to Judges while they are occupied in the exercise of their duty. Thus we read in the legal decisions of *Rabbenu Asher* <note>Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), a prominent Talmudic scholar</note>:

<margin>In the tractate Sanhedrin, at chapter 1, § 10.</margin>

**"A judge can receive a fee for his leisure** <note>original Latin: *mercedem vacationis suae*</note> **because he had to stop his own work so that he might be intent on judgment."** In the Greek and Latin languages, the words *schôlazein* <note>to have leisure</note>, *otiari* <note>to be at leisure</note>, and *vacare* <note>to be free/available</note> do not signify mere rest in which you do nothing at all. Rather, they mean rest from harder and servile works which tire the body more than the mind. I might call it, with Plato, **"an idleness from one's own affairs."** <note>original Greek: Τῶν οἰκείων ἔργων ἀργίαν (*Tōn oikeiōn ergōn argian*)</note> To this rank belong men of letters and scholars, such as the Teachers of the Churches and Academies. Because the common people see that these men are exempt from manual labor and perform tasks that the commoners themselves only do when they are "at leisure," the people name them **"Idle Men."**

Indeed, among the Greeks, the word *schôlazein* corresponds exactly with the Hebrew *batel* <note>to be idle or cease</note>, for it denotes being at leisure. But this same *schôlazein* also means to apply oneself to doing something, or to seize the opportunity for doing something. *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> says under the entry *schôlê*: **"Leisure is either doing nothing, or being occupied with something. To be free for a thing and to give it one's effort. As if to say: to be 'idle' around something."** However, many use the word *eukairein* <note>to have a good opportunity</note> instead of *schôlazein*. *Hesychius* <note>A 5th-century lexicographer</note> says: **"Leisure does not only denote doing nothing, but also devoting oneself and giving effort to a certain thing, even a chosen pursuit."**

In the writings of *Herodian* <note>A Roman historian who wrote in Greek</note>, you find phrases such as: **"to be at leisure for spectacles and festivals"** (meaning to attend them); **"to be at leisure for sacrifices"** (to perform them); **"to be at leisure for luxuries"** (to indulge in them); and **"to spend one's leisure in exercising tyranny."** Let us also compare the phrasing of Paul in his first Epistle to the Corinthians: **"Do not deprive one another, except by consent, for a certain time,"**

<margin>Chapter 7, verse 5.</margin>

**"so that you may be at leisure for** <note>original Greek: ἵνα σχολάζητε (*hina scholazēte*)</note> **fasting and prayer."**

# Chapter 7. On the Government of the Synagogue and the Church, etc.

**Clarification.** <note>original Dutch: *Verledigen*; meaning to explain or clear up a matter.</note> Indeed, every exercise of Youth and Teachers in places destined for that purpose was called *scholē* <note>original Greek: σχολὴ</note> or "Leisure" by Ancient Authors; from which, eventually, the place itself began to be named *scholē*—a School, or a place of leisure. Thus, it is entirely fitting that *men of letters, scholars, and those devoted to sacred matters* should be named *Batlanim* <note>original Hebrew: בטלניס; "Idle Men"</note> or *scholazontes* <note>original Greek: σχολάζοντες; "those at leisure"</note>—that is, the **Idle**. Hence, the word "School" <note>original Greek: σχολείον</note> is explained by Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> as a "literary gymnasium," and "having led a school" <note>original Greek: σχολαρχήσας</note> is explained as "one who leads a leisure," that is, one who presides over a School or the literary exercises of students. We leave other examples aside. Furthermore, the words *Vacare* <note>to be free for something</note> and *Otiari* <note>to be at leisure</note> have plainly the same power among the Latins. It would be trivial to dwell on the proof of this meaning in the word *VACARE*, since nothing is better known to schoolboys than that "to be free for letters and studies" is the same as consuming one's leisure in learning letters and giving labor to studies.

<margin>Letter to Celantia regarding the education of a mother of a family. Vol. 1. folio 4. col. 1.</margin>
Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century church father</note> elegantly uses the word *vacatio* <note>freedom/leisure</note> for every *Sacred occupation*. Thus he advises *Celantia*:

> *Maintain the care of the house in such a way that you still grant some* FREEDOM <note>original Latin: VACATIONEM</note> *to the soul.*

A few lines later:

> *Let there be such a study of Divine reading, such frequent turns of prayer, and such firm and persistent meditation on the future, that you easily compensate for the occupations of all the remaining time with this* FREEDOM <note>original Latin: VACATIONE</note>.

<margin>Book 3. On Duties.</margin>
Regarding the notion of LEISURE <note>original Latin: OTII</note>, it is quite certain among the Authors of the Latin Language that it signifies a "leisure" that is no less honorable than "sloth" is shameful. Cicero’s sentiment is very well known; he said that *Scipio* used to say,

> he was never less *Idle* than when he was AT LEISURE <note>original Latin: OTIOSUS</note>, nor less alone than when he was alone.

<margin>On the Nature of the Gods, book 3. at the beginning.</margin>
Plutarch puts it thus: *When he was* AT LEISURE, *he did more.* <note>original Greek: ὁ πότε σχολάζοι πλείονά πράττειν;</note> Again, Cotta in Cicero's work speaks excellently to our point:

> *For we are both* AT LEISURE <note>original Latin: OTIOSI</note>, *and we are dealing with those matters which are to be preferred even to business.*

<margin>In the Life of Caesar, chapter 4.</margin>
Suetonius says of *Caesar*:

> *Furthermore, after the civil sedition was settled, he prosecuted Cornelius Dolabella, a man of consular and triumphal rank, for extortion: and after Dolabella was acquitted, Caesar decided to retire to Rhodes, both to avoid ill-will and so that* THROUGH LEISURE <note>original Latin: PER OTIUM</note> *and rest he might give his attention to Apollonius Molo, the most famous teacher of oratory at that time.*

*This was the "leisure" of Caesar: to give his attention to Apollonius Molo.*

<margin>See Furetière under the word "Academy."</margin>
It would not be out of place to note here that the members of the Academy of Bologna are still to this day called THE IDLE ONES <note>original Latin: OTIOSOS</note>.

<margin>In the Itinerary, page 6.</margin>
Say, therefore, according to this familiar and accepted use of the word, that *the Idle are* those **"who are separated from the affairs and cares of the world and stand over the book of the Law day and night,"** <note>original Hebrew: שנפרשים מעניני העולם ועומדים על הספר יומם ולילה</note> as Benjamin says elsewhere. Or, if anyone desires a still more ample description of the *Idle*...

### Chapter 7. On the Governance of the Synagogue and Church, etc. 539

<margin>See the Lexicon for this word.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: פ' שעשרה אנשים בטלים מעסקיהם ועסקין בצרכי צבור</note>
By "Ten Idle Men," you should understand ten men who have ceased from their own private business and are **INTENT UPON THE CONVENIENCES OF PUBLIC AFFAIRS.**

Let us now see what the phrase <term>occupying oneself with the needs of the community</term> <note>original Hebrew: עסק בצרכי צבור (osek b'tzorchei tzibur)</note> signifies. The word *community* <note>original Hebrew: צבור (tzibur)</note> properly denotes the *entire assembly of the people* gathered in a house of prayer; and because all the people of a single district were accustomed to convene in the synagogue on Sabbaths and feast days, the term was sometimes taken more broadly to mean the "Republic" or "Public Commonwealth," as it is translated elsewhere by **Selden.** <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note> 
<margin>On the Sanhedrin, book 2, chapter 4, section 4. Book 1, Part 1, chapter 2.</margin>
This was discussed in the preceding sections. However, the *needs of the assembly* <note>original Hebrew: צרכי צבור (tzorchei tzibur)</note>—a very frequent phrase in the writings of **Maimonides** <note>The preeminent medieval Sephardic philosopher and legal codifier</note> and others—signify any duties and offices imposed on someone in the name of the assembly for the public benefit. Hence, to be *occupied in the needs of the assembly* (or *the needs of the many*) means the same as being intent upon the benefits of public affairs and fulfilling the office committed to you with the highest faith and diligence.

Since it is certain that the benefits of the Commonwealth or the necessities of the Synagogal Assembly are primarily cared for by the Prefects of the City or Synagogue and the public Ministers of the Synagogue, it follows that Judges, Pastors, Deacons, Doctors in the Academy, and Synagogue Ministers are usually encompassed by this phrase. In this very way, **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented the lives of Jewish communities across Europe, Africa, and Asia</note> correctly described the Judges of Baghdad: 
<margin>As cited above.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: הם הנקראים בטלנים שאין מתעסקים בדבר אחר אלא בצרכי צבור</note>
*These are called the "Idle Men," because they apply themselves to no other thing than the needs of the Assembly.* Regarding the Minister of the Synagogue, **Elias Levita** <note>A 15th-16th century Hebrew grammarian and scholar</note> writes in the same manner: 
<margin>In the Lexicon "Tisbi."</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: ונקרא גם כן חזן לפי שהוא צריך לראות מה הם צורכי צבור</note>
*He is also called an Inspector [Chazzan], because it is his duty to attend to the needs of the Synagogal Assembly.* Regarding Deacons, there is a passage already noted by others in the **Orach Chaiim**: <note>The section of the Shulchan Aruch (Jewish Code of Law) dealing with daily ritual life</note> 
<margin>Title 58, Section 26.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: קהל שנהגו למנות אנשים על צורכי הצבור בין לחזן בין לקופה של צדקה בין לשאר מנויים הצריכים לצבור וכו'</note>
**When a congregation is accustomed to appoint men over public business (the necessities of the community)—whether it appoints a synagogue minister, or collectors of alms, or distributes other duties for the benefit of the public affairs, etc.** It appears clearly from these few documents that the phrase *to be intent on the necessary actions of the Commonwealth* is applied throughout Jewish Law to such officials of the Synagogal Assembly who bring more benefit to the public or the Church than ten men for whom this task alone...

### Page 540

...it is supposed to be given so that they may *be at leisure* <note>original Latin: *otientur*</note>. I am not unaware, however, that there is a great breadth of meaning in this phrasing, and the force of the words is increased or diminished at the writer's discretion.

<margin>
Maimonides, *Laws of the Megillah*, chapter 1, § 9.
And in the Commentary on the Code *Megillah*, chapter 1, § 1.

As each of these points seems to suggest that these *Ten Idle Men* <note>The *Batlanim*, or men of leisure, whose presence ensured a quorum for synagogue services</note> should be granted more honor or duty than what is attributed to them by **Jarchi** <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note>, various arguments could be produced to diminish the weight of Jarchi’s authority in this case. For what Jarchi holds here, he must have received from tradition; indeed, you will find nothing about it in the Talmud itself. Moreover, that tradition would have been from a very long time ago and therefore more uncertain, because the *distinction between Greater and Smaller Cities*, which the *Ten Idle Men* once served, and the varying reading of the Book of Esther subordinated to this distinction of *Cities*, only took place in *Canaan* while the *Republic was flourishing*, according to the testimony of the Masters themselves. After the destruction of the Republic, as the distinction between *Greater and Smaller Cities* perished, the very use of the *Idle Men* seems to have gradually vanished as well, with the name being preserved, as often happens. But what is more, it is clear enough that the tradition of the Masters concerning the interpretation of this title is not constant or perpetual. We noted above that **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler and chronicler who documented the lives of Jewish communities in the East</note> asserts that the Presidents of the *Ten Baghdad Sanhedrins* were called the *Ten Idle Men*. Benjamin would not have done this unless he had understood from other sources that the name *Idle* most especially fits the heads of Schools and Synagogues, who live entirely dedicated to sacred things and are completely free from worldly business.

<margin>
On Alfasi, folio 360, column 2.
</margin>
**Rabbi Nissim** <note>Nissim ben Reuben, a 14th-century Talmudist and philosopher</note>, on the other hand, having rejected a large part of Jarchi's commentary, says that they are called *Idle Men* who: <gloss>ALL WHO ARE FOUND ASSIDUOUS IN THE SYNAGOGUE AT THE HOUR OF PRAYER, MORNING AND EVENING.</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: כל שמשכימין ומעריבין להיות מצוין בשעת תפלה לבית הכנסת</note> I confess, this exposition stands in the way of **Lightfoot** <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist and clergyman</note>; but it also stands in the way of the patrons of Jarchi's exposition. It is enough for us to have gathered from this that the tradition regarding the true interpretation of the name of the *Idle Men* fluctuates among the Hebrew interpreters themselves, and therefore Jarchi is not to be trusted too much in this case. And indeed, men highly skilled in Hebrew letters have frequently acted to desert the glosses of the Talmudic interpreters and even of Jarchi himself, when they saw that those glosses relied on no suitable foundations and reason suggested otherwise; and this all the more so because the Talmudic glossators [were known] to forge stories beyond necessity...

...through which they are inclined. However, as for the saying that this *Decade of Idle Men* <note>The *Batlanim*; the author uses the Latin *Numerum Denarium Otiosorum*</note> was required in Synagogues to recite the holier formulas of prayer, I certainly do not deny that the Jews require a number of *ten men* to recite certain prayer formulas; but they could surely fulfill this duty without *ten men* hired with money to sit as *Idle* and *Lazy* in the Synagogues for the greater part of the day, waiting for those coming to pray. For even today, it is so received among their customs that if *seven, six*, or even *one* (for the Teachers disagree here) enter the Synagogue after the blessings of the *Shema* <note>The central declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel..."</note> [שמע] have already been recited, and if they find enough others remaining in the Synagogue to make up the *number of ten* with them, then those remaining are forced to wait until they have recited the *Shema*. <margin>In the *Orach Chayim* <note>A section of the Jewish code of law</note>, Title 69.</margin>

And this is also said in the *Tractate Soferim* <note>A minor tractate of the Talmud concerning scribal laws and liturgy</note>: in a place where there are nine or ten who have heard *Kaddish* and *Barecu*, if there is even one among them who has not heard them, and he recites *Kaddish* and *Barecu* and the others respond after him, he has fulfilled his duty. # LIGHTFOOT’S OPINION ON BOOK 2.

And it seemed fitting to discuss these matters at somewhat greater length, more to defend Lightfoot's interpretation from absurdity and ill-will than to force it upon others as the absolute truth. # Chapter 8. On the Governance of the Synagogue and Church, etc.

That the most skilled men, and the arbiters of religious controversies in the Church, were often and above others chosen as Rulers of the Synagogue <note>original Latin: *Archisynagogos*</note>, there is no reason for us to doubt. However, I would have greatly desired that our *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), the English Hebraist whose theories the author is evaluating</note> had established, either from the explicit decrees of the Hebrews or at least from probable arguments, that the *Three-man Judges* were always the same as the *Princes of the Synagogue*. For if we grant Lightfoot that in the smaller Jewish societies, which did not contain *one hundred and twenty* inhabitants, a *Three-man Senate* held the first place in the Synagogues, what will become of the Synagogues of the *Greater Cities or Societies*, in which, if the Talmudic traditions are to be trusted, *Sanhedrins of Twenty-Three* <note>original: *Synedria Viginti-Triumviralia*; these were local courts for larger towns</note> were located? Indeed, since the highest power regarding the sacred matters of that place undoubtedly resided with the most distinguished Senate of twenty-three men in every larger city, who would dare to deny them the chief seat <note>original Greek: πρωτοκαθεδρίαν (*protokathedrian*)</note> in the Synagogue and the supreme governance of the Synagogue? For even if those larger Senates deliberated and judged on more serious legal cases, that certainly did not prevent the sacred matters of the Synagogue from depending on their judgment. Therefore, since Lightfoot has not fortified that opinion of his with any authority, nor does reason support it, I do not subscribe to it thus far. How much power should be granted to the Sanhedrins over the sacred matters of the Synagogues, in my opinion, I shall declare in its proper place in the following pages.

2. We grant to Lightfoot that the *Synagogue had its own* <term>Chazzan <note>Hebrew: חזן (*Chazzan*). In this context, an attendant or minister of the synagogue who performed various administrative and liturgical tasks.</note></term> *Minister*, who is also often called in the Jewish Constitutions the <term>Sheliach Tzibbur <note>Hebrew: שליח צבור (*Sheliach Tzibbur*). Literally the "Messenger of the Congregation," the person designated to lead the public prayers on behalf of the community.</note></term> *Minister* or *Envoy of the Synagogue*. But as for Lightfoot’s comparison of the name *Sheliach Tzibbur* with that of the *Angel of the Church*, which occurs in *Revelation* chapter 2:1, and his comparison of both the name and the office of the <term>Chazzan</term> *Minister of the Synagogue* with the name and office of the *Bishop* <note>original Greek: ἐπισκόπυ (*episkopou*)</note>, which Paul described in the *First Epistle to Timothy*, chapter 3:1—both points, at first consideration, commend themselves with a great appearance of truth. However, the latter is by no means to be approved, as will be established from the following treatise on the *Ministers of the Synagogue*; we shall look into the former in that same place.

3. The *three* <term>Gabbai Tzedakah <note>Hebrew: גבאי צדקה (*Gabbai Tzedakah*). Officials responsible for the collection and distribution of communal charity.</note></term> *Collectors of Alms*, whom *Lightfoot* places under the *Chazzans*, are indeed very well known in the Jewish State, but they were never reckoned among the *Officials of the Synagogue* during the height of the Hebrew Commonwealth, and therefore they are not to be so reckoned by us.

# Lightfoot’s Opinion on Book 2.

They belonged to the *City*, and they were regarded as its officials. For we recognize no synagogue office unless it revolves around the sacred matters of the synagogues themselves and is administered within the synagogue itself. For this must be warned beforehand, lest this whole dispute descend into a war of words <note>original Greek: *logomachia*</note>. However, this duty of the Collection of Alms was carried out outside the synagogues, and thus it is consistently referred by Hebrew authors to the **City** <note>Hebrew: *’Ir*</note>, that is, to the *Society of Jews* in each place, insofar as it is considered by us not as a *Sacred* but as a *Civil* entity.

<margin>chapter 9, 1. Book of the Laws of the Poor.</margin>
Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> writes: "Every city in which there are Israelites is bound to appoint from among themselves COLLECTORS OF CHARITY, known and faithful men, who go around among the people from the eve of the Sabbath to the eve of the Sabbath, receiving from each and every one what is appropriate for him to give and the amount assessed for him. And they distribute the money every Sabbath eve and give to each and every poor person food sufficient for seven days; and this is what is called the *Kuppah* <note>original Hebrew: *Kuppah*, meaning the 'basket' or communal charity chest</note>." It is clear from this testimony that Maimonides assigns the *Collectors of Alms* to the *City*; and he does this consistently throughout this entire treatise. Thus the *Curators of Alms*, or the Magistrate, or the General Society of inhabitants—to whom he assigns the power of disposing of the collected alms at their discretion—<margin>chapter 8, section 11.</margin> he calls the **Men of the City** <note>original Hebrew: *Anshei ha-’Ir*</note>. The *City’s* men, I say, not the **Synagogue’s** <note>original Hebrew: *Beit ha-Knesset*</note>. By the same reasoning, <margin>chapter 7, section 14.</margin> the poor who are supported are called the **Poor of the City** <note>original Hebrew: *Aniyei ’Ir*</note>, as they are undoubtedly to be considered members of the *City* in this case. Indeed, these very *Collectors of Alms* are named <margin>chapter 257, section 8.</margin> the COLLECTORS OF THE CITY <note>original Hebrew: *Gabbayei ha-’Ir*</note>. There is a passage in the *Yoreh De’ah* <note>a major section of the Shulchan Aruch, the standard code of Jewish law</note>: *If any poor person has wealthy relatives who are able to support him, the* COLLECTORS OF THAT CITY *are not bound to support him; even though these relatives of his also contribute to the purse according to their means.* Why then are they not called *Collectors of the Synagogue*? Why, I ask, *Collectors of the...*

### CHAPTER 8. On the Government of the Synagogue and the Church, etc.

**Collectors of the CITY** <note>original Hebrew: *Gabbae ’Ir*</note>—do these *Collectors of Alms* belong to the *Synagogue* or the *City*? I am certainly not unaware that the word **City** <note>Hebrew: *’Ir*</note> enjoys the broadest significance among Hebrew authors, and designates any Society of Jews dwelling in any location. I also know that, among the Jews of old, the *City* and the *Church* <note>The author uses "Ecclesia" here to mean the religious assembly or congregation</note> did not constitute two separate bodies of men, as is the case with us, but merged into one single Society. However, just as every *Society* has a dual aspect—either in how it fulfills its religion toward God in *Sacred Places*, or in how it strives for its own preservation and safety, which truly makes it a *City*—so it was similarly arranged within the *Jewish Societies*. They fulfilled their religious duties toward God in the *Temple* and the *Synagogues*. Those duties which were administered outside the *Temple* and *Synagogues* were regarded as *Civil* matters; and the very word **City** <note>Hebrew: *’Ir*</note> properly denotes the *Society of Jews* insofar as it constitutes a *City*, and that *City* strives to preserve and defend itself. To this point, consider that those *Collectors of Alms* were appointed by the *Sanhedrin* <note>The local Jewish court or council of elders</note> itself, insofar as that body exercised care over the *City* or *Civil Society*. The *Sanhedrin* prescribed to every *Citizen* the manner in which this charity was to be exercised; those who resisted this mandate were to be corrected with lashes. Let us hear Prideaux <note>Humphrey Prideaux, a 17th-century scholar who translated Maimonides</note>, the learned interpreter of this *Treatise by Maimonides*:

<margin>
Note on
Chapter 9 of
Maimonides,
Section 4.
</margin>

> It was not decreed how much each person should give to the Bowl <note>original: *Catinus*, referring to the *Tamchui* or daily food collection</note>, and therefore three Collectors were appointed who, possessing the authority of Judges, would judge during the collection whether each person was giving according to his means. The ALMS OF THE CHEST <note>original: *Cista*, referring to the *Kuppah* or weekly money collection</note>, however, since it was a fixed matter—being IMPOSED BY THE SANHEDRIN OF THE CITY—was not collected by more people than those to whose care it was to be entrusted.

<margin>
Chapter 7,
Section 2.
</margin>

Maimonides himself writes in this manner: "If there is anyone who does not wish to give alms, or who gives less than is fitting for him, the **SANHEDRIN** <note>original Hebrew: *Beth Din*, the house of judgment</note> shall compel him and strike him with the **lashes of rebellion** <note>original: *Makkat Mardut*, a form of disciplinary flogging for disobeying rabbinic law</note> until he gives what they have judged he must give, etc." It is established that this entire matter pertained to the care and direction of the *Sanhedrin of the City*, which commanded each Citizen to give as much as his condition allowed.

<margin>
Chapter 9,
Section 1.
</margin>

Thus *Maimonides* elsewhere reminds us again that the *Collectors of Alms* "take from each and every person what is fitting for him to give and the amount assessed upon him."

->**Lightfoot's Opinion on Book 2.**<-

...from each person <note>original Hebrew: *alav*</note> they receive what is appropriate for them to give, **AND WHAT HAS BEEN IMPOSED UPON THEM.** Namely, by the Sanhedrin <note>The local Jewish court or council of elders</note>. Indeed, the *Collectors of the Bowl* <note>original Latin: *Collectores Catini*; referring to the *Tamchui*, a daily food collection for the poor</note>, which I believe should be noted here, belong to the same body as the *Collectors of the Chest* <note>original Latin: *Collectores Cistæ*; referring to the *Kuppah*, a weekly money collection for resident poor</note>; for this is again most clearly evident from *Maimonides* <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, a preeminent medieval Jewish scholar</note>:

<margin>Chapter 9, Section 11.</margin> <gloss>In the same way, they appoint collectors who take every single day from every single courtyard, etc.</gloss> *In the same way* (he had been speaking of the *Collectors of the Chest* to be established in the City) *they appoint Collectors, who receive donations every day from every house, etc.* And from this, the **Chest** <note>Hebrew: *Kuppah*</note> and the **Bowl** <note>Hebrew: *Tamchui*</note>, or the *Alms of the Chest* and the *Alms of the Platter* or *Bowl*, could be exchanged and combined with one another, if the public interest required it:

<margin>Yoreh De'ah Chapter 256, Section 4.</margin> <gloss>The people of the city are permitted to turn the Chest into a Bowl, and the Bowl into a Chest, and to change them to whatever they wish for the needs of the community.</gloss> **THE INHABITANTS OF THE CITY HAVE THE POWER TO CONVERT ALMS OF THE CHEST INTO ALMS OF THE BOWL, AND THOSE OF THE *Bowl* INTO THOSE OF THE *Chest*, AND TO SPEND THEM ON ALL MATTERS WHICH THEY SHALL JUDGE TO PERTAIN TO THE ADVANTAGE OF THE PUBLIC GOOD.** Now who will say that the *Collectors of the Bowl*, so called among the Hebrews, should be referred to the Synagogue? Therefore, this was once the practice in the State of the Jews. The Collectors of the *Chest* and the *Bowl* were established by the same Magistrate. Both collected their alms throughout the town at the doors of the citizens. The collected alms were often changed from one to the other at the discretion of the Magistrate. What then was the difference, you ask? What was the reason that Overseers of the poor with different names were established?

The difference is quite small; so much so, that the *Collectors of the Bowl* were often neglected in Cities and their duty entrusted to the *Collectors of the Chest*. Where, however, in larger Cities, these Collectors were established by the Sanhedrin with distinct duties and names, this distinction existed between them: that the *Collectors of the Chest* provided only for the needs of the poor of that specific City and Town, while the *Collectors of the Bowl* cared for any other poor people coming from elsewhere, who were staying in the city for one or a few days, coming and going. That is the reason why these Collectors of the Bowl were required to go from door to door every single day and distribute to each person their daily portion <note>original Latin: *dimensum*; a measured ration or allowance</note>, whereas the *Collectors of the Chest* went from door to door only every Friday and distributed money to the poor of the City for the entire week. This also explains why the former would receive any kind of food into their bowl, while the latter collected only money. For the *Collectors of the Chest* and they themselves...

<meta>catchword: and they themselves</meta>
