### CHAPTER 9. THE GOVERNMENT OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

<margin>
On the Hebrew Republic, book 6, chapter 3.
</margin>
...more serious matters were consulted by the *Seven-Man Council* <note>original: *Septem-Viris*; a local governing body of seven elders mentioned by Josephus</note>. I have proposed this more confidently because *Carolus Sigonius* <note>An influential 16th-century Italian humanist who studied ancient states</note>, who applied himself with singular industry to understanding the states of various nations, observed that the *Jewish Republic, under the rule of the Hasmoneans* <note>The dynasty of the Maccabees who ruled Judea from 140 to 37 BCE</note>*, became more popular* <note>meaning more democratic or populist</note> *and was constituted in the Greek manner. Since, however, he says, the Republic of the Hebrews was not at all* POPULAR, *but rather* of the Nobility <note>original: *Optimatium*; an aristocracy</note> *or* Royal, *as was said above, for that reason the people did not have very great power in it, since in an Aristocracy the Senate, and in a Kingdom the Law, prevailed. But if there was any strength or majesty in the people, it was especially after the Kingdom was destroyed by the Babylonian exile, when the people adopted the Hasmonean Princes for themselves, and* CONSTITUTED THE REPUBLIC IN THE GREEK MANNER. *Sigonius* illustrates this matter with examples. Whatever the case may be, it is sufficiently clear that the words of *Josephus* <note>The 1st-century historian Flavius Josephus</note> cannot be understood as referring to an ordinary *Senate* of either *Leaders* or *Judges*, and therefore they do not subvert our hypothesis.

Now I further suppose that within these *Courts* <note>original: *Curias*; referring to local assemblies or administrative bodies</note> of every *City*, there resided an equal and supreme power for arranging *sacred matters* and the exercise of *Divine Worship* to be celebrated in those places. For indeed, civil and *sacred* matters among the *Jews* were not distinct, except in theory. Truly, God formed the Jewish Republic in such a way that sacred affairs were mixed with Civil ones, and the *City* <note>the State</note> was by no means distinct—nor to be distinguished—from the *Church*. Civil and *Sacred* laws were blended together by the Lawgiver <note>Moses</note>, and the obedience to be paid to them is urged by the same arguments. The *Magistrates* were established as the Interpreters and Protectors of this entire body of Laws; they sat in the *Chair of Moses* <note>term: *sella Mosis*; a symbol of teaching and judicial authority derived from the authority of Moses</note> and were called by the common name Judges <note>original Hebrew: *Elohim* (אלהים); though often meaning God, here used in its biblical sense for human judges or rulers</note>. These Magistrates, therefore, had no less *right* and power for establishing the *Church* and ordering sacred things than for governing the city. Whether a *Synagogue* was to be built in the city they oversaw, where it should be built, at what times sacred rites should be celebrated, which rites were to be preferred over others, what kind of men were to be admitted to the communion of those rites, and who should be kept away and excommunicated—all this stood for them to define, just as much as which men they wished to grant the Rights of Citizenship, and to whom they would deny the same. Indeed, since the *City* was the same thing as the *Church*, to be enrolled in the *City* carried as much weight as being received into the communion of the *Church*. If I wished to prove this from the Talmudic Institutions, I would be foolishly redundant. For the entire discipline of the *Teachers of the Oral Law* <note>term: *Deuterotarum*; from the Greek *deuterosis*, referring to the Tannaim or early Rabbinic scholars who transmitted the Mishnah</note> is founded as if upon this—

### ON THE TRUE FORM, BOOK 2.

The principle is resolved that the *power over sacred matters* <note>original Latin: *sacrorum potestas*</note> belonged to the **House of Judgment** <note>Hebrew: *Beth Din*</note>, the *Council* <note>original Greek: *Synedrion*</note>, or the *Senate* of each locality; these local Senates were, however, subordinate to the **Great House of Judgment** <note>Hebrew: *Beth Din HaGadol*</note> in Jerusalem. Furthermore, since no small knowledge of both divine and human affairs was required for that difficult duty of a *Senator* among the Hebrews, it was entrusted only to the most skilled and prudent men—or at least it ought to have been—who for that reason are called **Elders** <note>Hebrew: *Zekenim*; Greek: *presbyteroi*</note>, in respect to their *wisdom* and *skill* rather than their *age*. Besides the fact that clear reason teaches this, it is also so consistent with the teachings of the Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish civil and ceremonial law</note> that they err more by demanding too much skill in *their Senators* than too little. Regarding this, since others have written at length, and especially *Selden* <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a famous English jurist and scholar of Jewish law</note>, I will not provide further details now.

Based on these premises, the certainty of which I think no one will easily doubt, I now finally conclude that *this Sacred Senate of each city*, called the **House of Judgment** <note>Hebrew: *Beth Din*</note> by the Hebrews, *presided in the more famous synagogue of that city* and held the primary place there. Let us hear Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note>:

<margin>
Laws of Fasting <note>Hebrew: *Hilchot Taanith*</note>, chapter 1, § 17.
</margin>

**On every fast day that is decreed upon the community because of public troubles, the House of Judgment and the Elders sit in the synagogue and examine the conduct of the people of the city from the conclusion of morning prayers until the middle of the day, etc.**

> *On every day of Fasting, which they decree over the assembly because of public evils, the SENATE & ELDERS sit in the house of the Synagogue, and inquire into the conduct of the men of that city from the end of morning prayers until the middle of the day.*

Behold the *Sacred Senate*, as is proper, presiding in the *Synagogue*! I do not bring other proofs now, because that will be provided soon with dedicated effort. Just as the Jews administered their affairs, both civil and sacred, in Canaan as long as their Republic was intact, so they established them entirely in Exile under the rule of a foreign Magistrate, according to the measure of liberty granted to them by that Magistrate. Thus, in the larger and more famous cities where they lived in great numbers, they formerly had a **Session** <note>Hebrew: *Yeshiva*</note> or **Assembly of Elders**, or a **Sacred and Civil House of Judgment** <note>Hebrew: *Beth Din*</note>, both for rendering judgment (insofar as it was permitted by the Gentile Magistrate) and for resolving cases of conscience and deciding questions of Religion; this *Senate* held the highest power over the Jewish community of that place. ### CHAPTER 9. ON THE GOVERNMENT of the Ancient Synagogue.

In the account of *Susanna, regarding the Judges of the Jewish people living in Babylon*, two **ELDERS** <note>Hebrew: *Zekenim*; Latin: *Seniores*</note> are mentioned among others. These men were accustomed to meet with the whole people at the house of *Jojakim*, a man of primary dignity among them, and there they handled legal matters. Even if this story is fictional, it is nevertheless probable that its author wished to decorate his drama with such circumstances that would smack of truth and could be easily reconciled with accepted customs. Therefore, whatever the case may be regarding the rest of the story, this much at least seems to be true: that the multitude of Jews dwelling in the more famous places of the Exile were ruled by certain Elders of no small authority and power.

Just as the greater Senates in Judea had as their President the most learned and honored man of that Council, so too the most distinguished Senates outside Judea—such as those of **Alexandria, Antioch** (and perhaps **Damascus**), **Babylon**, and later **Baghdad**—were notable for a President, who, like a Prince, defended the rights and honor of his nation in those foreign places with the greatest splendor. These leaders were called **Ethnarchs** <note>Greek: *Ethnarchai*, meaning "rulers of a nation"</note> by the Greeks, and **Patriarchs and Primates** by the Latins. To these Sacred Senates of the Jews and their Princes, we again assign the primary role in the Synagogue, the first place, and the first honor; for indeed, no one denies that the supreme power concerning sacred matters rested with them.

<margin>
From the book: *That Every Good Man is Free*, page 679.
</margin>

Until now, we have been occupied with explaining our opinion on the government of the more famous ancient synagogues. Now it will be necessary to build up these suppositions of ours from the records of the Ancients and reconcile them with those records, and finally apply them to those holy places of Scripture that deal with the government of the synagogue. Let us begin with *Philo and Josephus*. *Philo* the Jew nowhere more clearly outlines the form of the ancient synagogue than where he discusses the **Essenes** <note>An ancient Jewish sect known for communal living and strict observance</note>, those practical philosophers, their customs, and their entire way of life. It serves our purpose now to transcribe these words from that book:

"In moral philosophy alone do they exercise themselves," he says, "using the ancestral laws as their trainers—laws which the human mind cannot grasp **WITHOUT DIVINE INSPIRATION** <note>Latin: *absque afflatu numinis*; Greek: *aneu katakōchēs entheou*</note>. They teach these things both at other times and especially on the seventh days; for the seventh day is considered holy, on which they abstain from other works; arriving at holy places which are called **synagogues**, sitting in order according to their age—"

### CHAPTER 9. THE GOVERNANCE of the Old Synagogue.

...someone, whom *Josephus* calls an <term>Archon</term> <note>original Greek: ἄρχοντα; a ruler or magistrate</note> **Prefect**, and a <term>Boule</term> <note>original Greek: βυλὴν; a council or legislative body</note> <margin>Josephus, Life, p. 1020 & 1022.</margin> **Senate** in the **Synagogue** deliberating on the public affairs of the people of Tiberias, both elsewhere throughout his work and specifically in these words: <term>But Jesus, seeing that the state of affairs had changed, ordered the common people to withdraw, but requested the Senate to remain</term> <note>original Greek: συνιδὼν δ' ἡ μεταβολὴν Ἰησῦς, τ' μὲν δῆμον ἐκέλευεν ἀναχωρεῖν, προσμεῖναι δὲ τὴν βυλὴν ἠξίωσε</note>; *seeing indeed that the state of things was altered, Jesus ordered the rest of the multitude to depart, with* **Only the Senate** *remaining behind; namely,* from the **Synagogue**. We have conjectured that the supreme **Senate** of the people of Tiberias is designated by this. I would like it to be observed, however, that *Josephus*, both in the *History of the War* and in his *Life*, distinguishes **Ten Men** of this **Senate** with a special mark as being more eminent than the others. He calls them the <term>Ten most powerful of the Tiberians</term> <note>original Greek: τὲς δέκα τῶν Τιβεριέων δυνατωτάτες</note>; the <term>Ten leaders of the people</term> <note>original Greek: δέκα τ' πλήθες προεςῶτας</note>; and the <term>Ten foremost men of the Tiberians</term> <note>original Greek: δέκα πρώτες Τιβεριέων</note>. Yet *Josephus* does not explain the basis of that dignity or excellence, nor does it please me to inquire into it too anxiously because of the uncertainty of the matter. Jesus the Prefect, namely, by his own will admitted this man into the Synagogue and excluded another. Indeed, compare also the other things that follow. Besides this Jesus and the Senate, no Prefect or Prefects of the Synagogue of the Tiberians are named; on the contrary, the judgment of all matters is left to them as the supreme Prefects of the Tiberian people.

### CHAPTER 9. ON THE GOVERNANCE of the Ancient Synagogue.

Beyond these, one may find excellent examples of this kind of Synagogue Governance in the writings of **Benjamin of Tudela** <note>A 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented the lives of Jewish communities across Europe, Asia, and Africa</note>, who, in almost all the major places where the descendants of Israel resided in significant numbers, records <note>original Hebrew: ישיבות (*Yeshivot*)</note> **ASSEMBLIES OF LEARNED MEN**, (which are <note>original Greek: πρεσבυτέρια (*presbyteria*)</note> **Councils of Elders** according to the style of the Scriptures). By their common counsel, the sacred matters of those places—both academic and ecclesiastical—are directed. It will be useful to extract certain examples from his work for our own use, since upon this hypothesis, our entire comparison between the *Governance of the Synagogue* and the *Church* will be built in the following sections. Let us first hear our traveler from Tudela regarding the Jews of Damascus:

...nourished with rewards, from that time either the titles of dignities were invented (I am not unaware that the Jews seek deeper origins) or they became more frequently used—titles by which the Students of *Jewish Law* were honored by their Teachers after completing the course of their studies. However, a common title of this kind, and one already most widely accepted in the time of Christ the Lord, was that of רבי *Ribbi* or *Rabbi Doctor*, sought with great ambition by students of Jewish Law, so that by it they might distinguish themselves from the common crowd of men. Indeed, Christ the Lord rebukes the Pharisees because they desired to be honored by men <margin>Chapter 23, 7. 8.</margin> [with the title] "Rabbi, Rabbi," <note>original Greek: ῥαββί, ῥαββί</note> and He warns His disciples to beware of that vice of arrogance; *But you, He says, shall not be called* RABBI <note>original Greek: Ὑμεῖς δὲ μὴ κληθῆτε, ῥαββί</note>. Moreover, this dignity of Mastery was usually conferred through סמיכה *Imposition of hands* <note>The Hebrew term "Semikha" refers to the formal ordination of a rabbi</note> (ordinarily; for it was also conferred without this rite through the mere pronunciation of words) by another, who himself had received this *title* from another *Doctor* through the <gloss>laying on of hands</gloss> <note>original Greek: χειροθεσίαν</note>. I will not add more about it now, because these things have long since been diligently described by most learned men.

<margin>Selden, *On the Sanhedrin*, book 1, chapter 14, § 1. Alting, *History of Academic Promotions*, page 325.</margin>
Nevertheless, it must not be overlooked that these Doctors were of different qualities and offices. *Some, says Selden (Presbyters or* DOCTORS), *they created for the* DIGNITY *of teaching, and of* BINDING <note>prohibiting an action based on law</note> *or Prohibiting, and* LOOSING <note>permitting an action</note>, *or Permitting—that is, defining cases of conscience and sacred doubts, or as if in the dignity of a Doctorate of universal Theology; others they created with the faculty for explaining only some particular chapters of Theology, which were called* דברי יחידים *individual matters* <note>original Hebrew: divrei yechidim; often refers to minority opinions or specific private rulings</note>, *as if circumscribed within the singular limits of a Doctorate of Theology; others, which was most frequent, they gifted with the Power, License, or rather capacity for hearing any kind of cases, thus creating Doctors of Law as well as of their Theology; others, finally, for only some cases, such as pecuniary ones, but not permitted for capital [crimes].*

The same thing is noted in words that are not obscure, though briefer, <margin>*History of Academic Promotions*, pages 318, 321. In the Lexicon at the word סמיכה. *Laws of the Sanhedrin*, chapter 4, throughout.</margin> by *Alting*; it is also noted by *Buxtorf* from *Maimonides*, whose text he brought forward and interpreted. At the discretion, therefore, of the Promoter and the candidates, this title of *Doctor* was conferred upon them according to both aptitude and desires, as Maimonides explicitly states. To some was given the faculty of hearing pecuniary cases; to others, heavier cases involving *fines* <note>original Hebrew: דיני קנסות (dinei kenasot); legal cases involving statutory penalties rather than simple restitution</note>; to others, again, the license of teaching what is permitted and what is forbidden. *The court has the power*—these are the words of Maimonides—*to ordain him and to give him permission to judge, but not to give instruction regarding what is forbidden...* <note>original Hebrew: יש לבית דין לסמוך אותו וליתן לו רשות לדון ולא להורות באסור</note>

The *Sanhedrin* <note>The high court and supreme council of ancient Israel</note> can promote that man (one who is very well-versed in the Law of God) and grant him the authority TO JUDGE, but not to TEACH what is permitted and forbidden; or they give him authority to pronounce on the permitted and prohibited, but not to judge monetary cases; or both to teach and to hear monetary lawsuits, but not to judge cases involving fines, etc. Indeed, this authority to teach or judge was also conferred upon someone for a set time, or was restricted by any other conditions that the Promoter <note>The teacher or official conferring the rank</note> saw fit to apply according to the various circumstances of the matters.

Just as those who were declared and held fit for *judging* exercised this authority whenever a suitable opportunity arose, so those who were promoted to *teaching* did not only answer questions about various everyday cases of conscience, regarding things forbidden and permitted, but also, having obtained permission from their Promoters, they opened *Schools* and interpreted the Divine Law in them. I say, with license obtained from their Promoters; for otherwise this was by no means permitted to them as long as the *Promoter* was alive. ### Chapter 10. OF THE GOVERNMENT of the Ancient Synagogue.

... a Jew] residing in Rome conducted himself as an **INTERPRETER OF THE MOSAIC LAW**, *having admitted into his circle three others, similar to him in every respect.* Nor were those of a different kind whom the same *Josephus* identifies as the authors of the <margin>Antiquities, Book 17, chapter 8.</margin> sedition stirred up in Jerusalem near the end of *Herod’s* life: *“There were,” he says, “Judas son of Sariphaeus, and Matthias son of Margalothus, the most learned of the Jews, and <note>original Greek: ἦν, inquit, Ἰούδας ὁ Σαριφαῖος, καὶ Ματθίας ὁ Μαργαλώθου Ἰουδαίων λογιώτατοι</note> **MOST EXCELLENT INTERPRETES OF THE ANCESTRAL LAW**, and for that reason dear to the people, because they instructed the youth in disciplines; for they devoted themselves through entire days to all those who desired to make progress in virtue.”* In the following discourse of *Josephus*, they are called “sophists” <note>original Greek: σοφισταί; in this context, the term refers to professional teachers of wisdom or law, rather than the modern negative connotation of a "sophist."</note>. *Josephus* repeats this history <margin>The Jewish War, Book 1, chapter 21.</margin> with the title of “sophists” in the *Books which he wrote concerning the Jewish War;* <margin>The Jewish War, Book 2, chapter 7.</margin> a word which he also uses elsewhere, where he speaks of *Simon the Galilean*. And indeed, that title of “sophists” corresponds with the Hebrew *Chachamim* <note>original Hebrew: חכמים</note> or **Wise Men**, <margin>Under the word "Rabatz" (to recline/settle)</margin> by which such Teachers are designated in Hebrew. *Elias Levita* <note>A famous 15th-century Hebrew grammarian and scholar</note> acts as a witness; who, although he writes that the laying on of hands (*semikhah*) <note>The formal ritual of rabbinic ordination</note> did not prevail in Spain, because the Spanish Doctors *thought the laying on of hands only had a place in the land of Canaan*, yet says the Presidents of the Spanish Academies, whose sect many disciples followed, were called *Marbitzei Torah* <note>original Hebrew: מרביצי תורה</note> meaning **“those who cause the Law to settle/recline,”** while the others were simply called *Rabbanim* or **Doctors**, and were termed **WISE MEN**. This title is certainly not new, but has been attributed to literate men from the most ancient times. For I am not looking only at the fact that all investigators of natural science before *Pythagoras* were called **WISE MEN** (*sophoi*), as reported by *Laertius*, but especially that this title <margin>Lives of the Philosophers, p. 8, 15, chapter 18, 18.</margin> *Chacham* <note>Wise Man</note> was already accepted in this sense in the ancient monuments of the Sacred Scriptures. These words of *Jeremiah* will give us an example: *“But they say: come and let us devise plans against Jeremiah, for the Law shall not perish from the Priest, nor counsel from the* **WISE MAN**, *nor the word from the Prophet.”* Who is this **WISE MAN** (*Chacham*)? Any learned man, experienced and proven by long use of things, and a man skilled in the Divine Law. *Josephus* says of his own Nation: <margin>Antiquities of the Jews, Book 20, chapter 9.</margin> *“They attribute wisdom only to those who clearly understand the legal customs and are able to interpret the power of the sacred writings.”* <note>original Greek: Μόνοις δὲ σοφίαν μαρτυροῦσι τοῖς τὰ νόμιμα σαφῶς ἐπισταμένοις καὶ ἱερῶν γραμμάτων δύναμιν ἑρμηνεῦσαι δυναμένοις</note>

### CHAPTER 10. On the Government of the Synagogue and Church, etc.

### CHAPTER 10. THE GOVERNANCE of the Ancient Synagogue. 573

They are called *Pharisees*. We readily grant that the word **Chaver** <note>original Hebrew: חבר; "Associate" or "Colleague"</note> should be explained in this way in the passages of *Demai* and *Bechoroth* <note>Tractates of the Mishnah dealing with tithes and firstborn animals</note> illustrated by William Guise. Certainly, *Bartenora* <note>A 15th-century commentator on the Mishnah</note> saw more sharply into the passage of *Demai* than *Maimonides* did; and after him, the distinguished *Coccejus* had already excellently interpreted the words of the Code of *Demai*—**He who takes upon himself to be a Chaver** <note>original Hebrew: המקבל עליו להיות חבר</note>, that is, *one who takes upon himself the* STATUS *of an Associate*—following the mind of Guise as: *One who undertakes that he will be an* ASSOCIATE. That is to say, "one of the brotherhood and society of those entrusted with matters of purity" <note>original Greek: ἕνα τῆς ἀδελφότητος καὶ ἐταιρείας τῶν πεπιστευμένων περὶ καθαρότητος</note>. According to this interpretation of the word, it was possible for someone to be a *Learned Man* and yet not a **Chaver** <note>Associate</note>; although such followers of Learning were of little value among the Jewish people. However, it is another matter when the name **Chaver** is attributed to some <term>Doctor</term> <note>In this context, a "Doctor" is a formal teacher or scholar of the Law</note> with respect to the **Rav** <note>original Hebrew: רב; "Master" or "Teacher"</note>, the excellent Master; it has been stated and proven from certain places that the term is most frequently used in this latter sense in Hebrew history. Concerning another title of similar meaning, the **Talmid Chacham** <note>original Hebrew: תלמיד חכם; "Disciple of a Wise Man," a term for a Torah scholar</note>, I have nothing separate to remark at this time.

Furthermore, how great a number of these *Doctors*, *Scribes*, and *Students of Divine Wisdom* there were in the land of *Canaan* <note>The Land of Israel</note> around the age of Christ the Lord, when the study of traditions was flourishing, is clear from the Gospel History, in which we see Christ the Lord surrounded and beset by them in every place. <margin>Those who seem to interpret the laws with precision. <note>original Greek: οἱ δοκοῦντες μετ' ἀκριβείας ἐξηγεῖσθαι τὰ νόμιμα</note> See Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book II, chapter VII. See also Maimonides, *Code on the Sanhedrin*, chapter IV.</margin> How great then was the multitude of *Pharisees*, of whom Josephus says that *they interpreted the Divine Laws more accurately*? Indeed, Jewish history records that around that time there was such an abuse of *Promotions* <note>The formal granting of scholarly titles or ordinations</note> that it had to be corrected by suitable laws. From this it happened that these **Doctors** were not only scattered throughout Canaan but were also spread through all the other regions of the world inhabited by Jews.

> The words of the Torah are like wood, as it is said: *It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it* <margin>Prov. III. 18.</margin>; this is to tell you that just as a small piece of wood ignites a larger one, so too do the minor scholars sharpen the greater ones; and this is what Rabbi Chanina said: "I have learned much from my **TEACHERS**, even more from my **COLLEAGUES** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν γνωρίμων με; "from my acquaintances"</note>, but from my **DISCIPLES** more than from them both."

<margin>fol. 90. col. 2.</margin>
Indeed, in the Code *Sanhedrin*, the term **Chaver** <note>Associate or Colleague</note> is clearly opposed to the **Am ha-aretz** <note>original Latin: populo terræ; "the people of the land," a term for common folk who were not strictly observant or learned</note>, that is, the illiterate common people. They dispute there concerning the sense of the Law: *And you shall give from it an offering to Aaron the Priest.*
<margin>Num. xviii. 28.</margin>
Rabbi Ishmael is said to have interpreted that text such that by "Aaron" one should understand any Priest who is like Aaron—namely, one who is erudite and learned. *What was Aaron? A Chaver <note>Associate</note>, or a Learned Man; likewise his sons were Chaverim <note>Viri Docti; Learned Men</note>.* It is added: *From here we learn that gifts are not to be given to an* **UNLEARNED PRIEST**.

<margin>Commentary on chapter II. §. III. of the Code Demai.</margin>
For this reason, I would not say as absolutely as the most learned Guise <note>William Guise, a 17th-century English scholar of Oriental languages</note> that Maimonides <note>The famous 12th-century Jewish philosopher and legalist</note> was most gravely mistaken when he interpreted **Chaver** as a *disciple of the Wise*. It seems more true that the word **Chaver** (Associate) occurs with a double meaning among the Hebrew authors. Sometimes it is used for a **Teaching Colleague**, as we have already described (specifically when it is used with respect, either express or silent, to the word *Rav* or *Rabbi*). At other times, it refers to a member of a certain society of men who have bound themselves by certain laws to mutual purity and holiness of life. "They were," says Guise, "**Chaverim** <note>Associates</note>, it seems to me, a class of men who were not a little scrupulous regarding the minutiae of ritual impurities, who had entered a Society and bound themselves by fixed laws, so that they might conduct themselves more safely among one another and avoid the impurities resulting from commerce with the common people." This was clearly stated and explained by Guise, and we embrace it with both arms. Just as we also embrace the idea that these "Associates" are nearly the same men who, in the Gospel, are call-

### CHAPTER 10. ON THE GOVERNANCE OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE. 575

...notes that the word *Rav* <note>Hebrew: רב</note> or *Rava* <note>Aramaic: רבא</note> among the Chaldeans <note>The author uses "Chaldeans" to refer to speakers of Aramaic</note> signifies a **Prince, Leader, Noble, Prefect, Lord, or Master**; a fact which he confirms with suitable arguments. This is correct; *Rav* denotes "the greater" <note>original Greek: τὸν μείζονα</note> or superior, and thus is conveniently applied to any **Prefect**. Christ the Lord, when he warned his disciples that none of them should arrogantly claim the title of **Teacher** <note>original Greek: καθηγητής, "kathēgētēs"</note>, immediately added to his words: *But he that is GREATEST among you shall be your servant* <margin>Matthew 23:11.</margin> Whoever is the GREATEST <note>original Latin: MAXIMUS</note> among you (that is, he who thinks he has the highest right to be called *Rav* or EXCELLENT), let him be the Minister of you all. Thus, the *Rav* (the "greater") and the *Minister* <note>original Greek: διάκονος, "diakonos"</note> are placed in opposition to one another. However, when the word *Rav* is used for the **Masters** and the presiding officers of the **Synagogue Religion**, it certainly carries more force and emphasis than when it is simply attributed to any promoted **Teacher**. It is much like how in **Germany** the title of **Doctor** is common to both **Professors** of sciences and all those who have graduated <note>original Latin: "Promotis," those who have received a degree</note>, yet it is usually given to the former with a greater "power of the voice" <note>original Greek: δυνάμει τῆς φωνῆς, meaning the title carries more weight when applied to a Professor</note>. Indeed, perhaps this very word *Rav* assigned to the **Prefects of the Synagogue** could be thought to refer to the word for the **Synagogue** itself <note>Aramaic: כנישתא, "Keneshta"</note>. For the Syriac version <margin>Mark 5:35, 38; Luke 8:49.</margin> of *Mark 5* usually translates the Greek *archisynagogos* <note>meaning "Ruler of the Synagogue"</note> as *Rav Keneshta* <note>literally "Master of the Assembly"</note>. It has the same sense and significance, if I am not mistaken, as when *Rav Beita* is used by the **Syrians** for the **Steward** <note>original Greek: ὁ οἰκονόμος, "oikonomos"</note> or **Prefect of the house**; and it has long been observed by the learned that the word **MASTER** <note>Latin: "Magister"</note> was taken up by **Roman writers**, both ancient and more recent, in this way. <margin>See the Observations of learned men in de Bauldri's notes on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapters 7 and 14.</margin> Thus, among them we find **Masters of the People, Masters of the Districts, of Societies, of Villages, of Colleges, of the Knights, of Offices, of Correspondence, of the Palace, etc.**

If the word *Rav*, used for a **Synagogue Prefect** as we have described, admits this latter interpretation, then it would entirely agree in meaning with the title **Prince of the Synagogue** <note>Hebrew: ראש הכנסת, "Rosh Ha-Knesset"; or Aramaic: ריש כנישתא, "Rish Keneshta"</note>. # ON THE TRUE FORM, BOOK 2. 578

<margin>Observations on Luke 6:13.</margin>
...under the yoke [of the Romans], you will not deny that at least some form of the Sanhedrin <note>original: "Synedrii"; the supreme council and court of the Jewish people</note> survived in that age. Heinsius <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous Dutch scholar</note> has already observed, from Eusebius, that the Apostle Paul, before he took up the Christian faith, was an Apostle <note>original: "Apostolum"; here used in the Jewish sense of an official messenger or envoy, known in Hebrew as a Shaliach</note> of that kind; and I need not pointlessly repeat after other learned men that the Apostles of Jesus Christ himself, the supreme Prince and Patriarch of the Church, are not undeservedly compared with these Apostles. Now, this title of **Father of the House of Judgment** <note>original: אב בית דין (Ab Beit Din); the vice-president of the Sanhedrin</note> was adopted by the heads of schools <note>original: "Gymnasiarchis"</note> and the teachers of famous schools, who, together with other teachers or learned youths, formed a type of **Academic Assembly** <note>original: ישיבת (Yeshivat); a formal sitting or session of scholars</note>. Since the President of the Academic Assembly usually presided in the Synagogue as well, the title of **Father of the House of Judgment** eventually also became attached to the Rectors of the Synagogue. They seem to have preferred this title over that of **Head of the Assembly** <note>original: ראש ישיבה (Rosh Yeshiva)</note> or **Prince** <note>original: נשיא (Nasi)</note>, because those terms sounded somewhat more grand and excellent, and properly belonged only to the Rectors of the most famous Sanhedrins or schools.

<margin>Regarding year 833. Millenium 4, page 97.</margin>
In the writings of Ganz <note>David Ganz (1541–1613), a Jewish chronicler and astronomer</note>, I read that Rabbi Joshua, son of Hananiah, was *Father of the Senate and Precentor <note>The leader of prayer or chanting</note> on the Platform.* Indeed, the name *Father of the Senate*, as far as I can gather from that passage, is not used there in an absolute sense for the supreme President of the Academy, but for the President's Assessor <note>A judicial assistant or deputy</note>, which is the meaning of the word we were just discussing. For he is called **Rabbi Joshua** there, the **Associate of Rabbi Eliezer the Great**, who, if I am not mistaken, acted as the supreme President of the Academic Assembly and the Synagogal Gathering.

<margin>
Laws of Prayer, chapter 11, section 4.
Laws of Fasting, chapter 1, section 17; chapter 3.
</margin>
It remains to be noted that, besides this **Rav** or **Prefect of the Sacred Rites of the Synagogue**, the Jews in larger places where they live in greater numbers have a certain **political** Senate of **Pastors** or **Consuls** <note>original: פרנסים (Parnassim); community leaders who managed civic affairs</note>, whom Maimonides <note>The influential 12th-century Jewish philosopher and jurist</note> calls **Those Appointed over the Congregation** <note>original: ממונים על הצבור (Memunim al ha-Tzibur)</note> and elsewhere **Elders** <note>original: זקנים (Zekenim)</note>, if I am not mistaken. I described them sufficiently at the beginning of this book. Among them is the supreme power concerning **matters outside the synagogue** <note>original: τὰ ἔξω τῆς συναγωγῆς (ta exo tes synagoges)</note>. They govern the Jewish community in the manner of **Consuls**. They ensure that the place of worship and its instruments are kept in good repair. They impose monetary taxes on their subjects according to each person's means, to be spent for sacred or civil use. They bring the disobedient back into line through Excommunication and other means, having no doubt obtained the prior consent of the **Master of the Synagogue**. Of the poor...

It seems to me that such a **Senate** of respected men from the common people was established by the Jews in certain more famous places of their Exile <note>original: "Exilii"; referring to the Jewish Diaspora, or the dispersion of Jews outside their homeland</note>, partly because they could not have a sufficient supply of learned men everywhere, and partly because the synagogue communities were not large enough to support many learned men. For truly, these **Synagogue Senates** seem to me to be considered as a shadow and <term>outward form <note>Greek: σχῆμα (schema)</note></term> of those **Judicial and Civil Senates**—those **Presbyters** <note>original: "Presbyterorum"; elders or community leaders</note>, I say, by whom we have said the Jews were formerly governed both in their Homeland and in famous places outside their Homeland. I have various arguments for this:

1. The names <term>Elders and Parnasim <note>Hebrew: זְקֵנִים & פַּרְנָסִים (Zekenim & Parnasim)</note></term> by which those modern consuls are honored, were, according to their ancient usage, appropriate for literate and learned men. 

2. Even now, the teacher of a Synagogue or Academy seems to me to be called, in respect to this Senate, the <term>Father of the House of Judgment <note>Hebrew: אב בית דין (Av Beit Din); traditionally the vice-president of the high court, but here used as a title for a communal head</note></term>. For although he does not preside over a **Senate** of men of his own rank and order in the Synagogue, it sometimes happens that he is invited by these Pastors or Rectors of the Synagogue into their Senate, both to deliver a legal opinion in more difficult cases and to deliberate with them on community affairs. And since there is no other high council over which he might preside, this Senate of "consuls" is held to be a shadow and a type of the <term>House of Judgment <note>Hebrew: בית דין (Beit Din); a rabbinical court</note></term>. 

3. These **Parnasim** also exercise certain **rights** which were formerly the property of the <term>Courts <note>Greek/Hebrew: τοῖς בּתי דינין (tois Battei Dinim)</note></term>. For unless I am mistaken, they also exercise the power of both Fining and Excommunicating, and even of punishing, where that custom prevails, for insolent behavior...

### CHAPTER II. OF THE GOVERNANCE of the Ancient Synagogue.

...it becomes clear, because Christ the Lord is said to have entered this *Synagogue* on the Sabbath day, **according to his custom** <note>original Greek: κατ' τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ; Latin: PROUTI CONSUEVERAT</note>. Indeed, on Sabbath days, the *Synagogue*—so named for its purpose <note>original: φερωνύμως (pheronumos), meaning "bearing the name" of its function as a gathering place</note>—is most frequently attended. The sacred solemnities of the **reading**, performed while standing, and the subsequent **explanation**, also align well with the nature of a *Synagogue*. However, the fact that Christ sat while teaching suggests the atmosphere of a School. Perhaps, therefore, we shall not err if we conclude that this *Nazarene Synagogue* served the inhabitants as both a *School* and a <term>House of Prayer <note>original: Proseucha; a term often used for a synagogue, specifically emphasizing its role as a place of prayer</note></term>. For we have elsewhere supposed that this was often the case in smaller locales.

Now, in this entire historical account, no official of the *Synagogue* is mentioned except for one **Attendant** <note>original Greek: ὑπηρέτην (hupereten)</note>, the *Minister* of the Synagogue, from whom the book was **given** to Christ, and to whom it was returned. <margin>verse 20</margin> In the following context of the narrative, the **eyes of all** are said to have been **fixed** upon him, <margin>verse 28</margin> and **all were filled with wrath**: yet, besides this *Minister of the Synagogue*, no *Prefect* of the Synagogue, nor any other member distinguished by rank, is encountered here. However, those who are not strangers to synagogue customs will not find this surprising. For the Presidents of the Synagogue had hardly any business in the ordinary religious solemnities (provided the President himself was not teaching), other than to maintain their dignity in the synagogue by their presence and, if anything extraordinary occurred, to moderate and settle it by their authority. When nothing out of the ordinary was done in the synagogue, they had almost nothing to do. Indeed, many religious acts could be carried out even in their absence, and even today, sermons in synagogues are not infrequently held while they are absent.

Therefore, what prevents us from considering the absence of the Prefects of the Synagogue in this case as well? But there is no difficulty here, since elsewhere explicit mention is made both of **several Rulers of the Synagogue**, and of **one**.

Luke indeed shows several in the Pauline History: <margin>Acts 13:14</margin> **But they (Paul and his companions), having departed from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia, and having entered the Synagogue on the Sabbath day, they sat down. After** the READING **of the** LAW and the PROPHETS, **the** RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGE <note>original Greek: οἱ Ἀρχισυνάγωγοι (hoi Archisynagogoi)</note> **sent to them, saying: "Men and brethren, etc."** It is clear that Luke is speaking of the *Synagogue* so-called. He mentions that the **Law and the Prophets** were read therein. Whether there was **one** reader of the **Law and the Prophets** in the synagogue, or several; whether the *Minister* of the Synagogue read the **Law and the Prophets**, or others...

## Concerning the True FORM, BOOK 2.

...Luke does not explain how he called [Paul] out from the assembly to read. This is not surprising, because he was speaking of a custom that was well-received and sufficiently well-known at that time. Besides this *Reader* or *Readers of the Law*, it is useful for our purpose to note from the words of *Luke* the **Rulers of the Synagogue** <note>original Greek: τοὺς Ἀρχισυναγώγους (tous Archisynagogous)</note>, that is, the **PREFECTS** or *Chiefs* of the SYNAGOGUE. Regarding their qualities and duties, you can gather nothing from the name itself except for the fact that they granted *Paul* and his companions the power to speak; from this, one may conclude that they presided in the Synagogue as the supreme judges and moderators of the solemnities to be performed therein. On this point, one thing deserves attention: several Prefects of the Synagogue are mentioned here, and, as far as can be gathered from this History, they were all of equal power, order, dignity, and office. These men would have granted the opportunity to speak, perhaps with the consent of the Master of the Synagogue, or in his absence, or even if that Synagogue had no Master at all. However, the former explanation now seems more probable to me. Furthermore, elsewhere as well, multiple Prefects of a single <margin>chapter 5, verse 22.</margin> Synagogue seem to be clearly indicated by Mark, when he calls *Jairus* **ONE of the rulers of the synagogue** <note>original Greek: ἕνα τῶν ἀρχισυναγώγων (hena tōn archisynagogōn)</note>. Is it truly believable that *Josephus*, who describes every famous location in his administrative district, would make no mention of this place at all if it could be compared to other cities in fame and size? He says there was a spring, arising in a pleasant tract of land, which we may believe first attracted people to build homes there; then, through frequent habitation, a **Village** <note>original Latin: *Pagus*, referring to a rural settlement or district</note> was formed. This village flourished greatly in the time of Christ, but was later diminished again according to Christ’s prophecy; we have no doubt that this decline had already occurred by the time of *Josephus*. Indeed, *Lightfoot* was persuaded—as I am most firmly persuaded—that *Josephus* was speaking of no other Capernaum than this very one, because our Capernaum was situated in the exact spot where *Josephus* reports this spring bubbled up.

The historians of the New Testament speak of *Capernaum* in such a way that it is difficult to accept there was more than one **Synagogue** there. For besides the fact that, although mention of Capernaum is made very frequently, multiple synagogues are never numbered there, we believe the words of *Luke* lead us to this conclusion. In 

<margin>Chapter 7.</margin>

recounting the story of the Centurion—a man who was certainly not a Jew—who wished to keep his dying servant among the living, *Luke* tells us he sent the **ELDERS OF THE JEWS** <note>original Greek: τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους τῶν Ἰουδαίων (tous presbyterous tōn Ioudaiōn)</note> to Christ to intercede for him. As we shall soon explain more clearly, these were the "rulers" or "synagogue leaders" <note>original Greek: τοὺς ἄρχοντας (tous archontas), τοὺς ἀρχισυναγώγους (tous archisynagōgous)</note>, one of whom was *Jairus*. These elders said: "For he loves our nation, and he himself built the **SYNAGOGUE** for us" <note>original Greek: Ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν, καὶ τὴν συναγωγὴν αὐτὸς ᾠκοδόμησεν ἡμῖν</note>. Is it likely or even probable that the inhabitants of Capernaum would owe the benefit of a built synagogue to a Gentile man if Capernaum had been such a famous city? Does it not rather suggest that we should think of it as a more celebrated village or hamlet? The dying servant belonged to a single Centurion;

# On the True FORM, BOOK 2.

This man <note>The Roman Centurion</note> approached the Elders of the Jews; they, in turn, went to Christ on behalf of a single servant at the Centurion's request. Are these the kind of circumstances that would make us dare to count Capernaum among the more famous and populous cities?

<margin>John, chapter 6, verse 59.</margin>
In the Gospel of John, only *one synagogue in Capernaum* is mentioned. "These things he said in the synagogue, teaching in Capernaum" <note>original Greek: Ταῦτα εἶπεν ἐν συναγωγῇ, διδάσκων ἐν Καπερναούμ (Tauta eipen en synagōgē, didaskōn en Kapernaoum)</note>. Is this to be understood as "in one of the synagogues" <note>original Greek: ἐν μίᾳ τῶν συναγωγῶν (en mia tōn synagōgōn)</note>, as Luke phrases it elsewhere?

<margin>Book 1, Part 1, chapter 14.</margin>
The very name *Kephar* <note>original Hebrew: כפר (Kfar), meaning a village or small settlement</note> indicates that Capernaum was a *Village* or a notable hamlet of the type described earlier as "Small Cities" <note>original Hebrew: עיירות (Ayayarot), a term for towns that were not large enough to be walled cities but were more than tiny clusters of homes</note> (for indeed, Capernaum is called a "city" <note>original Greek: πόλις (polis)</note> by the Evangelist). And did such villages have more than one synagogue? I will say it as it is: when I consulted the learned works of *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned scholar of biblical geography</note> on *Sacred Chorography*, it seemed clear to me that Capernaum was a village near *Tiberias*, situated by Lake Gennesaret. At first, as can be gathered from Christ's words, it was small; later, it became more notable when the synagogue was built there. It was very close to *Tiberias*, and it is not likely that on the same shore, at such a short distance from one another, there were two towns competing in fame.

<margin>on Matthew chapter 9, verse 18; chapter 11, verse 23; and chapter 7, verse 5.</margin>
Therefore, *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch humanist and legal scholar</note> correctly advised before me that *there was only ONE SYNAGOGUE IN CAPERNAUM*. Let us establish, then, that there was one synagogue in Capernaum, and that there were several leaders of that synagogue, one of whom was named *Jairus*. And who were those leaders, if not those "Elders of the Jews" <note>original Greek: τῶν Ἰουδαίων Πρεσβύτεροι (tōn Ioudaiōn Presbyteroi)</note> whom Luke mentions as interceding with Christ the Lord for the Centurion’s servant? These were the judges and rulers of that place according to our hypothesis, and they presided in the synagogue, forming a *council of elders* <note>original Greek: γερουσίαν (gerousian)</note>, or a certain *Yeshiva* <note>original Hebrew: ישיבה (Yeshiva), a session or council</note> or *Presbytery* <note>original Greek: Πρεσβυτέριον (Presbyterion)</note>. The very name *Presbyter* [Elder] easily leads us to this conclusion.

<margin>Acts 18:8, 17.</margin>
Indeed, in the synagogue at Corinth, two **RULERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>original Latin: ARCHISYNAGOGI</note> are also identified by their names: "Crispus and Sosthenes, rulers of the synagogue" <note>original Greek: Κρίσπος ϗ Σωσθένης ἀρχισυνάγωγοι (Krispos kai Sōsthenēs archisynagōgoi)</note>. It does not appear that there were multiple synagogues in Corinth; and therefore *Crispus and Sosthenes* seem to have been *leaders* of one and the same synagogue at one and the same time. Both of them also seem to have given their names to Christ <note>i.e., converted to Christianity</note> through the preaching of Paul.

<margin>verses 8, 17; chapter 1:1.</margin>
This is stated clearly regarding *Crispus*, but more obscurely regarding *Sosthenes*. For certainly this *Sosthenes* seems to be the same man mentioned by the Apostle in the *First Epistle to the Corinthians*.

### CHAPTER II. THE GOVERNMENT of the Ancient Synagogue.

<margin>chapter 5, verse 22.</margin>
Therefore, in the writings of the New Testament, *multiple* Leaders of the Synagogue are frequently assigned to *one* single *Synagogue*. However, there is one passage that presents only *one* *Leader of the Synagogue*. To be sure, *Luke* recounts that the Lord Christ, in a certain place on the Sabbath day, gave a sermon in the Synagogue according to custom, and granted health to an *infirmed woman*; but the Prefect of the Synagogue took offense at this, and for that reason rebuked the people. The words are: <margin>Luke 13:14</margin> "But the **LEADER OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>original Greek: ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος (apokritheis de ho archisynagōgos)</note> answered with indignation, because *Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, and said to the crowd; etc.*" Truly, since elsewhere *several* Leaders of the Synagogue are mentioned, there is no force or inconvenience in accepting what is called here the "Leader of the Synagogue" or *Prefect of the Synagogue* as referring to *one* of the Prefects of that Synagogue, which the *Belgians* <note>Likely referring to the Dutch Reformed scholars who produced the Statenvertaling Bible annotations</note> also noted regarding this text. *One* of the *Prefects* of the Synagogue is therefore here called the "Leader of the Synagogue" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος (ho archisynagōgos)</note>, the *Prefect of the Synagogue*. 

In a similar way of speaking, *Jairus*, who is called by *Mark* <margin>chapter 5, verse 22.</margin> "one of the Leaders of the Synagogue" <note>original Greek: εἷς τῶν Ἀρχισυναγώγων (heis tōn archisynagōgōn)</note>, is simply called by *Luke* "the Leader of the Synagogue" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος (ho archisynagōgos)</note>, which should certainly be translated: <margin>chapter 8, verse 49.</margin> *a certain Prefect of the Synagogue*. In exactly the same manner, *John* is to be understood regarding *Nicodemus*: *Now there was a certain man of the Pharisees, whose name was Nicodemus*, <margin>John 3:1</margin> a "Ruler of the Jews" <note>original Greek: ἄρχων Ἰυδαίων (archōn Ioudaiōn)</note>, a **PRINCE OF THE JEWS**. *Beza* <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a prominent Protestant theologian</note> correctly translates this as: *From the leading men of the Jews*. 

If, however, anyone prefers the simple sense of the phrase and chooses to feel that *one* specific *Prefect* of the Synagogue is being noted here, I will not draw the sword of contention with him in such an uncertain matter. For if this were some minor or common *Synagogue*, it is possible that its Government was entrusted by the local Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and court of justice among the ancient Jews</term> to a single Master, who is called the *Leader of the Synagogue* here; or, if the local Holy Senate itself presided in this Synagogue, it is possible that its President was specifically and emphatically called "the Leader of the Synagogue" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος (ho archisynagōgos)</note> by *Luke*; more on this shortly. 

Both views are sufficiently consistent with the hypotheses just illustrated. Indeed, what is found in the body of Civil Law, in the writings of *Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a prominent bishop and heresiologist</note>, and other authors—whether secular or Sacred—concerning the *Government of the Synagogue* (many of which have already been cited above where we disputed against *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit (1594–1643), a French scholar of law and antiquity</note> <margin>chapter 5</margin>), will be shed with no small amount of light if they are compared with our earlier hypotheses regarding the *Government of the Synagogue*. For even if we do not place as much confidence in their authority as we do in domestic testimonies <note>Referring to Jewish sources or the direct biblical text</note>, it is nevertheless not to be doubted that at least some things regarding the *Government of the Synagogue* and its rituals...

Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer</note> accepts this word in either of these senses when he says that Joseph the Apostle <note>A prominent Jewish convert to Christianity in the 4th century</note> *removed Leaders of the Synagogues, Priests, and Elders from their office*. By *these teaching Leaders of the Synagogue* we should understand either the *Presidents of the Elders*, or those singular *Masters of Sacred Matters* who are called **Teachers** <note>original: Didascali</note> in the statutes of **Roman Law**, and among the Jews are called **Rabbis** <note>original Hebrew: רבנים (Rabbanim)</note>. ### CHAPTER II. THE GOVERNANCE of the Ancient Synagogue.

...of every member of the synagogue, to moderate the sacred rites. But in those places where no such sacred authority <term>exousia</term> resided, there only that *Master of the Synagogue* <note>original Latin: Synagogæ Magister</note> was called *Archisynagogus*, whom we were just describing. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop and historian</note> accepts this word in either of these two meanings when he says that Joseph the Apostle removed *Archisynagogi*, Priests, and Elders from their office. For where he distinguishes *Archisynagogi* from *Presbyters* <note>Elders</note>, with Priests placed between them, he shows clearly enough that by "Presbyters" he means here either the *Assessors* and *Colleagues* of the *Archisynagogi* in the sacred council <term>Presbyterium</term>, or those very Seniors of the Synagogue who are elsewhere called <term>Memunim al ha-tzibbur</term> <note>original Hebrew: ממונים על הצבור, meaning "Those appointed over the community"</note> and <term>Parnasim</term> <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים, meaning "Pastors" or providers</note>, whom I described in the previous chapter. Once this is admitted, nothing remains except to understand by **ARCHISYNAGOGI** either the **PRESIDENTS** of the sacred councils, or those **MASTERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE** to whom the moderation of the synagogue’s sacred rites was alone entrusted. And the concept of **ARCHISYNAGOGI** is taken in one of these two senses by most other authors. Consider this passage from *Justin Martyr* concerning teaching Archisynagogi:

<margin>Dialogue with Trypho the Jew, page 366.</margin>
> *Therefore, meeting and talking together, he says, do not attack the Son of God with insults, nor following the* **PHARISEE TEACHERS** (obedient to the Pharisee teachers), *ever mock the King of Israel with taunts; such as your* **ARCHISYNAGOGI** **TEACH** *after the prayers are finished.*

By these teaching *Archisynagogi*, we should understand either the Presidents of the Elders, or those specific *Masters* of sacred rites who are called *Didascali* <note>Teachers</note> in the Constitutions of Roman Law, and among the Jews are called <term>Rabbanim</term> <note>original Hebrew: רבנים, Rabbis</note>. Nor does the term appear in any other sense in the writings of Lampridius. *He wanted it to appear*, so he says of *Alexander Severus*; <margin>In the Life of Alexander Severus, chapter 28.</margin> *that he traced his origin from the Roman people, because he was ashamed to be called a Syrian: especially because on a certain feast day, as is their custom, the people of Antioch, the Egyptians, and the Alexandrians had provoked him with little insults, calling him a* **SYRIAN ARCHISYNAGOGUS** *and a* **HIGH PRIEST** <note>original Latin/Greek: Archiereus</note>. Alexander was a Syrian, and he favored the Jewish nation and religion; therefore, by way of a rather bold insult, he was called by the people of Antioch and Alexandria a "Syrian Archisynagogus" and "High Priest," which were accepted names of dignity among the Jews. For it is certain that Severus, the best of the Roman Emperors, was devoted to the Jewish religion...

Among the Jews, there were also certain **FATHERS OF THE SYNAGOGUES**; likewise **PRIESTS**, **ELDERS** <note>original: *Presbyteri*</note>, and **DEACONS** <note>original: *Diaconi*</note> of the *Synagogues*, whom the *Jews* call *Chazzanim* <note>original: *Azanitas*; these were synagogue officials who served as assistants, cantors, or beadles</note>. There were also **APOSTLES**, and positioned above all these were the **PATRIARCHS**. However, in this passage by *Dionysius* <note>Dionysius of Alexandria, a 3rd-century bishop</note>, the term *Head of the Synagogue* <note>original: *archisynagogus*</note> signifies something else, which is obscure to me. We will pass over what *Valesius* <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century scholar and editor of ecclesiastical histories</note> has added here regarding the *Governance of the Ancient Synagogue*, drawn from *Epiphanius* and the *Imperial Constitutions*. These points agree with what we noted above from *Petit* <note>Samuel Petit, a scholar known for his work on ancient laws</note>; we discussed then to what extent those points were true or false. Now we only need to consider the fact that *Valesius* says it is *obscure to him what the word "Head of the Synagogue" signifies in this context*. It seems to me that this doubt can be easily resolved by saying that *Dionysius*, Bishop of *Alexandria* (where the term *Archisynagogus* was in common use), chose to use it rather than any other term to indicate that *Macrianus* <note>Fulvius Macrianus, a financial administrator under Emperor Valerian who was associated with Egyptian magicians and the persecution of Christians</note> was, as it were, the *Leader* and *Prefect* of a group of *Egyptian* magicians. This is especially true since the word *synagogue* <note>original: *synagoge*</note> had already begun to be used frequently by Christians of that time in a negative sense to mean a *gathering of wicked men*, following the example of the passage in the Apocalypse <margin>Revelation 2:9, 3:9</margin> which mentions a *synagogue* and *Satan*, the *Synagogue of Satan*. Therefore, for Dionysius, the *Head of the Synagogue* <note>original: *Archisynagogos*</note> here is the Prefect and Leader of any assembly of wicked and criminal men; in this same category, Christians everywhere tended to place the *Jewish Teachers* <note>original: *Didiscali*</note> and *Heads of Synagogues*. Jerome calls these same men the *Overseers of the Synagogue*. <margin>Jerome, *Letter to Algasia*, Part III, page 52, column 3.</margin> He says, "They have **OVERSEERS** in the **SYNAGOGUES**, the most learned men appointed to a foul task: if they cannot distinguish by sight whether a virgin's blood or menstrual flow is clean or unclean, they sample it by taste." <note>This graphic description reflects the intense anti-Jewish polemic common in the writings of Church Fathers like Jerome.</note> Who does not see that *Jerome* intended to describe the *Heads of Synagogues* of that latter kind, whom we have called the *Masters of Synagogue Rites*?

Let us now briefly touch upon the remaining names by which the dignity of the *Synagogal Prefecture* is expressed in Roman Laws. Therefore, besides the *Heads of Synagogues*, you may find there **ELDERS** <note>original: *Presbyteros*</note> and **SENIORS**, whose meaning I touched upon just now. These names are certainly used in the Laws either in a broader and more general sense to mean the entire Holy Senate of the *Synagogue Prefects* (not excluding the *Head of the Synagogue*), or in a stricter sense for the *Assistants of the Head of the Synagogue* who, along with him, formed the holy Presbytery, or for the *Political Consuls*—

The former significance is manifest in these Rescripts <note>Imperial decrees or formal responses to legal questions</note>; for example: *If any dispute should arise between Christians and Jews, it shall be settled not by the* **ELDERS OF THE JEWS** <note>original: *Senioribus Judæorum*</note> *but by the ordinary Judges.* Again: *Those who have devoted themselves with total devotion to the Synagogues of the Jews, to the Patriarchs, or to the* **ELDERS** <note>original: *Presbyteris*</note>, *and living in the aforementioned sects, preside over the Law itself, shall remain immune from all personal as well as civil duties.* This passage seems corrupt, but was quite successfully restored by Petit <note>Samuel Petit, a 17th-century legal scholar</note> in this manner: *And in the memorable sect of the Nation, they themselves preside over the Law.* Who can deny that the **ELDERS** and **PRESBYTERS** in these Constitutions <note>Imperial laws</note> are considered entirely as Sacred Persons, who preside over both the settling of disputes and the performance of sacred rites? And what could be clearer than the text of the *Novella* <note>The *Novellae Constitutiones*, laws issued by Emperor Justinian</note>, in which **Presbyters** are confounded with the **Chief Interpreters** and **Masters**. The words are as follows: *Neither shall those have the license, who are called the greatest of all by them,* **CHIEF INTERPRETERS** <note>original: *Archiperecitæ*; likely a Latinization of the Greek for "Chiefs of the study house"</note>, *or* **PRESBYTERS**, *or perhaps* **MASTERS**, *to prohibit this by any penalties or excommunications.* That by **Chief Interpreters** and **Masters** are designated the **Heads of the Synagogue** <note>original: *Archisynagogi*</note>, or the Prefects of the Sacred Sanhedrins, no one doubts. And yet, the very same people are here called **Presbyters**. You should, however, take these names in a more specific and restricted sense in those places where **Presbyters** or **Elders** are distinguished from the **Heads of the Synagogue**; whether you then understand them as *Assessors* to the Heads of the Synagogue, or as the *Consuls* and *Pastors* of the Synagogues. Indeed, in many texts, this cannot be defined with sufficient accuracy. This occurs in Law 14 of the Theodosian Code, *concerning the Jews and Worshippers of Heaven*, as well as in the writings of Epiphanius, in the words described above. By the **ELDERS** <note>original: *Majores*; literally "Greater ones"</note> (a title found in the inscription of Law 23 of the Theodosian Code), it is certain that those Lay Rulers and Consuls of the Synagogues are meant, who are called **Parnasim** <note>original Hebrew: פרנסים; administrative leaders who managed the community's needs and charity</note>. This is evident from the fact that they are distinguished from the **Teacher**. The inscription reads: *The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augustus to Annatus, the* **TEACHER** <note>original: *Didascalo*</note> *and* **ELDERS** <note>original: *Majoribus*</note> *of the Jews.* The **Teacher** in this place is the same as the Master <note>original Hebrew: רב / *Rav*</note> of the Synagogue, and the **Elders** are those Pastors from among the common people of the Synagogue, whom I described in the previous chapter. These same individuals are to be understood as the **FATHERS OF THE SYNAGOGUES** in a certain Rescript of Constantine, since they themselves are distinguished from the **Heads of the Synagogue**; unless you would rather interpret this title of honor as the **Fathers of the Houses of Judgment** <note>original Hebrew: אבות בתי דינין / *Avot Batei Din*</note>, concerning which, as well as the **PATRIARCHS** and **HIEROPHANTS**, we have argued above.

# CHAPTER II. THE GOVERNMENT of the Ancient Synagogue.

<margin>

Until now, we have said nothing about the title **Head of the Assembly** <note>Hebrew: *Rosh Ha-Knesset*</note>, to which the Greek term **Ruler of the Synagogue** <note>Greek: *Archisynagogos*</note> most closely corresponds. This title appears in the records of both ancient and more recent Teachers. We will provide one example from the Mishnah and another from Maimonides. The Mishnah tractate *Sotah* states the following: *By what ritual are the blessings of the High Priest performed?* **THE ATTENDANT OF THE SYNAGOGUE** <note>original: *Chazzan Ha-Knesset*</note> **takes the book of the Law and hands it to the HEAD OF THE ASSEMBLY.** Maimonides, in another place, writes in this manner: **Even the ATTENDANT OF THE SYNAGOGUE or the HEAD OF THE ASSEMBLY does not read of his own accord until the congregation, or the most distinguished person among them, calls upon him to read.** <note>original Hebrew: ואפילו חזן הכנסת או ראש הכנסת אינו קורא מעצמו עד שיאמרו לו הצבור או גדול שבהם לקרות</note>

But who is this **Head of the Assembly** in both of these passages? Certainly, in the first instance from *Sotah*, by **Head of the Assembly** one may understand either the Prince of the **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin: The supreme legal and religious council of ancient Israel, consisting of 71 judges</term>—the primary man of the Synagogal gathering, who was undoubtedly present alongside the Sacred Senate of seventy men for the solemn reading by the High Priest and the King mentioned there—or a specific Teacher who was specially appointed by the Sanhedrin to oversee a particular synagogue within the Temple. 

However, the first option seems much more likely to me, because this reading was performed not in the Temple Synagogue itself, but in the **Court** <note>The *Atrium* or outer courtyard of the Temple</note> by the High Priest and the King during the festivals of Atonement and Tabernacles. In the Court, whom else would we conceive as the Prince of the entire gathering of Israelites other than the Prince of the Great Sanhedrin, or his Deputy, if he were absent? For he was truly the Primary Member of the Gathering or the **Prince of the Assembly**, which is how Wagenseil <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil, a 17th-century German Hebraist</note> and Sheringham <note>Robert Sheringham, an English scholar who translated parts of the Mishnah</note> have interpreted this title; and these sacred rites were to be carried out according to the judgment of him and the High Senate. 

Nor was it beneath the dignity of the President of that Great Council of Elders to perform this service for the **Sagan** <term>Sagan: The Deputy High Priest, who stood next in rank to the High Priest</term> and the High Priest. This is partly because the High Priest and his deputy, the Sagan, were truly the most conspicuous in dignity within the Jewish nation after the King; partly because these rites were celebrated in the Temple, where the authority of the High Priest was undoubtedly greatest; and finally, because on the public Day of Atonement, the High Priest and his deputy were delegated to God on behalf of the Sanhedrin and the entire Jewish people, and therefore the highest honor was to be accorded to them during that festival. Similarly, in Maimonides, by **Head of the Assembly**, you may understand either the specific overseer of a synagogue, elsewhere called a **Parnas** <term>Parnas: A communal leader or administrator responsible for the physical and financial needs of the synagogue</term>, or a member of the Senate...

# CHAPTER XII.

*Various models of Synagogue Governance, proposed in the preceding chapters, are compared with the form of Governance of the early Christian Church; and it is proved by solid arguments that none of them can be applied to the form of Governance of the Apostolic Church except for the first one, in which the more famous Synagogues are supposed to have been ruled by a Council of several Teachers, who constituted a certain sacred Consistory or Presbytery.*

**W**e would have exhausted ourselves in vain up to this point in describing the *Various models of Synagogue Governance*, if we were unable to apply any of them to the true form of Governance of the Christian Church, which we claimed for it in the second Chapter of this Book. ...since in those places where the *Jews lived under foreign power*, the [scholastic regime] was everywhere the same as the *Ecclesiastical* one. Indeed, since they were not allowed to have *Schools* distinct from *Synagogues* in every place, for this reason the *Synagogues* themselves in many places were considered *Gymnasiums* <note>In this context, a "gymnasium" refers to a place of study or a secondary school, not a place for physical exercise.</note>, or, if you prefer, *Gymnasiums* were merged with *Synagogues*; with the same *Teachers of the Synagogue* presiding over both the assembly and the *School* at the same time. The *Christians*, since they always lived under *foreign power* whether in the land of *Canaan* or outside it, imitated this same practice. And we have a brilliant argument for this in the **Acts of the Apostles**, where it is preached concerning the Apostle *Paul* that he separated the *Disciples at Ephesus*, debating daily in the *School of a certain Tyrannus*. The *method* of teaching of the *Teachers of the First Christian Church* was so *Ecclesiastical* <note>Related to the church assembly or congregation.</note> that it shared not a little with the *Scholastic* <note>Academic or school-based.</note> method. Indeed, as I have just said, the *School & Synagogue* were merged among the Jews in many places outside the land of Canaan—and perhaps even in the less famous places of the land of Canaan itself—and the *Governance* of both was easily entrusted to the same people. This difficulty is so far from delaying us that, on the contrary, the *duties and circumstances of the Overseers of the First Church* can be explained from this very hypothesis, and from no other, as we shall see in what follows.

# On the True FORM, BOOK 2.

...to God. I concede that every **Academic Assembly** had its own **Presiding Officer**, 
<margin>Head of the Academy <note>Hebrew: *Rosh Yeshiva*</note>, who</margin> was called the **Head of the Assembly**. I would not deny that in the **Greater Assemblies**—such as those that flourished before and after the destruction of Jerusalem in Canaan, and in the more famous locations outside Canaan, such as Alexandria, Antioch, Damascus, and later also in **Babylonia**—a certain recognized dignity and authority was granted to him above the other **Elders** <note>Latin: *Presbyteris*</note> with whom he constituted the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and court of justice in ancient Israel.</note>. However, it must be observed:

1. That such a **President of the Senate** was always considered to be of the same order and office as the **entire Senate**, of which he was the most distinguished part; and, what is more, he was always subject to the **Senate**, which could remove him from his office whenever it wished. Therefore, this **Presiding Officer of the Jewish Elders** should be compared with the **Presidents of Civil Senates** or **Courts**, such as are accepted in many places. To be sure, the dignity of the **Presidency** wins them greater authority and reverence, and gives them certain prerogatives, yet they are not thereby removed from the same class and kind of men as the **Senate** over which they preside; as can be seen from the single example of the **Rectors of Academies** in our own time. Certainly, all the **Assessors** of the great and most venerable Senate of Jerusalem, the President not excluded, were called **Elders** <note>Hebrew: *Zekenim*</note> / **House of Judgment** <note>Hebrew: *Beit Din*</note> / **Sanhedrin** / **Council of Elders** <note>Greek: *presbyterion*</note>, **Senate** <note>Greek: *gerousia*</note>, and whatever other names were attributed to that Senate; and from this it is certain enough that those Sacred Colleges constituted homogeneous bodies of men, of the same kind and rank. For if the President possessed any greater dignity, it was reflected back upon the whole College from which it had been conferred upon him. But besides these things,

2. I would like it to be observed that in those common **Sacred Councils** <note>Hebrew: *Yeshivot*</note>, such as were settled indiscriminately in less populated places, the dignity of the **Head of the Academy** <note>Hebrew: *Rosh Yeshiva*</note> or **President of the Senate** was scarcely greater than the dignity of his colleagues. He was the first and perpetual **President** of this **Senate**, but of the same order, office, and power (since he was required to exercise all such power with them and through them) as his other colleagues, nor did he excel them in any dignity, except that **he was the first of a class of men of his own kind and office**. Let the testimonies we cited from **Benjamin** <note>Referring to Benjamin of Tudela, the 12th-century traveler.</note> be compared again, as reason itself supports this. For the dignity of a **President** in smaller Senates is always less and less conspicuous. To which is now added 

3. that Christ the Lord [chose] his Discip- <meta>Catchword: los (disciples)</meta>

### CHAPTER 12. OF THE GOVERNMENT of the Old Synagogue.

...his own [disciples] seriously about avoiding dominance, and more than once commended the equality of **Governance** <note>original: *Regiminis*</note>. Since these warnings of Christ were then recent, the **Presidents of the Christian Presbyteries** <note>The "Presbytery" was the council of elders governing a local church.</note> in the origins of the **Church** seem to have used this dignity and authority of theirs so moderately that they were scarcely distinguished from the other **Presbyters** <note>Elders</note> by any visible mark. 4. However, it is clear enough that the **Presbyteries** of the **Early Church** truly had their own **Presidents**, from the fact that **Bishops** <note>original: *Episcopi*</note> in a short time after the birth of **Christianity** acquired for themselves great authority and dignity above the other **Presbyters**. But regarding that, we shall speak more at length **in the following Book, in its own Place.**

3. Perhaps a difficulty may arise from my saying that the **Presbyteries of the Christian Church, after the pattern of those Jewish ones, consisted of learned men**, since it seems altogether that several **Presbyters** of the early **Church** were chosen **from the common people** <note>original: *de plebe*</note>, from the assembly of the **Church** itself.

It is possible to address this objection in a few words. I do not deny that in certain **Churches** of the first period, due to a lack of others, **uneducated Presbyters from the common people** were placed in charge—that is, those who before that time had not devoted effort in the **Academies** <note>original: *Gymnasiis*; referring to formal schools of Jewish learning</note> to the studies of **Religion and Jewish Law**, and had not brought back the title of **Doctor** <note>In this context, a "Doctor" is a formal teacher or scholar of the law.</note> from their Masters; however, I strongly deny that any men from the common people were promoted to that most grave office who had not been advanced in knowledge, whether through the extraordinary grace of the **Holy Spirit** or through **Apostolic** instructions, to the point that they could honorably maintain this dignity. Moreover, even if they were not then **Doctors**, through that very **Apostolic Laying on of Hands** <note>original: *Manuum Impositionem*</note> they were separated from the common people and co-opted into the order of **Doctors**; from which finally proceeded the distinction, observed far too strictly in the **Ancient Church**, between **Clergy and Laity** <note>original: *Clerum & Plebem*</note>.

Finally, if you ask what should be determined regarding the <term>פרנסים</term> <note>Hebrew: *Parnasīm*, meaning "providers" or community leaders who managed the physical and financial needs of the synagogue.</note> **Pastors** or <term>זקנים</term> <note>Hebrew: *Zekenīm*, meaning "Elders."</note> **Presbyters of the Synagogue** of our modern time; I respond: They are a shadow and image, though quite obscure, of **that Council** by which the **Old Synagogues** were governed when there was a more abundant supply of **Learned Men**. Learned men could not always be had: therefore necessity often demanded that the **Senate of the Synagogue** be constituted from the members of the synagogue themselves, who were often not as skilled in their Religion and Law. To them, however, was given the same name of <term>פרנסים</term> and <term>זקנים</term>, **Presbyters and Pastors**—

Having thus established and defended our hypothesis, nothing seems to remain except to bolster the same at the conclusion of this treatise with certain authorities; indeed, many are moved more by such authority than by a clear demonstration of the truth. Let us, therefore, first hear Bertram <note>Bonaventure Corneille Bertram (1531–1594), a Hebraist who wrote on the ancient Jewish state.</note>, who was among the first to undertake the task of explaining the Jewish Republic. *Therefore*, he says, *the place of the Levites and Prophets was taken in those synagogues by the* LEADERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE <note>original: *ARCHISYNAGOGI*</note>; *OF WHOM THERE WERE SEVERAL IN THE SAME SYNAGOGUE, as appears from Acts 13:15 and 18:8, 17, where TWO LEADERS OF THE SYNAGOGUE, CRISPUS AND SOSTHENES, ARE NAMED AS BEING OF THE SAME CORINTHIAN SYNAGOGUE. And from this it came about that these Leaders of the Synagogue would, on every feast day, not only conceive the prayers and read the Law and the Prophets, but also add an interpretation to them, as did others who seemed fit to them for that task. From this, perhaps, those practices regarding the interpretation of the Prophets were later introduced into the Church by Paul in Acts 13:15 and 1 Corinthians 14:28.* Bertram recognizes that there were multiple Leaders of the Synagogue, that these were learned men, and that the custom of the synagogues in explaining the Prophecies was transferred to the Christian Church. Let Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a polymath and expert on Jewish law.</note> follow Bertram; his authority will be all the greater here as he was more skilled in Hebrew matters. He argues throughout Chapter 14 of his first book *On the Sanhedrins* <note>original: *De Synedriis*</note> that the Rulers of the Christian Church took the Name of Elders <note>original: *Presbyterorum*</note> and the Rite of the Laying on of Hands—by which someone was ordained as a Doctor or Elder—from the Jewish Elders, such as those who were received into the Sacred Councils <note>original: *Consistoria*</note> of the Jews.

### CHAPTER 12. ON THE GOVERNANCE OF THE ANCIENT SYNAGOGUE.

...what we call *Ecclesiastical* is, according to *Talmudic Doctrine* and truth itself, very far from the reality. Depending on the *breadth of their jurisdictions*, THE VERY SAME COURT EVERYWHERE IN THAT REPUBLIC OR CHURCH JUDGED SACRED MATTERS AND RELIGION AS IT DID SECULAR MATTERS, OR THOSE WHICH ARE NOT SACRED.

<margin>Dissertation on the Hebrew Republic, § 39.</margin>
Indeed, *Conring* <note>Hermann Conring (1606–1681), a renowned German scholar of law and history.</note> followed this same point with clear testimony in his learned *Dissertation on the Hebrew Republic*. Hear his words: *“Fifthly, finally, it appears to be alien to the truth THAT JUDGMENTS WERE CONSTITUTED AS BEING OF TWO TYPES, ONE ECCLESIASTICAL AND THE OTHER SECULAR <note>original: forense</note>, since the cases submitted to that judgment were only of one kind. Neither is there any mention of such different kinds of lawsuits in the Holy Scriptures. Although it may sometimes happen that regarding the same matter there is one ecclesiastical and another civil forum, this occurs in only a few instances, and it was not necessary to establish two different courts because of those few cases. Therefore, if secular and sacred matters were submitted to one and the same Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish people.</note>, then certainly the primary place in the Synagogue, and consequently the supreme governance of the Synagogue, must be granted to that same Sanhedrin.”*

For suppose it happened that some member of the Synagogue assembly committed a crime worthy of censure, excommunication, or scourging; who would have the standing to hear the case and pass sentence on it? Would it be by some Leader of the Synagogue <note>original: *Archisynagogo*</note> distinct from the Sanhedrin, or from the ecclesiastical consistory of that place? Thus, when the Republic was flourishing among the Jews, were there in one place sacred tribunals of different types that could hear and judge the same crimes committed against religion? For all who have studied Hebrew letters know that the sacred tribunals, which are called <term>Batei Dinim</term> <gloss>Houses of Law or Courts</gloss> <note>original: <term>בתי דינין</term></note>, heard cases of excommunication and exercised the power to excommunicate. Shall we, therefore, grant the same right and the same power in one and the same place to the Leaders of the Synagogue, separate from these elders of the Sanhedrin? And if by chance the members of the Sanhedrins themselves should do wrong, would they also be judged to have been subject to the judgment of the Leaders of the Synagogue? Certainly, since these things would be entirely contrary to the laws of a well-constituted Republic, nothing remains except that our hypothesis, which is consistent in all its parts, should prevail. And there are indeed excellent points...
